HEMO defines u_P in HEMO-MS-FLAG-001 as "Utility of Progressed."; HEAO defines preference-based utility weight as "A valuation weight that expresses the preference for a health state on a scale on which full health is 1 and dead is 0, with values below 0 for states worse than dead, used to weight time lived in that state.".

column2: Regression-based EVPPI estimator from fitted incremental net benefits
column24: The regression-based estimator of the module is the HEAO regression-based EVPPI method (HEMO-HOOK-18). The module describes Regression-based EVPPI estimator from fitted incremental net benefits as "Regresses the incremental net benefit of each option against a baseline on the parameters of interest across the N runs of one probabilistic sample and treats the fitted values as the conditional expected net benefits, so no inner loop or extra model runs are needed. The estimate is the mean over runs of the largest fitted value, with zero for the baseline, less the largest mean fitted value. This is Equation 9 of Strong, Oakley and Brennan written for three options as incremental net benefits, which they note leaves the result unchanged and needs one regression fewer. Using the fitted values in both terms exploits the positive correlation between them and improves precision. Strong, Oakley and Brennan fit a generalised additive model or a Gaussian process, and Algorithm 4 of the second ISPOR report sets out the same scheme."; HEAO defines regression-based EVPPI method as "A value of information calculation method in which the EVPPI of a subset of parameters is estimated from a single probabilistic sensitivity analysis sample by regressing net benefit on those parameters with a nonparametric regression.".

column2: model structure
column24: HEO's model structure is the overall organisation of a model including its technique, and HEMO's is the set of equations a model evaluates, so the two are related rather than the same. HEMO defines model structure as "An information content entity that is the set of equations, recurrences and constraints a model evaluates, with their order of evaluation, independent of parameter values and of software."; HEO defines Model Structure as "The overall organisation of a health economic model, including its technique, the health states or events represented, and how they link together.".

column2: test case
column24: Running HEMO test cases against a formula or an implementation is one part of validating a model. HEMO defines test case as "An information content entity that states input values with an expected output and a tolerance, or a condition, that a formula, a computational function or an implementation must satisfy, and that is evidence that what it tests is stated and implemented correctly."; HEO defines Model Validation as "Model validation is the structured assessment of whether a model is sufficiently accurate, credible, and fit for its stated decision purpose.".

column2: decision tree
column24: Both name the branching model of chance and decision nodes evaluated without explicit time. HEMO defines decision tree as "A model type of a structure of chance and decision nodes evaluated without explicit time, for a cohort, by rolling back expected values over the branches."; HEO defines Decision Tree as "A decision tree is a branching model used in economic evaluation: strategies, chance events and end points give each option's expected costs and QALYs.".

column2: state-transition cohort model
column24: Both name the cohort model in which proportions move between states each cycle by the Markov property. HEMO defines state-transition cohort model as "A model type of a structure in which a cohort moves between mutually exclusive health states in discrete cycles by transition probabilities that depend only on the current state, the Markov model."; HEO defines Markov Cohort Model as "A Markov model tracking a hypothetical cohort collectively as proportions across health states over cycles, rather than simulating each patient separately.".

column2: state-transition cohort model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, covering any memoryless state-transition model, cohort or individual. HEMO defines state-transition cohort model as "A model type of a structure in which a cohort moves between mutually exclusive health states in discrete cycles by transition probabilities that depend only on the current state, the Markov model."; HEO defines Markov Model as "A Markov model is a memoryless state-transition model used in economic evaluation: people move between health states each cycle, accruing costs and QALYs.".

column2: state-transition cohort model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, the general state-transition model. HEMO defines state-transition cohort model as "A model type of a structure in which a cohort moves between mutually exclusive health states in discrete cycles by transition probabilities that depend only on the current state, the Markov model."; HEO defines State Transition Model as "A general term for a decision-analytic model, such as a Markov model, representing disease progression as movement between defined health states.".

column2: state-transition cohort model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any model of a patient group as a whole. HEMO defines state-transition cohort model as "A model type of a structure in which a cohort moves between mutually exclusive health states in discrete cycles by transition probabilities that depend only on the current state, the Markov model."; HEO defines Cohort Model as "A cohort model is a health economic decision model that estimates mean costs and outcomes for a patient group as a whole, without simulating individuals.".

column2: semi-Markov or tunnel-state model
column24: A tunnel state is how a semi-Markov cohort model carries time in a state. HEMO defines semi-Markov or tunnel-state model as "A model type of a state-transition cohort structure in which transition probabilities also depend on the time spent in a state, carried by tunnel states."; HEO defines Tunnel State as "A tunnel state is one of a fixed sequence of one-cycle temporary states in a Markov model, letting risks, costs or utilities vary with time in a state.".

column2: individual state-transition model
column24: Both name the individual-level state-transition model. HEMO defines individual state-transition model as "A model type of a state-transition structure run for simulated individuals, whose transitions may depend on their histories, also called microsimulation."; HEO defines Markov Microsimulation as "Markov microsimulation is an individual-level state-transition modeling method that simulates each person's sequence of health states over time using transition probabilities that may depend on current state, personal characteristics, time, and explicitly retained history.".

column2: individual state-transition model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any model of individuals one at a time. HEMO defines individual state-transition model as "A model type of a state-transition structure run for simulated individuals, whose transitions may depend on their histories, also called microsimulation."; HEO defines Microsimulation as "Microsimulation models individuals one at a time, allowing their characteristics and event histories to influence future outcomes.".

column2: individual state-transition model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any model that tracks simulated patients one at a time. HEMO defines individual state-transition model as "A model type of a state-transition structure run for simulated individuals, whose transitions may depend on their histories, also called microsimulation."; HEO defines Individual-Level Model as "A decision-analytic model tracking simulated patients one at a time rather than representing a population using aggregate cohort proportions.".

column2: continuous-time multi-state model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any decision model run in continuous time. HEMO defines continuous-time multi-state model as "A model type of a structure in which a cohort moves between states at any time by transition intensities."; HEO defines Continuous Model as "A continuous model is a decision model run in continuous time rather than fixed cycles, so health events can occur at any moment, governed by rates.".

column2: partitioned survival model
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, defined for cancer models with progression-free and overall survival curves, while the HEMO model type holds for any set of separately estimated survival curves. HEMO defines partitioned survival model as "A model type of a structure in which state occupancy over time is read from survival curves that are estimated separately, such as progression-free and overall survival, rather than from transitions between states."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: discrete event simulation
column24: Both name the model that follows individuals from event to event at any time. HEMO defines discrete event simulation as "A model type of a structure that follows individuals through events at any time, which may compete for resources and queues through which they affect one another."; HEO defines Discrete Event Simulation as "Discrete event simulation (DES) is a modelling method that follows each patient from event to event over time, tracking their history and use of resources.".

column2: dynamic transmission compartmental model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any model in which infection risk depends on the number infectious, individual-based ones included, while HEMO's type is the compartmental one. HEMO defines dynamic transmission compartmental model as "A model type of a structure in which compartments of an open population exchange members at rates that depend on the number infectious, through the force of infection, in continuous time or by difference equations."; HEO defines Dynamic Transmission Model as "A dynamic transmission model represents how an infectious disease spreads through a population while the risk of infection changes with the number and characteristics of infectious people.".

column2: dynamic transmission compartmental model
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, one structure of susceptible, infectious and recovered compartments. HEMO defines dynamic transmission compartmental model as "A model type of a structure in which compartments of an open population exchange members at rates that depend on the number infectious, through the force of infection, in continuous time or by difference equations."; HEO defines SIR Model as "A basic epidemic model dividing a population into susceptible, infectious, and recovered compartments, representing flow between them using differential equations.".

column2: dynamic transmission compartmental model
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any model that splits a population into compartments with flows between them. HEMO defines dynamic transmission compartmental model as "A model type of a structure in which compartments of an open population exchange members at rates that depend on the number infectious, through the force of infection, in continuous time or by difference equations."; HEO defines Compartmental Model as "A compartmental model splits a population into compartments, such as susceptible, infectious and recovered, and uses equations for the flows between them.".

column2: agent-based model
column24: Both name the model of interacting individual agents. HEMO defines agent-based model as "A model type of a structure that follows individual agents whose behaviour and contacts with one another drive the results."; HEO defines Agent-Based Model as "An agent-based model (ABM) simulates individuals as agents that follow rules and interact, so outcomes such as infections, costs and QALYs emerge.".

column2: system dynamics model
column24: Both name the model of stocks, flows and feedback loops. HEMO defines system dynamics model as "A model type of a structure of aggregate stocks and the flows between them, with feedback loops, also called a stock and flow model."; HEO defines System Dynamics Model as "A modelling approach representing a complex system using stocks, flows, and feedback loops to capture how it evolves through internal dynamics.".

column2: system dynamics model
column24: A stock and flow structure is the core of a system dynamics model. HEMO defines system dynamics model as "A model type of a structure of aggregate stocks and the flows between them, with feedback loops, also called a stock and flow model."; HEO defines Stock and Flow Model as "A system dynamics structure representing accumulations, called stocks, such as infected individuals, and the rates of change into and out of them, called flows.".

column2: hybrid model
column24: Both name a model that combines two or more model types. HEMO defines hybrid model as "A model type of a structure that combines two or more other model types, such as a decision tree feeding a state-transition model."; HEO defines Hybrid Model as "A decision-analytic model combining two or more approaches, such as a decision tree feeding into a Markov model, to represent a disease process.".

column2: probability
column24: Both name a number between 0 and 1 for the chance of a defined event. HEMO defines probability as "A quantity kind whose values lie between 0 and 1 and give the chance that an event occurs, within a stated interval or per event."; HEO defines Probability as "Probability is a number between zero and one assigned to the likelihood of a precisely defined event under stated conditions.".

column2: probability per cycle
column24: Both name the chance of moving between states, or staying, within one cycle. HEMO defines probability per cycle as "A quantity kind whose values are the probabilities of a transition within one model cycle of stated length, which change when the cycle length changes."; HEO defines Transition Probability as "A transition probability is the chance of moving from one health state to another, or staying, during one cycle of a Markov or state-transition model.".

column2: utility
column24: Both name the preference-based value of a health state on the scale of 1 for full health and 0 for dead. HEMO defines utility as "A quantity kind whose values are preference-based health state values with 1 for full health and 0 for dead, which can be below 0 and cannot exceed 1, and which give QALYs when multiplied by time. HEMO reads 0 for dead as the true zero of the scale, so that QALY totals, their ratios and proportional shortfalls are meaningful, a reading for the curator to confirm."; HEO defines Health State Utility Value as "A health state utility value, or HSU value, is a preference-based numerical weight assigned to a health state for use in economic evaluation.".

column2: utility
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any numerical measure of preference. HEMO defines utility as "A quantity kind whose values are preference-based health state values with 1 for full health and 0 for dead, which can be below 0 and cannot exceed 1, and which give QALYs when multiplied by time. HEMO reads 0 for dead as the true zero of the scale, so that QALY totals, their ratios and proportional shortfalls are meaningful, a reading for the curator to confirm."; HEO defines Utility as "Utility is a numerical measure of preference; in health economics, a health utility values a health state on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead.".

column2: QALYs
column24: Both name quality-adjusted life years. HEMO defines QALYs as "A quantity kind whose values are quality-adjusted life years, time weighted by utility, which can be negative for time in states worse than dead."; HEO defines Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) as "A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) combines length and quality of life in one measure: a year in full health counts as one QALY and death counts as zero.".

column2: DALYs
column24: Both name disability-adjusted life years. HEMO defines DALYs as "A quantity kind whose values are disability-adjusted life years, years of life lost plus years lived with disability."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: disability weight
column24: Both name the 0 to 1 rating of health loss used for DALYs. HEMO defines disability weight as "A quantity kind whose values give the health loss of a state between 0 for full health and 1 for a state equal to death, as used for DALYs."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: discount rate
column24: Both name the yearly rate at which future amounts are discounted. HEMO defines discount rate as "A quantity kind whose values are yearly rates written as decimals, such as 0.035, by which future amounts are discounted, and which must exceed minus 1."; HEO defines Discount Rate as "The discount rate is the annual rate, such as NICE's 3.5%, used in economic evaluation to convert future costs and health outcomes into present values.".

column2: rate per unit time
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, the instantaneous rate of an event in survival analysis. HEMO defines rate per unit time as "A quantity kind whose values are the number of events per unit of time at risk, such as a hazard, which unlike a probability can exceed 1."; HEO defines Hazard Rate as "In survival analysis, the instantaneous rate of an event at a given time among people still free of it; a rate, not a probability, so it can exceed 1.".

column2: event rate per person-time
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, new cases of a disease per person-time. HEMO defines event rate per person-time as "A quantity kind whose values are events per unit of person-time in a population, such as admissions per person-year."; HEO defines Incidence Rate as "A measure of disease frequency calculated as new cases divided by total person-time at risk observed, accounting for varying follow-up lengths.".

column2: relative effect ratio
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, one ratio of probabilities among the relative effects HEMO's kind covers. HEMO defines relative effect ratio as "A quantity kind whose values are ratios of a risk, a rate, a hazard or odds between two groups, such as a relative risk or a hazard ratio."; HEO defines Relative Risk as "Relative risk compares the probability of an event in one group with the probability in another group over a defined period.".

column2: currency conversion rate
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, a market rate between two currencies, while HEMO's kind also covers purchasing power parity factors. HEMO defines currency conversion rate as "A quantity kind whose values are units of one currency per unit of another, or per international dollar, such as a market exchange rate or a purchasing power parity factor."; HEO defines Exchange Rate as "The price of one currency expressed in terms of another, used to convert costs or prices between countries.".

column2: currency conversion rate
column24: The HEO concept is the method of comparing value across countries, whose factors are one source of HEMO's conversion rates. HEMO defines currency conversion rate as "A quantity kind whose values are units of one currency per unit of another, or per international dollar, such as a market exchange rate or a purchasing power parity factor."; HEO defines Purchasing Power Parity as "A method of comparing economic value across countries based on the relative cost of a common basket of goods and services, rather than exchange rates.".

column2: relative effect ratio
column24: The HEO concept is narrower, one ratio of odds among the relative effects HEMO's kind covers. HEMO defines relative effect ratio as "A quantity kind whose values are ratios of a risk, a rate, a hazard or odds between two groups, such as a relative risk or a hazard ratio."; HEO defines Odds Ratio as "A measure comparing the odds of an outcome in one group to the odds in another, common in case-control studies and logistic regression.".

column2: money per unit of resource
column24: A unit cost is the money per unit of a resource that HEMO's kind holds. HEMO defines money per unit of resource as "A monetary quantity kind whose values are sums of money per unit of a resource, such as a unit cost per bed day or per dose."; HEO defines Unit Cost as "The cost of producing or delivering a single unit of a good or service, such as the cost per hospital bed-day.".

column2: duration
column24: A time horizon is one duration that HEMO's kind holds. HEMO defines duration as "A quantity kind whose values are lengths of time, such as a time horizon, a cycle length or a time spent in a health state."; HEO defines Time Horizon as "The span of time over which an economic evaluation captures relevant differences in costs and outcomes among the options being compared.".

column2: duration
column24: A cycle length is one duration that HEMO's kind holds. HEMO defines duration as "A quantity kind whose values are lengths of time, such as a time horizon, a cycle length or a time spent in a health state."; HEO defines Cycle Length as "Cycle length is the duration of one cycle in a Markov or other discrete-time state-transition model, such as a month or a year, set before the model runs.".

column2: discount factor
column24: Discounting applies discount factors to future amounts. HEMO defines discount factor as "A quantity kind whose values are the weights by which a future amount is multiplied to give its present value, which lie above 0 and are at most 1 for a non-negative rate and time."; HEO defines Discounting as "Discounting converts future costs and health effects, such as QALYs, into present values so that options with different timings can be compared.".

column2: trapezoidal within-cycle correction
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any within-cycle adjustment, of which the trapezoid rule is one method. HEMO defines trapezoidal within-cycle correction as "A within-cycle correction in which the occupancy of each cycle is the mean of its start and end occupancy, the half-cycle correction by the trapezoid rule."; HEO defines Half-Cycle Correction as "Half-cycle correction is a within-cycle adjustment in discrete-time state-transition models that approximates time-accruing costs or health effects between recorded state-occupancy endpoints.".

column2: mid-period counting
column24: Counting at mid-period applies to any discounted stream, with or without cycles, while the HEO concept adjusts a model's cycles, so the two are related. HEMO defines mid-period counting as "A discount timing convention in which each period's amount is counted at the middle of the period."; HEO defines Half-Cycle Correction as "Half-cycle correction is a within-cycle adjustment in discrete-time state-transition models that approximates time-accruing costs or health effects between recorded state-occupancy endpoints.".

column2: cost-effectiveness wrapper
column24: Both name the comparison of options by extra cost per extra unit of health. HEMO defines cost-effectiveness wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that compares the costs and health outcomes of options from the results of any model structure, by incremental ratios or net benefit."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Analysis as "Cost-effectiveness analysis compares healthcare options by the extra cost of each extra unit of health gained, such as cost per life-year gained.".

column2: budget impact wrapper
column24: Both name the estimate of the change in a budget holder's spending. HEMO defines budget impact wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that estimates the change in spending of a budget holder over a short horizon when a technology is adopted."; HEO defines Budget Impact Analysis as "Budget impact analysis (BIA) estimates how adopting a new health technology would change spending for a particular budget holder over the next few years.".

column2: deterministic sensitivity analysis wrapper
column24: Both name the rerun of a model with inputs set to other fixed values. HEMO defines deterministic sensitivity analysis wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that reruns a model structure with one or more inputs set to other fixed values."; HEO defines Deterministic Sensitivity Analysis as "Deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) reruns a health economic model with chosen inputs set to fixed values to see how results and decisions change.".

column2: value of information wrapper
column24: Both name the valuation of reducing decision uncertainty. HEMO defines value of information wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that values the reduction of decision uncertainty from the draws of a probabilistic sensitivity analysis."; HEO defines Value of Information as "Value of information (VOI) analysis estimates the expected benefit of reducing decision uncertainty, to judge whether more research is worth its cost.".

column2: calibration wrapper
column24: Both name the search for input values whose outputs match observed data. HEMO defines calibration wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that searches for input values of a model structure whose outputs match observed targets."; HEO defines Calibration as "Calibration is the estimation of unobservable or uncertain parameters in a health economic model by adjusting them until model outputs match observed data.".

column2: probabilistic sensitivity analysis wrapper
column24: The HEO concept is broader, any repeated random sampling, of which probabilistic sensitivity analysis is one use. HEMO defines probabilistic sensitivity analysis wrapper as "An analysis wrapper that runs a model structure for repeated draws of its inputs from their distributions."; HEO defines Monte Carlo Simulation as "Monte Carlo simulation uses repeated random sampling to show how uncertainty in model inputs produces uncertainty in model outputs.".

column2: Present value of a single future value
column24: Both name the current worth of a future amount found by discounting. The module describes Present value of a single future value as "Converts one cost or health outcome occurring at time t to its value at the reference time."; HEO defines Present Value as "The current worth of a future sum of money or cash flow stream, found by discounting each future amount using a specified discount rate.".

column2: Present value of a single future value
column24: The formula applies exponential discounting at a constant rate. The module describes Present value of a single future value as "Converts one cost or health outcome occurring at time t to its value at the reference time."; HEO defines Exponential Discounting as "A discounting model in which future costs and benefits are reduced at a constant proportional rate each period, producing time-consistent preferences.".

column2: Total present value of a stream
column24: Both name the current worth of a stream of future amounts found by discounting each. The module describes Total present value of a stream as "Sums discounted values occurring across the selected time horizon."; HEO defines Present Value as "The current worth of a future sum of money or cash flow stream, found by discounting each future amount using a specified discount rate.".

column2: Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the end of each year
column24: The closed-form annuity sums exponential discount factors. The module describes Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the end of each year as "Gives the present value of the same amount q in each of T years when each year's amount is counted at the end of that year, so the first year carries the factor 1/(1 + r) and the last 1/(1 + r)^T. The fraction (1 minus (1 + r) to the power minus T) divided by r is the sum of the T yearly discount factors, the annuity form in the article's worked example. It tends to T as r falls towards zero, where the closed form itself cannot be evaluated."; HEO defines Exponential Discounting as "A discounting model in which future costs and benefits are reduced at a constant proportional rate each period, producing time-consistent preferences.".

column2: Population EVPI over the decision's lifetime
column24: Both name the EVPI for the whole affected population. The module describes Population EVPI over the decision's lifetime as "Multiplies per-person EVPI by the discounted number of people expected to face the decision in each period while it remains relevant. The result is compared with the cost of research: when it is below the cost of any feasible study, further research is not worthwhile on these grounds."; HEO defines Population EVPI as "The expected value of perfect information calculated for an entire affected patient population over time, rather than for a single patient.".

column2: Incremental net health benefit at threshold k
column24: Both name the QALYs gained less the QALYs forgone through the extra cost. The module describes Incremental net health benefit at threshold k as "Converts the incremental cost of an intervention into the health expected to be displaced elsewhere, Delta_C divided by k, and subtracts it from the incremental health gain. A positive value means population health increases overall; a negative value means the health gained does not offset the health lost from care not funded elsewhere. It gives the same decision as incremental net monetary benefit at the same threshold."; HEO defines Net Health Benefit as "Net health benefit (NHB) is the health an option gains, in QALYs, minus the QALYs its extra cost would buy elsewhere at the cost-effectiveness threshold.".

column2: Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall
column24: The formula computes the absolute QALY shortfall. The module describes Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall as "Absolute shortfall subtracts the expected remaining QALYs of people with the condition under current care from those of the matched general population. Proportional shortfall divides the same difference by the general-population QALYs. Both look forward from the point at which the technology would be used, so health already lost does not count, and both are discounted at the reference-case rate."; HEO defines QALY Shortfall as "QALY shortfall is the expected QALY gap between a matched general population and patients on current care, which NICE reads as absolute or proportional.".

column2: Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall
column24: The formula computes the proportional QALY shortfall. The module describes Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall as "Absolute shortfall subtracts the expected remaining QALYs of people with the condition under current care from those of the matched general population. Proportional shortfall divides the same difference by the general-population QALYs. Both look forward from the point at which the technology would be used, so health already lost does not count, and both are discounted at the reference-case rate."; HEO defines Proportional Shortfall as "A measure of disease severity calculated as the proportion, rather than absolute number, of expected quality-adjusted life years lost to a condition.".

column2: Severity QALY weight from the shortfall bands
column24: The formula gives the severity weight, the modifier NICE applies, from the shortfall bands. The module describes Severity QALY weight from the shortfall bands as "Returns the NICE severity weight from absolute and proportional shortfall. The weight is 1.7 if absolute shortfall is at least 18 or proportional shortfall at least 0.95, 1.2 if absolute shortfall is at least 12 or proportional shortfall at least 0.85, and 1 otherwise. The measure implying greater severity decides, and a value on a cut-off takes the higher band. Each comparison returns 1 when true and 0 when false."; HEO defines Severity Modifier as "The severity modifier is a weight of 1.2 or 1.7 that NICE applies to QALY gains for conditions with a high absolute or proportional QALY shortfall.".

column2: Price-year adjustment of a cost with an inflation index
column24: Both name restating a cost in the prices of another year by a price index. The module describes Price-year adjustment of a cost with an inflation index as "Moves a cost observed in price year a to price year b by multiplying it by the ratio of an appropriate price index in the two years. When the index is published as annual percentage increases, as the NHS Cost Inflation Index is, the index is built by chaining: each year's value is the previous value multiplied by one plus that year's increase. The NICE manual names the NHS Cost Inflation Index and the PSS Pay and Prices Index, both reported in the Unit Costs of Health and Social Care manual, or the ONS consumer price index."; HEO defines Inflation Adjustment as "The process of restating cost data from different time periods in constant, comparable price terms, typically using a relevant price index.".

column2: Absence cost by the human capital approach
column24: Both name valuing all time lost at the wage rate. The module describes Absence cost by the human capital approach as "Values every hour of absence at the value of an hour of work. D_a counts calendar days absent, so D_a divided by 7 gives weeks absent, and multiplying by the usual weekly hours and the hourly value gives the cost. The human capital approach usually values time at gross earnings including employer-paid costs such as payroll taxes and benefits, the full cost of employee compensation."; HEO defines Human Capital Approach as "A way to value productivity lost to illness or premature death by applying an economic value, often based on earnings, to forgone productive time.".

column2: Absence cost by the friction cost method
column24: Both name valuing time lost only until a worker is replaced. The module describes Absence cost by the friction cost method as "Counts absence only up to the friction period, the time an employer needs to restore production, usually by replacing the worker, and multiplies the counted hours by the value of an hour and by the elasticity of production with respect to working time. Absences shorter than the friction period count in full. When the hourly value already allows for the elasticity, as the Dutch reference price does, e is set to 1."; HEO defines Friction Cost Method as "A productivity loss valuation approach estimating only the cost of the finite period needed to restore normal production, generally lower than human capital estimates.".

column2: Foreign price or cost converted to the home currency at a market exchange rate
column24: The formula converts a price at a market exchange rate. The module describes Foreign price or cost converted to the home currency at a market exchange rate as "Multiplies a price or cost observed in another country's currency by the exchange rate expressed as home-currency units per unit of that currency, the p_i e_i term of the article's reference-price rule. The same step converts any cost record between currencies. A rate published the other way round, as local currency units per US dollar in the GLOBE Model final rule, is divided into the price instead. The converted prices feed the basket aggregates of HE-FM-BOC-003, and conversion at purchasing power parity is HE-FM-BOC-002."; HEO defines Currency Conversion as "The translation of cost or price data from one national currency into another, typically using exchange rates or purchasing power parity.".

column2: Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity
column24: The formula converts a cost between currencies by purchasing power parity factors. The module describes Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity as "Divides a cost in the source currency by the source country's PPP conversion factor, which gives international dollars, and multiplies by the target country's factor, which gives the target currency. Both factors are local currency units per international dollar, so the route through international dollars follows from their units (derived here), and a target factor of 1 returns international dollars. The World Bank describes PPPs as eliminating differences in price levels between countries in the process of conversion, and the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre Cost Converter page notes that pure exchange-rate conversion, the market rate of HE-FM-BOC-001, does not. Where the cost also comes from another price year, the year is moved first with HE-FM-COST-002 and HE-CF-BOC-001 sets out the two orders."; HEO defines Currency Conversion as "The translation of cost or price data from one national currency into another, typically using exchange rates or purchasing power parity.".

column2: Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity
column24: The formula uses purchasing power parity factors. The module describes Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity as "Divides a cost in the source currency by the source country's PPP conversion factor, which gives international dollars, and multiplies by the target country's factor, which gives the target currency. Both factors are local currency units per international dollar, so the route through international dollars follows from their units (derived here), and a target factor of 1 returns international dollars. The World Bank describes PPPs as eliminating differences in price levels between countries in the process of conversion, and the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre Cost Converter page notes that pure exchange-rate conversion, the market rate of HE-FM-BOC-001, does not. Where the cost also comes from another price year, the year is moved first with HE-FM-COST-002 and HE-CF-BOC-001 sets out the two orders."; HEO defines Purchasing Power Parity as "A method of comparing economic value across countries based on the relative cost of a common basket of goods and services, rather than exchange rates.".

column2: Pairwise dominance rule including ties
column24: Both name the rule that an option costs no more, is at least as effective and is strictly better on one. The module describes Pairwise dominance rule including ties as "Classifies whether an intervention dominates its comparator: it costs no more, produces no less health and is strictly better on at least one of the two. The intervention is dominated when the same rule holds with the comparison reversed."; HEO defines Weak Dominance as "Weak dominance is when another option costs no more and is at least as effective, and is strictly better on one, so the dominated option is dropped.".

column2: Strict dominance with tie tolerances
column24: Both name the rule that an option costs less and is more effective. HEMO defines Strict dominance with tie tolerances as "Gives 1 when an option costs less and is more effective than its comparator, each by more than its tie tolerance, and 0 otherwise."; HEO defines Strict Dominance as "Strict dominance in cost-effectiveness analysis is when one option both costs less and gives more health than another, so the other option is ruled out.".

column2: Dominated option, the mirror of the dominance rule
column24: The rule says when an option is a dominated alternative. HEMO defines Dominated option, the mirror of the dominance rule as "Gives 1 when an option costs no less and is no more effective than its comparator and is strictly worse on one of the two, with equality read within the tie tolerances, and 0 otherwise."; HEO defines Dominated Alternative as "An intervention that is both more costly and less effective than another option, or a combination of options, and so should not be selected.".

column2: Four-way dominance classification of an option against its comparator
column24: The classification applies dominance to a pair of options. HEMO defines Four-way dominance classification of an option against its comparator as "Classifies an option against its comparator as dominant, dominated, a duplicate when its cost and effect equal the comparator's within the tie tolerances, or neither, a trade-off in which one costs more and is more effective."; HEO defines Dominance as "Dominance in cost-effectiveness analysis excludes an option when another option, or a blend of two others, is no worse on cost or effect and better on one.".

column2: Informal care cost by the proxy good method
column24: The formula values informal care by the proxy good method. HEMO defines Informal care cost by the proxy good method as "Gives the cost of informal care valued at the market price of a close substitute, such as a paid home carer, for each hour of care given."; HEO defines Informal Care Cost as "The economic value of unpaid caregiving time from family or friends, typically estimated using replacement cost or the carer's forgone time.".

column2: MCDA weighted sum of three criterion values
column24: The weighted sum is the core of an MCDA. HEMO defines MCDA weighted sum of three criterion values as "Gives the overall value of an option in a multiple criteria decision analysis as the sum of its partial values on each criterion times the criterion weights, which add to 1."; HEO defines Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis as "Multi-criteria decision analysis is a family of structured methods that compares alternatives across multiple explicit criteria and incorporates judgments about the trade-offs among them.".

column2: Catastrophic health spending share, flag and amount in international dollars
column24: Both name out-of-pocket health spending above a set share of household consumption. HEMO defines Catastrophic health spending share, flag and amount in international dollars as "Gives the share of a household's consumption spent out of pocket on health, whether it exceeds a threshold share, and the out-of-pocket amount converted to international dollars."; HEO defines Catastrophic Health Expenditure as "Catastrophic health expenditure (CHE) is out-of-pocket health spending that exceeds a set share of a household's total budget or its capacity to pay.".

column2: Net budget impact from patient-years on treatment
column24: The formula gives the net budget impact of a year. HEMO defines Net budget impact from patient-years on treatment as "Gives the net budget impact of a year as the patient-years on treatment times the annual drug cost less the annual cost of the care it displaces."; HEO defines Net Budget Impact as "The overall change in spending from adopting a new technology, after accounting for offsetting savings elsewhere, such as avoided hospital admissions.".

column2: Stock balance over one period
column24: The stock balance applies to a waiting list. HEMO defines Stock balance over one period as "Gives the size of a stock at the end of a period, such as a waiting list, from its size at the start, the inflow and the outflow during the period."; HEO defines Waiting List as "An ordered list of patients awaiting a healthcare service, such as elective surgery, that exceeds available capacity to provide it.".

column2: Stock balance over one period
column24: The balance is the core equation of a stock and flow model. HEMO defines Stock balance over one period as "Gives the size of a stock at the end of a period, such as a waiting list, from its size at the start, the inflow and the outflow during the period."; HEO defines Stock and Flow Model as "A system dynamics structure representing accumulations, called stocks, such as infected individuals, and the rates of change into and out of them, called flows.".

column2: Donor funding share of programme spending
column24: The formula gives the share of spending that donor funding covers. HEMO defines Donor funding share of programme spending as "Gives the share of a programme's spending covered by donor grants earmarked for it, with the spending converted to the grants' currency."; HEO defines Donor Funding as "Financial resources provided by external organisations, such as development agencies or foundations, to support health programmes, particularly in lower-income countries.".

column2: GDP-adjusted reference price of a medicine in one reference country
column24: The adjusted price is one step of international reference pricing. HEMO defines GDP-adjusted reference price of a medicine in one reference country as "Gives a reference country's net price of a medicine adjusted by the ratio of the home country's GDP per capita at purchasing power parity to the reference country's."; HEO defines International Reference Pricing as "A pricing policy setting a country's drug price with explicit reference to prices charged for the same product in a defined basket of countries.".

column2: GDP-adjusted reference price of a medicine in one reference country
column24: The adjusted price is one step of external reference pricing. HEMO defines GDP-adjusted reference price of a medicine in one reference country as "Gives a reference country's net price of a medicine adjusted by the ratio of the home country's GDP per capita at purchasing power parity to the reference country's."; HEO defines External Reference Pricing as "A medicine-pricing policy that uses prices for the same or comparable product in other jurisdictions as benchmarks for a domestic price or reimbursement decision.".

column2: Kolm equally distributed equivalent health with absolute inequality aversion
column24: The Kolm equally distributed equivalent comes from a social welfare function. HEMO defines Kolm equally distributed equivalent health with absolute inequality aversion as "Gives the level of health which, if everyone had it, would be judged as good as the actual distribution, when concern for inequality depends on absolute differences in health between people."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health for epsilon other than 1
column24: The equally distributed equivalent is the quantity from which the Atkinson index is computed. The module describes Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health for epsilon other than 1 as "Gives the equally distributed equivalent health as the power mean of the n health values with exponent one minus epsilon. At epsilon of 0 it equals the arithmetic mean, so only total health counts; at epsilon of 2 it is the harmonic mean; and as epsilon rises it moves towards the health of the worst-off person, the maximin rule. Each h_i is the health of one person, or of one of n groups of equal size."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: Cost per DALY averted converted at a market exchange rate
column24: The formula gives a cost per DALY averted. HEMO defines Cost per DALY averted converted at a market exchange rate as "Gives a programme's cost per DALY averted in another currency, converting the cost at a market exchange rate and dividing by the DALYs without the programme less the DALYs with it."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: Nested Monte Carlo EVPPI estimator for K outer and J inner draws
column10: Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information
column24: The estimator gives the EVPPI. HEMO defines Nested Monte Carlo EVPPI estimator for K outer and J inner draws as "Gives the expected value of partial perfect information per person about a parameter set from a nested Monte Carlo sample of the incremental net benefit of one option over another, K outer draws of the parameters of interest and J inner draws of the others for each."; HEO defines Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information as "Expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) is the expected gain in net benefit from knowing selected model parameters exactly before deciding.".

column2: QALY-weighted incremental net health benefit
column24: The formula gives a net health benefit with the QALY gain weighted. HEMO defines QALY-weighted incremental net health benefit as "Gives the incremental net health benefit of an option with its QALY gain weighted by a decision modifier, such as a severity weight, at a stated money value of a QALY, as NICE asks for at GBP 25,000 and GBP 35,000 per QALY with and without the weighting."; HEO defines Net Health Benefit as "Net health benefit (NHB) is the health an option gains, in QALYs, minus the QALYs its extra cost would buy elsewhere at the cost-effectiveness threshold.".

column2: Flagship three-state Markov cohort model structure
column24: The flagship structure is a Markov cohort model. HEMO defines Flagship three-state Markov cohort model structure as "The equations of the three-state Stable, Progressed and Dead cohort model of the Build demonstrator, version 1.1, for one arm. Transition probabilities come from a progression probability, a relative risk of progression and death probabilities. The cohort trace is updated once a cycle, the trapezoidal half-cycle correction gives the occupancy of each cycle, and costs and QALYs are weighted by the cycle length and discounted at the start of each cycle."; HEO defines Markov Cohort Model as "A Markov model tracking a hypothetical cohort collectively as proportions across health states over cycles, rather than simulating each patient separately.".

column2: Cohort state-transition function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Model. The module describes Cohort state-transition function as "Maps a cohort's current state distribution and transition probabilities to its state distribution in the next model cycle."; HEO defines Markov Model as "A Markov model is a memoryless state-transition model used in economic evaluation: people move between health states each cycle, accruing costs and QALYs.".

column2: Incremental comparison function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Economic Evaluation. The module describes Incremental comparison function as "Maps the costs and effects of two healthcare alternatives to their incremental cost and incremental effect."; HEO defines Economic Evaluation as "Economic evaluation, often called health economic evaluation, compares the costs and outcomes of healthcare options to judge which offers the best value.".

column2: Fully incremental cost-effectiveness function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Analysis. The module describes Fully incremental cost-effectiveness function as "Maps an effectiveness-ordered set of non-dominated alternatives to sequential incremental cost-effectiveness ratios."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Analysis as "Cost-effectiveness analysis compares healthcare options by the extra cost of each extra unit of health gained, such as cost per life-year gained.".

column2: Incremental cost-utility function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Utility Analysis. The module describes Incremental cost-utility function as "Maps incremental cost and incremental quality-adjusted life years to the additional cost per QALY gained."; HEO defines Cost-Utility Analysis as "Cost-utility analysis is an economic evaluation that measures health gains in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and reports cost per QALY gained.".

column2: Monetised cost-benefit comparison function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Benefit Analysis. The module describes Monetised cost-benefit comparison function as "Maps the present values of monetised benefits and resource costs to measures of net social value and relative return."; HEO defines Cost-Benefit Analysis as "Cost-benefit analysis values the costs and benefits of healthcare options in money, so they can be compared by their net benefit, usually to society.".

column2: Equivalence-gated least-cost selection function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Minimisation Analysis. The module describes Equivalence-gated least-cost selection function as "Selects the lowest-cost feasible healthcare alternative only when reliable evidence shows that all decision-relevant outcomes do not differ meaningfully."; HEO defines Cost-Minimisation Analysis as "Cost-minimisation analysis compares only the costs of healthcare options, and is valid only when evidence shows their health outcomes are equivalent.".

column2: Budget-change function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Budget Impact Analysis. The module describes Budget-change function as "Maps reference- and adoption-scenario expenditure to periodic and cumulative changes in spending for a specified budget holder."; HEO defines Budget Impact Analysis as "Budget impact analysis (BIA) estimates how adopting a new health technology would change spending for a particular budget holder over the next few years.".

column2: Economic-burden estimation function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-of-Illness Study. The module describes Economic-burden estimation function as "Maps attributable resource use, losses, population counts and valuation assumptions to the economic burden of a disease, injury or risk factor."; HEO defines Cost-of-Illness Study as "A cost-of-illness study estimates the economic burden of a disease, including healthcare costs, patient and carer costs, and lost productivity.".

column2: Mixed-comparator construction function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Comparator. The module describes Mixed-comparator construction function as "Maps the treatment shares and expected results of current-care options to a weighted mixed comparator."; HEO defines Comparator as "A comparator is the alternative, such as current practice or another treatment, against which a new health intervention is compared in economic evaluation.".

column2: Present-value discounting function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discount Rate. The module describes Present-value discounting function as "Maps future costs or health outcomes to values at a common reference time using the applicable discount rate and timing convention."; HEO defines Discount Rate as "The discount rate is the annual rate, such as NICE's 3.5%, used in economic evaluation to convert future costs and health outcomes into present values.".

column2: Pairwise incremental cost-effectiveness function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER). The module describes Pairwise incremental cost-effectiveness function as "Maps the expected costs and expected health effects of an intervention and one comparator to the additional cost per additional unit of health effect."; HEO defines Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) as "The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is a treatment's extra cost divided by its extra health gain versus a comparator, such as cost per QALY.".

column2: Quality-adjusted survival function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY). The module describes Quality-adjusted survival function as "Maps a profile of health-state utility over time to quality-adjusted life years, the area under the utility-over-time curve."; HEO defines Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) as "A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) combines length and quality of life in one measure: a year in full health counts as one QALY and death counts as zero.".

column2: Net monetary benefit function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Net Monetary Benefit. The module describes Net monetary benefit function as "Values an option's expected health effect in money at a stated cost-effectiveness threshold and subtracts its expected cost, placing health and cost on one monetary scale."; HEO defines Net Monetary Benefit as "Net monetary benefit (NMB) is an option's health outcome valued in money at a cost-effectiveness threshold minus its cost, used to rank healthcare options.".

column2: Dominance classification function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dominance. The module describes Dominance classification function as "Maps the expected costs and expected health effects of mutually exclusive options to a classification of which options are dominated, a result that holds at every non-negative cost-effectiveness threshold."; HEO defines Dominance as "Dominance in cost-effectiveness analysis excludes an option when another option, or a blend of two others, is no worse on cost or effect and better on one.".

column2: Extended dominance function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Extended Dominance. The module describes Extended dominance function as "Maps the expected costs and effects of options that survive the dominance screen, ordered by effect, to a flag for each intermediate option that a blend of its neighbours would beat."; HEO defines Extended Dominance as "Extended dominance excludes an option in cost-effectiveness analysis when a blend of a less and a more effective option gives its health gain for less.".

column2: Cost-effectiveness acceptability function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC). The module describes Cost-effectiveness acceptability function as "Maps the simulated costs and health effects of mutually exclusive options from a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, together with a threshold, to the probability that each option has the highest net monetary benefit at that threshold. Evaluated across a range of thresholds, it traces the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC) as "A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC) plots, across cost-effectiveness thresholds, the probability that each option is the most cost-effective.".

column2: Expected net benefit function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Net Benefit. The module describes Expected net benefit function as "Maps the joint distribution of an option's uncertain costs and health effects, and a threshold, to the mean of its net benefit. The option with the highest expected net benefit is the one to adopt on current evidence, and the same quantity is the baseline for value of information analysis."; HEO defines Expected Net Benefit as "Expected net benefit is the mean net benefit of a healthcare option across parameter uncertainty at a set threshold; the option with the highest is chosen.".

column2: Value of information function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Value of Information. The module describes Value of information function as "Maps the joint distribution of net benefit across the options in a decision to the expected gain from resolving some or all of the uncertainty before choosing, compared with choosing the option with the highest expected net benefit on current information."; HEO defines Value of Information as "Value of information (VOI) analysis estimates the expected benefit of reducing decision uncertainty, to judge whether more research is worth its cost.".

column2: One-way sensitivity function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept One-Way Sensitivity Analysis. The module describes One-way sensitivity function as "Maps a model output to its value when a single input j is set to a stated value while every other input stays at its base-case value. Running it at the input's lower and upper values gives the endpoints of one bar in a tornado diagram."; HEO defines One-Way Sensitivity Analysis as "One-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) varies one model input at a time, holding the rest at base case, to show which inputs drive cost-effectiveness results.".

column2: Supply-side threshold function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Threshold. The module describes Supply-side threshold function as "Maps a change in health-care expenditure under a fixed budget, and the change in population health that results, to the cost at which the health system gains or loses one unit of health at the margin. This is the opportunity-cost basis of the threshold, distinct from a demand-side value placed on health."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Threshold as "A cost-effectiveness threshold is the maximum cost per QALY gained that a health system treats as value for money when deciding which treatments to fund.".

column2: Rate and transition probability conversion function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Transition Probability. The module describes Rate and transition probability conversion function as "Maps an event rate and a time interval to the probability that the event occurs within that interval, and back again. Rates are converted rather than probabilities divided, because a probability is tied to the length of the interval over which it was observed. The converted probability then enters a transition matrix used in the cohort update s_(t+1) = s_t P described on the Markov Model page."; HEO defines Transition Probability as "A transition probability is the chance of moving from one health state to another, or staying, during one cycle of a Markov or state-transition model.".

column2: Relative hazard function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hazard Ratio. The module describes Relative hazard function as "Maps the hazards of an event in a treatment group and a comparator group at the same time t to their ratio. Under proportional hazards the ratio is constant over time, and it can then be applied to a baseline survival curve or a baseline transition probability to obtain absolute outcomes for the treatment group."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Accelerated failure time function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accelerated Failure Time Model. The module describes Accelerated failure time function as "Models the logarithm of the time to an event as a linear function of covariates plus a scaled error term whose distribution defines the model, such as Weibull, log-logistic or log-normal. A covariate multiplies time itself, so the survival curve of the treated group is the reference curve stretched or shrunk along the time axis: S(t|x = 1) equals S_0(t / TR), where TR is the time ratio."; HEO defines Accelerated Failure Time Model as "An accelerated failure time (AFT) model is a survival model in which treatment or another factor stretches or shrinks time to an event by a time ratio.".

column2: Event time sampling function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discrete Event Simulation. The module describes Event time sampling function as "Maps a uniform random number and a fitted time-to-event distribution to a sampled time to the next event for one simulated patient. The sampled time is the value at which the survival function equals the random number, so repeated draws reproduce the fitted distribution. The simulation clock then advances to the earliest scheduled event."; HEO defines Discrete Event Simulation as "Discrete event simulation (DES) is a modelling method that follows each patient from event to event over time, tracking their history and use of resources.".

column2: Absorbing Markov chain function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absorbing State. The module describes Absorbing Markov chain function as "A state k is absorbing when p_kk = 1 and p_kj = 0 for every other state j, so no one who enters it can leave. Ordering the transient states first writes the transition matrix in canonical form, with Q the transitions among transient states, R the transitions from transient to absorbing states, a zero block and an identity block for the absorbing states. From Q and R the expected time before absorption and the probability of ending in each absorbing state follow without running the cohort trace s_(t+1) = s_t P."; HEO defines Absorbing State as "An absorbing state is a state in a Markov model that patients cannot leave once they enter it, usually death, so the whole cohort eventually ends there.".

column2: Absolute risk estimation function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk. The module describes Absolute risk estimation function as "Maps the number of people who have a new event during a stated period, and the number at risk at the start of that period, to the probability of the event over the period. The result is a risk, tied to the length of the period, not a rate per unit of time. Moving a risk to a different period, such as a model cycle, goes through a rate and is covered on the Transition Probability page."; HEO defines Absolute Risk as "The probability that an individual in a defined population will experience a specific outcome over a given period, without reference to a comparison.".

column2: Absolute risk reduction function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk Reduction. The module describes Absolute risk reduction function as "Maps the risks of an adverse event with the comparator and with the intervention, over the same period, to their difference, oriented so that a benefit is positive. The difference converts a relative treatment effect into events avoided per person treated, the quantity that costs and QALYs in an economic evaluation are built from."; HEO defines Absolute Risk Reduction as "Absolute risk reduction is the arithmetic difference in the probability of a specified adverse outcome between a comparator group and an intervention group over the same defined time horizon.".

column2: Network consistency function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Network Meta-Analysis. The module describes Network consistency function as "Expresses every pairwise relative effect in a connected network through effects relative to a common reference treatment A, on a scale where effects add, such as the log odds ratio. Here d_XY is the effect of Y relative to X, the NICE Decision Support Unit convention. Consistency is the assumption that direct and indirect evidence estimate the same d_XY."; HEO defines Network Meta-Analysis as "Network meta-analysis (NMA) compares three or more treatments in one analysis, pooling direct and indirect trial evidence to inform HTA decisions.".

column2: Severity shortfall function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Shortfall. The module describes Severity shortfall function as "Maps the remaining discounted QALYs expected for an age- and sex-matched general population, and for people with the condition under current NHS care, to absolute and proportional QALY shortfall. NICE uses whichever measure implies greater severity to set a weight on the incremental QALYs of a new technology."; HEO defines Absolute Shortfall as "Absolute shortfall is the future QALYs lost with a condition under current care versus the age- and sex-matched population, used by NICE to judge severity.".

column2: 15D index score function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept 15D. The module describes 15D index score function as "Maps a respondent's levels on the 15 dimensions of the 15D, each with 5 ordinal levels, to a single index on a 0 to 1 scale, where 0 is being dead and 1 is no problems on any dimension. The index is a preference-based utility that can weight survival in QALY calculations."; HEO defines 15D as "A generic, multi-attribute quality of life instrument measuring fifteen health dimensions, each scored on five levels, combined into a single utility index.".

column2: Resource costing function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost. The module describes Resource costing function as "Maps the resources used by an option, and the unit cost of each, to a single cost expressed in one currency, one price year and one time basis. Costing identifies the resources that differ between options, measures how much of each is used and values each with a unit cost; costs from other years are moved to the common price year, and capital used over several years is spread as an equivalent annual cost. Future costs are then discounted, as set out on the Discount Rate page."; HEO defines Cost as "In health economics, cost is the value of resources used by a healthcare intervention, measured as the benefit forgone from their best alternative use.".

column2: Absenteeism measurement and valuation function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absenteeism. The module describes Absenteeism measurement and valuation function as "Maps the time a worker is absent from paid work because of ill health, the usual hours worked and a value per hour to the share of working time lost and to a productivity cost. The value depends on the method: the human capital approach counts the whole absence, while the friction cost method counts only the period an employer needs to restore production."; HEO defines Absenteeism as "Time lost from work due to illness, injury, or caregiving responsibilities, resulting in a direct, measurable cost to employers through lost productivity.".

column2: Willingness-to-pay estimation function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Willingness to Pay. The module describes Willingness-to-pay estimation function as "Maps stated or modelled preferences for a change in health or health care to a sum of money: the marginal value of an attribute from the coefficients of a discrete choice model, or the mean of individual valuations from a contingent valuation survey, scaled to the affected population. Aggregate WTP is the monetary benefit that cost-benefit analysis sets against the present value of costs."; HEO defines Willingness to Pay as "Willingness to pay (WTP) is the most money a person would give up for a health gain or other benefit, used to value outcomes in cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Frontier efficiency measurement function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Efficiency. The module describes Frontier efficiency measurement function as "Maps a decision-making unit's observed inputs, outputs and costs, and a production or cost frontier estimated for comparable units, to efficiency scores between 0 and 1. A score of 1 places the unit on the estimated frontier. The frontier itself is usually estimated by data envelopment analysis, a linear programming method, or by stochastic frontier analysis, a parametric method that separates inefficiency from random noise."; HEO defines Efficiency as "Efficiency is getting the most health or other valued outcomes from scarce healthcare resources, avoiding waste and allocating them to their best uses.".

column2: Social marginal cost and benefit function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Externality. The module describes Social marginal cost and benefit function as "Adds the marginal effect that an activity has on third parties to the marginal cost or benefit that the decision-maker weighs, giving the marginal social cost or benefit. The efficient quantity is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost; a private decision that ignores the external term stops at a different quantity, and a Pigouvian tax or subsidy set at the marginal external effect at the efficient quantity closes the gap."; HEO defines Externality as "An externality is a cost or benefit, such as antimicrobial resistance or herd immunity, that falls on third parties and is ignored by the person deciding.".

column2: Ex post moral hazard welfare function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard. The module describes Ex post moral hazard welfare function as "Maps the resource cost of care, the share of that cost the insured patient pays and the quantities of care used at the full and insured prices to the welfare loss attributed to insurance-induced use, and maps observed spending under two cost-sharing arrangements to a price elasticity of demand. The welfare measures assume that the demand curve measures the patient's marginal benefit, an assumption that the access motive and behavioural hazard challenge."; HEO defines Moral Hazard as "Moral hazard is the change in behaviour, such as greater use of healthcare, that occurs when insurance shields people from the full cost of their choices.".

column2: Health capital accumulation and investment function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand for Health. The module describes Health capital accumulation and investment function as "In the Grossman model health is a durable capital stock that produces healthy time. The stock carried into the next period is the current stock less depreciation plus gross investment, which the individual produces with medical care and own time. The optimal stock in each period equates the marginal return on health capital with its user cost, the real rate of interest plus the rate of depreciation."; HEO defines Demand for Health as "Demand for health is the idea, from the Grossman model, that people value health as a capital stock, so their demand for healthcare is derived from it.".

column2: Welfare change measurement and aggregation function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Welfare Economics. The module describes Welfare change measurement and aggregation function as "Converts each person's gain or loss from a change into money, with the compensating or equivalent variation or the consumer surplus approximation, and then ranks the change for society: by adding the money measures, as the Kaldor-Hicks potential compensation test does, or by combining individual outcomes with an explicit social welfare function that states how gains to one person are set against losses to another."; HEO defines Welfare Economics as "Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that judges whether changes in the allocation of resources and health make society better off.".

column2: 340B ceiling price function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept 340B Drug Pricing Program. The module describes 340B ceiling price function as "Maps a covered outpatient drug's average manufacturer price and its Medicaid unit rebate amount for the preceding calendar quarter to the maximum price a covered entity can be required to pay for the smallest unit of the drug. The statute sets the ceiling as AMP reduced by the rebate percentage, the Medicaid rebate per unit divided by AMP, which is AMP minus the unit rebate amount."; HEO defines 340B Drug Pricing Program as "A US federal programme requiring manufacturers to provide outpatient drugs to eligible organisations serving low-income populations at reduced prices.".

column2: Average bioequivalence and generic price function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Abbreviated New Drug Application. The module describes Average bioequivalence and generic price function as "For an ANDA, bioequivalence to the reference listed drug is shown when the 90% confidence interval for the ratio of geometric means of a pharmacokinetic measure, such as AUC or Cmax, lies within 80.00% to 125.00% after rounding. The interval is computed on the log scale and exponentiated. For economic models, the approval of generic competitors is then translated into a post-entry price."; HEO defines Abbreviated New Drug Application as "A streamlined US regulatory application letting a generic manufacturer gain approval by demonstrating bioequivalence to an approved reference drug, without repeating full trials.".

column2: Adverse event rate to model input function
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Adverse event rate to model input function as "Maps the adverse event counts in a trial safety table, with their denominators of patients or person-time, to the probability of an event in one model cycle, and maps those probabilities to the expected adverse event cost and QALY loss per patient. The general rate and probability conversions are on the Transition Probability page (HE-FN-TP-001); the records here apply them to adverse event data and add the cost and QALY weighting."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Penalised-likelihood ranking of candidate survival models
column24: The module lists this mathematical function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes Penalised-likelihood ranking of candidate survival models as "Maps the maximised log-likelihood and the number of estimated parameters of each model fitted to the same data to an information criterion, a fit statistic with a penalty for each extra parameter. Lower values rank higher, and only differences between models fitted to the same observations carry meaning. In health technology assessment the candidates are usually parametric survival curves fitted to trial time-to-event data before extrapolation. The criteria measure fit within follow-up only, so they inform but do not settle the choice of curve."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Alpha spending function for group sequential trials
