The comparator curve supplies the absolute level; the ratio alone cannot."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Treatment-arm transition probability from a hazard ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hazard Ratio. The module describes Treatment-arm transition probability from a hazard ratio as "Applies a hazard ratio to a comparator transition probability for one model cycle. The comparator probability is converted to a rate, the rate is multiplied by the hazard ratio, and the result is converted back, which reduces to a single power. The conversions are set out on the Transition Probability page."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Time ratio from an accelerated failure time coefficient
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accelerated Failure Time Model. The module describes Time ratio from an accelerated failure time coefficient as "Converts the estimated treatment coefficient on the log-time scale into the time ratio, the factor by which treatment multiplies survival times. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Accelerated Failure Time Model as "An accelerated failure time (AFT) model is a survival model in which treatment or another factor stretches or shrinks time to an event by a time ratio.".

column2: Treated survival time at the same survival proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accelerated Failure Time Model. The module describes Treated survival time at the same survival proportion as "Multiplies the time by which a given proportion of the reference group has had the event by the time ratio to give the corresponding time in the treated group. Applied at the median it gives the treated median; applied at every percentile it traces the whole treated curve."; HEO defines Accelerated Failure Time Model as "An accelerated failure time (AFT) model is a survival model in which treatment or another factor stretches or shrinks time to an event by a time ratio.".

column2: Weibull hazard ratio implied by an accelerated failure time fit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accelerated Failure Time Model. The module describes Weibull hazard ratio implied by an accelerated failure time fit as "For the Weibull distribution, the only one that is both a proportional hazards and an accelerated failure time model, converts the treatment coefficient and the scale parameter sigma of the log-linear form into the hazard ratio. The Weibull shape parameter equals 1 divided by sigma, so the same result is TR raised to the power minus 1 divided by sigma."; HEO defines Accelerated Failure Time Model as "An accelerated failure time (AFT) model is a survival model in which treatment or another factor stretches or shrinks time to an event by a time ratio.".

column2: Exponential event time by inverse transform
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discrete Event Simulation. The module describes Exponential event time by inverse transform as "Samples a time to an event with a constant hazard lambda_j from a uniform random number U. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Discrete Event Simulation as "Discrete event simulation (DES) is a modelling method that follows each patient from event to event over time, tracking their history and use of resources.".

column2: Weibull event time by inverse transform
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discrete Event Simulation. The module describes Weibull event time by inverse transform as "Samples a time to an event from a Weibull distribution with scale beta and shape gamma, whose survival function is S(t) = exp(-(t/beta)^gamma), from a uniform random number U. A shape above 1 gives a rising hazard and a shape below 1 a falling hazard."; HEO defines Discrete Event Simulation as "Discrete event simulation (DES) is a modelling method that follows each patient from event to event over time, tracking their history and use of resources.".

column2: Little's law check on a simulated queue
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discrete Event Simulation. The module describes Little's law check on a simulated queue as "Relates the long-run average number of entities in a stable queueing system to their arrival rate and average time in the system. In a DES with constrained resources it is used as a validation check: the simulated average number in the system should match the arrival rate multiplied by the simulated average time in the system."; HEO defines Discrete Event Simulation as "Discrete event simulation (DES) is a modelling method that follows each patient from event to event over time, tracking their history and use of resources.".

column2: Expected cycles before absorption from the fundamental matrix
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absorbing State. The module describes Expected cycles before absorption from the fundamental matrix as "Inverts I minus Q to obtain the fundamental matrix N, whose entry in row i and column j is the expected number of cycles spent in transient state j by a person starting in transient state i, counting the starting cycle. Multiplying N by a column of ones sums each row, giving the expected number of cycles before absorption from each starting state. With death as the only absorbing state, this is the undiscounted expected number of cycles alive."; HEO defines Absorbing State as "An absorbing state is a state in a Markov model that patients cannot leave once they enter it, usually death, so the whole cohort eventually ends there.".

column2: Probability of ending in each absorbing state
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absorbing State. The module describes Probability of ending in each absorbing state as "Multiplies the fundamental matrix by R, the one-cycle probabilities of moving from each transient state to each absorbing state. Entry i, j of B is the probability that a person starting in transient state i is eventually absorbed in state j. It is useful when a model keeps separate death states, for example death from the disease and death from other causes."; HEO defines Absorbing State as "An absorbing state is a state in a Markov model that patients cannot leave once they enter it, usually death, so the whole cohort eventually ends there.".

column2: Absolute risk as an incidence proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk. The module describes Absolute risk as an incidence proportion as "Divides the number of new events during the period by the number of people at risk at its start. In epidemiology the same quantity is called the incidence proportion, attack rate or cumulative incidence. It gives the comparator-arm baseline risk that a decision model applies relative treatment effects to."; HEO defines Absolute Risk as "The probability that an individual in a defined population will experience a specific outcome over a given period, without reference to a comparison.".

column2: Absolute risk reduction from two arm risks
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk Reduction. The module describes Absolute risk reduction from two arm risks as "Subtracts the intervention-arm risk from the comparator-arm risk of an adverse event. A negative value is an absolute risk increase. The Cochrane Handbook computes the risk difference as intervention minus comparator, so for an adverse outcome ARR equals minus that risk difference."; HEO defines Absolute Risk Reduction as "Absolute risk reduction is the arithmetic difference in the probability of a specified adverse outcome between a comparator group and an intervention group over the same defined time horizon.".

column2: Absolute and relative risk reduction from a relative risk and baseline risk
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk Reduction. The module describes Absolute and relative risk reduction from a relative risk and baseline risk as "Applies a relative risk, for example a pooled estimate from a meta-analysis, to an assumed comparator risk for the population of interest. The intervention risk is p_C times RR, so the ARR is p_C times the relative risk reduction 1 minus RR. For a fixed relative risk, the ARR rises in direct proportion to baseline risk: at a relative risk of 0.75 a baseline risk of 0.04 gives an ARR of 0.01, a fifth of the value at 0.20."; HEO defines Absolute Risk Reduction as "Absolute risk reduction is the arithmetic difference in the probability of a specified adverse outcome between a comparator group and an intervention group over the same defined time horizon.".

column2: Number needed to treat and its confidence limits from the ARR
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Risk Reduction. The module describes Number needed to treat and its confidence limits from the ARR as "Takes the reciprocal of the ARR and of its confidence limits, which reverses their order. The NNT is the expected number of people who must receive the intervention rather than the comparator, over the stated period, for one additional person to avoid the event. By convention it is rounded up to the next whole number when reported."; HEO defines Absolute Risk Reduction as "Absolute risk reduction is the arithmetic difference in the probability of a specified adverse outcome between a comparator group and an intervention group over the same defined time horizon.".

column2: Bucher adjusted indirect comparison through a common comparator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Network Meta-Analysis. The module describes Bucher adjusted indirect comparison through a common comparator as "Estimates the effect of C relative to B from trials of B against A and trials of C against A. The indirect estimate is the difference of the two direct effects, and its variance is the sum of their variances because the two sets of trials are independent. Working with within-trial contrasts preserves randomisation, unlike a comparison of active arms taken from different trials."; HEO defines Network Meta-Analysis as "Network meta-analysis (NMA) compares three or more treatments in one analysis, pooling direct and indirect trial evidence to inform HTA decisions.".

column2: Indirect odds ratio and 95% interval from the log scale
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Network Meta-Analysis. The module describes Indirect odds ratio and 95% interval from the log scale as "Back-transforms an indirect log odds ratio and its variance into an odds ratio with a 95% confidence interval. The interval is built symmetrically on the log scale and becomes asymmetric on the odds ratio scale. The function exp is the exponential function and sqrt the square root."; HEO defines Network Meta-Analysis as "Network meta-analysis (NMA) compares three or more treatments in one analysis, pooling direct and indirect trial evidence to inform HTA decisions.".

column2: Bucher inconsistency estimate and z statistic for a single loop
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Network Meta-Analysis. The module describes Bucher inconsistency estimate and z statistic for a single loop as "Compares a direct estimate of the effect of C relative to B with the indirect estimate formed from the A versus B and A versus C evidence, the inconsistency factor IF in the article. The inconsistency is their difference, its variance is the sum of the two variances, and z is referred to the standard normal distribution. The function sqrt is the square root."; HEO defines Network Meta-Analysis as "Network meta-analysis (NMA) compares three or more treatments in one analysis, pooling direct and indirect trial evidence to inform HTA decisions.".

column2: Absolute event probability from a baseline risk and a network odds ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Network Meta-Analysis. The module describes Absolute event probability from a baseline risk and a network odds ratio as "Applies a treatment effect from a log odds ratio network to a baseline probability on the reference treatment, taken from a separate baseline natural history model. On the logit scale the effect adds, logit(p_k) = logit(p_0) + d_k, with OR_k = exp(d_k); the stated form is the same relation solved for p_k without logarithms. The ARR against the reference is then p_0 minus p_k."; HEO defines Network Meta-Analysis as "Network meta-analysis (NMA) compares three or more treatments in one analysis, pooling direct and indirect trial evidence to inform HTA decisions.".

column2: Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Shortfall. The module describes Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall as "Absolute shortfall subtracts the expected remaining QALYs of people with the condition under current care from those of the matched general population. Proportional shortfall divides the same difference by the general-population QALYs. Both look forward from the point at which the technology would be used, so health already lost does not count, and both are discounted at the reference-case rate."; HEO defines Absolute Shortfall as "Absolute shortfall is the future QALYs lost with a condition under current care versus the age- and sex-matched population, used by NICE to judge severity.".

column2: Discounted general-population QALYs from a life table
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Shortfall. The module describes Discounted general-population QALYs from a life table as "Sums, over each year of remaining life from the starting age, the expected years lived multiplied by the age-specific utility norm and discounted to the starting age. Here t counts years from the starting age i, so t equals x minus i for age x, and the sum runs to the last age in the life table, usually 100. It is carried out separately for each sex, and the two results are weighted by the proportion female to give Q_h."; HEO defines Absolute Shortfall as "Absolute shortfall is the future QALYs lost with a condition under current care versus the age- and sex-matched population, used by NICE to judge severity.".

column2: Severity QALY weight from the shortfall bands
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absolute Shortfall. The module describes Severity QALY weight from the shortfall bands as "Returns the NICE severity weight from absolute and proportional shortfall. The weight is 1.7 if absolute shortfall is at least 18 or proportional shortfall at least 0.95, 1.2 if absolute shortfall is at least 12 or proportional shortfall at least 0.85, and 1 otherwise. The measure implying greater severity decides, and a value on a cut-off takes the higher band. Each comparison returns 1 when true and 0 when false."; HEO defines Absolute Shortfall as "Absolute shortfall is the future QALYs lost with a condition under current care versus the age- and sex-matched population, used by NICE to judge severity.".

column2: 15D score as an additive weighted sum of level values
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept 15D. The module describes 15D score as an additive weighted sum of level values as "Multiplies the value of the level reported on each dimension by the importance weight of that dimension at that level, and adds the products over the 15 dimensions. This is the additive multi-attribute utility model of the 15D valuation system, v_H = sum of I_j(x_j) times w_j(x_j), with the level x_j written into I_j and w_j here."; HEO defines 15D as "A generic, multi-attribute quality of life instrument measuring fifteen health dimensions, each scored on five levels, combined into a single utility index.".

column2: Total cost from resource quantities and unit costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost. The module describes Total cost from resource quantities and unit costs as "Multiplies the quantity of each resource used by its unit cost and adds the products over all resource types. Keeping quantities and unit costs separate shows whether a cost difference comes from different resource use or from different prices, and lets an analyst in another setting substitute local unit costs. The same sum over options gives the cost terms C_j used in the ICER and net monetary benefit."; HEO defines Cost as "In health economics, cost is the value of resources used by a healthcare intervention, measured as the benefit forgone from their best alternative use.".

column2: Price-year adjustment of a cost with an inflation index
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost. The module describes Price-year adjustment of a cost with an inflation index as "Moves a cost observed in price year a to price year b by multiplying it by the ratio of an appropriate price index in the two years. When the index is published as annual percentage increases, as the NHS Cost Inflation Index is, the index is built by chaining: each year's value is the previous value multiplied by one plus that year's increase. The NICE manual names the NHS Cost Inflation Index and the PSS Pay and Prices Index, both reported in the Unit Costs of Health and Social Care manual, or the ONS consumer price index."; HEO defines Cost as "In health economics, cost is the value of resources used by a healthcare intervention, measured as the benefit forgone from their best alternative use.".

column2: Equivalent annual cost of a capital asset
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost. The module describes Equivalent annual cost of a capital asset as "Spreads the cost of a capital asset, such as equipment or a building, over its useful life as an equal annual amount whose present value equals the purchase cost less the discounted resale value. The annuity factor A(n,r), one minus (1 + r) to the power minus n, all divided by r, is the present value of 1 a year for n years at rate r. Unlike straight-line depreciation, the equivalent annual cost includes the opportunity cost of the funds tied up in the asset."; HEO defines Cost as "In health economics, cost is the value of resources used by a healthcare intervention, measured as the benefit forgone from their best alternative use.".

column2: WPAI proportion of work time missed because of health
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absenteeism. The module describes WPAI proportion of work time missed because of health as "Divides the hours missed from work because of health problems by the sum of those hours and the hours actually worked, over the seven-day recall period of the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire, general health version. Multiplying by 100 gives the percentage of work time missed. Hours missed for other reasons, such as holidays, are excluded from both terms."; HEO defines Absenteeism as "Time lost from work due to illness, injury, or caregiving responsibilities, resulting in a direct, measurable cost to employers through lost productivity.".

column2: Absence cost by the human capital approach
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absenteeism. The module describes Absence cost by the human capital approach as "Values every hour of absence at the value of an hour of work. D_a counts calendar days absent, so D_a divided by 7 gives weeks absent, and multiplying by the usual weekly hours and the hourly value gives the cost. The human capital approach usually values time at gross earnings including employer-paid costs such as payroll taxes and benefits, the full cost of employee compensation."; HEO defines Absenteeism as "Time lost from work due to illness, injury, or caregiving responsibilities, resulting in a direct, measurable cost to employers through lost productivity.".

column2: Absence cost by the friction cost method
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Absenteeism. The module describes Absence cost by the friction cost method as "Counts absence only up to the friction period, the time an employer needs to restore production, usually by replacing the worker, and multiplies the counted hours by the value of an hour and by the elasticity of production with respect to working time. Absences shorter than the friction period count in full. When the hourly value already allows for the elasticity, as the Dutch reference price does, e is set to 1."; HEO defines Absenteeism as "Time lost from work due to illness, injury, or caregiving responsibilities, resulting in a direct, measurable cost to employers through lost productivity.".

column2: Marginal willingness to pay from a discrete choice experiment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Willingness to Pay. The module describes Marginal willingness to pay from a discrete choice experiment as "Divides the utility coefficient of an attribute, or the difference in coefficients between two of its levels, by the negative of the coefficient on the cost attribute. The cost coefficient measures the marginal utility of money, so the ratio is the payment that leaves utility unchanged when the attribute improves by one unit or moves between the two levels."; HEO defines Willingness to Pay as "Willingness to pay (WTP) is the most money a person would give up for a health gain or other benefit, used to value outcomes in cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Mean willingness to pay and aggregate benefit from a survey sample
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Willingness to Pay. The module describes Mean willingness to pay and aggregate benefit from a survey sample as "Averages the stated values of the n respondents in the analysis sample to give mean WTP, and multiplies the mean by the number of people in the population to give aggregate WTP, the monetary benefit used in cost-benefit analysis. Mean WTP multiplied by the population equals the sum of individual values; median WTP describes the typical respondent and is reported alongside, but it is not a welfare total."; HEO defines Willingness to Pay as "Willingness to pay (WTP) is the most money a person would give up for a health gain or other benefit, used to value outcomes in cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Output-oriented technical efficiency
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Efficiency. The module describes Output-oriented technical efficiency as "Divides the output a unit actually produces by the maximum output that the estimated frontier says is feasible from the same inputs. The shortfall from 1 is the proportion by which output could rise without extra inputs. It measures waste in the production process only and says nothing about whether the right services are produced."; HEO defines Efficiency as "Efficiency is getting the most health or other valued outcomes from scarce healthcare resources, avoiding waste and allocating them to their best uses.".

column2: Cost efficiency and its decomposition into technical and allocative efficiency
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Efficiency. The module describes Cost efficiency and its decomposition into technical and allocative efficiency as "Compares three costs of producing the unit's observed output at its input prices: the actual cost, the cost of the technically efficient input bundle found by shrinking all inputs in proportion to the frontier, and the minimum cost with the least-cost mix of inputs. Cost efficiency is the minimum cost over the actual cost; input-oriented technical efficiency is the technically efficient cost over the actual cost; allocative efficiency in this production-frontier sense, the choice of input mix at given prices, is the minimum cost over the technically efficient cost. Cost efficiency equals technical efficiency multiplied by allocative efficiency."; HEO defines Efficiency as "Efficiency is getting the most health or other valued outcomes from scarce healthcare resources, avoiding waste and allocating them to their best uses.".

column2: Scale efficiency from constant and variable returns frontiers
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Efficiency. The module describes Scale efficiency from constant and variable returns frontiers as "Divides technical efficiency measured against a constant returns to scale frontier by technical efficiency against a variable returns to scale frontier for the same unit and orientation. The variable returns score removes the effect of size, so the ratio isolates the part of inefficiency due to operating at a size other than the most productive scale."; HEO defines Efficiency as "Efficiency is getting the most health or other valued outcomes from scarce healthcare resources, avoiding waste and allocating them to their best uses.".

column2: Marginal social cost, social benefit and net benefit at one margin
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Externality. The module describes Marginal social cost, social benefit and net benefit at one margin as "Marginal social cost is the marginal private cost borne by the decision-maker plus the marginal external cost imposed on others; marginal social benefit is the marginal private benefit plus the marginal external benefit received by others. Subtracting cost from benefit with and without the external terms gives the net gain to society and to the decision-maker from one more unit. When the two net gains differ in sign, the private decision goes against the social one, and a subsidy or tax larger than the private shortfall at that margin reverses it. By convention production externalities enter the cost side and consumption externalities the benefit side, so an external cost of consumption, such as the contribution of antibiotic use to resistance, is entered as a negative MEB."; HEO defines Externality as "An externality is a cost or benefit, such as antimicrobial resistance or herd immunity, that falls on third parties and is ignored by the person deciding.".

column2: Pigouvian subsidy and deadweight loss for vaccination with linear curves
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Externality. The module describes Pigouvian subsidy and deadweight loss for vaccination with linear curves as "Takes a linear marginal private benefit (demand) curve a minus b × Q, a constant marginal cost c with no external cost, and a marginal external benefit m minus g × Q that falls as coverage rises, as herd immunity would suggest. The private quantity Q_p sets marginal private benefit equal to c; the efficient quantity Q_s sets marginal social benefit equal to c. The Pigouvian subsidy s is the marginal external benefit at Q_s, and the deadweight loss of leaving the market alone is the triangle between marginal social benefit and cost from Q_p to Q_s. The tax on a negative externality mirrors this: t equals the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity."; HEO defines Externality as "An externality is a cost or benefit, such as antimicrobial resistance or herd immunity, that falls on third parties and is ignored by the person deciding.".

column2: Welfare loss triangle of insurance-induced care
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard. The module describes Welfare loss triangle of insurance-induced care as "With coinsurance rate c the patient pays c × p per unit of care that costs p to provide and uses q_1 units instead of the q_0 chosen at the full price. Each extra unit costs p but is valued by the patient at between c × p and p, so with a linear demand curve the loss is the triangle whose height is the price reduction p minus c × p and whose base is the extra use. The notation follows the moral hazard article."; HEO defines Moral Hazard as "Moral hazard is the change in behaviour, such as greater use of healthcare, that occurs when insurance shields people from the full cost of their choices.".

column2: Extra use and welfare loss from a linear demand curve
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard. The module describes Extra use and welfare loss from a linear demand curve as "When demand for care is linear with slope D, a fall in the price the patient faces from p to c × p raises use by D × (p minus c × p). Substituting into the triangle gives a welfare loss of one half of D × (p minus c × p) squared. The loss therefore rises with the square of the price reduction: halving the coinsurance rate from 0.5 to 0.25 more than doubles it."; HEO defines Moral Hazard as "Moral hazard is the change in behaviour, such as greater use of healthcare, that occurs when insurance shields people from the full cost of their choices.".

column2: RAND arc elasticity of medical spending
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard. The module describes RAND arc elasticity of medical spending as "Divides the change in spending, as a proportion of the average of the two spending levels, by the change in price, as a proportion of the average of the two prices. The RAND investigators used arc elasticities because the free care plan had a price of zero, from which an ordinary percentage change cannot be computed. The widely quoted RAND elasticity of about minus 0.2 comes from arc elasticities of this kind computed from an episode-based model; Aron-Dine and colleagues identify Keeler and Rolph 1988 as its underlying source."; HEO defines Moral Hazard as "Moral hazard is the change in behaviour, such as greater use of healthcare, that occurs when insurance shields people from the full cost of their choices.".

column2: Health capital stock carried into the next period
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand for Health. The module describes Health capital stock carried into the next period as "Grossman's equation (2-2) sets net investment, the change in the stock, equal to gross investment minus depreciation. Rearranged, the stock at the start of the next period is the current stock, less the share delta_t that depreciates during the period, plus gross investment. Holding the stock constant requires gross investment equal to delta_t × H_t."; HEO defines Demand for Health as "Demand for health is the idea, from the Grossman model, that people value health as a capital stock, so their demand for healthcare is derived from it.".

column2: Pure investment condition for the optimal health stock
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand for Health. The module describes Pure investment condition for the optimal health stock as "In the pure investment version of the Grossman model, health yields no direct utility and is valued only for the healthy time it adds to earnings. The marginal monetary return on health capital, gamma_t, is the wage multiplied by the marginal product of health capital in healthy time, divided by the marginal cost of gross investment. At the optimal stock it equals the opportunity cost of health capital, the real-own rate of interest r minus pi_tilde_(t-1) plus the rate of depreciation. The formula returns both sides so that the condition can be checked."; HEO defines Demand for Health as "Demand for health is the idea, from the Grossman model, that people value health as a capital stock, so their demand for healthcare is derived from it.".

column2: Compensating and equivalent variation from the expenditure function
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Welfare Economics. The module describes Compensating and equivalent variation from the expenditure function as "For a change in prices with income unchanged, the compensating variation is the income that could be taken away after the change while leaving the person at the original utility level u0; the equivalent variation is the income that would have to be given before the change to reach the new utility level u1. Each is a difference in the minimum expenditure needed to reach a utility level at old and new prices: CV = e(p0,u0) minus e(p1,u0) and EV = e(p0,u1) minus e(p1,u1). The formula takes the four expenditure values as inputs."; HEO defines Welfare Economics as "Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that judges whether changes in the allocation of resources and health make society better off.".

column2: Change in consumer surplus from a price change on a linear demand curve
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Welfare Economics. The module describes Change in consumer surplus from a price change on a linear demand curve as "When demand is linear between the old and new prices, the change in consumer surplus is the trapezoid between the two prices out to the demand curve: the price change multiplied by the average of the quantities bought before and after. The result is positive for a price fall and negative for a rise. It is the Marshallian approximation to CV and EV and lies between them for a single price change."; HEO defines Welfare Economics as "Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that judges whether changes in the allocation of resources and health make society better off.".

column2: Kaldor-Hicks aggregate net gain across groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Welfare Economics. The module describes Kaldor-Hicks aggregate net gain across groups as "Adds the money measure of each group's gain or loss, weighted by the number of people in the group. A change passes the Kaldor potential compensation test when the total is greater than zero, because the gainers could then compensate the losers and still be better off, whether or not compensation is paid. The sum is the welfare-economic basis of net benefit in cost-benefit analysis, where the programme's resource cost enters as a loss."; HEO defines Welfare Economics as "Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that judges whether changes in the allocation of resources and health make society better off.".

column2: Weighted two-group social welfare and the switching weight
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Welfare Economics. The module describes Weighted two-group social welfare and the switching weight as "Scores each option as total QALYs of group A plus a weight w times total QALYs of group B, where w is the value placed on a QALY accruing to the worse-off group relative to group A. A weight of 1 gives the utilitarian sum. The switching weight is the value of w at which two options X and Y score the same, found by setting their weighted totals equal; above it the option that does more for group B is preferred."; HEO defines Welfare Economics as "Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that judges whether changes in the allocation of resources and health make society better off.".

column2: 340B ceiling price per unit with the penny floor
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept 340B Drug Pricing Program. The module describes 340B ceiling price per unit with the penny floor as "42 CFR 10.10(a) sets the ceiling price as the AMP from the preceding calendar quarter for the smallest unit of measure minus the URA, calculated to six decimal places; HRSA publishes it rounded to two. Under 10.10(b), a calculation below 0.01 dollars gives a ceiling price of 0.01 dollars, the penny pricing policy."; HEO defines 340B Drug Pricing Program as "A US federal programme requiring manufacturers to provide outpatient drugs to eligible organisations serving low-income populations at reduced prices.".

column2: Medicaid unit rebate amount for a single-source or innovator drug
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept 340B Drug Pricing Program. The module describes Medicaid unit rebate amount for a single-source or innovator drug as "The unit rebate amount that enters the ceiling price is the basic rebate plus the additional inflation rebate. For a single-source or innovator multiple-source drug the basic rebate is the greater of AMP minus best price and 23.1% of AMP. The additional rebate is the amount, if any, by which AMP exceeds the drug's base-period AMP increased by the rise in the consumer price index for all urban consumers since the base period. The 100% of AMP cap on the total applied only to rebate periods before 1 January 2024, so since then URA can exceed AMP."; HEO defines 340B Drug Pricing Program as "A US federal programme requiring manufacturers to provide outpatient drugs to eligible organisations serving low-income populations at reduced prices.".

column2: Spread between reimbursement and the 340B price
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept 340B Drug Pricing Program. The module describes Spread between reimbursement and the 340B price as "The revenue a covered entity keeps on a unit bought at the ceiling price is the payer's reimbursement for the unit minus the price paid. The spread depends on the payer's payment rule, not on the 340B statute, so the same ceiling price produces different spreads across payers; a unit dispensed to a Medicaid fee-for-service patient must not also attract a Medicaid rebate."; HEO defines 340B Drug Pricing Program as "A US federal programme requiring manufacturers to provide outpatient drugs to eligible organisations serving low-income populations at reduced prices.".

column2: 90 per cent confidence interval for the geometric mean ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Abbreviated New Drug Application. The module describes 90 per cent confidence interval for the geometric mean ratio as "The mean difference d between test and reference in natural logs of AUC or Cmax is exponentiated to give the geometric mean ratio, and the limits of the 90% interval are d plus or minus the one-sided 95% t quantile times the standard error, exponentiated. This interval corresponds to the two one-sided tests procedure at the 5% level. Average bioequivalence is concluded when the interval, expressed in per cent and rounded to two decimal places, is at least 80.00 and no more than 125.00."; HEO defines Abbreviated New Drug Application as "A streamlined US regulatory application letting a generic manufacturer gain approval by demonstrating bioequivalence to an approved reference drug, without repeating full trials.".

column2: Standard error of the log difference in a balanced two-period crossover
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Abbreviated New Drug Application. The module describes Standard error of the log difference in a balanced two-period crossover as "In a two-treatment, two-period, two-sequence crossover with n subjects split equally between sequences, the variance of the estimated mean log difference is twice the within-subject variance divided by n, where the within-subject variance is the residual mean square from the analysis of the log data. The within-subject coefficient of variation on the original scale is the square root of exp(MSE) minus 1."; HEO defines Abbreviated New Drug Application as "A streamlined US regulatory application letting a generic manufacturer gain approval by demonstrating bioequivalence to an approved reference drug, without repeating full trials.".

column2: Post-entry generic price and annual drug cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Abbreviated New Drug Application. The module describes Post-entry generic price and annual drug cost as "Applies a proportional price reduction associated with a given number of generic competitors to the brand price before entry, then multiplies by the doses used in a year. This is the simplest way to reflect generic entry in a cost-effectiveness model, and it assumes immediate and complete switching at a single reduction."; HEO defines Abbreviated New Drug Application as "A streamlined US regulatory application letting a generic manufacturer gain approval by demonstrating bioequivalence to an approved reference drug, without repeating full trials.".

column2: Adverse event proportion over a trial follow-up period
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Adverse event proportion over a trial follow-up period as "Divides the number of patients with at least one episode of a stated adverse event by the number of patients at risk at the start of follow-up. The result is the cumulative incidence over that period, so it belongs to the period and is not a rate per week or a probability per model cycle."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Adverse event rate per unit of person-time
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Adverse event rate per unit of person-time as "Divides the number of adverse events counted by the total person-time at risk. The result is an incidence rate: it can exceed 1, depends on the time unit, and allows a fair comparison between arms treated for different lengths of time."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Per-cycle adverse event probability rescaled from a trial proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Per-cycle adverse event probability rescaled from a trial proportion as "Turns the proportion of patients with an adverse event over the trial follow-up period T into the probability of a first episode within a model cycle of length t in two steps: it recovers the implied constant rate r, then converts that rate to the cycle probability with the constant-rate conversion HE-FM-TP-001 on the Transition Probability page. The second step also applies to a rate per person-time from HE-FM-AER-002. The two steps together equal the single-step form 1 minus (1 minus P) raised to the power t/T, the rescaling formula HE-FM-TP-003 applied to trial safety data. Dividing P by the number of cycles is not equivalent, because probabilities do not add over time in the way rates do. The function log is the natural logarithm and exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Expected adverse event cost per patient
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Expected adverse event cost per patient as "Weights the cost of managing one episode of each adverse event type by the probability of that event and adds the products over the K event types included. The probabilities cover the period that the model costs, for example the 24-week trial period or the cycles on treatment."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Expected QALY loss from adverse events per patient
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Expected QALY loss from adverse events per patient as "Multiplies the probability of each adverse event type by the utility decrement during an episode and by the episode's duration in years, and adds the products over the K event types. The result is subtracted from the QALY total of the arm as a one-off decrement."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: Akaike information criterion from the maximised log-likelihood
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes Akaike information criterion from the maximised log-likelihood as "Akaike's criterion charges a penalty of 2 for each estimated parameter. A more complex model is therefore preferred only if each extra parameter raises the maximised log-likelihood by more than one unit. Because it compares maximised likelihoods rather than testing one model against another, it can rank survival distributions that are not nested within one another."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: AIC difference from the best-scoring candidate model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes AIC difference from the best-scoring candidate model as "Rescales each model's AIC to its distance from the smallest AIC in the candidate set, so the best model scores 0 and the arbitrary constant cancels. On Burnham and Anderson's rule of thumb, a difference of 2 or less indicates substantial support, 4 to 7 considerably less, and above 10 almost none."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Akaike weight of a candidate model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes Akaike weight of a candidate model as "Converts AIC differences into weights that sum to 1 across the R candidate models. The weight w_i equals exp(-delta_i/2) divided by S, where S is the sum of exp(-delta_r/2) over all R candidates. It is read as the weight of evidence that the model is the best approximating model in the set, given the data. Adding or removing a candidate changes every weight."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Bayesian information criterion as a companion to AIC
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes Bayesian information criterion as a companion to AIC as "Schwarz's criterion replaces the AIC penalty of 2 per parameter with the natural logarithm of the sample size, so the penalty grows with n. With 300 patients it is about 5.70 per parameter, and BIC leans towards simpler distributions. NICE DSU TSD 14 recommends presenting AIC and BIC, or other suitable tests of internal validity, when survival models are compared. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Small-sample corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc)
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes Small-sample corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc) as "Adds a second-order correction to AIC that matters when the number of parameters is large relative to the sample size. The correction shrinks towards 0 as n grows, so AICc converges to AIC. Burnham and Anderson recommend AICc unless the ratio of sample size to parameters exceeds about 40, which makes it relevant for small trial arms."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Information fraction from deaths for alpha spending
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Information fraction from deaths for alpha spending as "Measures trial progress on the information scale that a spending function uses: the information available at analysis k divided by the information planned for the final analysis. For a survival outcome compared with the log-rank test, the fraction is approximated by the deaths observed so far divided by the deaths expected by the end of the trial. For a comparison of means it is the number of patients analysed divided by the target sample size."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming type spending function
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming type spending function as "Gives the cumulative one-sided type I error spent by information fraction t under the function Lan and DeMets proposed to approximate the O'Brien-Fleming boundary. Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and Phi^-1 its inverse. The function spends almost nothing at early looks and equals alpha at t = 1 whatever the number of looks. Excel evaluates Phi with NORM.S.DIST and its inverse with NORM.S.INV."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Lan-DeMets Pocock type spending function
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Lan-DeMets Pocock type spending function as "Gives the cumulative one-sided type I error spent by information fraction t under the function Lan and DeMets proposed to approximate the Pocock boundary. The function log is the natural logarithm and exp(1) is e, the base of natural logarithms. It spends more evenly than the O'Brien-Fleming type, giving nearly constant boundaries and a higher chance of stopping early, and equals alpha at t = 1."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Alpha spending increment at an interim look
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Alpha spending increment at an interim look as "Gives the additional type I error that may be used at analysis k: the cumulative spend at t_k minus the cumulative spend at the previous analysis, with alpha_(k-1) equal to 0 at the first look. The increments over all analyses sum to the overall level alpha."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Hazard ratio needed to cross an alpha spending boundary
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Hazard ratio needed to cross an alpha spending boundary as "Converts the efficacy critical value at analysis k into the largest observed hazard ratio that crosses the boundary, using the approximation that with equal allocation the variance of the estimated log hazard ratio is about 4 divided by the number of deaths. The critical value comes from the numerically solved boundary; exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Annuity-due instalment for a one-off therapy price
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annuity Payment. The module describes Annuity-due instalment for a one-off therapy price as "Gives the equal instalment paid at the start of each year, the first at the point of treatment, so that the n payments have the same present value at the financing rate i as the upfront price P. It is the present value of an annuity due rearranged for the payment. When payments fall at the end of each year instead, the final division by (1 + i) is dropped, which gives the ordinary annuity used to annualise capital costs."; HEO defines Annuity Payment as "Annuity payment is an agreement to pay for a one-off therapy in yearly instalments, not upfront, with later ones sometimes stopping if the therapy fails.".

column2: Present value of a fixed annuity payment schedule at the evaluation discount rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annuity Payment. The module describes Present value of a fixed annuity payment schedule at the evaluation discount rate as "Values n equal instalments A, the first at treatment, at the discount rate r used in the economic evaluation. It equals the sum of A divided by (1 + r) to the power t for t from 0 to n minus 1, written here in closed form. This present value, not the list price or the nominal total, is the cost of the therapy in the model. When r equals the financing rate, the result equals the upfront price."; HEO defines Annuity Payment as "Annuity payment is an agreement to pay for a one-off therapy in yearly instalments, not upfront, with later ones sometimes stopping if the therapy fails.".

column2: Expected present value of an outcomes-based annuity payment schedule
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annuity Payment. The module describes Expected present value of an outcomes-based annuity payment schedule as "Values a schedule in which each later instalment is due only if the patient still meets a pre-agreed response criterion on that date. The sum runs over the years t from 0, the payment at treatment, to T, the year of the last instalment, which is the number of instalments minus 1. Each instalment A is weighted by the probability S_t that it falls due and discounted at the evaluation rate r. The probabilities should be the same ones that drive the modelled health benefit, so that a patient who stops responding stops generating both QALYs and payments."; HEO defines Annuity Payment as "Annuity payment is an agreement to pay for a one-off therapy in yearly instalments, not upfront, with later ones sometimes stopping if the therapy fails.".

column2: Wald large-sample confidence interval for an estimate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Asymptotic Normality. The module describes Wald large-sample confidence interval for an estimate as "Subtracts and adds a multiple of the estimated standard error to the estimate. With z equal to 1.96, the 97.5th percentile of the standard normal distribution, the interval has approximately 95% coverage in large samples. The interval is symmetric by construction."; HEO defines Asymptotic Normality as "Asymptotic normality means an estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples, the basis of Wald confidence intervals.".

column2: Delta-method confidence interval for an ICER
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Asymptotic Normality. The module describes Delta-method confidence interval for an ICER as "Linearises the ratio of the two estimated differences around their point estimates to obtain a large-sample standard error for the ICER, then forms a symmetric Wald interval around the ratio. The function abs returns the absolute value, so the standard error stays positive when the ICER is negative. The method is also called the Taylor series method."; HEO defines Asymptotic Normality as "Asymptotic normality means an estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples, the basis of Wald confidence intervals.".

column2: Fieller confidence limits for an ICER
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Asymptotic Normality. The module describes Fieller confidence limits for an ICER as "Applies the normal approximation to the two differences rather than to their ratio. The limits are the values of R at which the squared difference between Delta_C and R times Delta_E equals z squared times its variance; rearranged, they are the roots of a quadratic in R with coefficients a, b and c. The roots bound the interval when a is positive."; HEO defines Asymptotic Normality as "Asymptotic normality means an estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples, the basis of Wald confidence intervals.".

column2: Normal-approximation interval and probability for incremental net benefit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Asymptotic Normality. The module describes Normal-approximation interval and probability for incremental net benefit as "Incremental net benefit at a threshold lambda is linear in the two differences, so its variance follows directly and no ratio is involved. A Wald interval follows, and z_INB, the estimate divided by its standard error, gives the normal-approximation probability that net benefit is positive as the standard normal cumulative distribution function evaluated at z_INB. That probability is one point on the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve. The calculator returns z_INB; Excel NORM.S.DIST and R pnorm convert it to the probability."; HEO defines Asymptotic Normality as "Asymptotic normality means an estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples, the basis of Wald confidence intervals.".

column2: Atkinson index from equally distributed equivalent health
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Atkinson Index. The module describes Atkinson index from equally distributed equivalent health as "Compares the equally distributed equivalent health at a chosen epsilon, from HE-FM-ATK-002 or HE-FM-ATK-003, with mean health. The index is one minus their ratio, so it lies between 0, complete equality, and 1. Atkinson's own reading is that a value of 0.3 means an equal distribution would need only 70% of present national income to give the same social welfare; in health, an index of 0.04 means an equal distribution at 96% of current mean health would be judged as good."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health for epsilon other than 1
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Atkinson Index. The module describes Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health for epsilon other than 1 as "Gives the equally distributed equivalent health as the power mean of the n health values with exponent one minus epsilon. At epsilon of 0 it equals the arithmetic mean, so only total health counts; at epsilon of 2 it is the harmonic mean; and as epsilon rises it moves towards the health of the worst-off person, the maximin rule. Each h_i is the health of one person, or of one of n groups of equal size."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health at epsilon of 1
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Atkinson Index. The module describes Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health at epsilon of 1 as "Gives the equally distributed equivalent health when epsilon equals 1, where the general formula HE-FM-ATK-002 is undefined. The EDE is then the geometric mean of the n health values, the nth root of their product, written here as the exponential of the mean natural logarithm. The function log is the natural logarithm. It corresponds to Atkinson's logarithmic welfare function and is the limit of the general formula as epsilon tends to 1."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: Relative weight on a health gain implied by Atkinson inequality aversion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Atkinson Index. The module describes Relative weight on a health gain implied by Atkinson inequality aversion as "Gives the weight on a small health gain to a less healthy person or group relative to the same gain to a healthier one, implied by an Atkinson epsilon. It follows from the EDE formula, in which the weight on a small gain to person i is proportional to h_i raised to the power minus epsilon. It turns epsilon into a statement a decision committee can read: how many times a QALY to the less healthy group counts."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: AUC estimated by counting case and non-case pairs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Area Under Curve. The module describes AUC estimated by counting case and non-case pairs as "Compares every person with the outcome with every person without it. A pair in which the person with the outcome has the higher score counts 1, a tied pair counts one half, and the total is divided by the number of such pairs. This is the article's double sum of psi(s_i, s_j) over all n_1 times n_0 pairs, written with pair counts, and it is the quantity estimated by the Wilcoxon rank statistic."; HEO defines Area Under Curve as "Area under the curve (AUC), or C-statistic, is the probability a test or risk model scores a random case above a random non-case (0.5 chance, 1 perfect).".

column2: AUC as the trapezoidal area under the empirical ROC curve
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Area Under Curve. The module describes AUC as the trapezoidal area under the empirical ROC curve as "Adds the areas of the trapezoids beneath the empirical ROC curve, which plots sensitivity (the true positive rate) against the false positive rate (one minus specificity) at every threshold. Each segment between consecutive points contributes its width on the false positive axis multiplied by the mean of its two heights. Vertical segments add nothing, and the diagonal segment drawn through tied scores supplies the half credit of the pair count, so the result equals HE-FM-AUC-001."; HEO defines Area Under Curve as "Area under the curve (AUC), or C-statistic, is the probability a test or risk model scores a random case above a random non-case (0.5 chance, 1 perfect).".

column2: Gini index from the discrimination AUC
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Area Under Curve. The module describes Gini index from the discrimination AUC as "Converts the AUC to the Gini index, defined as twice the area between the ROC curve and the diagonal, using the relation that the Gini index plus 1 equals twice the AUC. The index is 0 for no discrimination and 1 for perfect discrimination. It is a different quantity from the Gini coefficient of income or health inequality."; HEO defines Area Under Curve as "Area under the curve (AUC), or C-statistic, is the probability a test or risk model scores a random case above a random non-case (0.5 chance, 1 perfect).".

column2: Common-effect inverse-variance pooled estimate and standard error
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes Common-effect inverse-variance pooled estimate and standard error as "Pools the study estimates y_i with weights equal to the inverse of their variances v_i, under the assumption that every study estimates the same underlying effect. The weight of study i is 1/v_i, and the standard error of the pooled estimate is the square root of one over the summed weights. For a ratio measure the result is on the log scale and is exponentiated for presentation."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: Cochran's Q statistic for an aggregate data meta-analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes Cochran's Q statistic for an aggregate data meta-analysis as "Sums each study's squared deviation from the common-effect estimate, weighted by the inverse of its variance. Under the common-effect model Q follows approximately a chi-squared distribution with k-1 degrees of freedom, so values well above k-1 suggest heterogeneity. Q is the input to I-squared and to the DerSimonian and Laird estimate of tau2."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: I-squared from Cochran's Q in an aggregate data meta-analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes I-squared from Cochran's Q in an aggregate data meta-analysis as "Rescales Q to the percentage of total variation across studies attributed to heterogeneity rather than chance. Negative values, which arise when Q is below its degrees of freedom, are set to zero so that the result lies between 0% and 100%."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: DerSimonian and Laird between-study variance estimate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes DerSimonian and Laird between-study variance estimate as "The moment-based estimate of the between-study variance tau2, the simplest of the available estimators. The excess of Q over its degrees of freedom is divided by a scaling term built from the common-effect weights 1/v_i, and the result is truncated at zero."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: Random-effects inverse-variance pooled mean and standard error
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes Random-effects inverse-variance pooled mean and standard error as "Pools the study estimates with weights 1/(v_i + tau2), so that the between-study variance is added to each study's own variance. The result estimates the mean of a distribution of true effects rather than one common effect. Larger tau2 makes the weights more equal and the standard error larger."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: Random-effects prediction interval for the effect in a new setting
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes Random-effects prediction interval for the effect in a new setting as "Gives an approximate 95% range for the true effect in a new study or setting, combining the between-study variance with the squared standard error of the random-effects mean and using the 97.5th percentile of a t distribution with k-1 degrees of freedom. The square root term is also the standard deviation of the predictive distribution that NICE DSU TSD 3 suggests may be more relevant to decision making than the distribution of the mean."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: AR(1) correlation between measurements s visit steps apart
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Autoregressive Correlation. The module describes AR(1) correlation between measurements s visit steps apart as "Gives the correlation between two outcomes of the same patient, for example utilities or costs, measured s equally spaced visits apart, when the correlation between adjacent visits is rho. With rho between 0 and 1 the correlation is highest for adjacent visits and falls geometrically towards zero as the gap grows. For four visits the correlation matrix has 1 on the diagonal, rho beside it, then rho^2 and rho^3 in the corners."; HEO defines Autoregressive Correlation as "Autoregressive correlation is a structure for repeated measures in which correlation falls by a constant factor with each time step between measurements.".

column2: Continuous-time AR(1) correlation for unequally spaced visits
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Autoregressive Correlation. The module describes Continuous-time AR(1) correlation for unequally spaced visits as "Uses elapsed time instead of visit steps, so a 3-month gap and a 6-month gap receive different correlations. phi is the correlation between two measurements one time unit apart and d is the elapsed time between them in that unit. With equally spaced visits it reduces to HE-FM-AR1-001, with rho equal to phi raised to the visit interval."; HEO defines Autoregressive Correlation as "Autoregressive correlation is a structure for repeated measures in which correlation falls by a constant factor with each time step between measurements.".

column2: Variance of a three-visit QALY total under AR(1) correlation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Autoregressive Correlation. The module describes Variance of a three-visit QALY total under AR(1) correlation as "Gives the variance of a patient's 12-month QALY total, calculated by the trapezium rule from utilities at baseline, 6 and 12 months, when the utilities share a common variance sigma2 and follow AR(1) correlation with adjacent-visit correlation rho. It is the general double sum, sigma2 times the sum over all pairs of visits of w_j * w_k * r_jk, written out for three visits: the squared weights, plus twice the cross-products for the two adjacent pairs at rho and for the outer pair at rho^2."; HEO defines Autoregressive Correlation as "Autoregressive correlation is a structure for repeated measures in which correlation falls by a constant factor with each time step between measurements.".

column2: Variance of a change between two visits under AR(1) correlation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Autoregressive Correlation. The module describes Variance of a change between two visits under AR(1) correlation as "Gives the variance of the difference between a patient's outcomes at two visits s steps apart, such as the change in utility from baseline to 12 months, when both visits share a common variance sigma2 and the correlation follows AR(1). Because the correlation falls with distance, the variance of a change grows with the gap between the visits, which is where the choice of correlation structure matters most."; HEO defines Autoregressive Correlation as "Autoregressive correlation is a structure for repeated measures in which correlation falls by a constant factor with each time step between measurements.".

column2: Average length of stay from bed-days and discharges
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Average length of stay from bed-days and discharges as "Divides the bed-days of the stays that ended in a period by the number of those discharges. BD is the sum of the individual stays L_i, each the discharge date minus the admission date, so the result equals the patient-level mean in the article. Deaths in hospital count as discharges in the OECD definition."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Annual discharges from beds, occupancy and average length of stay
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Annual discharges from beds, occupancy and average length of stay as "States the steady-state accounting identity linking capacity to stay length: a year's occupied bed-days, 365 times beds times occupancy, divided by the average stay gives the discharges those beds can support. Halving L_bar doubles potential throughput. Dividing D by B gives the bed turnover rate."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: NHS Payment Scheme length of stay trim point and excess bed days
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes NHS Payment Scheme length of stay trim point and excess bed days as "Sets the length of stay trim point for a spell healthcare resource group (HRG) at the larger of 5 days and the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the interquartile range of adjusted length of stay, rounded to the nearest whole number. Days of a spell beyond the trim point are excess bed days, paid at a separate daily long-stay rate. The calculator omits the rounding step."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Case-mix adjusted length of stay ratio by indirect standardisation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Case-mix adjusted length of stay ratio by indirect standardisation as "Computes the bed-days a hospital would use if each of its case-mix groups stayed as long as a reference average, and divides its observed bed-days by that figure. A ratio above 1 means longer stays than expected for its case mix. The relative stay index in Australia's Report on Government Services is of this form."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Top-down cost per admission from average length of stay
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Top-down cost per admission from average length of stay as "Multiplies the average length of stay by a cost per bed day to give a cost per admission. This top-down shortcut spreads staffing, buildings and overheads evenly across every day of a stay."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Cost change from a shorter average length of stay
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Cost change from a shorter average length of stay as "Values the bed-days released when the average stay of a patient group falls, at a stated cost per bed day. The answer depends on which cost is used: an average cost gives the apparent saving, a marginal cost the cash saving."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Poisson probability of n arrivals in a window
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process. The module describes Poisson probability of n arrivals in a window as "Gives the probability that exactly n arrivals occur in a window of length t when arrivals follow a homogeneous Poisson process with rate lambda. The expected number of arrivals is lambda times t. The function exp is the exponential function and factorial(n) is n!, the product of the whole numbers from 1 to n, with factorial(0) equal to 1."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Expected arrivals over a window with two arrival-rate periods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process. The module describes Expected arrivals over a window with two arrival-rate periods as "Gives the expected number of arrivals in a non-homogeneous Poisson process whose rate is constant within each of two periods, such as day and night. In general the expected count is the area under the rate curve, the integral of lambda(u) from a to b; for a rate that is constant within periods the integral becomes the sum of rate times length over the periods. The count over the window is then Poisson with mean m, so the Poisson probability formula on this page applies with m in place of lambda times t."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Inter-arrival gap sampled by inverse transform
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process.
