The module describes Inter-arrival gap sampled by inverse transform as "Samples the gap to the next arrival in a homogeneous Poisson process by inverting the exponential distribution function. The function log is the natural logarithm. In a discrete event simulation the sampled gap is added to the current arrival time, S_n equal to S_(n-1) plus X, and the next arrival is placed on the event queue."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Thinning acceptance probability for time-varying arrivals
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process. The module describes Thinning acceptance probability for time-varying arrivals as "Gives the probability with which a candidate arrival at time t is kept when arrivals with rate lambda(t) are generated by thinning. Candidates are first generated from a homogeneous Poisson process at a constant rate lambda_star that is at least lambda(t) throughout the period, and the kept points form a non-homogeneous Poisson process with rate lambda(t). The method avoids integrating the rate function."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Expected wait before service in a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process. The module describes Expected wait before service in a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals as "Gives the expected time a patient waits before service starts in a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals at rate lambda and exponential service at rate mu, in steady state with lambda below mu. The utilisation rho is computed first and then used in the wait. As rho approaches 1 the expected wait grows without limit, so a small rise in arrivals near full utilisation produces a large rise in waiting."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Variance of the antithetic variates estimator with within-pair correlation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Antithetic Variates. The module describes Variance of the antithetic variates estimator with within-pair correlation as "Gives the variance of the antithetic estimate based on n model evaluations arranged as n/2 independent pairs. Ordinary sampling with n independent evaluations has variance sigma2/n, so the factor 1 + rho measures the gain: a negative within-pair correlation lowers the variance and a positive one raises it. Because rho cannot be below -1 or above +1, the factor runs from 0 to 2: in the best case one pair gives the exact answer, and in the worst case the variance doubles."; HEO defines Antithetic Variates as "Antithetic variates are a variance reduction method that pairs each random draw with its mirror image so errors tend to cancel in Monte Carlo simulation.".

column2: Standard error of the antithetic estimate from pair means
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Antithetic Variates. The module describes Standard error of the antithetic estimate from pair means as "Gives the Monte Carlo standard error of the antithetic estimate by treating each pair as one observation. Each pair mean is the average of the two outputs in a pair, s_anti is the sample standard deviation of the m pair means and m equals n/2. The same rule applies to mean costs and QALYs, the probability that a strategy is cost-effective and each point on the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve estimated from paired PSA iterations."; HEO defines Antithetic Variates as "Antithetic variates are a variance reduction method that pairs each random draw with its mirror image so errors tend to cancel in Monte Carlo simulation.".

column2: Antithetic variance reduction factor and equivalent independent sample size
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Antithetic Variates. The module describes Antithetic variance reduction factor and equivalent independent sample size as "Converts the within-pair correlation into the variance reduction factor, the variance of ordinary sampling divided by that of antithetic sampling at the same number of evaluations, and into the number of independent evaluations that would match the precision of n antithetic evaluations. A factor above 1 means pairing helps and a factor below 1 means it harms."; HEO defines Antithetic Variates as "Antithetic variates are a variance reduction method that pairs each random draw with its mirror image so errors tend to cancel in Monte Carlo simulation.".

column2: Total-form average cost-effectiveness ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio. The module describes Total-form average cost-effectiveness ratio as "Divides an option's expected total cost by its expected total health effect. The denominator counts all the health the patient group experiences while receiving the option, including health that would have occurred anyway, so the result is a cost per QALY lived rather than a cost per QALY gained."; HEO defines Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio as "The average cost-effectiveness ratio (ACER) is an option's cost per unit of health effect, in total or against doing nothing, without comparing options.".

column2: Average cost-effectiveness ratio against doing nothing
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio. The module describes Average cost-effectiveness ratio against doing nothing as "Divides the cost of option i minus the cost of doing nothing by its health effect minus the health effect of doing nothing. It is the pairwise ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001) with doing nothing as the comparator, so it is informative when doing nothing is the real alternative and misleading when another option is available. When C_0 and E_0 are both zero it equals the total-form ratio HE-FM-ACER-001."; HEO defines Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio as "The average cost-effectiveness ratio (ACER) is an option's cost per unit of health effect, in total or against doing nothing, without comparing options.".

column2: Overall attack rate from new cases and the population at risk
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Overall attack rate from new cases and the population at risk as "Divides the number of new cases meeting the case definition during a stated period by the number of people at risk at the start of that period. The result is an incidence proportion, usually reported as a percentage. A food-specific attack rate uses the same formula with the people who ate a given food as the denominator."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Secondary attack rate among household contacts of primary cases
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Secondary attack rate among household contacts of primary cases as "Divides the cases that arise among contacts after the primary cases, for example within one incubation period, by the number of contacts. The number of contacts is often taken as the total population of the households of the primary cases minus the primary cases themselves. The measure separates spread within households, barracks or other closed settings from spread in the wider community."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Attack rate ratio between exposed and unexposed groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Attack rate ratio between exposed and unexposed groups as "Divides the attack rate in the exposed group, such as people who ate a suspected food, by the attack rate in the unexposed group. The result is a risk ratio that measures the association between the exposure and illness: a ratio of 1 indicates the same risk in both groups, and a ratio above 1 a higher risk among the exposed."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Vaccine efficacy or effectiveness from attack rates in vaccinated and unvaccinated people
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Vaccine efficacy or effectiveness from attack rates in vaccinated and unvaccinated people as "Measures the proportionate reduction in risk among vaccinated people as 1 minus the ratio of the attack rate among the vaccinated to the attack rate among the unvaccinated. The same quantity is the risk difference divided by the attack rate among the unvaccinated. It is called efficacy when measured in a trial under ideal conditions and effectiveness when measured under field conditions."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Basic reproduction number from the final attack rate of a completed epidemic
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Basic reproduction number from the final attack rate of a completed epidemic as "In the simple susceptible, infectious and recovered model, the final attack rate z of an epidemic satisfies the final size relation z = s_0(1 minus exp(minus R_0 z)), where s_0 is 1 when almost everyone is susceptible at the start. Taking logarithms of 1 minus z/s_0 = exp(minus R_0 z) rearranges the relation to give R_0 from an observed final attack rate. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Actuarial value as the plan-paid share of total allowed cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Value. The module describes Actuarial value as the plan-paid share of total allowed cost as "Divides the plan's total payment for covered care by the total allowed cost of that care, both summed over a standard population for one benefit year. The population is held as G spending groups of n_g people with the same allowed cost per person, the layout of the article's worked example and of a continuance table. With one person in every group the formula is the article's ratio of summed plan payments to summed allowed costs over N people, and it equals 1 minus the members' share of total allowed cost."; HEO defines Actuarial Value as "Actuarial value (AV) is the share of the total allowed cost of covered care that a health plan is expected to pay for a standard population.".

column2: Member cost sharing under a deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Value. The module describes Member cost sharing under a deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum as "Gives the cost sharing paid by a member with annual allowed cost X under a simple plan with one deductible, one coinsurance rate and an annual out-of-pocket maximum. The member pays all allowed cost up to the deductible and the coinsurance share of the cost above it, but no more than the out-of-pocket maximum in total, and the plan pays the remainder P. The functions min and max return the smaller and the larger of their arguments."; HEO defines Actuarial Value as "Actuarial value (AV) is the share of the total allowed cost of covered care that a health plan is expected to pay for a standard population.".

column2: Allowed cost at which the out-of-pocket maximum is reached
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Value. The module describes Allowed cost at which the out-of-pocket maximum is reached as "Gives the annual allowed cost at which the deductible plus coinsurance on the excess equals the out-of-pocket maximum, the point at which the member cost sharing in HE-FM-AV-002 stops rising. Above it every extra unit of allowed cost is paid in full by the plan."; HEO defines Actuarial Value as "Actuarial value (AV) is the share of the total allowed cost of covered care that a health plan is expected to pay for a standard population.".

column2: Aggregate stop-loss carrier payment and employer retention for one contract year
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Stop-Loss. The module describes Aggregate stop-loss carrier payment and employer retention for one contract year as "Gives the aggregate stop-loss carrier's payment for a contract year as the excess of the employer's net claims over the aggregate attachment point, capped at the policy's maximum aggregate payment, and the employer's retained claims as the remainder. Net claims S are the sum over covered members of each member's eligible claims net of specific stop-loss recoveries, so the calculator takes the total directly. The functions min and max return the smaller and the larger of their arguments. With no maximum the retained claims equal the smaller of S and A, so they never exceed the attachment point."; HEO defines Aggregate Stop-Loss as "Aggregate stop-loss is insurance that reimburses a self-funded employer for total health claims above an agreed attachment point in a plan year.".

column2: Aggregate attachment point set as a multiple of expected claims
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Stop-Loss. The module describes Aggregate attachment point set as a multiple of expected claims as "Sets the aggregate attachment point by applying an attachment factor to the group's expected annual claims, for example 1.25 for an attachment point at 125% of expected claims. Expected claims are defined on the same net basis as the claims that accumulate towards the attachment point. A lower factor transfers more risk to the carrier and costs more."; HEO defines Aggregate Stop-Loss as "Aggregate stop-loss is insurance that reimburses a self-funded employer for total health claims above an agreed attachment point in a plan year.".

column2: Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of a group's total net claims

column2: Standardised distance from expected claims to the aggregate attachment point
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Stop-Loss. column2: Expected aggregate stop-loss payment under a normal approximation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Stop-Loss. column2: Administrative cost ratio as administrative cost over a chosen denominator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Cost Ratio. The module describes Administrative cost ratio as administrative cost over a chosen denominator as "Divides administrative cost over a period by a denominator for the same period: premium revenue for an insurer (written ACR_P in the article), the payer's total spending on claims, quality improvement and administration (ACR_S), or current health expenditure for a country. The result is a proportion, usually reported as a percentage, and two ratios are comparable only when both parts are defined in the same way."; HEO defines Administrative Cost Ratio as "Administrative cost ratio is the share of an insurer's premium income, or a health system's spending, used for administration rather than claims or care.".

column2: Medical loss ratio as the regulatory counterpart of the administrative cost ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Cost Ratio. The module describes Medical loss ratio as the regulatory counterpart of the administrative cost ratio as "Divides incurred claims for clinical services plus expenditure on activities that improve health care quality by earned premium less federal and state taxes and licensing and regulatory fees, the medical loss ratio defined for United States health insurance issuers in 45 CFR 158.221. The regulation also adjusts the denominator for risk adjustment, risk corridors and reinsurance, applies any credibility adjustment and rounds the result to three decimal places; this simplified form leaves out the adjustments, as the article's example does."; HEO defines Administrative Cost Ratio as "Administrative cost ratio is the share of an insurer's premium income, or a health system's spending, used for administration rather than claims or care.".

column2: Complement of the medical loss ratio as administration plus margin
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Cost Ratio. The module describes Complement of the medical loss ratio as administration plus margin as "Rewrites one minus the medical loss ratio, often called the administrative share, using the identity that premium after taxes and fees equals claims, quality improvement, other non-claims costs and the underwriting margin. MLR_comp stands for one minus MLR. The complement mixes administration with profit, so a saving on administration that is kept as margin leaves the medical loss ratio unchanged."; HEO defines Administrative Cost Ratio as "Administrative cost ratio is the share of an insurer's premium income, or a health system's spending, used for administration rather than claims or care.".

column2: Medical loss ratio rebate from the shortfall against the standard
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Cost Ratio. The module describes Medical loss ratio rebate from the shortfall against the standard as "Gives the rebate an issuer owes for a reporting year under 45 CFR 158.240: premium after taxes and licensing and regulatory fees multiplied by the gap between the required medical loss ratio and the issuer's ratio. The function max returns the larger of its arguments, so the rebate is zero when the issuer meets or exceeds the standard. Under 45 CFR 158.210 the standard is 0.85 in the large group market and 0.80 in the small group and individual markets, unless a state sets a higher one or the individual market standard has been adjusted for a state."; HEO defines Administrative Cost Ratio as "Administrative cost ratio is the share of an insurer's premium income, or a health system's spending, used for administration rather than claims or care.".

column2: Expected claims cost per covered person from utilisation and unit cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Analysis. The module describes Expected claims cost per covered person from utilisation and unit cost as "Builds the expected claims cost per covered person per year service by service, as the sum over benefit categories of the utilisation rate times the unit cost, and multiplies it by the number of covered persons to give total expected claims for the year. The per-person cost is the net or risk premium for the group."; HEO defines Actuarial Analysis as "Actuarial analysis uses probability and statistics to estimate expected health insurance claims for pricing premiums or contributions and holding reserves.".

column2: Gross health insurance premium from net premium with fixed and proportional loadings
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Analysis. The module describes Gross health insurance premium from net premium with fixed and proportional loadings as "Converts the net premium, the expected claims cost per covered person, into the gross annual premium by adding a fixed loading per person and a proportional loading set as a share of the gross premium. Because the proportional loading is a share of the result, the net premium plus the fixed loading is divided by one minus that share."; HEO defines Actuarial Analysis as "Actuarial analysis uses probability and statistics to estimate expected health insurance claims for pricing premiums or contributions and holding reserves.".

column2: Standard deviation of the average claims cost in an insured pool
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Analysis. The module describes Standard deviation of the average claims cost in an insured pool as "Gives the standard deviation of the average annual claims cost per person across a pool of N people whose costs are independent with a common standard deviation. The spread of the average falls with the square root of the pool size, which is why large rating groups give reliable averages."; HEO defines Actuarial Analysis as "Actuarial analysis uses probability and statistics to estimate expected health insurance claims for pricing premiums or contributions and holding reserves.".

column2: Incurred claims and unpaid claims from a completion factor
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Analysis. The module describes Incurred claims and unpaid claims from a completion factor as "Estimates the total claims incurred for a month of service by dividing the amount paid so far by the completion factor, the cumulative share of a month's eventual claims that past experience shows to be paid by the same lag. The difference between estimated incurred and paid claims is the unpaid claims liability for that month, covering both unreported claims and claims reported but not yet paid."; HEO defines Actuarial Analysis as "Actuarial analysis uses probability and statistics to estimate expected health insurance claims for pricing premiums or contributions and holding reserves.".

column2: ATE as the share-weighted sum of subgroup effects
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Treatment Effect. The module describes ATE as the share-weighted sum of subgroup effects as "Computes the population average treatment effect from the conditional average effects of K non-overlapping subgroups, each weighted by its share of the population of interest. It is the law of total expectation applied to the mean of Y(1) minus Y(0), and the same weights apply to effects on cost and on QALYs."; HEO defines Average Treatment Effect as "The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean change in costs or health outcomes if a whole population received a treatment rather than its comparator.".

column2: ATT as the treated-mix weighted sum of subgroup effects
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Treatment Effect. The module describes ATT as the treated-mix weighted sum of subgroup effects as "Computes the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) from the same subgroup effects as HE-FM-ATE-001, reweighted to the subgroup mix of the patients who were actually treated. The product P_x times e_x is the share of the whole population that is treated and in subgroup x, and dividing by the sum of these products gives each subgroup's share of the treated group. When treatment is more likely where the effect is larger, the ATT exceeds the ATE."; HEO defines Average Treatment Effect as "The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean change in costs or health outcomes if a whole population received a treatment rather than its comparator.".

column2: Inverse probability weighted ATE estimator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Treatment Effect. The module describes Inverse probability weighted ATE estimator as "Estimates the ATE from patient-level observational data. Each treated patient is weighted by one over the propensity score and each untreated patient by one over one minus the propensity score, so that each weighted arm resembles the whole sample, and the estimate is the difference between the two weighted means. Applied with the same weights to costs and to QALYs, it gives the incremental cost and QALYs for the ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001) and the incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002)."; HEO defines Average Treatment Effect as "The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean change in costs or health outcomes if a whole population received a treatment rather than its comparator.".

column2: Static value of targeting treatment by subgroup
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Treatment Effect. The module describes Static value of targeting treatment by subgroup as "Measures the expected net monetary benefit per member of the population gained by treating only the subgroups with a positive incremental net monetary benefit, rather than making one decision for everyone on the population average. Each INMB_x comes from HE-FM-NMB-002 with the subgroup's effects on QALYs and cost, and the population value is their share-weighted sum, as in HE-FM-ATE-001. Espinoza and colleagues call this gain the static value of heterogeneity, separate from the value of further research on subgroups."; HEO defines Average Treatment Effect as "The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean change in costs or health outcomes if a whole population received a treatment rather than its comparator.".

column2: Survival and life-years in one interval of a piecewise bathtub hazard
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes Survival and life-years in one interval of a piecewise bathtub hazard as "For an interval of length L_j with constant hazard h_j, survival at the end of the interval is survival at its start multiplied by exp(-h_j L_j), and the expected life-years lived in the interval per person entering the cohort are the area under the survival curve across the interval. Chaining intervals with a high early hazard, a low middle hazard and higher late hazards reproduces a bathtub shape exactly, without fitting a single distribution. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: Mean survival under a bathtub hazard with an open final interval
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes Mean survival under a bathtub hazard with an open final interval as "Adds the life-years from the closed intervals to the life-years in the open final interval, where a constant hazard h_K applies for ever. The open interval contributes survival at the last cut point divided by h_K, the area under an exponential tail. The result is the undiscounted mean survival per person entering the cohort."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: Constant hazard fitted to early follow-up of a bathtub-hazard cohort
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes Constant hazard fitted to early follow-up of a bathtub-hazard cohort as "Fits an exponential model to follow-up that covers only the early part of a bathtub hazard. The fitted hazard is the deaths divided by the person-years at risk, the rate formula of the Adverse Event Rate page (HE-FM-AER-002), and the exponential model then implies survival exp(-lambda_hat t) and mean survival 1 divided by lambda_hat. Comparing these with the bathtub values shows how a constant hazard misplaces deaths and overstates the tail."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: Bathtub hazard as the sum of two Weibull hazards
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes Bathtub hazard as the sum of two Weibull hazards as "The poly-Weibull model of Demiris, Lunn and Sharples adds a falling Weibull hazard, with shape gamma_1 below 1, to a rising one, with shape gamma_2 above 1, so the total hazard falls at first and rises later. Survival is the exponential of minus the summed Weibull cumulative hazards, which is the product of the two component survival curves. The symbol ^ denotes a power."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: All-cause bathtub hazard as background plus excess hazard
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes All-cause bathtub hazard as background plus excess hazard as "Splits the all-cause hazard into a background hazard from population mortality and an excess hazard attributed to the disease or procedure. When the excess hazard declines after the early period, the background hazard, which rises with age, supplies the late arm of the bathtub. On the survival scale the same relation makes all-cause survival equal to background survival multiplied by relative survival. The per-cycle probability follows from h_all with the conversion HE-FM-TP-001."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: Nash bargaining price between a reservation price and a payer's maximum price
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bargaining Theory. The module describes Nash bargaining price between a reservation price and a payer's maximum price as "Gives the negotiated price when both parties' payoffs are in money and move one for one with the price: the manufacturer gains the price minus its reservation price c, and the payer gains its maximum price p_bar minus the price paid. Maximising the weighted Nash product of the two gains gives a weighted average of the two limits, so the manufacturer receives the share beta of the surplus p_bar minus c and the payer the share 1 minus beta. Berdud, Ferraro and Towse state the same weighted average in cost-effectiveness ratio units, from the developer's reserve ratio to the payer's maximum."; HEO defines Bargaining Theory as "Bargaining theory explains how negotiating parties divide the gains from reaching agreement, as when a payer and a manufacturer agree a drug price.".

column2: Payer's maximum price per patient from a cost-effectiveness threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bargaining Theory. The module describes Payer's maximum price per patient from a cost-effectiveness threshold as "Gives the highest price per patient at which a payer that funds technologies with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio at or below the threshold k still funds the product. At this price the ratio equals k and the incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002) is zero. In bargaining terms it is the payer's walk-away price, the top of the range over which the price is negotiated."; HEO defines Bargaining Theory as "Bargaining theory explains how negotiating parties divide the gains from reaching agreement, as when a payer and a manufacturer agree a drug price.".

column2: Rubinstein first proposer's share of the surplus under alternating offers
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bargaining Theory. The module describes Rubinstein first proposer's share of the surplus under alternating offers as "Gives the share of a surplus of size one obtained by the party that makes the first offer in the unique perfect equilibrium of Rubinstein's alternating-offers model, in which each party discounts agreement by a fixed factor per round of delay. The more patient a party, the larger its share, and the responder receives 1 minus s_1. Multiplied by the surplus p_bar minus c it gives the first proposer's gain, so s_1 can serve as the weight beta in HE-FM-BARG-001 for the party that opens."; HEO defines Bargaining Theory as "Bargaining theory explains how negotiating parties divide the gains from reaching agreement, as when a payer and a manufacturer agree a drug price.".

column2: Negotiated price when the payer holds a binding outside option
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bargaining Theory. The module describes Negotiated price when the payer holds a binding outside option as "Applies the outside option principle to the payer. An outside option, the net monetary benefit per patient v_P available by walking away for good, for example to a competing therapy, changes the price only if it is worth more than the payer's gain from the bargain without it, p_bar minus p_star. In that case the price falls until the payer's gain just equals the outside option; otherwise the threat is empty and the Nash price stands. The function min returns the smaller of its arguments."; HEO defines Bargaining Theory as "Bargaining theory explains how negotiating parties divide the gains from reaching agreement, as when a payer and a manufacturer agree a drug price.".

column2: Partially pooled basket response under a normal approximation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket Trial. The module describes Partially pooled basket response under a normal approximation as "Shrinks the observed response proportion of basket j towards a common mean mu. The weight w_j on the basket's own data is the between-basket variance tau2 divided by the sum of tau2 and the sampling variance s2_j of a proportion near the common mean in a basket of n_j patients. Because s2_j uses the common mean rather than the basket's own proportion, the weight depends only on basket size, so small baskets receive low weight and move furthest towards the mean. This is the simplified approximation in the article; a full hierarchical model estimates mu and tau2 jointly on the log-odds scale."; HEO defines Basket Trial as "A basket trial tests one targeted treatment in several diseases, usually tumour types, that share the same biomarker, with each disease forming a basket.".

column2: Expected response for a tumour-type mix from basket estimates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket Trial. The module describes Expected response for a tumour-type mix from basket estimates as "Weights each basket's response estimate by the share of that tumour type in the population expected to be treated, rather than by its share of trial enrolment. With enrolment shares and the observed proportions the result equals the pooled trial response, which reflects whoever was easiest to recruit. The same weighting applies to separate or partially pooled basket estimates."; HEO defines Basket Trial as "A basket trial tests one targeted treatment in several diseases, usually tumour types, that share the same biomarker, with each disease forming a basket.".

column2: Basket response probability from log-odds in a hierarchical model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket Trial. The module describes Basket response probability from log-odds in a hierarchical model as "Converts the log-odds of response theta_j back to a response probability. The hierarchical model for a basket trial links the baskets on this scale, with each theta_j drawn from a normal distribution with mean mu and variance tau2, so its estimates and priors are stated as log-odds. The function exp is the exponential function; the reverse step is theta_j equal to the natural log of p_j divided by one minus p_j."; HEO defines Basket Trial as "A basket trial tests one targeted treatment in several diseases, usually tumour types, that share the same biomarker, with each disease forming a basket.".

column2: Relative unit labour cost of health care from output per hour
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Baumol Effect. The module describes Relative unit labour cost of health care from output per hour as "Gives the labour cost of one unit of health care relative to one unit of other output. Labour cost per unit is the hourly wage divided by output per hour, w/a_h in health care and w/a_o elsewhere, and with the same wage w in both sectors the ratio of the two reduces to the ratio of output per hour. Health care is therefore relatively dearer whenever output per hour is lower there, whatever the level of pay."; HEO defines Baumol Effect as "The Baumol effect is the rising relative cost of labour-intensive services such as health care as their pay tracks faster productivity growth elsewhere.".

column2: Growth of the relative unit cost of health care over a horizon
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Baumol Effect. The module describes Growth of the relative unit cost of health care over a horizon as "Projects the relative unit labour cost of health care T years ahead when output per hour grows at a constant annual rate g_h in health care and g_o elsewhere. Each year the relative cost is multiplied by (1 + g_o)/(1 + g_h), so health care becomes relatively dearer whenever g_o exceeds g_h. The wage does not appear, so the result is the same whether pay rises with productivity in the progressive sector or not."; HEO defines Baumol Effect as "The Baumol effect is the rising relative cost of labour-intensive services such as health care as their pay tracks faster productivity growth elsewhere.".

column2: Health care share of working hours with the output mix held fixed
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Baumol Effect. The module describes Health care share of working hours with the output mix held fixed as "Gives the hours needed in health care when the ratio of health output to other output is held constant, for example because a publicly financed service keeps pace with the rest of the economy. The ratio of health hours to other hours grows by the same annual factor as the relative cost, and the share of total hours follows from that ratio. With equal wages and only labour costs, the share of hours is also health care's share of total spending."; HEO defines Baumol Effect as "The Baumol effect is the rising relative cost of labour-intensive services such as health care as their pay tracks faster productivity growth elsewhere.".

column2: Baumol component of real health spending growth in OBR projections
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Baumol Effect. The module describes Baumol component of real health spending growth in OBR projections as "Gives the contribution of the Baumol effect to annual real growth in health spending as a coefficient times projected economy-wide productivity growth. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) uses this top-down form, with an OECD estimate of the coefficient, within the other cost pressures that it adds to demographic and income effects."; HEO defines Baumol Effect as "The Baumol effect is the rising relative cost of labour-intensive services such as health care as their pay tracks faster productivity growth elsewhere.".

column2: Absolute and relative health gap between the extreme groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Absolute and relative health gap between the extreme groups as "Compares mean health in the most advantaged group J with mean health in the most disadvantaged group 1, as a difference in the units of the health variable and as a ratio without units. The WHO handbook calls these the difference and the ratio; Harper and colleagues call them the rate difference and the rate ratio."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Slope index of inequality for grouped health data
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Slope index of inequality for grouped health data as "Gives the slope of the line fitted by population-weighted least squares to group mean health against the midpoint rank of each group, with the population ranked from the most disadvantaged (rank 0) to the most advantaged (rank 1). The slope equals predicted health at rank 1 minus predicted health at rank 0, so the index is in the units of the health variable. From group values, cov_hr is the sum over groups of f_j times (h_j minus mu) times (r_j minus 0.5), and var_r is the sum of f_j times (r_j minus 0.5) squared, because the population-weighted mean rank is 0.5. The computational function HE-CF-HINQ-001 carries out the full procedure from group means and population shares."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Relative index of inequality as a ratio of predicted health
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Relative index of inequality as a ratio of predicted health as "Divides predicted health at rank 1 by predicted health at rank 0 from the same fitted line as the slope index. The line passes through mean health at the mean rank of 0.5, so the intercept alpha, the predicted value at rank 0, is mean health minus half the slope index, and the predicted value at rank 1 is alpha plus the slope index. A value above 1 shows higher health in the advantaged groups."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Relative index of inequality as the slope index over mean health
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Relative index of inequality as the slope index over mean health as "Divides the slope index of inequality by population-weighted mean health. The relative index values reported in the distributional cost-effectiveness tutorial by Asaria and colleagues equal their slope index divided by mean QALE, so this form appears in that literature alongside the ratio form of the WHO handbook. Both forms rise with relative inequality but take different values, so the form used is stated with the result."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Concentration index of health for grouped data
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Concentration index of health for grouped data as "Gives the concentration index from the covariance between health and fractional rank in the socioeconomic distribution. For grouped data the fractional rank of each group is the cumulative population share up to the midpoint of the group, and the mean and covariance are weighted by population share, so cov_hr is the same covariance as in the slope index. The index is positive when health is concentrated among the better-off and negative when it is concentrated among the worse-off."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Kakwani index of progressivity for a health financing source
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vertical Equity. The module describes Kakwani index of progressivity for a health financing source as "Measures how far one source of health finance departs from proportionality to ability to pay, as the concentration index of the payment minus the Gini coefficient of ability to pay. It equals twice the area between the Lorenz curve of ability to pay and the concentration curve of the payment. A positive value indicates a progressive source, a negative value a regressive one, and zero is consistent with proportionality."; HEO defines Vertical Equity as "Vertical equity is the principle that those in greater need should get appropriately more care, and those more able to pay should pay more.".

column2: Grouped-data concentration index by trapezoids for vertical equity analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vertical Equity. The module describes Grouped-data concentration index by trapezoids for vertical equity analysis as "Computes a concentration index, or a Gini coefficient when the curve is a Lorenz curve, from T groups ranked from poorest to richest. The curve joins the group points with straight lines, so the area under it is a sum of trapezoids and the index is one minus twice that area. The result is the same as the grouped-data formula of Fuller and Lury given in the World Bank guide."; HEO defines Vertical Equity as "Vertical equity is the principle that those in greater need should get appropriately more care, and those more able to pay should pay more.".

column2: Revenue-weighted Kakwani index for a health financing mix
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vertical Equity. The module describes Revenue-weighted Kakwani index for a health financing mix as "Measures the progressivity of a whole health financing system as the average of the Kakwani indices of its sources, each weighted by that source's share of total health payments. Overall progressivity therefore depends both on how progressive each source is and on how much revenue it raises."; HEO defines Vertical Equity as "Vertical equity is the principle that those in greater need should get appropriately more care, and those more able to pay should pay more.".

column2: Vertical redistributive effect of compulsory health payments
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vertical Equity. The module describes Vertical redistributive effect of compulsory health payments as "Gives the fall in the Gini coefficient of income that a compulsory health payment would produce through its progressivity alone, as the Kakwani index scaled by the average payment rate. It is the vertical term V in the decomposition of the redistributive effect into vertical redistribution, horizontal inequity and reranking. A larger payment rate magnifies the redistribution from a given degree of progressivity."; HEO defines Vertical Equity as "Vertical equity is the principle that those in greater need should get appropriately more care, and those more able to pay should pay more.".

column2: Need-expected use of health care by indirect standardisation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Need-expected use of health care by indirect standardisation as "Predicts the use of care each person would be expected to have given their need, from a linear regression of use on need variables and non-need control variables. Each person's own need values enter the prediction, while every control is set to its sample mean, so the controls protect the need coefficients from omitted-variable bias without being standardised for. This is the first step of indirect standardisation; the second is HE-FM-HEQ-002."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Need-standardised use of health care in a horizontal equity analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Need-standardised use of health care in a horizontal equity analysis as "Gives the use of care a person would have irrespective of differences in need across income, as actual use minus need-expected use plus the sample mean of actual use. Its distribution across income groups shows the inequality in use that remains after differences in need are allowed for. Because the formula is linear, it applies equally to the group means of a quintile table."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Horizontal inequity index as a difference of concentration indices
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Horizontal inequity index as a difference of concentration indices as "Measures horizontal inequity in the delivery of care as the concentration index of actual use minus the concentration index of need-expected use, with people ranked by income or another living standards measure from poorest to richest. It equals the concentration index of need-standardised use and is sometimes labelled HI_WV after Wagstaff and van Doorslaer. Zero is consistent with horizontal equity, a positive value indicates pro-rich inequity and a negative value pro-poor inequity. Each concentration index is computed as in HE-FM-HINQ-005 on the Health Inequality page."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Rule of 75 reading of a horizontal inequity index
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Rule of 75 reading of a horizontal inequity index as "Turns a concentration index into the percentage of the variable that would have to be redistributed linearly from the richer half of the population to the poorer half to bring the index to zero, by multiplying the index by 75. Applied to the horizontal inequity index, the variable is need-standardised use. A negative index gives a negative percentage, a redistribution from the poorer half to the richer half."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Decomposition of the redistributive effect of health payments with horizontal inequity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Decomposition of the redistributive effect of health payments with horizontal inequity as "Splits the redistributive effect of a compulsory health payment, the fall in the Gini coefficient from income before payment to income after it, into vertical redistribution minus horizontal inequity minus reranking, as shown by Aronson, Johnson and Lambert. H measures unequal payments among households with the same pre-payment income and R the change in the order of households. V is computed as in HE-FM-VEQ-004 on the Vertical Equity page."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Conditional posterior mean of the mean effect given the between-study variance
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis. The module describes Conditional posterior mean of the mean effect given the between-study variance as "Gives the posterior mean and standard deviation of the mean effect mu when the between-study variance tau2 is held at one value and mu has a flat prior. Each trial is weighted by 1/(s_i^2 + tau2), so the arithmetic is that of random-effects inverse-variance pooling (HE-FM-ADMA-005), read here as a conditional posterior. A full Bayesian analysis averages this result over the posterior for tau, as in the computational function attached to this formula."; HEO defines Bayesian Meta-Analysis as "Bayesian meta-analysis combines prior distributions with results from several studies to give posterior and predictive distributions for an effect.".

column2: Shrinkage factor and shrunken trial estimate in a Bayesian meta-analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis. The module describes Shrinkage factor and shrunken trial estimate in a Bayesian meta-analysis as "Gives the posterior mean of one trial's true effect theta_i given the mean effect mu and the between-study variance tau2. The trial estimate y_i is pulled towards mu by the shrinkage factor B_i, the share of the trial's total variance that comes from sampling error. Small trials, with large s_i, are pulled further, and every trial is pulled further when tau2 is small."; HEO defines Bayesian Meta-Analysis as "Bayesian meta-analysis combines prior distributions with results from several studies to give posterior and predictive distributions for an effect.".

column2: Median and central 95% range of a log-normal heterogeneity prior
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis. The module describes Median and central 95% range of a log-normal heterogeneity prior as "Summarises a log-normal prior for the between-study variance tau2, the form of the empirical priors published by Turner and colleagues, by its median and central 95% range. LN(m_LN, s_LN^2) means that the logarithm of tau2 is normal with mean m_LN and standard deviation s_LN, so the median and limits follow by exponentiating m_LN and m_LN plus or minus 1.96 s_LN. Square roots of the three values give the same summaries for tau."; HEO defines Bayesian Meta-Analysis as "Bayesian meta-analysis combines prior distributions with results from several studies to give posterior and predictive distributions for an effect.".

column2: Predictive draw of a new-setting effect and the resulting treated mortality risk
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis. The module describes Predictive draw of a new-setting effect and the resulting treated mortality risk as "Draws the true effect in a new setting at one iteration of a posterior sample and converts it to an annual mortality risk on treatment for a decision model. At each iteration theta_new is drawn from N(mu, tau^2) using that iteration's mu and tau, and the odds ratio exp(theta_new) is applied to the baseline odds o_0. The conversion is the baseline and odds ratio relation of HE-FM-NMA-004, applied here to a predictive draw. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of p_1 across iterations give the 95% predictive range of the treated risk."; HEO defines Bayesian Meta-Analysis as "Bayesian meta-analysis combines prior distributions with results from several studies to give posterior and predictive distributions for an effect.".

column2: Bed turnover rate from discharges and average available beds
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Bed turnover rate from discharges and average available beds as "Divides the discharges of a period, including deaths, by the average daily number of available beds over the same period. The result is the number of patients each bed served, a partial productivity ratio of one output, discharges, to one input, beds. NHS Wales reports it as the bed use factor (indicator IP03). B_bar is the mean of the daily bed counts, which the computational function under this formula derives from those counts."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Bed turnover interval from available and occupied bed-days
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Bed turnover interval from available and occupied bed-days as "Divides the bed-days on which available beds stood empty in a period by the number of discharges, giving the average time a bed is empty between one patient leaving and the next arriving. n times B_bar is the available bed-days. NHS Wales reports the same quantity as the bed turnover interval (indicator IP04), written as average unoccupied beds times days in the period, divided by deaths and discharges."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Annual bed turnover rate from occupancy and average length of stay
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Annual bed turnover rate from occupancy and average length of stay as "Expresses the annual turnover rate through bed occupancy and average length of stay. It follows from dividing both sides of the throughput identity on the Average Length of Stay page (HE-FM-ALOS-002) by the number of beds, with o equal to U divided by 365 times B_bar and L_bar equal to U divided by D. A high turnover rate can come from short stays, from full beds or from both, so the rate is ambiguous on its own. On a Pabón Lasso chart, which plots T against o, each line from the origin joins points with the same L_bar."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Bed turnover interval from occupancy and average length of stay
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Bed turnover interval from occupancy and average length of stay as "Expresses the turnover interval through occupancy and average length of stay. Adding the stay and the interval gives 365 divided by the annual turnover rate, so each bed cycles through one stay and one empty interval per patient, and the stay is the share o of that cycle. On a Barber-Johnson diagram, which plots L_bar against TI, lines from the origin join points of equal occupancy and diagonals with equal intercepts join points of equal turnover."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Fixed bed cost per discharge from the bed turnover rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Fixed bed cost per discharge from the bed turnover rate as "Spreads the annual cost of a staffed bed that does not vary with patient numbers over the patients the bed served in the year, as in top-down costing. A higher turnover rate lowers this average only because the same cost is shared among more patients; whether cash is saved depends on what happens to the freed capacity."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Mean, variance and standard error of a beta-distributed probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Mean, variance and standard error of a beta-distributed probability as "Gives the expected value and the variance of a probability that follows Beta(alpha, beta), and its standard error as the square root of the variance. The mean depends only on the ratio of the two parameters, while their sum acts like a sample size: the larger alpha + beta, the narrower the distribution. The function sqrt is the square root."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Beta parameters for a probability from binomial event counts and a conjugate prior
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Beta parameters for a probability from binomial event counts and a conjugate prior as "Updates a beta prior for a probability with r events among n patients at risk. Because the beta is the conjugate prior for a binomial probability, the result is again a beta distribution. With the limiting prior alpha_0 = beta_0 = 0 the rule reduces to alpha equal to the number of events and beta equal to the number of non-events, n minus r, so the mean is the observed proportion r/n. A uniform prior, alpha_0 = beta_0 = 1, adds one to each parameter."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Beta shape parameters from a reported mean and standard error by the method of moments
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Beta shape parameters from a reported mean and standard error by the method of moments as "Sets the beta mean and variance equal to a reported mean probability and the square of its standard error and solves for the two parameters. The sum alpha + beta equals mu (1 minus mu) divided by s squared, minus one, and alpha and beta are that sum multiplied by mu and by 1 minus mu. A solution exists only when s squared is below mu (1 minus mu)."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Gamma shape and scale for a utility decrement fitted by moments
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Gamma shape and scale for a utility decrement fitted by moments as "Describes a mean utility as a decrement from full health, one minus the utility, and fits a gamma distribution to the decrement by matching its mean and standard error. The shape is the squared mean decrement over the squared standard error and the scale is the squared standard error over the mean decrement. Each sampled utility, one minus a gamma draw, is at most one with no lower limit, which suits states where a mean utility below zero is plausible."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Dirichlet transition probabilities from three normalised gamma draws
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Dirichlet transition probabilities from three normalised gamma draws as "Samples one row of a transition matrix for a state with three exits by drawing an independent gamma variable for each destination, with shape equal to that destination's count plus any prior and a scale of one, and dividing each draw by their total. The result is a draw from a Dirichlet distribution, the multivariate generalisation of the beta, and the three probabilities add to one in every iteration. Each component has a beta marginal: the second probability from Dirichlet(90, 24, 6) follows Beta(24, 96)."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Net present value recovered from a benefit-cost ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Net present value recovered from a benefit-cost ratio as "Recovers net present value from a benefit-cost ratio and the present value of costs it was built on. It rearranges the identity that the ratio minus one equals net present value per unit of cost, so a ratio above one and a positive net present value are the same finding whenever costs are positive. The ratio minus one is also the return on investment as defined in public health reviews, so a reported return converts to a ratio by adding one."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Incremental benefit-cost ratio between two mutually exclusive options
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Incremental benefit-cost ratio between two mutually exclusive options as "Divides the extra present-value benefits of option Y over option X by its extra present-value costs. When Y costs more than X, an incremental ratio above one is the same condition as Y having the higher net present value, so the ratio applied incrementally gives the same choice as net present value. Average ratios of each option against doing nothing do not."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Benefit-cost ratio with averted costs counted gross or netted
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Benefit-cost ratio with averted costs counted gross or netted as "Gives the two ratios that arise when averted treatment costs are counted as a benefit (gross) or subtracted from programme costs (netted). Net present value, H plus S minus C, is the same under both, but the ratios differ, and the netted ratio is undefined or negative when averted costs reach or exceed programme costs."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Benefit-cost ratio with a transfer counted on both sides
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Benefit-cost ratio with a transfer counted on both sides as "Gives the ratio when a transfer, such as an incentive payment, is counted as a cost to the payer and an equal benefit to the recipient. The transfer cancels in net present value but moves the ratio towards one: a ratio above one falls and a ratio below one rises."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: Return on public sector cost from benefits, non-public and public costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Return on public sector cost from benefits, non-public and public costs as "Divides present-value benefits net of costs borne outside the public sector by present-value public sector costs, as set out in the Green Book (2026). Costs that fall on patients, families or other sectors move from the denominator to the numerator, so the ratio measures social value per pound of public spending. It suits ranking options when the public sector budget is the binding constraint."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: BIC with the number of uncensored events as the penalty count
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Information Criterion. The module describes BIC with the number of uncensored events as the penalty count as "Volinsky and Raftery's revision for censored survival data replaces the number of patients in the BIC penalty with the number of uncensored events d. With heavy censoring d is much smaller than the number of patients, so each parameter costs less and BIC moves closer to AIC. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Bayesian Information Criterion as "Bayesian information criterion (BIC) ranks models fitted to the same data, such as HTA survival curves, by fit with a penalty that grows with sample size.".

column2: Approximate Bayes factor from a difference in BIC
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Information Criterion. The module describes Approximate Bayes factor from a difference in BIC as "Kass and Raftery show that the Schwarz criterion is a rough approximation to the log Bayes factor, so twice the natural log of the Bayes factor in favour of model 1 over model 2 is approximately BIC_2 minus BIC_1. Exponentiating half the difference gives an approximate Bayes factor. On the Kass and Raftery scale, a difference of 0 to 2 is not worth more than a bare mention, 2 to 6 is positive, 6 to 10 strong and above 10 very strong evidence against the higher-BIC model."; HEO defines Bayesian Information Criterion as "Bayesian information criterion (BIC) ranks models fitted to the same data, such as HTA survival curves, by fit with a penalty that grows with sample size.".

column2: Approximate posterior probability of a candidate model from BIC differences
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Information Criterion. The module describes Approximate posterior probability of a candidate model from BIC differences as "Converts BIC differences into approximate posterior probabilities for each candidate model, assuming every model has the same prior probability. S is the sum of exp(-Delta_r / 2) over all R candidate models, so the probabilities add to 1 across the set. Burnham and Anderson view such model weights as a step towards model averaging."; HEO defines Bayesian Information Criterion as "Bayesian information criterion (BIC) ranks models fitted to the same data, such as HTA survival curves, by fit with a penalty that grows with sample size.".

column2: Monte Carlo bootstrap standard error from B replicates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bootstrap Standard Error. The module describes Monte Carlo bootstrap standard error from B replicates as "Estimates the bootstrap standard error as the standard deviation, with divisor B minus 1, of the statistic recalculated on B bootstrap samples. As B grows the estimate approaches the ideal bootstrap standard error over every possible resample. The replicate standard deviation is itself the standard error and is not divided by the square root of B."; HEO defines Bootstrap Standard Error as "Bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of an estimate, such as mean trial cost, recalculated across many resamples of the observed data.".

column2: Ideal bootstrap standard error of a sample mean
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bootstrap Standard Error. The module describes Ideal bootstrap standard error of a sample mean as "For a sample mean the ideal bootstrap standard error, the value over every possible resample, has a closed form derived by Efron and Tibshirani. It equals the usual standard error, s divided by the square root of n, multiplied by the square root of n minus 1 over n, so the bootstrap understates the usual value in small samples."; HEO defines Bootstrap Standard Error as "Bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of an estimate, such as mean trial cost, recalculated across many resamples of the observed data.".

column2: Variance of incremental net monetary benefit across paired bootstrap replicates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bootstrap Standard Error. The module describes Variance of incremental net monetary benefit across paired bootstrap replicates as "Gives the bootstrap variance of incremental net monetary benefit from the variances of the differences in mean effect and mean cost and their covariance across replicates. Resampling each patient's cost and effect together keeps the covariance; resampling them separately forces it to zero, which understates the standard error when costlier patients have worse outcomes."; HEO defines Bootstrap Standard Error as "Bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of an estimate, such as mean trial cost, recalculated across many resamples of the observed data.".

column2: Coefficient of variation of a bootstrap standard error from B replicates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bootstrap Standard Error. The module describes Coefficient of variation of a bootstrap standard error from B replicates as "Efron and Tibshirani's approximation splits the variability of a bootstrap standard error into the sampling variability of the ideal value and the simulation noise from using B replicates. The second term shrinks as B grows, which is why 50 to 200 replicates are adequate for a standard error in most situations."; HEO defines Bootstrap Standard Error as "Bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of an estimate, such as mean trial cost, recalculated across many resamples of the observed data.".

column2: Brier score from patient-level predicted risks and outcomes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Brier Score. The module describes Brier score from patient-level predicted risks and outcomes as "Averages the squared differences between each patient's predicted probability of the event and the observed outcome, coded 1 for an event and 0 otherwise. The score runs from 0 for perfect predictions to 1 for predictions that are confidently and completely wrong, and its square root is a typical distance between prediction and outcome on the probability scale."; HEO defines Brier Score as "The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted risks and observed binary outcomes, used to judge prediction models; lower is better.".

column2: Murphy partition of the Brier score into reliability, resolution and uncertainty
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Brier Score. The module describes Murphy partition of the Brier score into reliability, resolution and uncertainty as "When predictions take a limited set of K distinct values, the Brier score splits exactly into a reliability term, which measures miscalibration, minus a resolution term, which measures how far the group event rates spread from the overall rate, plus an uncertainty term, the score of the non-informative model. Refinement, uncertainty minus resolution, is the average uncertainty left within the groups, and the score also equals reliability plus refinement."; HEO defines Brier Score as "The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted risks and observed binary outcomes, used to judge prediction models; lower is better.".

column2: Scaled Brier score against the non-informative model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Brier Score. The module describes Scaled Brier score against the non-informative model as "Scales the Brier score against a non-informative model that predicts the overall event rate for every patient, so that 0 means no improvement on that model and 1 means perfect prediction. Steyerberg and colleagues write the reference in terms of the mean predicted risk; basing it on the observed rate keeps it fixed when models that are miscalibrated in the large are compared. A negative value means the model does worse than predicting the overall rate."; HEO defines Brier Score as "The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted risks and observed binary outcomes, used to judge prediction models; lower is better.".

column2: Binomial probability of exactly r patients with an event
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Binomial probability of exactly r patients with an event as "Gives the probability that exactly r of n patients at risk have the event within the period. C(n, r) is the binomial coefficient, n! divided by r! (n minus r)!, the number of ways of choosing which r of the n patients have the event; Excel returns it with COMBIN. A single patient, the case n = 1, is a Bernoulli trial."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Binomial probability of no events among n patients
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Binomial probability of no events among n patients as "The binomial probability function with r = 0. The chance of a zero count depends on the expected count n p: it stays high when n p is small, so a rare event in a small study often gives no events at all, and a zero count does not show that the probability is zero."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Mean, variance and standard deviation of a binomial event count
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Mean, variance and standard deviation of a binomial event count as "Gives the expected number of patients with the event and the variance and standard deviation of that count. In a cohort model the number moving is the mean n p, with no chance variation. In a microsimulation of n patients with a fixed probability, the count varies around that mean with variance n p (1 minus p), the stochastic or first-order uncertainty of the ISPOR-SMDM task force. The variance is largest when p is one half.
