The function sqrt is the square root."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Maximum likelihood estimate of a binomial probability and its standard error
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Maximum likelihood estimate of a binomial probability and its standard error as "The binomial likelihood, proportional to p^r (1 minus p)^(n minus r), peaks at the observed proportion r/n, the maximum likelihood estimate. Its standard error is estimated by putting p_hat in place of p in the sampling variance p (1 minus p)/n, so larger studies give more precise estimates."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Wald confidence interval for a binomial proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Wald confidence interval for a binomial proportion as "The normal-approximation interval for a binomial proportion, the form most often quoted. It is symmetric about p_hat, has zero width when r is 0 or n, and its lower limit can fall below zero. Brown, Cai and DasGupta showed that its coverage behaves erratically and that the problem is far more persistent than had been appreciated. The general Wald interval for any estimate is on the Asymptotic Normality page (HE-FM-AN-001)."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion as "Inverts the large-sample test for a proportion instead of plugging p_hat into the standard error. Its centre is pulled from p_hat towards one half, it is asymmetric near the bounds and its limits cannot fall outside the possible range for a probability. Brown, Cai and DasGupta recommend it, or the equal-tailed Jeffreys interval, for small n."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Binomial arm event probability from the logit model in NICE DSU TSD 2
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Binomial Distribution. The module describes Binomial arm event probability from the logit model in NICE DSU TSD 2 as "In the TSD 2 framework the number of events r_ik in arm k of trial i is binomial with probability p_ik among n_ik patients, and the logit of p_ik is the trial's baseline log odds mu_i plus, for arms other than the control, the trial-specific log odds ratio delta_ik. Inverting the logit gives the arm probability below; for the control arm delta_ik is zero. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Binomial Distribution as "The binomial distribution models how many of a fixed number of patients have an event when each has the same probability and outcomes are independent.".

column2: Chi-square probability density with k degrees of freedom
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Chi-square probability density with k degrees of freedom as "Gives the density of the chi-square distribution at a value x above zero. Gamma(.) is the gamma function, which equals (m minus 1)! for a whole number m and the square root of pi at one half. With k = 2 the density reduces to one half of exp(minus x/2), the exponential density with mean 2."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Mean, variance and skewness of a chi-square distribution
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Mean, variance and skewness of a chi-square distribution as "A statistic that follows chi-square on k degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis has expected value k, so only values well above k give small p-values. The skewness falls towards zero as k grows, and because the variable is a sum of k independent terms the central limit theorem makes it close to a normal distribution with the same mean and variance. The function sqrt is the square root."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Right-tail probability of a chi-square statistic on two degrees of freedom
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Right-tail probability of a chi-square statistic on two degrees of freedom as "With k = 2 the chi-square distribution is exponential with mean 2, so the p-value for an observed statistic has a closed form. It gives the p-value for the generalised gamma against the exponential, which differ by two parameters, and for Cochran's Q from three studies in the article's worked example. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Chi-square critical value on two degrees of freedom at level alpha
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Chi-square critical value on two degrees of freedom at level alpha as "Inverts the closed-form tail on two degrees of freedom: a statistic above x_crit has a p-value below alpha. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: One-degree-of-freedom chi-square statistic as a squared normal deviate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes One-degree-of-freedom chi-square statistic as a squared normal deviate as "With one degree of freedom the chi-square variable is a single squared standard normal deviate, so a two-sided normal test at a given level and a chi-square test on one degree of freedom give the same answer. A Wald test of one parameter can be reported as z or as its square, and the p-value of a one-degree-of-freedom statistic equals the two-sided normal tail beyond its square root."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Likelihood ratio statistic and chi-square degrees of freedom for nested models
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Likelihood ratio statistic and chi-square degrees of freedom for nested models as "The likelihood ratio statistic is twice the gain in maximised log-likelihood when the parameters fixed in the restricted model are freed. Under Wilks' theorem, in large samples, under the null model and when certain regularity conditions hold, LR is compared with chi-square on df degrees of freedom, the difference in the number of free parameters. The p-value is the right-hand tail, from the computational function below or, when df is 2, from HE-FM-CHISQ-003."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Pearson chi-square score for model calibration targets with its degrees of freedom
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chi-Square Distribution. The module describes Pearson chi-square score for model calibration targets with its degrees of freedom as "Scores a candidate parameter set by scaling each squared gap between an observed count and the model's predicted count by the predicted count, so a gap of 7 cases matters more for a target of 45 than for one of 450. When the score is read against chi-square, the NIST/SEMATECH rule subtracts the number of parameters estimated from the same counts, plus one, from the number of targets, which gives df. The one is subtracted because the predicted counts are constrained to add to the observed total, as in the article's example where both parameter sets total 350, the same as the observed counts. Treating the counts as independent with expectations fixed in advance gives m degrees of freedom instead, and the article's example shows how far the two readings can differ."; HEO defines Chi-Square Distribution as "The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared independent standard normals and is the reference for likelihood ratio, heterogeneity and fit tests.".

column2: Administrative censoring time and observed follow-up from staggered entry and a data cut-off
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Censoring. The module describes Administrative censoring time and observed follow-up from staggered entry and a data cut-off as "The administrative censoring time C_i of patient i is the gap between the calendar date of the data cut-off d and the patient's own entry date e_i. The observed follow-up Y_i is the smaller of the true event time T_i and C_i, and the event indicator delta_i is 1 when the event happened by the cut-off and 0 when the patient was censored. All times after entry are measured from entry or randomisation. When patients can also be lost to follow-up, the censoring time becomes the smaller of d minus e_i and the time of loss, and only the first part is administrative."; HEO defines Administrative Censoring as "Administrative censoring is right censoring that occurs when a trial's planned end of follow-up or data cut-off arrives before a patient has the event.".

column2: Kaplan-Meier survival under administrative censoring
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Censoring. The module describes Kaplan-Meier survival under administrative censoring as "The product-limit estimate multiplies survival before each distinct event time t_j by one minus the deaths at t_j divided by the number still at risk just before t_j. Chaining the step over all event times up to t gives the product of the factors, the Kaplan-Meier curve S(t). Patients censored at the cut-off leave the risk set at their censoring time, and because administrative censoring removes the latest recruits first, the number at risk falls steadily towards the end of follow-up."; HEO defines Administrative Censoring as "Administrative censoring is right censoring that occurs when a trial's planned end of follow-up or data cut-off arrives before a patient has the event.".

column2: Restricted mean survival time to the last observed follow-up
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Censoring. The module describes Restricted mean survival time to the last observed follow-up as "The restricted mean survival time is the area under the Kaplan-Meier curve from time 0 to a restriction time tau no later than the last observed follow-up. Because the curve is a step function, the area is the sum over the K intervals between 0, the successive event times and tau of the survival in each interval multiplied by its length."; HEO defines Administrative Censoring as "Administrative censoring is right censoring that occurs when a trial's planned end of follow-up or data cut-off arrives before a patient has the event.".

column2: Share of mean survival from an exponential tail beyond the last observed follow-up
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Censoring. The module describes Share of mean survival from an exponential tail beyond the last observed follow-up as "When survival at the last observed follow-up tau is S_tau and a constant hazard h is assumed afterwards, the area under the tail is S_tau divided by h. The share of mean survival that comes from that tail is the tail area divided by the restricted mean plus the tail area. The denominator is the mean survival of HE-FM-BTH-002 with the restricted mean in place of the closed-interval life-years, and a trial estimate of h is events divided by person-time, HE-FM-AER-002."; HEO defines Administrative Censoring as "Administrative censoring is right censoring that occurs when a trial's planned end of follow-up or data cut-off arrives before a patient has the event.".

column2: Pigouvian tax and efficient quantity with linear demand and rising marginal external cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Tax. The module describes Pigouvian tax and efficient quantity with linear demand and rising marginal external cost as "With marginal private benefit (the demand curve) a minus b × Q, a constant marginal private cost c and a marginal external cost m plus g × Q, consumers left alone choose Q_0, where marginal private benefit equals c. The efficient quantity Q_star sets marginal private benefit equal to marginal social cost, c plus the marginal external cost. The Pigouvian tax t_star is the marginal external cost at Q_star, and adding it to the private cost moves the private choice to Q_star."; HEO defines Pigouvian Tax as "A Pigouvian tax is a tax on an activity that harms others, set equal to its marginal external cost at the efficient level of that activity.".

column2: Deadweight loss of an untaxed negative externality with linear curves
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Tax. The module describes Deadweight loss of an untaxed negative externality with linear curves as "Without a tax, every unit between Q_star and Q_0 costs society more than it is worth to consumers. With linear curves the loss is a triangle: its base is Q_0 minus Q_star, and its height is the gap between marginal social cost and marginal private benefit at Q_0, which equals the marginal external cost at Q_0 because marginal private benefit equals c there. The Pigouvian tax removes the whole triangle."; HEO defines Pigouvian Tax as "A Pigouvian tax is a tax on an activity that harms others, set equal to its marginal external cost at the efficient level of that activity.".

column2: Quantity and remaining welfare loss when the tax is set at the pre-tax marginal external cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Tax. The module describes Quantity and remaining welfare loss when the tax is set at the pre-tax marginal external cost as "Sets the tax t_0 at the marginal external cost observed before the tax, at Q_0, rather than at Q_star. When marginal external cost rises with consumption, t_0 exceeds the Pigouvian rate and consumers cut back to Q_t, below the efficient quantity. The remaining loss L_t is the triangle between Q_t and Q_star, with height equal to marginal private benefit less marginal social cost at Q_t."; HEO defines Pigouvian Tax as "A Pigouvian tax is a tax on an activity that harms others, set equal to its marginal external cost at the efficient level of that activity.".

column2: Directly age-standardised rate for comparing social groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequity. The module describes Directly age-standardised rate for comparing social groups as "Weights the age-specific rates of one social group by the age structure of a common standard population, so that groups with different age structures are compared as if they had the same one. In a health inequity analysis this removes the part of a difference that is due to age, which Whitehead places partly under natural, biological variation and so treats as a legitimate source of difference. The weights sum to 1. With a group's own age shares as the weights, the same sum returns the group's crude rate."; HEO defines Health Inequity as "Health inequity is a difference in health judged avoidable, unfair and unjust, often arising from social or economic disadvantage rather than biology.".

column2: Direct unfairness measure of health inequity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequity. The module describes Direct unfairness measure of health inequity as "Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define direct unfairness through the variation that remains when every legitimate source of difference is held at a common reference value, written h_i^DU = f(c_i, l_bar) in the article's simplified notation. Applied to a gap between two groups that has been attributed additively to causes, holding the legitimate causes constant leaves only the parts attributed to causes judged illegitimate, so the inequity is the sum of those parts. The unexplained remainder is dropped, which treats it as acceptable. This group-gap formula is this page's simplification: Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define a hypothetical distribution across individuals and then apply an inequality index to it."; HEO defines Health Inequity as "Health inequity is a difference in health judged avoidable, unfair and unjust, often arising from social or economic disadvantage rather than biology.".

column2: Fairness gap measure of health inequity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequity. The module describes Fairness gap measure of health inequity as "Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define the fairness gap as the difference between the actual distribution and a hypothetical one in which every illegitimate source of difference is set to a common reference value, written h_i^FG = h_i minus f(c_bar, l_i) in the article's simplified notation. Applied to a gap between two groups that has been attributed additively to causes, removing the illegitimate causes leaves only the legitimate parts in the hypothetical gap, so the inequity is the whole gap minus those legitimate parts. The unexplained remainder stays in the result, which treats it as unfair. This group-gap formula is this page's simplification: Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define the fairness gap distribution across individuals and then apply an inequality index to it."; HEO defines Health Inequity as "Health inequity is a difference in health judged avoidable, unfair and unjust, often arising from social or economic disadvantage rather than biology.".

column2: Inequity share of a decomposed health gap under stated fairness judgements
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequity. The module describes Inequity share of a decomposed health gap under stated fairness judgements as "Expresses the inequity in a decomposed gap as a share of the whole gap. The gap is first rebuilt from its explained parts and the unexplained remainder, and the inequity counts each explained part judged unfair and the remainder when it is judged unfair. An indicator of 0 for the remainder gives the direct unfairness result of HE-FM-INEQ-002 and an indicator of 1 the fairness gap result of HE-FM-INEQ-003. Asada and colleagues report results in this form for survey data, with about 60% of health inequality inequitable when unexplained variation was treated as acceptable and almost all of it when it was treated as unfair."; HEO defines Health Inequity as "Health inequity is a difference in health judged avoidable, unfair and unjust, often arising from social or economic disadvantage rather than biology.".

column2: Community-rated premium as the member-weighted mean expected cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Community Rating. The module describes Community-rated premium as the member-weighted mean expected cost as "Under pure community rating every member of a pool pays the same premium, set at the average expected cost of the pool before any loading for administration and profit. Under adjusted community rating the same calculation applies within each permitted rating cell, such as an age band in a rating area. The premium is the mean of the risk groups' expected costs weighted by the number of members in each group."; HEO defines Community Rating as "Community rating is a health insurance pricing rule that stops premiums varying with health or claims, allowing at most limited variation by age or area.".

column2: Implicit cross-subsidy per member under community rating
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Community Rating. The module describes Implicit cross-subsidy per member under community rating as "The community-rated premium minus a member's expected cost. A positive value is the amount a member pays above expected cost towards others, as low-risk members do; a negative value is the amount by which a high-risk member's expected cost exceeds the premium. Weighted by the number of members, the cross-subsidies sum to zero across the pool, because the premium equals the pool's mean expected cost. Read from the insurer's side, the same quantity is the expected profit on that member in HE-FM-CSKM-001."; HEO defines Community Rating as "Community rating is a health insurance pricing rule that stops premiums varying with health or claims, allowing at most limited variation by age or area.".

column2: Risk equalisation transfer that offsets community-rating cross-subsidies
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Community Rating. The module describes Risk equalisation transfer that offsets community-rating cross-subsidies as "A payment from a central fund to an insurer for each member of risk group i, or from the insurer to the fund when negative, equal to the group's expected cost minus the community-rated premium. After the transfer each member brings the insurer an expected result of zero, because premium plus transfer equals expected cost. When the transfers use the same members and premium as the pool they sum to zero, so the fund balances. Van de Ven and colleagues report a consensus that removing the predictable over- and undercompensation of subgroups that community rating creates is part of the goal of risk equalisation."; HEO defines Community Rating as "Community rating is a health insurance pricing rule that stops premiums varying with health or claims, allowing at most limited variation by age or area.".

column2: Lifetime community rating late-entry loading
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Community Rating. The module describes Lifetime community rating late-entry loading as "A percentage added to the community-rated premium of a person who first buys cover late, equal to a fixed rate for each counted year without cover up to a maximum. Ireland's Lifetime Community Rating, introduced from 1 May 2015, adds 2% of the gross premium for each year a person spent aged 35 or over without cover, up to a maximum of 70%; since a 2017 amendment the loading is withdrawn after 10 years of cover. Australia's Lifetime Health Cover, introduced on 1 July 2000, adds 2% for each year a person is over 30 when taking out hospital cover after the 1 July following their 31st birthday, up to 70%, and the loading stops after 10 years of continuous cover. The function min returns the smaller of its two arguments."; HEO defines Community Rating as "Community rating is a health insurance pricing rule that stops premiums varying with health or claims, allowing at most limited variation by age or area.".

column2: Expected profit per member under a fixed or risk-adjusted payment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cream Skimming. The module describes Expected profit per member under a fixed or risk-adjusted payment as "The payment received for a member, whether a community-rated premium, a capitation payment or a risk-adjusted payment, minus the member's expected cost of care, written pi_i = R_i minus E[C_i] in the article. A plan has an incentive to attract members with a positive expected profit and deter those with a negative one whenever it can tell them apart and influence who joins. Under community rating with no risk equalisation the payment is the premium, and the expected profit equals the cross-subsidy of HE-FM-CRAT-002."; HEO defines Cream Skimming as "Cream skimming is when an insurer or provider attracts people expected to cost less than it is paid for them and deters those expected to cost more.".

column2: Expected profit per member from an enrolled risk mix
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cream Skimming. The module describes Expected profit per member from an enrolled risk mix as "The payment per member minus the average expected cost of the members a plan actually enrols, where the payment is the same for every member of the payment cell and the plan's mix of risk groups may differ from the cell's population. The profit comes entirely from the mix, since the expected cost of each type of member is unchanged. Multiplying by the number of members gives the plan's total expected profit, which is an upper bound on the gain from selection because attracting the mix has costs of its own."; HEO defines Cream Skimming as "Cream skimming is when an insurer or provider attracts people expected to cost less than it is paid for them and deters those expected to cost more.".

column2: Over- or under-compensation and predictive ratio for a risk group
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cream Skimming. The module describes Over- or under-compensation and predictive ratio for a risk group as "Two group-level measures of the selection incentive a payment system leaves. Over- or undercompensation is the average payment minus the average cost for the group, in money, and is the usual European measure; the predictive ratio is payment divided by cost, without units, and is the usual US measure. A positive difference or a ratio above 1 indicates overcompensation, and a negative difference or a ratio below 1 undercompensation, so a group with a ratio well below 1 is a likely target for selection. Both are computed over the same members, so the ratio of total payment to total cost equals the ratio of the averages."; HEO defines Cream Skimming as "Cream skimming is when an insurer or provider attracts people expected to cost less than it is paid for them and deters those expected to cost more.".

column2: Expected cost and health outcome at a chance node
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chance Node. The module describes Expected cost and health outcome at a chance node as "Replaces a chance node with the probability-weighted averages of the costs and of the health outcomes at the ends of its k branches. Costs and health outcomes are averaged separately because they are measured in different units; in a cost-utility analysis the health outcome is usually QALYs. When a branch leads to a further chance node, its C_j and E_j are the expected values already calculated at that node."; HEO defines Chance Node as "A chance node is a point in a decision tree where an uncertain event, not a choice, decides the pathway, and its branch probabilities sum to one.".

column2: Pathway probability to a terminal node
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Chance Node. The module describes Pathway probability to a terminal node as "Multiplies the conditional branch probabilities along a pathway to give the probability of reaching its terminal node, the multiplication rule for a joint probability. The formula is written for a pathway through two chance nodes, as in the article's test-and-treat example; a pathway through m chance nodes multiplies one further conditional factor for each node. Probabilities of successive events along a pathway are multiplied, while probabilities of mutually exclusive pathways may be summed."; HEO defines Chance Node as "A chance node is a point in a decision tree where an uncertain event, not a choice, decides the pathway, and its branch probabilities sum to one.".

column2: Expected outcome per person from a cohort simulation trace with counting weights and discounting
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cohort Simulation. The module describes Expected outcome per person from a cohort simulation trace with counting weights and discounting as "Sums the reward earned by the cohort in each recorded cycle, m_t r, after multiplying it by a within-cycle counting weight w_t and a discount factor delta_t. Here m_t is the row of the cohort trace at cycle t and r the column of rewards per cycle in each state, so m_t r is the reward per person at cycle t; where only one state carries a reward, m_t r is that state's proportion times its reward, the form used in the worked examples. The counting weights for the common rules are: end of cycle 0 at t = 0 and 1 afterwards; start of cycle 1 up to T minus 1 and 0 at T; half-cycle correction (trapezoidal rule) one half at t = 0 and t = T and 1 in between; Simpson's 1/3 rule, for T even, one third at t = 0 and t = T, four thirds at odd t and two thirds at even t. The half-cycle and Simpson weights appear here only as counting options; the Half-Cycle Correction page covers the correction itself."; HEO defines Cohort Simulation as "Cohort simulation runs a Markov or other state-transition model by moving the expected shares of a hypothetical cohort between health states each cycle.".

column2: Cohen's d from two group means and the pooled standard deviation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cohen's d. The module describes Cohen's d from two group means and the pooled standard deviation as "Divides the difference between two observed group means by the pooled standard deviation of the two groups, the usual sample estimate of Cohen's d. The pooled standard deviation weights each group's variance by its degrees of freedom. The sign carries the direction of the effect, so instruments that run in opposite directions have to be aligned first. The function sqrt is the square root."; HEO defines Cohen's d as "Cohen's d is a standardised effect size: the difference between two group means divided by their pooled standard deviation, used to compare studies.".

column2: Log odds ratio from a standardised mean difference by the logistic conversion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cohen's d. The module describes Log odds ratio from a standardised mean difference by the logistic conversion as "Re-expresses a standardised mean difference as a log odds ratio for responding by multiplying it by pi divided by the square root of 3, about 1.814, the factor Chinn derived from the logistic distribution. The odds ratio is the exponential of the log odds ratio. Combined with a comparator response probability, the odds ratio gives the intervention response probability by HE-FM-NMA-004, a quantity a decision model can use. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Cohen's d as "Cohen's d is a standardised effect size: the difference between two group means divided by their pooled standard deviation, used to compare studies.".

column2: Relative cost weight of a case group from group mean costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Weight. The module describes Relative cost weight of a case group from group mean costs as "Divides the mean cost per case in one group by the mean cost per case across all groups of the costing sample, the calculation that the European Observatory study of DRG systems describes in greatly simplified terms. The overall mean is the case-weighted mean of the group means, so the case-weighted average of the weights equals 1 in the costing year. Real systems refine the ratio, for example with IHACPA's inlier and outlier cost model for each AR-DRG, but keep the same scaling to a reference cost."; HEO defines Case Weight as "Case weight is a relative value for a diagnosis-related group showing its expected cost against the average case, used to scale payment from a base rate.".

column2: Case-weighted payment per hospital case
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Weight. The module describes Case-weighted payment per hospital case as "Converts a case weight into money by multiplying it by a base rate, the money paid per unit of weight, and by any adjustment factor for the hospital. In the Medicare inpatient prospective payment system, the base payment rate, with its labour-related share adjusted by the area wage index, is multiplied by the DRG relative weight. Summed over a hospital's cases, the payment equals its casemix multiplied by the base rate and the adjustment."; HEO defines Case Weight as "Case weight is a relative value for a diagnosis-related group showing its expected cost against the average case, used to scale payment from a base rate.".

column2: Casemix-adjusted cost ratio of a hospital
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Weight. The module describes Casemix-adjusted cost ratio of a hospital as "Divides a hospital's actual total cost by the cost expected if each of its cases cost the reference amount for its group. The ratio has the form of an indirect standardisation, as in the SMR (an analogy drawn here). CM_h is the hospital's casemix, the sum of the weights of its cases, so the ratio equals cost per weighted case divided by the reference cost of one unit of weight. A value above 1 means spending above the reference for that casemix. HE-FM-ALOS-004 applies the same structure to bed-days."; HEO defines Case Weight as "Case weight is a relative value for a diagnosis-related group showing its expected cost against the average case, used to scale payment from a base rate.".

column2: Price of an Australian admitted acute episode from national weighted activity units
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Weight. The module describes Price of an Australian admitted acute episode from national weighted activity units as "Applies IHACPA's adjustments to the price weight of an AR-DRG to give the episode's national weighted activity units (NWAU), the Australian case weight in which the average hospital service is worth 1, and multiplies the result by the national efficient price (NEP). The formula is the 2026-27 admitted acute formula without the private patient deductions and without the hospital-acquired complication and avoidable readmission terms, which the 2026-27 determination states are shadow priced rather than applied as penalties."; HEO defines Case Weight as "Case weight is a relative value for a diagnosis-related group showing its expected cost against the average case, used to scale payment from a base rate.".

column2: Case fatality rate among confirmed cases
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Fatality Rate. The module describes Case fatality rate among confirmed cases as "Divides the deaths from the disease among the counted cases by the number of cases that meet the case definition. The numerator is restricted to deaths among the cases in the denominator, so the CFR is a proportion rather than a true rate. It applies over the period in which those deaths were counted, which a precise definition states, for example a one-month CFR."; HEO defines Case Fatality Rate as "Case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of people diagnosed with a disease who die of it within a defined period, a measure of severity.".

column2: Case fatality rate among resolved cases
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Fatality Rate. The module describes Case fatality rate among resolved cases as "Restricts the calculation to detected cases whose outcome is known, dividing deaths by deaths plus recoveries. The WHO scientific brief on estimating mortality from COVID-19 sets it out as a simple response to the delay between becoming a case and dying, but the estimate is still biased when deaths and recoveries happen at different speeds."; HEO defines Case Fatality Rate as "Case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of people diagnosed with a disease who die of it within a defined period, a measure of severity.".

column2: Understatement factor of a crude case fatality rate during exponential growth
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Fatality Rate. The module describes Understatement factor of a crude case fatality rate during exponential growth as "Gives the approximate factor by which cumulative deaths divided by cumulative cases understates the case fatality rate when an epidemic grows exponentially and deaths are reported a fixed delay after cases. The exponent is the number of epidemic doubling times that pass between case reporting and death reporting, a heuristic given by Lipsitch and colleagues."; HEO defines Case Fatality Rate as "Case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of people diagnosed with a disease who die of it within a defined period, a measure of severity.".

column2: Population mortality from attack rate and case fatality rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case Fatality Rate. The module describes Population mortality from attack rate and case fatality rate as "Links the case fatality rate to the proportion of a closed population that dies of the disease over an outbreak. Deaths over the population equal cases over the population multiplied by deaths over cases, so the identity holds only when both measures share the case definition, the period and the population. The result is a cumulative incidence of death for the period, not a rate per person-year. The attack rate is computed with HE-FM-ATR-001."; HEO defines Case Fatality Rate as "Case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of people diagnosed with a disease who die of it within a defined period, a measure of severity.".

column2: Proportion of days covered as unique covered days over days in the observation period
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Proportion of Days Covered. The module describes Proportion of days covered as unique covered days over days in the observation period as "Divides the number of days in the observation period on which at least one fill provides medicine, after shifting overlapping supply of the same drug, by the number of days in the period, counted from the index date (the first fill) to the end date inclusive. Each day counts once however many fills cover it, and only days inside the period count, so the PDC cannot exceed 1. It is reported as a proportion or multiplied by 100 as a percentage, and is often dichotomised at 0.8."; HEO defines Proportion of Days Covered as "The proportion of days covered (PDC) is the share of days in a period on which pharmacy refill records show a patient had medicine, each day counted once.".

column2: Overlap shifting rule, start day of an early same-drug refill in the proportion of days covered
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Proportion of Days Covered. The module describes Overlap shifting rule, start day of an early same-drug refill in the proportion of days covered as "Moves the start of a refill of the same drug, collected before the previous supply has run out, to the day after that supply ends, on the PQA premise that the patient finishes the old supply before starting the new one. Fills are taken in date order and the rule is applied in sequence, so each start is compared with the end of the previous fill as already shifted. The first fill starts on its dispensing day, and a refill collected after the previous supply has ended keeps its own date. CMS defines the same drug by the active ingredient at generic name level."; HEO defines Proportion of Days Covered as "The proportion of days covered (PDC) is the share of days in a period on which pharmacy refill records show a patient had medicine, each day counted once.".

column2: Covered days in the PDC observation period from shifted same-drug fills
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Proportion of Days Covered. The module describes Covered days in the PDC observation period from shifted same-drug fills as "Adds, over the n fills of one drug after shifting, the days of each fill's supply that fall on or before the last day of the period. Shifting leaves the fills without overlap, so the sum counts each day once; a fill that starts after the end day adds nothing, and supply running past the end day is ignored. Day numbers run from the index date as day 1, so every fill starts on or after day 1 and the end day E equals the number of days in the period. Each comparison in parentheses inside the bracket equals 1 when it is true and 0 otherwise, so a fill adds its full supply when the supply ends on or before the end day, only the days up to the end day when it runs past it, and nothing when it starts after the end day."; HEO defines Proportion of Days Covered as "The proportion of days covered (PDC) is the share of days in a period on which pharmacy refill records show a patient had medicine, each day counted once.".

column2: Proportion of days covered adjusted for inpatient and skilled nursing facility stays
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Proportion of Days Covered. The module describes Proportion of days covered adjusted for inpatient and skilled nursing facility stays as "Applies the CMS adjustment for inpatient (IP) and skilled nursing facility (SNF) stays, during which the facility is assumed to supply the medicine. Stay days in the measurement period, including the discharge date, are removed from both numerator and denominator, and days' supply that overlaps a stay is shifted to uncovered days after discharge, if there are any. A patient whose stays span the whole treatment period is excluded."; HEO defines Proportion of Days Covered as "The proportion of days covered (PDC) is the share of days in a period on which pharmacy refill records show a patient had medicine, each day counted once.".

column2: Fixed-interval medication possession ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Medication Possession Ratio. The module describes Fixed-interval medication possession ratio as "Divides the total days' supply of the fills dispensed in the observation period by the number of days from the first dispensing to the end of the period, the most common variant in the review by Raebel and colleagues. Time after the last refill counts in the denominator, so stopping treatment lowers the ratio. Supply that runs past the end of the period still counts unless the analyst truncates it, so the ratio can exceed 1."; HEO defines Medication Possession Ratio as "The medication possession ratio (MPR) is the total days' supply dispensed divided by the days in the period. Unlike PDC, it can exceed 1 unless capped.".

column2: Refill-interval medication possession ratio including the last fill
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Medication Possession Ratio. The module describes Refill-interval medication possession ratio including the last fill as "Divides the total days' supply from the first to the last dispensing by the days between the first and last dispensing plus the days' supply of the last fill. Sikka and colleagues describe it as an often-used definition; Raebel and colleagues list it as less common and note that it has also been called MPRm. The clock stops when the last fill's supply ends, so the ratio does not account for discontinuation, and early refilling takes it above 1."; HEO defines Medication Possession Ratio as "The medication possession ratio (MPR) is the total days' supply dispensed divided by the days in the period. Unlike PDC, it can exceed 1 unless capped.".

column2: Modified medication possession ratio excluding the last fill (MPRm)
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Medication Possession Ratio. The module describes Modified medication possession ratio excluding the last fill (MPRm) as "Divides the days' supply of every fill except the last by the days between the first and last dispensing. Raebel and colleagues list it as MPR modified (MPRm). Because the last fill's supply and the time it would cover are both left out, the ratio describes refilling between the first and last dispensing and ignores any stop after the last refill."; HEO defines Medication Possession Ratio as "The medication possession ratio (MPR) is the total days' supply dispensed divided by the days in the period. Unlike PDC, it can exceed 1 unless capped.".

column2: Medication possession ratio capped at 1
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Medication Possession Ratio. The module describes Medication possession ratio capped at 1 as "Truncates any of the MPR variants at 1, so supply beyond the days in the denominator no longer raises the ratio. Sikka and colleagues note that early refilling takes the MPR above 1.0 and that it is often truncated there; Vollmer and colleagues define their capped measures as the minimum of the uncapped ratio and 1. Capping limits the upward skew of averages but still credits surplus supply against days without medicine."; HEO defines Medication Possession Ratio as "The medication possession ratio (MPR) is the total days' supply dispensed divided by the days in the period. Unlike PDC, it can exceed 1 unless capped.".

column2: Kendall's tau and normal test statistic of the Begg test from concordant and discordant study pairs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Begg Test. The module describes Kendall's tau and normal test statistic of the Begg test from concordant and discordant study pairs as "Compares every pair of studies once. A pair is concordant when the study with the larger variance also has the larger standardised effect (HE-FM-BEGG-002), and discordant when it has the smaller one. Kendall's score S, the difference between the two counts, is divided by the number of pairs to give tau, and by the square root of its null variance without ties to give a statistic compared with the standard normal distribution. When benefit is negative, as with log hazard ratios, exaggerated benefit in the smaller studies gives a negative tau. Stata's Kendall routine, to which its meta bias command refers, uses abs(S) minus 1 in the numerator as a continuity correction, and metafor's ranktest reports an exact p-value where it can, so a report states which version it used."; HEO defines Begg Test as "The Begg test is a rank correlation test (Kendall's tau) for small-study effects in a meta-analysis, a possible sign of publication bias.".

column2: Standardised effect of one study for the Begg test
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Begg Test. The module describes Standardised effect of one study for the Begg test as "Subtracts the inverse-variance pooled estimate from a study's effect estimate and divides by the standard deviation of that difference. The variance of the difference is the study's own variance less the variance of the pooled estimate, one over the sum of the weights, which allows for the study's own contribution to the pooled value. Without small-study effects the standardised values show no trend with study variance."; HEO defines Begg Test as "The Begg test is a rank correlation test (Kendall's tau) for small-study effects in a meta-analysis, a possible sign of publication bias.".

column2: Break-even and cost-neutral unit prices of a health technology
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Break-Even Analysis. The module describes Break-even and cost-neutral unit prices of a health technology as "Splits the incremental cost per patient into the acquisition cost of the technology, u units at unit price p, and every other cost difference, Delta_C_0, which is negative when the technology avoids more cost than it adds. Setting incremental net monetary benefit, lambda times Delta_E less (u times p plus Delta_C_0), to zero gives the break-even price, the highest unit price at which the technology is cost-effective at threshold lambda. Setting the incremental cost alone to zero gives the cost-neutral price. The gap between them, lambda times Delta_E divided by u, is the money value of the health gain per unit, so for a technology that improves health the break-even price lies above the cost-neutral price. With u equal to 1 the break-even price is the payer's maximum price per patient of HE-FM-BARG-002. Solving the same condition for the effect gives Delta_C divided by lambda, the health displaced of HE-FM-CET-002."; HEO defines Break-Even Analysis as "Break-even analysis finds the price, effect or volume at which a health technology or service becomes cost-effective, cost-neutral or self-financing.".

column2: Break-even activity volume and margin of safety for a health service paid per unit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Break-Even Analysis. The module describes Break-even activity volume and margin of safety for a health service paid per unit as "Applies the cost-volume form of break-even analysis from management accounting to a service paid a fixed price or tariff per unit of activity. Each unit contributes the price less the variable cost, so the break-even volume is the fixed cost for the period divided by the contribution per unit, and the margin of safety is the share by which expected activity could fall before the service makes a loss. When fixed costs step up with capacity, as when a second team is needed, the calculation is repeated for each block of capacity."; HEO defines Break-Even Analysis as "Break-even analysis finds the price, effect or volume at which a health technology or service becomes cost-effective, cost-neutral or self-financing.".

column2: Compensating variation for a health change under log-income utility
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Compensating Variation. The module describes Compensating variation for a health change under log-income utility as "With utility equal to the natural log of income plus b times a health index h, the compensating variation of a change in h solves ln(Y less CV) plus b times h_1 equals ln Y plus b times h_0. Because utility is concave in income, the money value is not proportional to the health change: for a gain it is below the linear value Y times b times Delta_h, and for a loss its absolute value is above it. HM Treasury's wellbeing guidance gives the same form for the compensating surplus of a large change in life satisfaction, with b equal to the coefficient on the outcome divided by the coefficient on log income, and presents it as a sensitivity test for the high end of the range, not the central value."; HEO defines Compensating Variation as "Compensating variation (CV) is the sum that restores original utility after a health or policy change: willingness to pay for a gain or to accept a loss.".

column2: Compensating variation from a multinomial logit model by the log-sum formula
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Compensating Variation. The module describes Compensating variation from a multinomial logit model by the log-sum formula as "Values a change in the attributes of the alternatives, or in the set of alternatives, in a discrete choice experiment or another logit model. Expected utility from the choice is the log of the sum of the exponentiated representative utilities, and the change in it is converted to money by dividing by the marginal utility of income, the negative of the coefficient on the cost attribute. Train attributes the closed form to Williams and to Small and Rosen; it holds for independent extreme value errors and utility linear in income, so it gives a single figure that is both the compensating and the equivalent variation, per person per choice occasion."; HEO defines Compensating Variation as "Compensating variation (CV) is the sum that restores original utility after a health or policy change: willingness to pay for a gain or to accept a loss.".

column2: Equivalent variation for a health change under log-income utility
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equivalent Variation. The module describes Equivalent variation for a health change under log-income utility as "With utility equal to the natural log of income plus b times a health index h, the equivalent variation solves ln(Y plus EV) plus b times h_0 equals ln Y plus b times h_1. For a gain it exceeds both the linear value Y times b times Delta_h and the compensating variation of the same gain; for a loss of the same size it equals minus the compensating variation of the gain, so the two measures swap values between a gain and a loss. HM Treasury's wellbeing guidance gives the same form for the equivalent surplus of a large change in life satisfaction and notes that, under its ln(income) formulae, the equivalent surplus always exceeds the compensating surplus for a gain."; HEO defines Equivalent Variation as "Equivalent variation (EV) is the income change, made instead of a price, health or policy change, that leaves a person as well off as that change would.".

column2: Equivalent variation of an option that changes both health and income under log-income utility
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equivalent Variation. The module describes Equivalent variation of an option that changes both health and income under log-income utility as "Values an option that moves both the health index and the person's income, for example a treatment with a copayment, from the same status quo income Y_0 and health. Solving ln(Y_0 plus EV_k) plus b times h_0 equals ln Y_k plus b times h_k gives the formula. Because each option is valued at the same status quo, the option with the larger equivalent variation gives the higher utility, the ranking property that compensating variation lacks when there are income effects. With Y_k equal to Y_0 the formula reduces to HE-FM-EVAR-001."; HEO defines Equivalent Variation as "Equivalent variation (EV) is the income change, made instead of a price, health or policy change, that leaves a person as well off as that change would.".

column2: Hazard ratio from event counts and person-time under constant hazards
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hazard Ratio. The module describes Hazard ratio from event counts and person-time under constant hazards as "Estimates each arm's hazard as its number of events divided by its person-time at risk and divides the treatment rate by the comparator rate, which gives the rate ratio. Under an exponential model each hazard is constant, so the rate ratio estimates the hazard ratio, and the approximate standard error of its natural logarithm depends only on the two event counts. The time unit cancels, so person-years and person-months give the same ratio when both arms use the same unit. The interval around the estimate follows HE-FM-HR-006."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Approximate confidence interval for a hazard ratio from the log scale
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hazard Ratio. The module describes Approximate confidence interval for a hazard ratio from the log scale as "Builds the interval on the natural log scale, where ratio measures are analysed, by adding and subtracting z standard errors to the log hazard ratio, and exponentiates the two limits. The interval is symmetric about the log hazard ratio and asymmetric about the hazard ratio itself. The log hazard ratio and its standard error come from a Cox model (HE-FM-HR-002) or from event counts and person-time (HE-FM-HR-005); z is 1.96 for a 95% interval."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Standard error of a log hazard ratio recovered from a reported confidence interval
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hazard Ratio. The module describes Standard error of a log hazard ratio recovered from a reported confidence interval as "Recovers the standard error of the log hazard ratio from a published interval: the difference between the natural logs of the upper and lower limits divided by twice the z value for the interval's coverage, 3.92 for a 95% interval. It is the inverse of HE-FM-HR-006 and supplies the standard error wherever a model or a meta-analysis on the log scale needs one but the report gives only the hazard ratio and its interval."; HEO defines Hazard Ratio as "A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the event rates (hazards) in two groups, the usual measure of a treatment effect on survival in trials and HTA models.".

column2: Cumulative hazard from a survival probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cumulative Hazard. The module describes Cumulative hazard from a survival probability as "Takes minus the natural logarithm of the probability of being event free beyond time t, which gives the cumulative hazard at t, and sets it beside the probability of having had the event by t. The two agree only when both are small: the cumulative hazard has no upper limit and passes 1 when survival falls below exp(minus 1), about 0.3679, while the event probability never exceeds 1. The reverse step is S_t = exp(minus H_t)."; HEO defines Cumulative Hazard as "Cumulative hazard, H(t), is the hazard rate summed over time in survival models. Survival equals exp(-H(t)), and unlike a probability H(t) can exceed 1.".

column2: Cycle transition probability from the rise in cumulative hazard across a cycle
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cumulative Hazard. The module describes Cycle transition probability from the rise in cumulative hazard across a cycle as "Gives the probability that a person event free at the start of a model cycle has the event by its end, from the cumulative hazard at the end of the cycle and at its start. Because survival is exp(minus H), the ratio S(t) / S(t minus Delta) is exp of minus the rise in H, so the conversion is exact for any hazard shape and the cohort trace reproduces the fitted curve. Time t runs from the origin of the fitted curve, so in a cohort model it is the time since model start at the cycle's end. With a constant hazard it reduces to HE-FM-TP-001."; HEO defines Cumulative Hazard as "Cumulative hazard, H(t), is the hazard rate summed over time in survival models. Survival equals exp(-H(t)), and unlike a probability H(t) can exceed 1.".

column2: Weibull cumulative hazard and its straight line on the log-cumulative hazard scale
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cumulative Hazard. The module describes Weibull cumulative hazard and its straight line on the log-cumulative hazard scale as "Gives the cumulative hazard of a Weibull curve written as S(t) = exp(minus lambda t^gamma), and its natural logarithm, which is a straight line in log time with intercept log(lambda) and gradient gamma. A gradient of 1 is the exponential model with a constant hazard, above 1 a rising hazard and below 1 a falling hazard. Under proportional hazards two arms' lines are parallel, separated by the log hazard ratio. This is the scale of the log-cumulative hazard plot that TSD 14 uses as its first step in choosing survival curves."; HEO defines Cumulative Hazard as "Cumulative hazard, H(t), is the hazard rate summed over time in survival models. Survival equals exp(-H(t)), and unlike a probability H(t) can exceed 1.".

column2: Deadweight loss triangle from a price wedge and the quantity change it causes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deadweight Loss. The module describes Deadweight loss triangle from a price wedge and the quantity change it causes as "Multiplies half the wedge between the demand price and the supply price at the distorted quantity by the change in quantity the wedge causes. For an excise tax the height is the tax per unit and the base the fall in sales; for insurance the height is the gap between the cost of care and the patient's price and the base the extra use. The coinsurance case written in terms of the coinsurance rate is HE-FM-MH-001."; HEO defines Deadweight Loss as "Deadweight loss is the net loss of total surplus when a tax, subsidy, market power or insurance drives a wedge between price and marginal cost.".

column2: Harberger approximation to deadweight loss from a small ad valorem tax
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deadweight Loss. The module describes Harberger approximation to deadweight loss from a small ad valorem tax as "Writes the triangle in terms of spending before the tax and the price elasticity of demand. With constant marginal cost the wedge is tau times p and quantity falls by about eps times tau times q, so the loss is half their product. Zero elasticity gives zero loss, and doubling the tax rate roughly quadruples it. The expression is the single-tax case of the second-order approximation that Auerbach and Hines attribute to Harberger, with the quantity response written through the elasticity."; HEO defines Deadweight Loss as "Deadweight loss is the net loss of total surplus when a tax, subsidy, market power or insurance drives a wedge between price and marginal cost.".

column2: Feldstein and Gruber reduction in the deadweight loss of insurance when coinsurance rises
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deadweight Loss. The module describes Feldstein and Gruber reduction in the deadweight loss of insurance when coinsurance rises as "Measures the fall in the deadweight loss of insurance-induced care when the coinsurance rate rises from P_0 to P_1. Care is measured in units whose price without insurance is 1, so quantities are spending at full cost. The reduction is a rectangle, the forgone care times the gap between its cost and the new patient price, plus a triangle above it. With a constant elasticity eta, E_1 = E_0 * (P_0 / P_1)^eta, and the triangle term then treats demand as straight between E_1 and E_0, an approximation."; HEO defines Deadweight Loss as "Deadweight loss is the net loss of total surplus when a tax, subsidy, market power or insurance drives a wedge between price and marginal cost.".

column2: Social cost of tax-financed spending with a marginal excess burden of taxation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deadweight Loss. The module describes Social cost of tax-financed spending with a marginal excess burden of taxation as "Scales an option's net call on tax-financed public budgets by one plus the marginal excess burden, the deadweight loss per unit of extra revenue at the margin; one plus it is the marginal cost of public funds. Guidance differs: the 1992 US OMB Circular A-94 takes 25 cents per dollar for a supplementary analysis, Norway's circular R-109/2021 sets 20 øre per krone for all sectors, and the UK Green Book (2026) says the costs of raising public funds should not generally be included."; HEO defines Deadweight Loss as "Deadweight loss is the net loss of total surplus when a tax, subsidy, market power or insurance drives a wedge between price and marginal cost.".

column2: Balanced incomplete block design parameters for object case best-worst scaling
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Best-Worst Scaling. The module describes Balanced incomplete block design parameters for object case best-worst scaling as "Gives the number of times each object appears and the number of times each pair of objects appears together in a balanced incomplete block design with v objects shown in b sets of k. The first identity counts object appearances two ways, b times k equals v times r; the second counts one object's pairings two ways, lambda times (v minus 1) equals r times (k minus 1). Whole-number values of r and lambda are needed for such a design."; HEO defines Best-Worst Scaling as "Best-worst scaling (BWS) is a stated preference method in which people pick the best and worst item in each set, to rank priorities or value health states.".

column2: Standardised best-minus-worst score in object case best-worst scaling
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Best-Worst Scaling. The module describes Standardised best-minus-worst score in object case best-worst scaling as "Divides the difference between the number of times an item was chosen best and the number of times it was chosen worst by the number of times it could have been chosen: the number of respondents times its appearances in each respondent's design. Scores run from minus 1, always worst, to plus 1, always best, and across all items the differences sum to zero."; HEO defines Best-Worst Scaling as "Best-worst scaling (BWS) is a stated preference method in which people pick the best and worst item in each set, to rank priorities or value health states.".

column2: Maxdiff model probability of a best and worst pair in one choice set
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Best-Worst Scaling. The module describes Maxdiff model probability of a best and worst pair in one choice set as "Gives the probability that item b is chosen best and item w worst from a set of J items when the respondent picks, from all ordered pairs of distinct items, the pair with the largest utility difference. The denominator is the sum of exp(V_j minus V_k) over all J(J minus 1) ordered pairs with j not equal to k, which equals S_pos times S_neg minus J, where S_pos sums exp(V_j) and S_neg sums exp(minus V_j) over the set; the J terms with j equal to k each equal 1. The probabilities over all ordered pairs sum to 1."; HEO defines Best-Worst Scaling as "Best-worst scaling (BWS) is a stated preference method in which people pick the best and worst item in each set, to rank priorities or value health states.".

column2: Sequential best-then-worst model probability in one choice set
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Best-Worst Scaling. The module describes Sequential best-then-worst model probability in one choice set as "Treats the best choice as a logit choice from the whole set and the worst choice as a logit choice on minus the utilities from the items left once the best is removed, and multiplies the two. S_neg minus exp(minus V_b) is the sum of exp(minus V_k) over the set without item b. From the same utilities it gives different probabilities from the maxdiff model (HE-FM-BWS-003), so a study should state which it assumed."; HEO defines Best-Worst Scaling as "Best-worst scaling (BWS) is a stated preference method in which people pick the best and worst item in each set, to rank priorities or value health states.".

column2: Normal prior to posterior update of a treatment effect at an interim analysis
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Adaptive Design. The module describes Normal prior to posterior update of a treatment effect at an interim analysis as "Combines a normal prior for the treatment effect with a normally distributed interim estimate of known standard error. The posterior precision is the prior precision plus the data precision, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the estimate. Dividing the posterior mean minus the minimum effect a by the posterior standard deviation gives z_1, and the posterior probability that the effect exceeds a is Phi(z_1), the standard normal distribution function, which a success criterion of the form Pr(d > a | y) > c compares with c."; HEO defines Bayesian Adaptive Design as "Bayesian adaptive design is a clinical trial design in which pre-set rules on posterior or predictive probabilities trigger changes such as early stopping.".

column2: Predictive probability of final success for a normal two-stage Bayesian design
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Adaptive Design. The module describes Predictive probability of final success for a normal two-stage Bayesian design as "Projects an interim look forward to the final analysis. Final success is a final posterior probability of a positive effect above Phi(z_c), so the final posterior mean must exceed z_c final standard deviations. Solving for the second-stage estimate gives y2_crit, and given the interim posterior that estimate is predicted to be normal with mean m_1 and variance v_1 plus s_2 squared. The predictive probability of success is 1 minus Phi(z_pp). Unlike the posterior probability it asks how likely the trial is to succeed, not how strong the evidence is now."; HEO defines Bayesian Adaptive Design as "Bayesian adaptive design is a clinical trial design in which pre-set rules on posterior or predictive probabilities trigger changes such as early stopping.".

column2: Thall and Wathen response-adaptive allocation probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Adaptive Design. The module describes Thall and Wathen response-adaptive allocation probability as "Sets the probability that the next patient is allocated to the experimental arm from the current posterior probability that the experimental arm has the higher success rate. The tuning constant c controls how hard allocation follows the posterior: c of 0 gives equal randomisation, c of 1 gives Thompson sampling, and one half, or a value rising with the number enrolled such as i / (2n), has been suggested to reduce the variability of allocation."; HEO defines Bayesian Adaptive Design as "Bayesian adaptive design is a clinical trial design in which pre-set rules on posterior or predictive probabilities trigger changes such as early stopping.".

column2: Lee and Liu predictive probability for a single-arm trial with a binary response
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Adaptive Design. The module describes Lee and Liu predictive probability for a single-arm trial with a binary response as "With x responses in n patients so far, a beta(a_0, b_0) prior and a maximum of N_max patients, the number of responses Y among the m = N_max minus n patients still to come is beta-binomial(m, a_0 + x, b_0 + n minus x), with weight w_i for Y = i. For each i, B_i is the final posterior probability that the response rate exceeds p_0, from a beta(a_0 + x + i, b_0 + N_max minus x minus i) distribution. The predictive probability sums the weights of the future results for which B_i exceeds theta_T; the trial stops for futility if it falls below theta_L and for efficacy if it exceeds theta_U."; HEO defines Bayesian Adaptive Design as "Bayesian adaptive design is a clinical trial design in which pre-set rules on posterior or predictive probabilities trigger changes such as early stopping.".

column2: Arc cross-price elasticity between two observed price and quantity pairs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Price Elasticity. The module describes Arc cross-price elasticity between two observed price and quantity pairs as "Divides the change in the quantity of good i, as a proportion of the average of its two values, by the change in the price of good j, as a proportion of the average of its two prices. Using averages gives the same answer whichever observation is treated as the start; the factors of 2 in the averages cancel. With i equal to j the same formula gives the arc own-price elasticity, as in the RAND form HE-FM-MH-003."; HEO defines Cross-Price Elasticity as "Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a change in another good's price: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.".

column2: Point cross-price elasticity on a straight-line demand relation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Price Elasticity. The module describes Point cross-price elasticity on a straight-line demand relation as "Multiplies the slope of good i's demand with respect to the price of good j by the ratio of that price to the quantity at the point of interest. On a straight line the slope is constant but the elasticity changes along it, and at the midpoint of two observations it equals the arc elasticity."; HEO defines Cross-Price Elasticity as "Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a change in another good's price: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.".

column2: Quantity response to own and cross price changes under constant elasticities
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Price Elasticity. The module describes Quantity response to own and cross price changes under constant elasticities as "Projects the new quantity of good i when its own price and the price of good j both change, using the log-log demand form in which each coefficient is an elasticity: the proportional change in log quantity is the elasticity-weighted sum of the log price changes. For small changes this equals the article's approximation, proportional change in Q_i about equal to the sum of eps_ij times the proportional change in P_j."; HEO defines Cross-Price Elasticity as "Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a change in another good's price: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.".

column2: Compensated cross-price elasticity from the gross elasticity by the Slutsky equation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Price Elasticity. The module describes Compensated cross-price elasticity from the gross elasticity by the Slutsky equation as "Separates a gross (uncompensated) cross-price elasticity, which mixes substitution with an income effect, into its compensated part. In elasticity form the Slutsky equation is eps_ij = eps_c_ij minus w_j times eta_i, so the compensated elasticity adds back the budget share of good j times the income elasticity of good i. With a small budget share, as for most co-payments, the two nearly coincide."; HEO defines Cross-Price Elasticity as "Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a change in another good's price: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.".

column2: Reverse compensated cross-price elasticity from Slutsky symmetry and budget shares
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Price Elasticity. The module describes Reverse compensated cross-price elasticity from Slutsky symmetry and budget shares as "Uses the symmetry of the Slutsky matrix of compensated price derivatives, which in elasticity form reads w_i eps_c_ij = w_j eps_c_ji, to obtain the compensated response of good j to the price of good i from the response of i to the price of j. The two compensated elasticities have the same sign but are equal only when the budget shares are equal."; HEO defines Cross-Price Elasticity as "Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a change in another good's price: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.".

column2: Two-group two-period difference-in-differences estimate from group means
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Difference-in-Differences. The module describes Two-group two-period difference-in-differences estimate from group means as "Subtracts the comparison group's change in mean outcome from the treated group's change between one period before and one period after the policy. The first change removes what is fixed about the treated group, such as case mix; subtracting the second removes changes common to both groups, such as a national trend. Under parallel trends and no anticipation it estimates the average treatment effect on the treated."; HEO defines Difference-in-Differences as "Difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates a policy's causal effect by comparing outcome changes over time in an exposed group and a comparison group.".

column2: Difference-in-differences regression with group, period and interaction terms
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Difference-in-Differences. The module describes Difference-in-differences regression with group, period and interaction terms as "Writes each group-period mean as a constant, a fixed group gap, a common period change and an interaction that is non-zero only for the treated group after the policy. Fitted by ordinary least squares to unit-level data, the interaction coefficient equals the two-by-two estimate, and the regression also gives its standard error. gamma_D and lambda_P are the article's gamma and lambda, written with subscripts naming the indicator each one multiplies."; HEO defines Difference-in-Differences as "Difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates a policy's causal effect by comparing outcome changes over time in an exposed group and a comparison group.".

column2: Difference-in-differences estimate adjusted for a linearly extrapolated pre-policy differential trend
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Difference-in-Differences. The module describes Difference-in-differences estimate adjusted for a linearly extrapolated pre-policy differential trend as "Removes from the estimate the gap that the pre-policy difference in trends would produce if it continued in a straight line over the post-policy interval.
