The pre-policy difference comes from a placebo estimate between two pre-policy periods (HE-FM-DID-001 applied before the policy). Linear extrapolation is one assumption among several; bounded sensitivity analysis reports how conclusions change under a range of departures."; HEO defines Difference-in-Differences as "Difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates a policy's causal effect by comparing outcome changes over time in an exposed group and a comparison group.".

column2: Group-time average treatment effect for one adoption cohort against never-treated units
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Difference-in-Differences. The module describes Group-time average treatment effect for one adoption cohort against never-treated units as "Compares the change in mean outcome for units first treated in period g, from the last period before adoption (g minus 1) to period t, with the same change for units never treated. Estimating one effect per cohort and period avoids the comparisons with already-treated units that bias the two-way fixed effects coefficient under staggered adoption; the effects are then combined with weights the analyst states."; HEO defines Difference-in-Differences as "Difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates a policy's causal effect by comparing outcome changes over time in an exposed group and a comparison group.".

column2: Annual net cost of a policy from a difference-in-differences event rate estimate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Difference-in-Differences. The module describes Annual net cost of a policy from a difference-in-differences event rate estimate as "Turns an estimated change in an event rate per 1,000 people into events per year for the population covered and values them, then adds the policy's running cost. A negative result is a net saving. Health effects are valued separately in a cost-effectiveness analysis, and the estimate's standard error should be carried into probabilistic analysis."; HEO defines Difference-in-Differences as "Difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates a policy's causal effect by comparing outcome changes over time in an exposed group and a comparison group.".

column2: Net benefit of a risk model at one threshold probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Decision Curve Analysis. The module describes Net benefit of a risk model at one threshold probability as "Counts patients whose predicted risk is at or above the threshold as positive. True positives per patient are credited in full and false positives per patient are charged at the odds of the threshold, p_t / (1 minus p_t), the exchange rate between an unnecessary intervention and a case found. A net benefit of 0.07 equals intervening in 7 patients per 100, all of whom have the event, and in no one else. The maximum is the prevalence and there is no lower limit."; HEO defines Decision Curve Analysis as "Decision curve analysis (DCA) plots the net benefit of a prediction model or test across risk thresholds against treating all or no patients.".

column2: Net benefit of intervening in every patient at a threshold probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Decision Curve Analysis. The module describes Net benefit of intervening in every patient at a threshold probability as "Classes every patient as positive, so true positives per patient equal the prevalence and false positives per patient its complement. The line falls as the threshold rises and crosses zero, the net benefit of intervening in no one, where the threshold equals the prevalence. A model is of value at a threshold only if it beats both defaults."; HEO defines Decision Curve Analysis as "Decision curve analysis (DCA) plots the net benefit of a prediction model or test across risk thresholds against treating all or no patients.".

column2: Net unnecessary interventions avoided per 100 patients by a risk model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Decision Curve Analysis. The module describes Net unnecessary interventions avoided per 100 patients by a risk model as "Restates the gain in net benefit over intervening in everyone as unnecessary interventions avoided, net of extra missed cases, by dividing by the false positive weight. It is recommended when intervening in everyone is current practice and does not change which strategy has the highest net benefit."; HEO defines Decision Curve Analysis as "Decision curve analysis (DCA) plots the net benefit of a prediction model or test across risk thresholds against treating all or no patients.".

column2: Decision curve threshold probability from the benefit to a case and the harm to a non-case
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Decision Curve Analysis. The module describes Decision curve threshold probability from the benefit to a case and the harm to a non-case as "Sets the threshold at which a rational decision maker is indifferent between intervening and not, given the expected benefit of intervening for a patient who has or will have the event and the expected harm of intervening for one who does not. Equivalently the odds p_t / (1 minus p_t) equal L / G. Harm can include money, time, stress and adverse health effects, as long as G and L share a unit."; HEO defines Decision Curve Analysis as "Decision curve analysis (DCA) plots the net benefit of a prediction model or test across risk thresholds against treating all or no patients.".

column2: Expected monetary gain per patient from decision curve net benefit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Decision Curve Analysis. The module describes Expected monetary gain per patient from decision curve net benefit as "Values the classifications at a threshold with an explicit benefit per case found and harm per unnecessary intervention, compared with intervening in no one. When the threshold is set at L / (G + L), the result equals G times decision curve net benefit, which links the decision curve to an economic model's values."; HEO defines Decision Curve Analysis as "Decision curve analysis (DCA) plots the net benefit of a prediction model or test across risk thresholds against treating all or no patients.".

column2: Years lived with disability from prevalent cases and a disability weight
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Years lived with disability from prevalent cases and a disability weight as "Multiplies the number of people living with a sequela over one year by its disability weight, the GBD 2010 prevalence method, without age weighting or discounting. A weight of 0.05 means that 20 years lived in the state count as one year of healthy life lost. YLDs for a disease are the sum over its sequelae."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Combined disability weight for a person with two conditions under the multiplicative model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Combined disability weight for a person with two conditions under the multiplicative model as "Combines two weights so that the second condition removes its share of the health remaining after the first: one minus the product of one minus each weight. The result is below the sum of the two weights and never exceeds 1. GBD 2010 applied this rule to every combination of sequelae in its comorbidity simulation."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Share of a combined disability weight attributed to one condition
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Share of a combined disability weight attributed to one condition as "Splits a combined weight among the conditions that produce it in proportion to their stand-alone weights, so that cause-specific YLDs add to the comorbidity-adjusted total. The attributed share is not the gain from curing that condition, which compares the weights with and without it."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Comorbidity-adjusted years lived with disability per person for two independent conditions
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Comorbidity-adjusted years lived with disability per person for two independent conditions as "Combines the YLD rates of two conditions, each prevalence times weight, under independent co-occurrence and the multiplicative weight rule. Because the expected combined weight over people with neither, one or both conditions equals one minus the product of one minus each YLD rate, the adjustment needs no count of comorbid people. Multiplying by the population gives total YLDs."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: DALYs averted by an intervention that lowers disability weights in two groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes DALYs averted by an intervention that lowers disability weights in two groups as "Adds, over the groups treated, the number of people times the fall in their disability weight for the year, for an intervention that changes non-fatal health only. For people with another condition the before and after weights are combined weights, so the gain from relieving one condition is smaller than its stand-alone weight. Dividing the intervention cost by the result gives cost per DALY averted, as in HE-FM-ICER-001 with DALYs averted as the effect."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Disability weight from the first person trade-off question (life extension)
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Disability weight from the first person trade-off question (life extension) as "Derives a weight from the number of people with a condition whose one-year life extension a respondent judges equal to extending the lives of a reference number of people without it: one minus the ratio. This GBD 1990 question (PTO1) was criticised by Arnesen and Nord for presupposing that extending a disabled person's life is worth less."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Disability weight from the second person trade-off question (cures)
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability Weight. The module describes Disability weight from the second person trade-off question (cures) as "Derives a weight from the number of cures of a chronic condition that a respondent judges equal to prolonging the lives of a reference number of people: the reference number divided by the number of cures. Unlike PTO1, this question does not presuppose that disabled people's lifetime is devalued."; HEO defines Disability Weight as "A disability weight is a value from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death) rating health loss in a non-fatal state, used to calculate YLDs and DALYs.".

column2: Squared Euclidean distance between two patient profiles on two clustering variables
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cluster Analysis. The module describes Squared Euclidean distance between two patient profiles on two clustering variables as "Adds the squared differences between two units on each clustering variable. It is the dissimilarity k-means minimises, written here for two variables, such as annual emergency department attendances and outpatient appointments; with p variables the sum has p terms. Because differences are squared, variables with larger spread carry more weight, which is why scaling is a separate decision (HE-FM-CLU-002)."; HEO defines Cluster Analysis as "Cluster analysis is an unsupervised method that sorts patients, providers or countries into groups whose members are more alike than those in other groups.".

column2: Weighted squared distance between two units with variable weights
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cluster Analysis. The module describes Weighted squared distance between two units with variable weights as "Multiplies each squared difference by a weight that sets the variable's influence. Each variable's influence on squared Euclidean distance is proportional to its variance, so weights in inverse proportion to the variance give equal influence; this is what standardising the variables does. Multiplying every weight by the same constant rescales all distances equally and leaves the grouping unchanged."; HEO defines Cluster Analysis as "Cluster analysis is an unsupervised method that sorts patients, providers or countries into groups whose members are more alike than those in other groups.".

column2: Share of total scatter removed by a K-cluster k-means solution
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cluster Analysis. The module describes Share of total scatter removed by a K-cluster k-means solution as "Compares the within-cluster sum of squares W(K), the squared distances of units from their own cluster mean that k-means minimises, with its value for one cluster, the total sum of squares about the overall mean. The share removed rises as clusters are added, so the number of clusters is judged by where the gains flatten (the kink or elbow), not by maximising it."; HEO defines Cluster Analysis as "Cluster analysis is an unsupervised method that sorts patients, providers or countries into groups whose members are more alike than those in other groups.".

column2: Posterior probability of latent class membership with two classes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cluster Analysis. The module describes Posterior probability of latent class membership with two classes as "Applies Bayes' rule to give the probability that a unit belongs to a class, given its observed data: the class share times the likelihood of the data under that class, divided by the same quantity summed over classes. Units are commonly allocated to their most probable class, but the probability shows how uncertain the allocation is. With K classes the denominator has K terms."; HEO defines Cluster Analysis as "Cluster analysis is an unsupervised method that sorts patients, providers or countries into groups whose members are more alike than those in other groups.".

column2: Silhouette of one unit in a cluster solution
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cluster Analysis. The module describes Silhouette of one unit in a cluster solution as "Compares a unit's mean distance to the other members of its own cluster, a_i, with its mean distance to the members of the nearest other cluster, b_i. Values run from minus 1 to 1: near 1 the unit sits well inside a dense, well-separated cluster, around 0 the clusters overlap and below 0 the unit is closer to another cluster than to its own. The mean over all units summarises a solution."; HEO defines Cluster Analysis as "Cluster analysis is an unsupervised method that sorts patients, providers or countries into groups whose members are more alike than those in other groups.".

column2: Part-worth of a two-level attribute from mean ratings in a balanced orthogonal design
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conjoint Analysis. The module describes Part-worth of a two-level attribute from mean ratings in a balanced orthogonal design as "In a balanced orthogonal design with dummy coding, the least-squares part-worth of a two-level attribute equals the mean rating of the profiles showing the coded level minus the mean rating of those showing the reference level. Any design can be fitted by multiple regression on the dummy codes (HE-CF-CJA-001); the difference of means is a shortcut that holds only in a balanced orthogonal design, where every pair of levels of any two attributes appears equally often, as in a full factorial or an orthogonal fraction of it."; HEO defines Conjoint Analysis as "Conjoint analysis is a family of stated preference methods estimating how people value treatment or service attributes from ratings, rankings or choices.".

column2: Predicted rating of a clinic profile under the additive part-worth model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conjoint Analysis. The module describes Predicted rating of a clinic profile under the additive part-worth model as "Adds the part-worths of a profile's levels to the intercept, the predicted rating of the reference profile. With three two-level attributes it scores every one of the eight possible clinic designs, including ones not shown to respondents in a fractional design, as long as they combine levels used in the study."; HEO defines Conjoint Analysis as "Conjoint analysis is a family of stated preference methods estimating how people value treatment or service attributes from ratings, rankings or choices.".

column2: Relative importance of a conjoint attribute as its share of the total part-worth range
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conjoint Analysis. The module describes Relative importance of a conjoint attribute as its share of the total part-worth range as "Takes the range of an attribute's part-worths, the difference between its most and least preferred levels over the levels in the study, and divides it by the sum of the ranges of all attributes. Written here for three attributes; with K attributes the denominator has K ranges. The share depends on the levels chosen, so it describes the study's design as much as the respondent."; HEO defines Conjoint Analysis as "Conjoint analysis is a family of stated preference methods estimating how people value treatment or service attributes from ratings, rankings or choices.".

column2: Marginal rate of substitution between two conjoint attributes from part-worths
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conjoint Analysis. The module describes Marginal rate of substitution between two conjoint attributes from part-worths as "Gives the change in a continuous attribute b that offsets a one-unit change in attribute a, so that the profile's value is unchanged: minus the ratio of their part-worths. With waiting time as b it expresses a preference in weeks of waiting; with cost as b it is read as willingness to pay (HE-FM-WTP-001), which is a welfare measure only for choice data analysed under random utility theory."; HEO defines Conjoint Analysis as "Conjoint analysis is a family of stated preference methods estimating how people value treatment or service attributes from ratings, rankings or choices.".

column2: Exact interval probabilities in a progressive illness-death model with constant rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Continuous Model. The module describes Exact interval probabilities in a progressive illness-death model with constant rates as "Gives the closed-form matrix exponential for a three-state model in which Well people can fall Sick or die and Sick people can die, with no recovery. Staying Well depends on the total exit rate; being Sick at the end of the interval allows for people who fall Sick and then die within it; the remainder is death by either route. The single-rate conversion is HE-FM-TP-001 and the competing-risk split HE-FM-TP-004; neither includes the two-step path through Sick."; HEO defines Continuous Model as "A continuous model is a decision model run in continuous time rather than fixed cycles, so health events can occur at any moment, governed by rates.".

column2: Expected undiscounted time in the Well and Sick states with constant rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Continuous Model. The module describes Expected undiscounted time in the Well and Sick states with constant rates as "Gives life expectancy in a progressive illness-death model directly from the rates. A stay in a state with constant total exit rate lasts 1 over that rate on average (the mean sojourn time); the share of people leaving Well who go to Sick is q_WS over the total Well exit rate, and each spends on average 1 / q_SD in Sick. The sum is life expectancy, the value a cycle model of the same process should reproduce."; HEO defines Continuous Model as "A continuous model is a decision model run in continuous time rather than fixed cycles, so health events can occur at any moment, governed by rates.".

column2: Continuous discount rate equivalent to an annual discount rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Continuous Model. The module describes Continuous discount rate equivalent to an annual discount rate as "Converts an annual (discrete) discount rate d into the continuous rate rho that gives the same discount factor at every time, so that exp(minus rho t) equals (1 plus d) to the power minus t. Continuous-time models integrate costs and QALYs against exp(minus rho t), so rho, not d, belongs in the exponent."; HEO defines Continuous Model as "A continuous model is a decision model run in continuous time rather than fixed cycles, so health events can occur at any moment, governed by rates.".

column2: Discounted QALYs in a progressive illness-death model with continuous discounting
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Continuous Model. The module describes Discounted QALYs in a progressive illness-death model with continuous discounting as "Solves the article's integral of state utilities times state occupancy times exp(minus rho t) in closed form when rates are constant: discounting adds rho to every exit rate, so discounted time Well is 1 / (q_WS plus q_WD plus rho) and discounted time Sick is q_WS / (q_WS plus q_WD plus rho) / (q_SD plus rho). Weighting by utilities gives discounted QALYs; state costs in place of utilities give discounted costs."; HEO defines Continuous Model as "A continuous model is a decision model run in continuous time rather than fixed cycles, so health events can occur at any moment, governed by rates.".

column2: Unstabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dependent Censoring. The module describes Unstabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval as "Divides a patient's weight at the end of the previous interval by the probability of remaining unswitched (uncensored) through the current interval, given no earlier switch, baseline and time-dependent covariates and survival to the interval's start. Starting from 1, repeated division builds the product over intervals in the article's formula. Patients who cannot be censored in an interval keep their weight."; HEO defines Dependent Censoring as "Dependent censoring occurs when the chance of being censored is linked to a patient's risk of the event, so standard survival estimates can be biased.".

column2: Stabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dependent Censoring. The module describes Stabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval as "Multiplies the previous stabilised weight by the probability of remaining uncensored given baseline covariates only, divided by the same probability given baseline and time-dependent covariates. The numerator shrinks the weights towards 1, which makes the weighted analysis more efficient; when the time-dependent covariates do not affect censoring every stabilised weight is 1."; HEO defines Dependent Censoring as "Dependent censoring occurs when the chance of being censored is linked to a patient's risk of the event, so standard survival estimates can be biased.".

column2: IPCW-weighted Kaplan-Meier survival through one interval with two prognostic groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dependent Censoring. The module describes IPCW-weighted Kaplan-Meier survival through one interval with two prognostic groups as "Applies one Kaplan-Meier step with weighted counts: weighted deaths divided by the weighted number at risk give the interval's hazard, and survival is carried forward by the product-limit rule (unweighted form HE-FM-ADMC-002). Weighting non-switchers rebuilds the risk set that censoring at switch removed. Written for two prognostic groups; with more groups each adds a term to both sums."; HEO defines Dependent Censoring as "Dependent censoring occurs when the chance of being censored is linked to a patient's risk of the event, so standard survival estimates can be biased.".

column2: Bang and Tsiatis simple weighted estimator of mean cost with censored data
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dependent Censoring. The module describes Bang and Tsiatis simple weighted estimator of mean cost with censored data as "Estimates mean cost over a restricted period from all N patients, counting only complete cases (death or full follow-up to the limit) and weighting each by the inverse of the Kaplan-Meier probability of remaining uncensored at its time, with censoring treated as the event. Censored patients contribute through the weights given to complete cases with longer follow-up. Survival methods applied directly to cumulative cost are not valid, because cost at censoring and cost at death are linked through the same patient's spending."; HEO defines Dependent Censoring as "Dependent censoring occurs when the chance of being censored is linked to a patient's risk of the event, so standard survival estimates can be biased.".

column2: Mean survival from one-year survival and a constant later hazard, under dependent censoring
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dependent Censoring. The module describes Mean survival from one-year survival and a constant later hazard, under dependent censoring as "Extrapolates mean survival from one-year survival S_1 and conditional survival through year 2, q_2, assuming a constant hazard in year 1 and the year-2 hazard thereafter. The first term is the area under the curve in year 1 and the second the area of the exponential tail; it is the two-interval case of HE-FM-BTH-002, written in survival probabilities. Fed with a q_2 biased by dependent censoring, it shows how a small gap at two years becomes a large gap in life expectancy."; HEO defines Dependent Censoring as "Dependent censoring occurs when the chance of being censored is linked to a patient's risk of the event, so standard survival estimates can be biased.".

column2: Weighted absolute-difference calibration loss for two targets
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Optimisation. The module describes Weighted absolute-difference calibration loss for two targets as "Folds the distances between model predictions and calibration targets into one weighted score for the search to minimise. The article's general form sums over J targets with any distance d; two targets with the absolute difference are written out here, and a single target is the case w_2 = 0. Each evaluation needs a full model run, so the loss has no formula or derivatives the search can use."; HEO defines Bayesian Optimisation as "Bayesian optimisation seeks the inputs that optimise a costly function, such as a model's fit to calibration targets, using a surrogate to pick each run.".

column2: Squared exponential kernel covariance between losses at two parameter values
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Optimisation. The module describes Squared exponential kernel covariance between losses at two parameter values as "Gives the prior covariance between the calibration losses at two parameter values: the prior variance times a correlation that falls with the squared distance between them, scaled by the length-scale. Nearby values are expected to have similar losses. For several parameters the squared difference becomes the squared Euclidean distance."; HEO defines Bayesian Optimisation as "Bayesian optimisation seeks the inputs that optimise a costly function, such as a model's fit to calibration targets, using a surrogate to pick each run.".

column2: Gaussian process posterior mean and variance of the loss after two noise-free runs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Optimisation. The module describes Gaussian process posterior mean and variance of the loss after two noise-free runs as "Writes the posterior mean and variance at an untried value in closed form when two runs have been made without noise. The weights a_1 and a_2 solve the two-by-two correlation system of the runs; the posterior mean moves the prior mean towards the observed losses by those weights, and the posterior variance is the prior variance less the part the runs explain. Correlations come from the kernel (HE-FM-BOPT-002); for more runs or noisy runs the matrix form is HE-CF-BOPT-001."; HEO defines Bayesian Optimisation as "Bayesian optimisation seeks the inputs that optimise a costly function, such as a model's fit to calibration targets, using a surrogate to pick each run.".

column2: Expected improvement of a candidate run for a loss that is minimised
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Optimisation. The module describes Expected improvement of a candidate run for a loss that is minimised as "Values a candidate by how far its loss is expected to fall below the best loss so far, given a normal posterior with mean mu_n and standard deviation s_n. The first term rewards candidates predicted to fit well and the second rewards uncertainty. The site's calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_z, the standard normal distribution function at z, is entered as an input (NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) in Excel, pnorm(z) in R); the normal density is computed as exp(minus z^2 / 2) / 2.5066283, the constant being the square root of 2 times pi."; HEO defines Bayesian Optimisation as "Bayesian optimisation seeks the inputs that optimise a costly function, such as a model's fit to calibration targets, using a surrogate to pick each run.".

column2: Demographic projection of service use from age-specific base-year rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand Forecasting. The module describes Demographic projection of service use from age-specific base-year rates as "Applies the base-year use rate of each age group to that group's projected population and adds the results. The article's form sums over any number of age groups; three are written out here so that the calculator can run. Only the size and age structure of the population change; the rates stay at base-year levels unless a scenario changes them. Converting the forecast to beds is HE-FM-ALOS-002 solved for beds."; HEO defines Demand Forecasting as "Demand forecasting projects future use of health services and medicines, and the staff needed, from past utilisation, population change and other drivers.".

column2: Simple exponential smoothing forecast for the next period
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand Forecasting. The module describes Simple exponential smoothing forecast for the next period as "Forecasts the next period as a weighted average of the latest observation and the forecast that had been made for it, or equivalently the previous forecast corrected by a share alpha of its error. Unrolled, the weights on past observations decline exponentially with age. The method suits series with no clear trend or seasonal pattern; Holt's method adds a trend and seasonal versions add a seasonal component."; HEO defines Demand Forecasting as "Demand forecasting projects future use of health services and medicines, and the staff needed, from past utilisation, population change and other drivers.".

column2: Mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error over three test periods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Demand Forecasting. The module describes Mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error over three test periods as "Summarises forecast errors, observed minus forecast, over periods held back from fitting. The MAE is in the units of the data; the MAPE expresses each error as a percentage of the observed value, so it is unit-free but undefined when an observed value is zero and extreme when values are close to zero. The general forms average over any number of test periods; three are written out here so that the calculator can run. Evaluating Stockholm's forecasts of annual growth in drug expenditure, Linnér and colleagues reported a mean absolute error of 1.9 percentage points."; HEO defines Demand Forecasting as "Demand forecasting projects future use of health services and medicines, and the staff needed, from past utilisation, population change and other drivers.".

column2: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a diagnostic two-by-two table
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Diagnostic Accuracy. The module describes Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a diagnostic two-by-two table as "Sensitivity and specificity are proportions of the people with and without the target condition who receive the correct index test result, so they are conditional on disease status (the columns of the table). The predictive values are proportions of the positive and negative results that are correct, so they are conditional on the test result (the rows) and carry the prevalence of the study sample. Likelihood ratios are HE-FM-DXA-002 and predictive values at another prevalence HE-FM-DXA-003."; HEO defines Diagnostic Accuracy as "Diagnostic accuracy is how well a test agrees with a reference standard in detecting a target condition, usually reported as sensitivity and specificity.".

column2: Likelihood ratios and diagnostic odds ratio from sensitivity and specificity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Diagnostic Accuracy. The module describes Likelihood ratios and diagnostic odds ratio from sensitivity and specificity as "The positive likelihood ratio says how many times more likely a positive result is in people with the condition than in people without it, and the negative likelihood ratio the same for a negative result. Multiplying pre-test odds by a likelihood ratio gives post-test odds. The diagnostic odds ratio is their ratio, equal to TP times TN over FP times FN."; HEO defines Diagnostic Accuracy as "Diagnostic accuracy is how well a test agrees with a reference standard in detecting a target condition, usually reported as sensitivity and specificity.".

column2: Positive and negative predictive values at a given prevalence by Bayes' theorem
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Diagnostic Accuracy. The module describes Positive and negative predictive values at a given prevalence by Bayes' theorem as "Recomputes the predictive values for the population where the test will be used from sensitivity, specificity and the prevalence (pre-test probability) there. As prevalence falls, false positives from the larger disease-free group make up more of the positive results, so PPV falls and NPV rises. The odds form, post-test odds equal pre-test odds times the likelihood ratio (HE-FM-DXA-002), gives the same result."; HEO defines Diagnostic Accuracy as "Diagnostic accuracy is how well a test agrees with a reference standard in detecting a target condition, usually reported as sensitivity and specificity.".

column2: Proportion of correct test results as a prevalence-weighted average
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Diagnostic Accuracy. The module describes Proportion of correct test results as a prevalence-weighted average as "The share of results that are correct, often reported simply as accuracy, weights sensitivity by prevalence and specificity by its complement. At low prevalence it is dominated by specificity, and it counts a missed case and an unnecessary referral as equally bad."; HEO defines Diagnostic Accuracy as "Diagnostic accuracy is how well a test agrees with a reference standard in detecting a target condition, usually reported as sensitivity and specificity.".

column2: Net monetary benefit per person of a triage test against no testing
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Diagnostic Accuracy. The module describes Net monetary benefit per person of a triage test against no testing as "Values each true positive at its net gain G and each false positive at its cost L, both in money at a stated value of health, and subtracts the cost of the test. False negatives and true negatives fare as they would without testing, so they add nothing. Divided by G and with the test cost removed, the expression is decision-curve net benefit (HE-FM-DCA-001) at the threshold L / (G + L) (HE-FM-DCA-004)."; HEO defines Diagnostic Accuracy as "Diagnostic accuracy is how well a test agrees with a reference standard in detecting a target condition, usually reported as sensitivity and specificity.".

column2: Survival conditional on reaching a late entry time
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Left Truncation. The module describes Survival conditional on reaching a late entry time as "A person who enters observation at time l after the origin informs only survival beyond l given survival to l. Dividing survival at t by survival at entry, both measured from the same origin, gives that conditional probability; it is the quantity a late entrant's follow-up estimates and the quantity the article's correction restores to its place."; HEO defines Left Truncation as "Left truncation (delayed entry) occurs when people join a survival analysis risk set after time zero and are observed only if still event free at entry.".

column2: Kaplan-Meier step with a risk set restricted to people who have already entered
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Left Truncation. The module describes Kaplan-Meier step with a risk set restricted to people who have already entered as "Counts the risk set at an event time as those who have entered and not yet left. With follow-up intervals open at entry and closed at exit, a person is at risk at t_j when L_i < t_j <= X_i, so the count is the number who entered before t_j less the number who exited before t_j (anyone who left before t_j had also entered before it). The product-limit step itself is HE-FM-ADMC-002; only the risk set changes."; HEO defines Left Truncation as "Left truncation (delayed entry) occurs when people join a survival analysis risk set after time zero and are observed only if still event free at entry.".

column2: Exponential event rate and mean from person-time counted after entry
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Left Truncation. The module describes Exponential event rate and mean from person-time counted after entry as "With an exponential curve, S(t) = exp(minus lambda t), the left-truncated log-likelihood sums delta_i log lambda minus lambda (X_i minus L_i), because the entry term minus log S(L_i) cancels the time before entry. It is maximised by the number of events over the person-time from entry to exit, and the fitted mean time from the origin is 1 / lambda."; HEO defines Left Truncation as "Left truncation (delayed entry) occurs when people join a survival analysis risk set after time zero and are observed only if still event free at entry.".

column2: Weibull log-likelihood contribution of a left-truncated record
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Left Truncation. The module describes Weibull log-likelihood contribution of a left-truncated record as "Writes the article's contribution, delta_i log f(X_i) plus (1 minus delta_i) log S(X_i) minus log S(L_i), for a Weibull curve with S(t) = exp(minus (t / b)^k) and density (k / b)(t / b)^(k minus 1) S(t). The last term, (L_i / b)^k, is what a fit without entry times leaves out. Summed over records and maximised over k and b it gives the left-truncated Weibull fit used for extrapolation; with k = 1 it reduces to the exponential case of HE-FM-LTR-003."; HEO defines Left Truncation as "Left truncation (delayed entry) occurs when people join a survival analysis risk set after time zero and are observed only if still event free at entry.".

column2: Revenue and provider margin per case under an Ellis and McGuire mixed payment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Contract Theory. The module describes Revenue and provider margin per case under an Ellis and McGuire mixed payment as "A mixed payment pays a fixed prospective amount per case plus a share r of the cost of the care given, so revenue rises by r times c for each extra unit and the provider bears the rest, (1 minus r) times c. Pure case payment is r = 0 and full cost reimbursement is P = 0 with r = 1. The margin is revenue minus cost, written in Ellis and McGuire's equation (12) as P + (r minus 1) c q."; HEO defines Contract Theory as "Contract theory studies how contracts, such as provider payment rules, can align incentives when actions or information are hidden or cannot be verified.".

column2: Bed-days chosen under a mixed payment with a linear marginal benefit of care
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Contract Theory. The module describes Bed-days chosen under a mixed payment with a linear marginal benefit of care as "Ellis and McGuire's first-order condition alpha b(q) = (1 minus r) c sets the weighted marginal benefit of care equal to the cost the provider bears. With the marginal benefit falling in a straight line, b(q) = b_0 minus b_1 q, the condition solves for the stay; the max function returns no care when even the first unit is not worth its cost to the provider. The article's patient benefit B(q) = 1200q minus 50q squared gives b_0 = 1,200 and b_1 = 100."; HEO defines Contract Theory as "Contract theory studies how contracts, such as provider payment rules, can align incentives when actions or information are hidden or cannot be verified.".

column2: Efficient reimbursed share of cost and the budget-matched prospective amount
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Contract Theory. The module describes Efficient reimbursed share of cost and the budget-matched prospective amount as "Efficiency requires the patient's marginal benefit to equal the marginal cost of care. Comparing this with the provider's condition (HE-FM-CTH-002) gives Ellis and McGuire's optimal reimbursed share r_star = 1 minus alpha, so the provider's own cost share equals the index of agency. The fixed part is then set so that the payment for an efficient stay equals its cost, the article's choice; Ellis and McGuire note that the prospective amount can be lowered as r rises to keep the same total payment per case."; HEO defines Contract Theory as "Contract theory studies how contracts, such as provider payment rules, can align incentives when actions or information are hidden or cannot be verified.".

column2: Geographically adjusted Medicare physician fee schedule amount for a service in a locality
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conversion Factor. The module describes Geographically adjusted Medicare physician fee schedule amount for a service in a locality as "Each of the three relative value components of a service is multiplied by its geographic practice cost index for the payment locality, and the adjusted total is multiplied by the conversion factor. The regulation writes the same amount as total relative value units times a geographic adjustment factor (GAF) times the conversion factor, where the GAF weights each index by the component's share of the total. In the article's notation Fee is P_s,l and PE and MP are E_s and M_s. The amount is for a participating supplier; a non-participating supplier receives 95 per cent of it."; HEO defines Conversion Factor as "Conversion factor (CF) is the money amount per relative value unit that turns fee schedule relative values, such as Medicare RVUs, into payment amounts.".

column2: Medicare conversion factor for a calendar year as a chain of budget neutrality, update and one-year increase
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conversion Factor. The module describes Medicare conversion factor for a calendar year as a chain of budget neutrality, update and one-year increase as "CMS takes the previous year's conversion factor and multiplies it by the budget neutrality adjustment, the statutory update for the payment group and any temporary statutory increase. For 2026 the starting point was the single 2025 factor, the updates were 0.75 per cent for qualifying participants in advanced alternative payment models and 0.25 per cent for everyone else, and the one-year increase was 2.50 per cent. Factors are published to four decimals."; HEO defines Conversion Factor as "Conversion factor (CF) is the money amount per relative value unit that turns fee schedule relative values, such as Medicare RVUs, into payment amounts.".

column2: Budget neutrality multiplier and adjusted conversion factor after a revaluation of relative value units
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conversion Factor. The module describes Budget neutrality multiplier and adjusted conversion factor after a revaluation of relative value units as "When relative value units are revised, the conversion factor is scaled so that the projected volume of services, priced at the new units, costs the same as before. The multiplier is the ratio of total weighted units before to after the change, so a cut to some services' units raises the factor and with it the fee of every service whose units were not cut. Two services are written out so that the calculator can run; SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number. This is the article's simplified version: CMS estimates the adjustment from prior-year utilisation and handles several adjustments in sequence."; HEO defines Conversion Factor as "Conversion factor (CF) is the money amount per relative value unit that turns fee schedule relative values, such as Medicare RVUs, into payment amounts.".

column2: Cost per relative value unit for a category of outpatient care in the HERC average cost method
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Conversion Factor. The module describes Cost per relative value unit for a category of outpatient care in the HERC average cost method as "Keeps Medicare's relative values as the measure of resource use but replaces Medicare's price level with a health system's own spending: total spending on a category of care divided by the total relative value units of its encounters gives a cost per unit, and each encounter is costed at that rate times its units. This is the article's simplified stylisation of the method used by HERC, the health economics unit of the US Department of Veterans Affairs, which in practice scales a hypothetical Medicare reimbursement for each visit so that the estimates tally to national VA spending."; HEO defines Conversion Factor as "Conversion factor (CF) is the money amount per relative value unit that turns fee schedule relative values, such as Medicare RVUs, into payment amounts.".

column2: Rogan-Gladen corrected prevalence from the share flagged by an imperfect algorithm
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Criterion Validity. The module describes Rogan-Gladen corrected prevalence from the share flagged by an imperfect algorithm as "The share flagged, the apparent prevalence, mixes true positives and false positives: a = Se p + (1 minus Sp)(1 minus p). Solving for p gives the Rogan-Gladen estimator, which removes the false positive rate from the flagged share and divides by Youden's index, Se + Sp minus 1. Values outside the range 0 to 1 are truncated, the usual convention, and arise when the flagged share lies below the false positive rate or above the sensitivity."; HEO defines Criterion Validity as "Criterion validity is the degree to which a measure's scores agree with a gold standard for the same concept, assessed at the same time or later.".

column2: Mean cost of an algorithm-flagged cohort weighted by the positive predictive value
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Criterion Validity. The module describes Mean cost of an algorithm-flagged cohort weighted by the positive predictive value as "When cost depends only on true disease status, the flagged cohort is a mix of true cases, in proportion PPV, and false positives, in proportion 1 minus PPV, so its mean cost is the PPV-weighted average of the two group costs. The bias against the true mean cost of cases is minus (1 minus PPV) times the cost gap. The PPV to use is the one in the population the cohort is drawn from (HE-FM-DXA-003), not the validation sample's (HE-FM-DXA-001)."; HEO defines Criterion Validity as "Criterion validity is the degree to which a measure's scores agree with a gold standard for the same concept, assessed at the same time or later.".

column2: Survey-weighted prevalence from a cross-sectional health survey with three weighting classes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Sectional Design. The module describes Survey-weighted prevalence from a cross-sectional health survey with three weighting classes as "Each respondent counts in proportion to the survey weight, which corrects for unequal selection, non-response and the population profile, so the prevalence is the weighted share of respondents with the condition, the sum over respondents i of w_i y_i divided by the sum of w_i, with y_i equal to 1 for a respondent with the condition and 0 otherwise. When respondents in a weighting class share one weight, the sum reduces to the class form below; three classes are written out so that the calculator can run, and SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number. The formula gives the point estimate only: its standard error needs the strata and primary sampling units of the design."; HEO defines Cross-Sectional Design as "A cross-sectional design is an observational design that measures exposure and outcome in a population at one point in time, often to estimate prevalence.".

column2: Steady-state point prevalence from incidence and mean duration
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Sectional Design. The module describes Steady-state point prevalence from incidence and mean duration as "In a steady state, where incidence, duration and population size are stable and there is no net migration of cases, the prevalence odds equal the incidence rate in the population at risk times the mean duration, P / (1 minus P) = I times D. Solved for P this is I D / (1 + I D). When prevalence is small, (1 minus P) is close to 1 and P is approximately I times D, the form used in the article's worked example; the approximation overstates P by the factor 1 / (1 minus P)."; HEO defines Cross-Sectional Design as "A cross-sectional design is an observational design that measures exposure and outcome in a population at one point in time, often to estimate prevalence.".

column2: Prevalence-weighted and incidence-weighted mean utility of a condition with two forms
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cross-Sectional Design. The module describes Prevalence-weighted and incidence-weighted mean utility of a condition with two forms as "In a steady state the prevalent pool holds each form of a condition in proportion to its incidence times its mean duration, so a survey of everyone currently living with the condition averages utility with those weights. A model of newly diagnosed patients needs the mean at onset, weighted by incidence alone. The prevalent shares are exact under the steady state even without the small-prevalence approximation, because the common factor (1 minus P) cancels. Two forms are written out so that the calculator can run; SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number."; HEO defines Cross-Sectional Design as "A cross-sectional design is an observational design that measures exposure and outcome in a population at one point in time, often to estimate prevalence.".

column2: Gamma unit deviance and deviance residual of one patient's cost in a generalised linear model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deviance Residual. The module describes Gamma unit deviance and deviance residual of one patient's cost in a generalised linear model as "For a gamma GLM of positive costs, the unit deviance compares the observed cost with its fitted mean through the proportional gap minus the log of their ratio, so it depends only on y / mu. The deviance residual takes its square root with the sign of y minus mu, and the squared residuals add up to the model deviance. In the Math line the sign is written (y minus mu) / |y minus mu|; at y = mu the residual is 0 by convention, a case the calculator cannot show because it divides by zero there."; HEO defines Deviance Residual as "A deviance residual is a signed measure of how poorly a generalised linear or survival model fits each patient; in a GLM its squares sum to the deviance.".

column2: Martingale residual and survival deviance residual of one patient from a fitted cumulative hazard
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Deviance Residual. The module describes Martingale residual and survival deviance residual of one patient from a fitted cumulative hazard as "The martingale residual is the event indicator minus the fitted cumulative hazard at the patient's observed time, the Cox-Snell residual. It cannot exceed 1 and has no lower bound, so it is skewed; the deviance residual rescales it to be roughly symmetric about zero. Since delta minus M equals the fitted cumulative hazard, the log term is always defined, and for a censored patient, with delta = 0, the residual reduces to minus the square root of twice the cumulative hazard. Treating delta as a Poisson count with mean H, the quantity under the square root is the Poisson unit deviance given in Stata's glm Methods and formulas, which links the survival residual to the GLM residual of HE-FM-DEVR-001."; HEO defines Deviance Residual as "A deviance residual is a signed measure of how poorly a generalised linear or survival model fits each patient; in a GLM its squares sum to the deviance.".

column2: Minimal important difference as a multiple of the baseline standard deviation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distribution-Based MID. The module describes Minimal important difference as a multiple of the baseline standard deviation as "Multiplies the baseline standard deviation of scores by a chosen multiple: 0.5 for the half standard deviation rule of Norman, Sloan and Wyrwich, or 0.2 for Cohen's small effect size benchmark. The result is in the instrument's own units and grows with the heterogeneity of the sample."; HEO defines Distribution-Based MID as "A distribution-based MID is a minimal important difference estimated from score spread or instrument reliability, such as half a standard deviation.".

column2: Standard error of measurement from the score standard deviation and reliability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distribution-Based MID. The module describes Standard error of measurement from the score standard deviation and reliability as "The standard error of measurement (SEM) is the standard deviation of scores times the square root of one minus a reliability coefficient, and estimates in the instrument's units how far an observed score is likely to stray from a person's true score. Test-retest reliability in a stable population suits change between two time points better than Cronbach's alpha. One SEM equals half a standard deviation when reliability is 0.75."; HEO defines Distribution-Based MID as "A distribution-based MID is a minimal important difference estimated from score spread or instrument reliability, such as half a standard deviation.".

column2: Minimally detectable change and reliable change index from the standard error of measurement
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distribution-Based MID. The module describes Minimally detectable change and reliable change index from the standard error of measurement as "A change score involves two measurements, so its standard error is the square root of 2 times the SEM. The minimally detectable change (MDC) is 1.96 of these standard errors, the 95 per cent limit for no change, and the reliable change index (RC) of Jacobson and Truax divides one person's change by the same standard error; a value beyond 1.96 in either direction would arise from measurement error alone with probability of 5 per cent or less. Both thresholds apply to one person's change, not to a difference in group means."; HEO defines Distribution-Based MID as "A distribution-based MID is a minimal important difference estimated from score spread or instrument reliability, such as half a standard deviation.".

column2: Disutility as a utility decrement from a stated baseline and its QALY loss over the harm's duration
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disutility. The module describes Disutility as a utility decrement from a stated baseline and its QALY loss over the harm's duration as "A disutility is the baseline utility without the harm minus the utility with it, both from the same instrument and value set, and the QALY loss is the decrement times the time the harm lasts. Some studies report decrements as negative numbers; here a loss is positive."; HEO defines Disutility as "Disutility is the loss of utility caused by a health state, adverse event or treatment, measured from a stated baseline and used to reduce QALYs.".

column2: Utility of two conditions combined by the additive, multiplicative and minimum rules on a shared baseline
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disutility. The module describes Utility of two conditions combined by the additive, multiplicative and minimum rules on a shared baseline as "When utilities exist only for people with one condition each, TSD 12 sets out three conventional estimates for people with both: the additive rule subtracts both absolute decrements, the multiplicative rule applies both proportional effects, and the minimum rule assumes no further loss beyond the worse single condition. With a shared baseline U_0 the multiplicative value equals U_0 minus d_A minus d_B plus d_A d_B / U_0, so with two positive decrements it is higher than the additive value by d_A d_B / U_0. TSD 12 advises the multiplicative rule when combined data are unavailable."; HEO defines Disutility as "Disutility is the loss of utility caused by a health state, adverse event or treatment, measured from a stated baseline and used to reduce QALYs.".

column2: QALY gain and cost per QALY from avoiding a second condition under a chosen combination rule
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disutility. The module describes QALY gain and cost per QALY from avoiding a second condition under a chosen combination rule as "A person who avoids condition B stays at the utility of condition A alone instead of the combined utility, so the QALY gain per case avoided is the difference times the years B would have lasted, and the cost per QALY gained divides the cost per case avoided by that gain. The combined utility comes from HE-FM-DISU-002 under the rule chosen."; HEO defines Disutility as "Disutility is the loss of utility caused by a health state, adverse event or treatment, measured from a stated baseline and used to reduce QALYs.".

column2: Ara and Brazier general population EQ-5D baseline by age and sex with a proportional decrement
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disutility. The module describes Ara and Brazier general population EQ-5D baseline by age and sex with a proportional decrement as "Ara and Brazier's regression of EQ-5D index scores from the 2003 and 2006 Health Survey for England gives mean general population utility as a quadratic in age with a shift for men. Applying a proportional decrement m to this baseline, as the multiplicative rule does, makes the absolute loss shrink as the baseline falls with age, whereas a fixed additive decrement costs the same at every age. The equation is shown for illustration; PMG36 asks for a recent source, and the norms used should match the instrument and value set of the other utilities."; HEO defines Disutility as "Disutility is the loss of utility caused by a health state, adverse event or treatment, measured from a stated baseline and used to reduce QALYs.".

column2: Expected response at a dose under the sigmoid Emax model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dose Response. The module describes Expected response at a dose under the sigmoid Emax model as "The sigmoid Emax model, the standard four-parameter dose-response curve, rises from the placebo response E_0 towards E_0 plus E_max, reaching half the maximum added effect at the dose ED_50; the Hill coefficient h sets how steeply it rises around ED_50, and with h = 1 it reduces to the hyperbolic Emax model. Because acquisition cost usually rises in proportion to dose while the effect flattens, each extra milligram buys less response than the one before once the dose is past the steep part of the curve."; HEO defines Dose Response as "Dose response is the relationship between the amount of a drug or exposure and the size or probability of its effect, used in dose selection and HTA.".

column2: Share of the maximum added effect at a dose expressed as a multiple of ED50
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dose Response. The module describes Share of the maximum added effect at a dose expressed as a multiple of ED50 as "Dividing the added effect by E_max shows that the share of the maximum depends only on k, the dose as a multiple of ED_50, and on the Hill coefficient. At k = 1 the share is one half for any h; above ED_50 a larger h gives a larger share."; HEO defines Dose Response as "Dose response is the relationship between the amount of a drug or exposure and the size or probability of its effect, used in dose selection and HTA.".

column2: Drug cost of one administration with whole single-use vials and with vial sharing
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dose Response. The module describes Drug cost of one administration with whole single-use vials and with vial sharing as "When the dose is set by weight or body surface area and the drug comes in single-use vials, the amount paid for is the vials opened: n_v is the dose divided by the vial content rounded up to a whole number. With vial sharing, or payment per mg used, the cost is in proportion to the dose, and the difference is the cost of the drug discarded. The calculator has no rounding-up function, so n_v is entered."; HEO defines Dose Response as "Dose response is the relationship between the amount of a drug or exposure and the size or probability of its effect, used in dose selection and HTA.".

column2: Drug cost per cycle scaled by relative dose intensity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dose Response. The module describes Drug cost per cycle scaled by relative dose intensity as "Relative dose intensity (RDI) is the delivered dose per unit of time divided by the planned dose per unit of time, and models multiply the cost of the planned dose for a cycle by it to reflect dose reductions, delays and missed doses."; HEO defines Dose Response as "Dose response is the relationship between the amount of a drug or exposure and the size or probability of its effect, used in dose selection and HTA.".

column2: Incremental cost per QALY of a programme with two cost instalments and one later QALY gain under separate cost and health rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Differential Discounting. The module describes Incremental cost per QALY of a programme with two cost instalments and one later QALY gain under separate cost and health rates as "Discounts a cost paid at the start (year 0) and a second cost in year a at the cost rate, discounts a QALY gain that arrives in year b at the health rate, and divides the discounted cost by the discounted QALY gain. It is the article's prevention programme, whose costs fall early and whose health gain falls late, so the pair of rates can change its ratio a great deal; a treatment with all its cost in year 0 is the special case with no second instalment."; HEO defines Differential Discounting as "Differential discounting applies a lower annual discount rate to future health effects, such as QALYs, than to future costs in an economic evaluation.".

column2: Health discount rate from the cost discount rate and growth in the consumption value of health
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Differential Discounting. The module describes Health discount rate from the cost discount rate and growth in the consumption value of health as "When the money value of a unit of health grows at g_v a year, discounting the volume of health at r_H gives the same present value as inflating each year's QALYs at g_v and discounting them at the cost rate, provided one plus r_H equals one plus r_C divided by one plus g_v. Gravelle and Smith derive this exact form and summarise it as the cost rate minus the growth rate, the subtraction rule the Dutch guideline uses."; HEO defines Differential Discounting as "Differential discounting applies a lower annual discount rate to future health effects, such as QALYs, than to future costs in an economic evaluation.".

column2: Effective cost discount rate and health forgone when the cost-effectiveness threshold grows
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Differential Discounting. The module describes Effective cost discount rate and health forgone when the cost-effectiveness threshold grows as "With a fixed budget, a cost in year t displaces health equal to the cost divided by the threshold in that year, and the forgone health is then discounted at the health rate. If the threshold grows at g_k a year, a pound spent later displaces less health, so costs carry an effective rate r_C_star with one plus r_C_star equal to (one plus r_H) times (one plus g_k), approximately the health rate plus the threshold growth."; HEO defines Differential Discounting as "Differential discounting applies a lower annual discount rate to future health effects, such as QALYs, than to future costs in an economic evaluation.".

column2: Change in a programme's discounted cost per QALY when the whole programme is delayed under differential rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Differential Discounting. The module describes Change in a programme's discounted cost per QALY when the whole programme is delayed under differential rates as "Moving every cost and QALY of a programme s years later multiplies its discounted cost by (1 + r_C)^(-s) and its discounted QALYs by (1 + r_H)^(-s), so the ratio is multiplied by ((1 + r_H) / (1 + r_C))^s. The factor is below one whenever the health rate is below the cost rate, so the ratio improves with every year of delay, the postponement paradox of Keeler and Cretin; under equal rates it is one."; HEO defines Differential Discounting as "Differential discounting applies a lower annual discount rate to future health effects, such as QALYs, than to future costs in an economic evaluation.".

column2: Mean, variance, covariance and correlation of two components of a three-destination Dirichlet row
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dirichlet Distribution. The module describes Mean, variance, covariance and correlation of two components of a three-destination Dirichlet row as "For a row with parameters alpha_1, alpha_2 and alpha_3, the mean of each component is its parameter over the sum alpha_0, the variances and covariances shrink as alpha_0 grows, and every covariance is negative, so a sampled row that sends more of the cohort to one destination sends less to the others. The correlation depends only on the means, while alpha_0 sets the precision."; HEO defines Dirichlet Distribution as "The Dirichlet distribution is a multivariate distribution for proportions that sum to one, used for uncertain transition probabilities from a model state.".

column2: Dirichlet posterior parameter, mean and beta marginal for one destination from transition counts and a Dirichlet prior
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Dirichlet Distribution. The module describes Dirichlet posterior parameter, mean and beta marginal for one destination from transition counts and a Dirichlet prior as "A Dirichlet prior combined with multinomial counts gives a Dirichlet posterior in which each parameter is its prior parameter plus its count. The posterior mean of one destination is that parameter over the prior total plus the number of patients, and the destination's probability on its own follows Beta(alpha_j, alpha_0 minus alpha_j), whose second parameter is written b_j here. A zero prior reproduces the observed proportions; a prior of one per destination is uniform over all valid rows."; HEO defines Dirichlet Distribution as "The Dirichlet distribution is a multivariate distribution for proportions that sum to one, used for uncertain transition probabilities from a model state.".

column2: Between-group minimal important difference from mean changes in two anchor groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference. The module describes Between-group minimal important difference from mean changes in two anchor groups as "Subtracts the mean change of patients who rate themselves about the same from the mean change of patients who rate themselves a little better (or a little worse, for deterioration). The mean change of the minimally improved group on its own is the Jaeschke estimate of a within-person change; the difference between the two groups is, in the terms of Terwee and colleagues, a minimal important difference between groups, the quantity suited to a difference between trial arms."; HEO defines Minimal Clinically Important Difference as "The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as important, beneficial or harmful.".

column2: Sensitivity, specificity and misclassification of one candidate change-score cut-off against an anchor
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference. The module describes Sensitivity, specificity and misclassification of one candidate change-score cut-off against an anchor as "Treats the change score as a diagnostic test and the anchor as the reference standard. At a candidate cut-off, sensitivity is the share of anchor-improved patients whose change reaches it and specificity the share of all other patients whose change falls below it; the ROC cut-off is the candidate with the smallest sum of the two misclassification proportions, the same as the largest Youden index."; HEO defines Minimal Clinically Important Difference as "The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as important, beneficial or harmful.".

column2: Ninety-five per cent limit cut-off above the change scores of patients not importantly changed
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference. The module describes Ninety-five per cent limit cut-off above the change scores of patients not importantly changed as "Places the threshold for improvement at the mean change of the patients the anchor classes as not importantly changed plus 1.645 standard deviations of their change scores, the one-sided 95 per cent point of a normal distribution. De Vet and colleagues note that it corresponds to 95 per cent specificity on the ROC curve, so it is stricter than the ROC cut-off."; HEO defines Minimal Clinically Important Difference as "The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as important, beneficial or harmful.".

column2: Shares of each trial arm reaching a responder threshold when changes are normal with a common standard deviation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference. The module describes Shares of each trial arm reaching a responder threshold when changes are normal with a common standard deviation as "If changes in each arm are normally distributed with a common standard deviation, the share of an arm reaching a threshold is one minus the standard normal distribution function at the threshold's distance from the arm's mean in standard deviations, and the responder difference is the treated share minus the control share. The site's calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_C and Phi_T, its values at z_C and z_T, are entered as inputs (NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) in Excel, pnorm(z) in R)."; HEO defines Minimal Clinically Important Difference as "The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as important, beneficial or harmful.".

column2: Patients per arm for a two-arm trial with a continuous outcome and a minimal important difference as the target
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference. The module describes Patients per arm for a two-arm trial with a continuous outcome and a minimal important difference as the target as "The usual normal approximation for two equal arms and a two-sided test sets the number per arm to twice the squared sum of the two standard normal quantiles, times the outcome variance, over the squared target difference. Because the target is a difference between arms, a between-group estimate such as MID_between is the relevant MCID; halving it quadruples the trial."; HEO defines Minimal Clinically Important Difference as "The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as important, beneficial or harmful.".

column2: Six-month matrix as the square root of a progressive three-state annual transition matrix
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Transition Matrix. The module describes Six-month matrix as the square root of a progressive three-state annual transition matrix as "For a progressive model with states progression-free (1), progressed (2) and dead (3), no return from 2 to 1 and death absorbing, the annual matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries and the square root has diagonal entries equal to their square roots. The progression entry follows from requiring the root squared to return the annual progression probability, the death entries are the row remainders, and two six-month cycles then reproduce every entry of the annual matrix."; HEO defines Transition Matrix as "A transition matrix is the table of probabilities of moving between, or staying in, health states in one cycle of a Markov model, with rows summing to one.".

column2: Incidence-based years lived with disability for one sequela without discounting
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years Lived with Disability. The module describes Incidence-based years lived with disability for one sequela without discounting as "Counts the new cases of a sequela in the reference year and multiplies them by the disability weight and by the average duration of a case until remission or death, so all of each case's future health loss is assigned to the year, and the age, in which it begins. This is the form used by the GBD 1990 study and WHO's updates before 2010, here without their discounting and age weighting."; HEO defines Years Lived with Disability as "Years lived with disability (YLDs) measure non-fatal health loss, usually as prevalence times disability weight; adding years of life lost gives the DALY.".

column2: Continuously discounted years lived with disability per incident case and for a cohort of new cases
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years Lived with Disability. The module describes Continuously discounted years lived with disability per incident case and for a cohort of new cases as "Under the pre-2010 convention each new case's future years with the condition were discounted from onset. With continuous discounting at rate r and no age weighting, L years at weight DW are worth DW times (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r present years, so a long-lasting condition loses most in the conversion."; HEO defines Years Lived with Disability as "Years lived with disability (YLDs) measure non-fatal health loss, usually as prevalence times disability weight; adding years of life lost gives the DALY.".

column2: Prevalence-based years lived with disability k years after incidence of a fixed-duration condition changes
