column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years Lived with Disability. The module describes Prevalence-based years lived with disability k years after incidence of a fixed-duration condition changes as "For a condition that lasts exactly L years, the people living with it in the reference year are the last L annual cohorts. If incidence changed from I_old to I_new k years ago, with this year counted as one of the k, then k cohorts are of the new size and L minus k of the old, and the prevalence-based count is their person-years times the weight. It reaches the new incidence-based count only when the last of the old cohorts has recovered, L years after the change."; HEO defines Years Lived with Disability as "Years lived with disability (YLDs) measure non-fatal health loss, usually as prevalence times disability weight; adding years of life lost gives the DALY.".

column2: Cohort recursion through a chain of one-cycle tunnel states and a long-term state
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Tunnel State. The module describes Cohort recursion through a chain of one-cycle tunnel states and a long-term state as "Moves the cohort one cycle through a tunnel of K one-cycle states T_1 to T_K feeding a long-term state L. New entrants from every state with a route into the tunnel collect in T_1; everyone in T_k who neither dies nor leaves by another route moves to T_(k+1), so no one stays in a tunnel state for a second cycle; survivors of T_K join those who stay in L. These are the tunnel rows of the expanded transition matrix written out, with a zero on each tunnel diagonal. Summing T_1 to L gives the clinical state for reporting, while each column keeps its own cost and utility."; HEO defines Tunnel State as "A tunnel state is one of a fixed sequence of one-cycle temporary states in a Markov model, letting risks, costs or utilities vary with time in a state.".

column2: Number of states in a cohort model after splitting one state into a tunnel
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Tunnel State. The module describes Number of states in a cohort model after splitting one state into a tunnel as "Gives the size of the expanded model when one state is replaced by a chain of tunnel states. Following Alarid-Escudero and colleagues, n_tunnels counts every state the original state is split into, including the long-term state, so with K one-cycle tunnel states n_tunnels is K+1. One is subtracted because the tunnel replaces the original state. The expanded transition matrix has n_S_tunnels rows and columns."; HEO defines Tunnel State as "A tunnel state is one of a fixed sequence of one-cycle temporary states in a Markov model, letting risks, costs or utilities vary with time in a state.".

column2: Average per-cycle death probability across three tunnel states and a long-term state
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Tunnel State. The module describes Average per-cycle death probability across three tunnel states and a long-term state as "Gives the share of people in a tunnelled clinical state who die in the next cycle, as the occupancy-weighted mean of the probabilities in T1, T2, T3 and L. Here m_T1 to m_L are the values m_(T_k,t) and m_(L,t) of HE-FM-TUN-001 at one cycle, and q_k equals 1 minus s_k when death is the only exit. The average depends on when people entered, which is why a single memoryless state with a cycle-specific probability cannot reproduce a tunnel once entry is staggered. Longer tunnels add one term to each sum for each extra state."; HEO defines Tunnel State as "A tunnel state is one of a fixed sequence of one-cycle temporary states in a Markov model, letting risks, costs or utilities vary with time in a state.".

column2: Three-state occupancy from PFS and OS curves in a partitioned survival model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Partitioned Survival Model. The module describes Three-state occupancy from PFS and OS curves in a partitioned survival model as "Gives the proportions progression-free, progressed and dead at time t from the PFS and OS survival functions of one treatment arm. The PFS curve gives the progression-free share directly, the dead share is 1 minus OS, and the progressed share is the gap between the two curves. Each arm has its own pair of curves."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: Four-state occupancy with a time to treatment discontinuation curve
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Partitioned Survival Model. The module describes Four-state occupancy with a time to treatment discontinuation curve as "Extends the three-state partition with a third curve, time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), which splits progression-free time into on-treatment and off-treatment states. It applies the general N-state rule of TSD 19: the first state is its own curve, each later alive state is its curve minus the curve of the state before it, and the dead state is 1 minus OS. Five of the appraisals reviewed in TSD 19 used this structure."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: Partitioned survival QALYs as utility-weighted areas under PFS and OS
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Partitioned Survival Model. The module describes Partitioned survival QALYs as utility-weighted areas under PFS and OS as "Values mean progression-free time at the progression-free utility and mean progressed time, the area between the OS and PFS curves, at the progressed utility; death carries zero. A_PF and A_OS are the areas under the PFS and OS curves up to the time horizon, which equal mean progression-free and overall survival when the horizon is lifetime. Within follow-up an area can come from a Kaplan-Meier curve (HE-FM-ADMC-003) and beyond it from a fitted parametric curve. Costs follow the same pattern, and discounting weights each part of the curves before the areas are taken (HE-FM-DR-002)."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: Lifetime partitioned survival QALYs with exponential PFS and OS curves
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Partitioned Survival Model. The module describes Lifetime partitioned survival QALYs with exponential PFS and OS curves as "Closed form of HE-FM-PSM-003 when both curves are exponential and the horizon is lifetime. The area under an exponential curve with constant hazard lambda is 1 divided by lambda, or 1 divided by (lambda + rho) when time is discounted continuously at rate rho. Setting rho to 0 gives undiscounted results; rho = log(1 + d) converts an annual rate d (HE-FM-CONT-003)."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: Partitioned survival QALYs with utilities by time to death
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Partitioned Survival Model. The module describes Partitioned survival QALYs with utilities by time to death as "Values time alive by closeness to death instead of by progression status, using only the OS curve. Over a lifetime horizon each person's time in the final window of length a before death is the smaller of a and their survival time, and its mean W is the area under the OS curve from 0 to a. For an exponential OS curve W is (1 minus exp(minus lambda_OS a)) divided by lambda_OS, and the remaining 1 divided by lambda_OS minus W years are valued at the utility for time further from death."; HEO defines Partitioned Survival Model as "A partitioned survival model is a cancer economic model that uses PFS and OS curves to split a cohort into progression-free, progressed and dead states.".

column2: Discounted fundamental matrix of a time-homogeneous Markov chain at a constant discount rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Chain. The module describes Discounted fundamental matrix of a time-homogeneous Markov chain at a constant discount rate as "Discounting membership at the start of cycle k by (1 + r) to the power minus k Delta multiplies every cycle by the same factor, so the discount folds into Q and the series of discounted powers of Q sums to a matrix inverse. Entry i, j of N_disc is the expected discounted number of cycles spent in transient state j by a person starting in transient state i, with the starting cycle counted in full and undiscounted. The row sums t_disc are the discounted expected cycles before absorption, which with death as the only absorbing state is discounted life expectancy in cycles. With r equal to zero the formula returns the fundamental matrix of HE-FM-ABS-001."; HEO defines Markov Chain as "A Markov chain is a random process moving between states in which the next state depends only on the current state. It underlies Markov cohort models.".

column2: Episode decomposition of time in a re-enterable state of a Markov chain
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Chain. The module describes Episode decomposition of time in a re-enterable state of a Markov chain as "Splits the expected time that a person starting in transient state i spends in another transient state j into the expected number of separate episodes in j and the mean length of each episode, and gives the probability of ever entering j. Each cycle begun in i leads into j with probability p_ij, so the expected number of entries is n_ii, the expected cycles in i from the fundamental matrix of HE-FM-ABS-001, times p_ij; n_ii already includes the cycles spent in i after each return from j. Each episode lasts a geometric number of cycles with mean 1 divided by 1 minus p_jj."; HEO defines Markov Chain as "A Markov chain is a random process moving between states in which the next state depends only on the current state. It underlies Markov cohort models.".

column2: Mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cure Rate Model. The module describes Mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form as "Writes all-cause survival at time t as the expected survival of the matched general population multiplied by relative survival, which is the cure fraction plus the uncured share times the survival of the uncured from the excess hazard. As the uncured die out, relative survival falls to pi and all-cause survival to S_star times pi. This is equation 11 of NICE DSU TSD 21."; HEO defines Cure Rate Model as "A cure rate model is a survival model that estimates the cure fraction and survival of uncured patients, used in HTA to extrapolate long-term survival.".

column2: Non-mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cure Rate Model. The module describes Non-mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form as "Bounds the excess cumulative hazard instead of splitting the cohort: relative survival is the cure fraction raised to the power F_z(t), a cumulative distribution function that is 0 at the start and approaches 1 as time tends to infinity, so relative survival falls from 1 towards pi. Multiplying by expected survival gives all-cause survival. TSD 21 gives pi to the power F_z(t) as equation 12 and notes that the model extends to the relative survival setting in the same way as the mixture model."; HEO defines Cure Rate Model as "A cure rate model is a survival model that estimates the cure fraction and survival of uncured patients, used in HTA to extrapolate long-term survival.".

column2: Mean overall survival as a cure-fraction weighted average of group means
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cure Rate Model. The module describes Mean overall survival as a cure-fraction weighted average of group means as "Mean survival of a population with a cure fraction is the weighted average of the mean survival of cured and uncured patients, weighted by their proportions. E_B is the area under background survival S_star(t) and E_U the area under S_star(t) times S_u(t). Because T_bar is linear in pi, each unit of cure fraction adds E_B minus E_U years."; HEO defines Cure Rate Model as "A cure rate model is a survival model that estimates the cure fraction and survival of uncured patients, used in HTA to extrapolate long-term survival.".

column2: Discounted QALYs from a cure fraction under constant background and excess hazards
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cure Rate Model. The module describes Discounted QALYs from a cure fraction under constant background and excess hazards as "Values each group's survival with a constant utility and discounts it continuously at rate r. With exponential survival the area under exp(minus h t) times exp(minus r t) is 1/(h plus r), so each group's discounted mean is one over its total hazard plus r. With r = 0 and both utilities 1 the formula returns T_bar of HE-FM-CRM-003. The continuous rate equivalent to an annual rate d is r = log(1 plus d), HE-FM-CONT-003."; HEO defines Cure Rate Model as "A cure rate model is a survival model that estimates the cure fraction and survival of uncured patients, used in HTA to extrapolate long-term survival.".

column2: Expected value of a product of two correlated quantities
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value. The module describes Expected value of a product of two correlated quantities as "Gives the expected value of a product, such as the number of admissions times the cost per admission, from the two means and their covariance. The identity is exact for any joint distribution with finite variances. The product of the means equals the expected product only when the covariance is zero, for example when the two quantities are independent; a positive covariance raises the expected product above the product of the means and a negative one lowers it."; HEO defines Expected Value as "Expected value is the probability-weighted mean of an uncertain outcome, such as a cost or QALY total, across all its possible values.".

column2: Second-order approximation to the expected value of a curved model output
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value. The module describes Second-order approximation to the expected value of a curved model output as "Approximates the expected value of an output g(theta) that depends on one uncertain parameter by its value at the parameter mean plus half its second derivative at the mean times the parameter variance. The correction shows the direction of Jensen's inequality: it is negative for a concave output, positive for a convex one and zero for a linear one. With several parameters the article's double sum adds a term for each pair, weighted by their covariance; for the product N times U the only second derivative is the cross term, equal to 1, so the expansion is exact and gives HE-FM-EV-001. The approximation indicates sign and rough size; the simulated mean (HE-FM-ENB-001) or a closed form is the estimate."; HEO defines Expected Value as "Expected value is the probability-weighted mean of an uncertain outcome, such as a cost or QALY total, across all its possible values.".

column2: Expected survival and event probability under a gamma-distributed constant hazard
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value. The module describes Expected survival and event probability under a gamma-distributed constant hazard as "When a constant hazard h is uncertain and follows a gamma distribution with shape k and scale s, so that its mean is k times s and its variance k times s squared, the expected value of exp(minus h t) is the gamma Laplace transform evaluated at t, and the expected event probability over the horizon t is one minus that value. It replaces the deterministic 1 minus exp(minus h t) at the mean hazard (HE-FM-TP-001), which overstates the expected probability because the probability is concave in h. The same identity gives population survival under a gamma frailty with a constant baseline hazard."; HEO defines Expected Value as "Expected value is the probability-weighted mean of an uncertain outcome, such as a cost or QALY total, across all its possible values.".

column2: Mean and median of a log-normal cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value. The module describes Mean and median of a log-normal cost as "When the natural log of cost is normally distributed with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the median cost and the geometric mean cost both equal exp(mu), and the expected cost is the median multiplied by exp(sigma squared over 2). The factor is Jensen's inequality for the convex exponential: exponentiating the mean log cost returns the median, not the mean. The expected cost is the figure that, multiplied by the number of patients, gives the total budget."; HEO defines Expected Value as "Expected value is the probability-weighted mean of an uncertain outcome, such as a cost or QALY total, across all its possible values.".

column2: Years of life lost from deaths in one age group under a standard life table
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years of Life Lost. The module describes Years of life lost from deaths in one age group under a standard life table as "Multiplies the deaths from a cause in one age group by the standard remaining life expectancy for that age group, the years of life lost per death in the standard life table. Summing the products over age groups gives the cause's total, as in the computational function below. GBD 2021 calculated YLLs this way for each cause, age, sex, location and year; GBD 2010 dropped discounting and age weighting."; HEO defines Years of Life Lost as "Years of life lost (YLL) measure premature mortality as deaths times standard remaining life expectancy at the age of death, the fatal part of the DALY.".

column2: Potential years of life lost before a cut-off age for deaths in one age group
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years of Life Lost. The module describes Potential years of life lost before a cut-off age for deaths in one age group as "Counts, for each death before a cut-off age, the years between the midpoint of its age group and the cut-off, and nothing for deaths at or above the cut-off, following the method described by the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Unlike HE-FM-YLL-001 it uses no life table, so deaths in old age drop out of the total. The function max returns the larger of its arguments."; HEO defines Years of Life Lost as "Years of life lost (YLL) measure premature mortality as deaths times standard remaining life expectancy at the age of death, the fatal part of the DALY.".

column2: Continuously discounted years of life lost per death and for a group of deaths
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Years of Life Lost. The module describes Continuously discounted years of life lost per death and for a group of deaths as "Before GBD 2010 the standard DALY discounted future years at 3 per cent a year. With continuous discounting from the time of death and no age weighting, the L standard years remaining at the age of death are worth (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r present years, so discounting reduces the loss from a young death much more than from an old one. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Years of Life Lost as "Years of life lost (YLL) measure premature mortality as deaths times standard remaining life expectancy at the age of death, the fatal part of the DALY.".

column2: Incremental utility-cost ratio in QALYs gained per one million of net expenditure
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Incremental Cost-Utility Ratio. The module describes Incremental utility-cost ratio in QALYs gained per one million of net expenditure as "Divides the incremental QALYs by the incremental cost, both taken as the intervention minus the comparator and both discounted, and multiplies by one million. PHARMAC calls the result the incremental utility-cost ratio (IUCR) and describes the incremental cost per QALY as in effect its inverse, so 1,000,000 divided by the IUCR returns the ICUR of HE-FM-CUA-001. For a QALY gain at extra cost a higher IUCR indicates better value, the opposite direction to the ICUR."; HEO defines Incremental Cost-Utility Ratio as "The incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR) is the ICER of a cost-utility analysis: extra cost over a comparator divided by extra QALYs gained.".

column2: Log risk ratio and its variance from the two-by-two counts of one head-to-head trial
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pairwise Meta-Analysis. The module describes Log risk ratio and its variance from the two-by-two counts of one head-to-head trial as "Divides the risk of the event on drug A, a/n1, by the risk on drug B, c/n2, takes the natural log, and computes the variance of the log risk ratio as one over a plus one over c, minus one over n1 and one over n2. This is the square of the standard error of the log risk ratio in the RevMan statistical algorithms, and one over v is the trial's inverse-variance weight in HE-FM-ADMA-001. The formula is applied to each trial in turn, so the trial subscript i of the article is dropped; y and v become the y_i and v_i that the pooling records take."; HEO defines Pairwise Meta-Analysis as "Pairwise meta-analysis is the statistical pooling of trials of the same two treatments, such as head-to-head RCTs, into one estimate of relative effect.".

column2: Wagstaff normalised concentration index for a binary health variable
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Concentration Index. The module describes Wagstaff normalised concentration index for a binary health variable as "For a variable that takes only the values 0 and 1, such as being ill, immunised or dead, the concentration index is bounded below by the mean minus 1 and above by 1 minus the mean in large samples, so its feasible range shrinks as the mean rises (Wagstaff 2005). Dividing the index by 1 minus the mean restores a range of minus 1 to 1, so indices for binary outcomes with different means can be compared. The sign is unchanged: a negative value still means that the variable is concentrated among the poor."; HEO defines Concentration Index as "The concentration index measures socioeconomic inequality in a health variable; a negative value means it is disproportionately held by the poor.".

column2: Erreygers corrected concentration index for a bounded health variable
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Concentration Index. The module describes Erreygers corrected concentration index for a bounded health variable as "Multiplies the standard concentration index by 4 times the mean and divides by the range of the measurement scale, b minus a. Because C equals 2 cov_hr / mu, the corrected index also equals 8 times the covariance of health and fractional rank divided by b minus a, a scaled version of the generalised concentration index mu C. Erreygers designed it to satisfy four requirements: transfer, level independence, cardinal invariance and mirror. For a binary variable a is 0 and b is 1."; HEO defines Concentration Index as "The concentration index measures socioeconomic inequality in a health variable; a negative value means it is disproportionately held by the poor.".

column2: Prevalence ratio from a cross-sectional two-by-two table
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Prevalence Ratio. The module describes Prevalence ratio from a cross-sectional two-by-two table as "Divides the proportion of exposed people who have the condition by the proportion of unexposed people who have it, using the four cells of a cross-sectional two-by-two table with exposure in rows. A value of 1 means the condition is equally common in both groups, above 1 more common among the exposed and below 1 less common. Because P_1 cannot exceed 1, the ratio cannot exceed 1 / P_0."; HEO defines Prevalence Ratio as "The prevalence ratio (PR) is the prevalence of a condition in an exposed group divided by that in an unexposed group, used to compare disease burden.".

column2: Prevalence odds ratio from a prevalence ratio and the unexposed prevalence
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Prevalence Ratio. The module describes Prevalence odds ratio from a prevalence ratio and the unexposed prevalence as "Converts a prevalence ratio into the prevalence odds ratio that logistic regression reports for the same cross-sectional data, given the prevalence among the unexposed. The cross-product a d / (b c) of the two-by-two table gives the same value. The factor (1 minus P_0) / (1 minus P_1) exceeds 1 whenever P_1 exceeds P_0 and falls below 1 whenever P_1 is lower, so the POR lies further from 1 than the PR whenever the two prevalences differ."; HEO defines Prevalence Ratio as "The prevalence ratio (PR) is the prevalence of a condition in an exposed group divided by that in an unexposed group, used to compare disease burden.".

column2: Population attributable fraction of prevalent cases from a prevalence ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Prevalence Ratio. The module describes Population attributable fraction of prevalent cases from a prevalence ratio as "Applies the attributable-risk formula that Jo describes for top-down cost-of-illness studies, with the crude prevalence ratio in place of the relative risk. With cross-sectional evidence the result equals (P minus P_0) / P, the share of prevalent cases in excess of the unexposed prevalence, so it refers to prevalent cases and their annual costs, not to new cases and lifetime costs. Multiplying it by aggregate annual costs gives the top-down attributable burden HE-FM-COI-002."; HEO defines Prevalence Ratio as "The prevalence ratio (PR) is the prevalence of a condition in an exposed group divided by that in an unexposed group, used to compare disease burden.".

column2: Subgroup prevalences from an overall prevalence, an exposed share and a prevalence ratio
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Prevalence Ratio. The module describes Subgroup prevalences from an overall prevalence, an exposed share and a prevalence ratio as "Recovers the prevalence among the unexposed and among the exposed when local records give only the overall prevalence and the exposure mix, and a published PR gives the relative prevalence. It rearranges P = e P_1 + (1 minus e) P_0 with P_1 = PR x P_0, and multiplies the exposed prevalence by the exposed population to size an eligible population for a budget impact analysis."; HEO defines Prevalence Ratio as "The prevalence ratio (PR) is the prevalence of a condition in an exposed group divided by that in an unexposed group, used to compare disease burden.".

column2: Economically justifiable price per unit and per patient at one threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Economically Justifiable Price. The module describes Economically justifiable price per unit and per patient at one threshold as "Splits the incremental cost per patient into the medicine's acquisition cost, U units at the price EJP, and every other cost difference, Delta_C_other. Setting the ICER, EJP times U plus Delta_C_other, all divided by Delta_E, equal to the threshold lambda and solving gives the per-patient EJP, lambda times Delta_E minus Delta_C_other: the most the payer could spend on the medicine for each patient. Dividing by U gives the EJP per unit, so with U equal to 1 the two results coincide. When Delta_C_other equals or exceeds lambda times Delta_E both are zero or negative, and no positive price makes the medicine cost-effective at that threshold."; HEO defines Economically Justifiable Price as "The economically justifiable price (EJP) is the top price a manufacturer can defend on cost-effectiveness grounds at a given payer's threshold.".

column2: Economically justifiable price range between a lower and an upper threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Economically Justifiable Price. The module describes Economically justifiable price range between a lower and an upper threshold as "Applies HE-FM-EJP-001 at two thresholds to give the range of justifiable prices per unit that an EJP analysis reports, for example at the ends of NICE's GBP 25,000 to GBP 35,000 per QALY range (PMG36 sections 6.3.4 to 6.3.8). The range is the gap between the thresholds times Delta_E divided by U wide, so it widens with the QALY gain, and each extra 0.1 QALY raises each end by its threshold times 0.1 divided by U."; HEO defines Economically Justifiable Price as "The economically justifiable price (EJP) is the top price a manufacturer can defend on cost-effectiveness grounds at a given payer's threshold.".

column2: Severity-weighted economically justifiable price under NICE QALY weights
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Economically Justifiable Price. The module describes Severity-weighted economically justifiable price under NICE QALY weights as "NICE's committee may apply a greater weight to QALYs for conditions with a high degree of severity, 1.2 or 1.7 depending on the absolute and proportional QALY shortfall (PMG36 sections 6.2.16 to 6.2.18). Multiplying Delta_E by the weight w in HE-FM-EJP-001 raises the EJP by w minus 1, times lambda times Delta_E, divided by U. With w equal to 1 the formula returns the unweighted EJP."; HEO defines Economically Justifiable Price as "The economically justifiable price (EJP) is the top price a manufacturer can defend on cost-effectiveness grounds at a given payer's threshold.".

column2: Analysed final-visit mean after LOCF as a mixture of the earlier and final means
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Last Observation Carried Forward. The module describes Analysed final-visit mean after LOCF as a mixture of the earlier and final means as "When a fraction tau of final-visit values is missing completely at random and replaced by values from an earlier visit, the completed final-visit data are a mixture of two distributions. Their expected mean, mu_tilde, is tau times the mean at the earlier visit plus one minus tau times the true final-visit mean (Lachin 2016, equation 1). The bias, mu_tilde minus mu_end, is tau times the change in the mean between the two visits, so it is zero only when the mean does not change after the last observed visit."; HEO defines Last Observation Carried Forward as "Last observation carried forward (LOCF) fills missing trial follow-up values with each participant's last observed value, assuming no change after dropout.".

column2: Bias of the LOCF between-arm difference with unequal dropout fractions
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Last Observation Carried Forward. The module describes Bias of the LOCF between-arm difference with unequal dropout fractions as "Applies the mixture mean of HE-FM-LOCF-001 to each arm with its own fraction imputed and subtracts. The analysed difference, Delta_tilde, departs from the true final difference, Delta, by the treatment arm's bias minus the control arm's bias. With equal fractions the analysed difference reduces to tau times the earlier difference plus one minus tau times the final difference (Lachin 2016, equation 5), which is too large when the earlier difference exceeds the final one and too small when it is smaller. With unequal fractions that rule no longer holds."; HEO defines Last Observation Carried Forward as "Last observation carried forward (LOCF) fills missing trial follow-up values with each participant's last observed value, assuming no change after dropout.".

column2: Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the end of each year
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discounting. The module describes Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the end of each year as "Gives the present value of the same amount q in each of T years when each year's amount is counted at the end of that year, so the first year carries the factor 1/(1 + r) and the last 1/(1 + r)^T. The fraction (1 minus (1 + r) to the power minus T) divided by r is the sum of the T yearly discount factors, the annuity form in the article's worked example. It tends to T as r falls towards zero, where the closed form itself cannot be evaluated."; HEO defines Discounting as "Discounting converts future costs and health effects, such as QALYs, into present values so that options with different timings can be compared.".

column2: Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the start of each year
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discounting. The module describes Discounted total of a level yearly amount counted at the start of each year as "Credits each year's amount at the start of the year, so the T amounts fall in years 0 to T minus 1 and the first is not discounted. Every factor is one period earlier than under end-of-year counting, so the total is (1 + r) times the total in HE-FM-DISC-001. Larson describes this convention as the same as a stream of payments each made at the beginning of the year."; HEO defines Discounting as "Discounting converts future costs and health effects, such as QALYs, into present values so that options with different timings can be compared.".

column2: Continuously discounted total of an even yearly flow over a time horizon
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discounting. The module describes Continuously discounted total of an even yearly flow over a time horizon as "Treats the amount q as arising evenly through each year instead of at one point, and integrates it against the continuous discount factor exp(minus rho t) from 0 to T. Larson gives the same integral, with an amount of 1, for years of life lost. The continuous rate rho, the natural log of (1 + r), gives the same factor at every whole year as the annual rate r, so the result lies between the end-of-year and start-of-year totals of HE-FM-DISC-001 and HE-FM-DISC-002. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Discounting as "Discounting converts future costs and health effects, such as QALYs, into present values so that options with different timings can be compared.".

column2: Discounted cost per QALY of a one-off treatment cost with a level yearly QALY gain
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discounting. The module describes Discounted cost per QALY of a one-off treatment cost with a level yearly QALY gain as "Divides an incremental cost paid entirely at the start (year 0), which discounting leaves unchanged, by the discounted total of a level yearly QALY gain counted at the end of each year, as in HE-FM-DISC-001. Only the QALYs shrink, so the ratio rises with the rate. This is the calculation behind the article's worked example."; HEO defines Discounting as "Discounting converts future costs and health effects, such as QALYs, into present values so that options with different timings can be compared.".

column2: Annualised capital charge net of discounted resale value
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annualisation. The module describes Annualised capital charge net of discounted resale value as "Divides the purchase price, net of the resale value discounted over the useful life, by the annuity factor A, the present value of one unit of currency received at the end of each of n years. The result is the economic cost of using the asset for one year, covering both the value used up and the opportunity cost of the funds tied up in it. Rearranged, E equals K minus S divided by A, plus r times S, so the resale value attracts only a yearly holding charge of r times S and no wear."; HEO defines Annualisation as "Annualisation is the conversion of a capital outlay into an equal yearly cost over the asset's useful life, using an annuity factor and the discount rate.".

column2: Annualised capital charge with no resale value
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annualisation. The module describes Annualised capital charge with no resale value as "The special case of HE-FM-ANLS-001 with S equal to zero, used for inputs that have no value at the end of their life, such as training that has to be repeated. The purchase price is divided by the annuity factor, so the charge works like a loan repayment at rate r, paying a return on the balance still tied up and recovering part of the price each year."; HEO defines Annualisation as "Annualisation is the conversion of a capital outlay into an equal yearly cost over the asset's useful life, using an annuity factor and the discount rate.".

column2: Ratio of the annualised capital charge to straight-line depreciation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annualisation. The module describes Ratio of the annualised capital charge to straight-line depreciation as "With no resale value, the annualised charge, K divided by A, and the straight-line charge, K divided by n, differ by the ratio n divided by A, which depends only on the useful life and the rate. Because A is smaller than n at any positive rate, the ratio exceeds 1 and rises with the useful life, and it tends to 1 as r approaches zero."; HEO defines Annualisation as "Annualisation is the conversion of a capital outlay into an equal yearly cost over the asset's useful life, using an annuity factor and the discount rate.".

column2: Random-effects meta-regression model with one study-level covariate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Meta-Regression. The module describes Random-effects meta-regression model with one study-level covariate as "Writes the effect estimate of study i as a point on a regression line in the covariate x_i plus two error terms, the study's deviation u_i from the line, with u_i ~ N(0, tau2), and its sampling error e_i, with e_i ~ N(0, v_i) and v_i treated as known. The slope beta_1 is the change in the expected effect per unit increase in x_i, and tau2 is the residual between-study variance not accounted for by the covariate. A fixed-effect meta-regression omits u_i, so sampling error is the only random variation. Further covariates enter as further terms, with a categorical characteristic of J groups coded as J minus 1 dummy variables."; HEO defines Meta-Regression as "Meta-regression is a precision-weighted regression of study effect estimates on study characteristics, explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses for HTA.".

column2: Random-effects precision weight of a study in a meta-regression
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Meta-Regression. The module describes Random-effects precision weight of a study in a meta-regression as "Weight given to study i when the regression coefficients are estimated by weighted least squares. The weight is the inverse of the study's within-study variance plus the residual between-study variance, so larger studies have more influence on the slope, but less than in a fixed-effect meta-regression, where tau2 is zero and the weight is 1/v_i."; HEO defines Meta-Regression as "Meta-regression is a precision-weighted regression of study effect estimates on study characteristics, explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses for HTA.".

column2: Proportion of between-study variance accounted for by meta-regression covariates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Meta-Regression. The module describes Proportion of between-study variance accounted for by meta-regression covariates as "Compares the between-study variance of a random-effects meta-analysis without covariates with the residual between-study variance of the meta-regression, and expresses the fall as a share of the first. It describes heterogeneity among true effects only, not the sampling error in the observed estimates."; HEO defines Meta-Regression as "Meta-regression is a precision-weighted regression of study effect estimates on study characteristics, explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses for HTA.".

column2: Relative change in a ratio measure for a change in a meta-regression covariate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Meta-Regression. The module describes Relative change in a ratio measure for a change in a meta-regression covariate as "When a ratio measure is regressed on the log scale, the exponential of the slope is the factor by which the ratio measure changes per unit increase in the covariate. For a change of Delta_x units the factor is the exponential of beta_1 times Delta_x."; HEO defines Meta-Regression as "Meta-regression is a precision-weighted regression of study effect estimates on study characteristics, explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses for HTA.".

column2: Treatment effect at a chosen covariate value from a centred meta-regression
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Meta-Regression. The module describes Treatment effect at a chosen covariate value from a centred meta-regression as "TSD 3 centres the covariate at its mean, so the fitted effect d applies at the mean covariate value x_bar, and the effect at any other value z is recovered by un-centring. A decision model uses it to take the relative effect for its own population, for example its baseline risk, instead of the average over the trials."; HEO defines Meta-Regression as "Meta-regression is a precision-weighted regression of study effect estimates on study characteristics, explaining heterogeneity in meta-analyses for HTA.".

column2: Simple hyperbolic discount factor at a delay of t periods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hyperbolic Discounting. The module describes Simple hyperbolic discount factor at a delay of t periods as "Gives the weight on an outcome t periods ahead under the simple hyperbola that Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue attribute to Herrnstein and to Mazur. The weight is 1 for an outcome now and falls as the delay grows, but more slowly at long delays than the constant-rate factor 1/(1 + r)^t of HE-FM-DR-001, so distant outcomes keep more weight. The parameter alpha sets how quickly the rate of impatience declines, and the per-period rate it implies is in HE-FM-HYPD-002."; HEO defines Hyperbolic Discounting as "Hyperbolic discounting is time preference in which the discount rate falls as delay grows, so plans made for later are often reversed when the time comes.".

column2: Per-period discount rate implied by the simple hyperbola at a delay of t periods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hyperbolic Discounting. The module describes Per-period discount rate implied by the simple hyperbola at a delay of t periods as "The per-period rate between delays t and t + 1 is the ratio of the two weights minus 1, D_H(t)/D_H(t + 1) minus 1, which simplifies to alpha/(1 + alpha t). It equals alpha for the first period and falls steadily as the delay grows, whereas the same calculation on the constant-rate factor of HE-FM-DR-001 returns r at every delay. A declining per-period rate is what Frederick and colleagues mean by hyperbolic discounting."; HEO defines Hyperbolic Discounting as "Hyperbolic discounting is time preference in which the discount rate falls as delay grows, so plans made for later are often reversed when the time comes.".

column2: Generalised hyperbolic discount factor of Loewenstein and Prelec
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hyperbolic Discounting. The module describes Generalised hyperbolic discount factor of Loewenstein and Prelec as "Raises 1 + alpha t to the power minus beta divided by alpha, the form that Frederick and colleagues attribute to Loewenstein and Prelec. Beta sets the overall level of discounting and alpha how far the curve departs from a constant rate. Setting beta equal to alpha returns the simple hyperbola of HE-FM-HYPD-001, and as alpha approaches zero the weight approaches exp(minus beta t), the continuous constant-rate factor (HE-FM-CONT-003 gives the continuous rate for an annual rate). The beta here is not the present-bias factor of HE-FM-HYPD-004."; HEO defines Hyperbolic Discounting as "Hyperbolic discounting is time preference in which the discount rate falls as delay grows, so plans made for later are often reversed when the time comes.".

column2: Quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta discount weight with its short-run and long-run per-period rates
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hyperbolic Discounting. The module describes Quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta discount weight with its short-run and long-run per-period rates as "For a delay of one period or more the weight is beta times delta to the power t, while an outcome now keeps a weight of 1, so beta is a one-off discount on everything that is not immediate. The per-period rate is r_0 between now and the next period and r_L between any two later periods, as Frederick and colleagues give them. Setting beta = 1 returns exponential discounting with the factor delta, the HE-FM-DR-001 factor with r equal to (1 minus delta)/delta, and Wang and Sloan read beta below 1 as present bias."; HEO defines Hyperbolic Discounting as "Hyperbolic discounting is time preference in which the discount rate falls as delay grows, so plans made for later are often reversed when the time comes.".

column2: Net value of waiting for a larger-later outcome judged today and one period ahead
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hyperbolic Discounting. The module describes Net value of waiting for a larger-later outcome judged today and one period ahead as "Compares a smaller-sooner amount a with a larger-later amount b that arrives one period after it, using the weights w_0, w_1 and w_2 of any discount function at delays 0, 1 and 2 seen from today. M_0 is the advantage of waiting when the choice is immediate and M_1 the advantage, judged today, of waiting when the same choice comes one period later. A negative M_0 with a positive M_1 is a preference reversal, a plan to wait that is dropped when the time comes. Under constant-rate weights M_1 equals delta times M_0, so the two share a sign and no reversal occurs."; HEO defines Hyperbolic Discounting as "Hyperbolic discounting is time preference in which the discount rate falls as delay grows, so plans made for later are often reversed when the time comes.".

column2: EVSI of a study with a positive or negative result for two options
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Sample Information. The module describes EVSI of a study with a positive or negative result for two options as "Evaluates the EVSI expectation exactly when the proposed study can give only two results and the choice is between standard care A and a new option B whose net benefit depends on whether B works (state F) or not (state U). Bayes theorem turns the prior probability p of state F and the chance q that the result points the right way into the probability of each result and the posterior probability of F after it. The better option is chosen after each result, and the expected value of choosing after the study, V_S, is compared with the value of choosing now, V_0. A result adds value only when it changes the choice, so EVSI is zero when every result leaves the current choice in place and equals EVPI when q is 1."; HEO defines Expected Value of Sample Information as "Expected value of sample information (EVSI) is the expected net benefit gained by deciding after a specific proposed study reports instead of deciding now.".

column2: Preposterior variance of incremental net benefit for a study of size n
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Sample Information. The module describes Preposterior variance of incremental net benefit for a study of size n as "Gives the variance, across the results a proposed study could produce, of the posterior mean of incremental net benefit, the preposterior variance, when the prior and the study estimate are both normal. The prior variance v0 is written as the per-patient sampling variance sigma2 divided by a prior effective sample size n0, and a study of n patients then resolves the fraction nu, n divided by n plus n0, of the prior variance. The preposterior variance is zero when n is zero, rises with n and tends to the prior variance as n grows without limit. It also equals the prior variance less the posterior variance, the known reduction in variance on which the analytic EVSI depends."; HEO defines Expected Value of Sample Information as "Expected value of sample information (EVSI) is the expected net benefit gained by deciding after a specific proposed study reports instead of deciding now.".

column2: Closed-form EVSI for two options with normal incremental net benefit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Sample Information. The module describes Closed-form EVSI for two options with normal incremental net benefit as "Applies the unit normal loss integral to the preposterior distribution of incremental net benefit, which is normal with the prior mean m0 and the preposterior variance s2 of HE-FM-EVSI-002. EVSI is the expected gain from switching away from the option preferred now in the results that reverse the sign of the posterior mean, s times phi_z less the absolute value of m0 times Q_z, where z is the absolute prior mean in preposterior standard deviations. phi_z is the standard normal density written out with exp and sqrt, and Q_z is the standard normal upper-tail probability at z, entered from Excel's 1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) because the calculator has no normal distribution function. With s2 equal to the prior variance the same expression gives per-person EVPI under normality, the bound in HE-FM-VOI-001."; HEO defines Expected Value of Sample Information as "Expected value of sample information (EVSI) is the expected net benefit gained by deciding after a specific proposed study reports instead of deciding now.".

column2: Population EVSI for a constant annual beneficiary population over the decision's lifetime
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Sample Information. The module describes Population EVSI for a constant annual beneficiary population over the decision's lifetime as "Scales per-person EVSI to everyone whose treatment the study result would inform, N people a year for Y years, with later cohorts discounted at rate r, the population value of research in equation 15 of the second ISPOR value of information report. The factor D is the present value of one person a year in years 0 to Y minus 1, so the first cohort is not discounted, as in population EVPI (HE-FM-VOI-002), which allows a different N_t in each period. Population EVSI is the figure set against the cost of the study, and their difference, the expected net benefit of sampling, has its own package."; HEO defines Expected Value of Sample Information as "Expected value of sample information (EVSI) is the expected net benefit gained by deciding after a specific proposed study reports instead of deciding now.".

column2: Equity-weighted QALY gain summed over population groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Weighted Analysis. The module describes Equity-weighted QALY gain summed over population groups as "Multiplies the incremental QALY gain in each group by that group's equity weight to give the group's equity-weighted value, and adds these values over the groups that the programme affects. The calculator form is written for two groups, V_1 and V_2, and each further group adds one more term w_g times Delta_E_g to the sum. A weight above 1 counts each QALY gained in a priority group as more than one QALY, and a weight of 1 leaves a group's gain unchanged. The result replaces the unweighted QALY gain in the ICER and in net health benefit, so the comparison with costs follows the usual rules once the weights are fixed."; HEO defines Equity-Weighted Analysis as "Equity-weighted analysis is a cost-effectiveness analysis in which health gains for priority groups, such as the severely ill, are weighted more heavily.".

column2: Equity-weighted ICER for one group and the equivalent threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Weighted Analysis. The module describes Equity-weighted ICER for one group and the equivalent threshold as "Divides the incremental cost by the weighted QALY gain of a group that carries a single weight w. Because the weight is the same for everyone in the group, the weighted ICER equals the unweighted ICER divided by w, and judging it against a threshold lambda gives the same decision as judging the unweighted ICER against w times lambda. The second part of the formula returns that equivalent threshold, the route the Norwegian committee proposed in 2014 through differential threshold ranges by severity."; HEO defines Equity-Weighted Analysis as "Equity-weighted analysis is a cost-effectiveness analysis in which health gains for priority groups, such as the severely ill, are weighted more heavily.".

column2: Equity-weighted incremental net health benefit with and without the weight
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Weighted Analysis. The module describes Equity-weighted incremental net health benefit with and without the weight as "Converts the incremental cost into the health displaced elsewhere, Delta_C divided by lambda, and subtracts it from the weighted and from the unweighted QALY gain. The displaced health is not weighted, so the two results differ by w minus 1, times Delta_E. A negative unweighted value with a positive weighted value marks a programme that lowers total population health and would be recommended only on the strength of the equity judgement."; HEO defines Equity-Weighted Analysis as "Equity-weighted analysis is a cost-effectiveness analysis in which health gains for priority groups, such as the severely ill, are weighted more heavily.".

column2: Equity switching weight at which a programme breaks even
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Weighted Analysis. The module describes Equity switching weight at which a programme breaks even as "Sets the weighted net health benefit to zero and solves for the weight, giving the incremental cost divided by lambda times the QALY gain, which is the unweighted ICER divided by lambda. A weight at or above w_star makes the programme acceptable at lambda, so the value states how much concern for the group is needed to justify a programme that is not cost-effective without weights. A value below 1 means the programme is cost-effective unweighted."; HEO defines Equity-Weighted Analysis as "Equity-weighted analysis is a cost-effectiveness analysis in which health gains for priority groups, such as the severely ill, are weighted more heavily.".

column2: DALYs for a cause as the sum of its years of life lost and years lived with disability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability-Adjusted Life Year. The module describes DALYs for a cause as the sum of its years of life lost and years lived with disability as "Adds the fatal and non-fatal parts of the health loss from one cause, both calculated for the same cause, sex, age group and year, as in WHO's Global Health Estimates and the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. One DALY is one lost year of healthy life, so a death and a period of illness are counted on one scale. Each part comes from its own formula, and the DALY is their sum."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: Undiscounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths at one age and survivors living with a condition for a fixed time
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability-Adjusted Life Year. The module describes Undiscounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths at one age and survivors living with a condition for a fixed time as "Gives the DALYs a cohort incurs in one scenario when D people die at once at an age where the standard remaining life expectancy is L years, and S survivors live T years at disability weight DW before recovering fully. The first term is the YLLs of HE-FM-YLL-001 and the second the incidence-based YLDs of HE-FM-YLD-001, so the result is HE-FM-DALY-001 for the cohort. The article applies it to one cohort with and without a treatment programme."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: DALYs averted and cost per DALY averted by a programme against its comparator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability-Adjusted Life Year. The module describes DALYs averted and cost per DALY averted by a programme against its comparator as "Subtracts the DALYs a cohort incurs with the programme from those it incurs without it, and divides the extra cost by the difference. Because DALYs count health lost, the comparator's DALYs come first in the denominator, which makes the ratio HE-FM-ICER-001 with the effect measured as DALYs averted. Both scenarios cover the whole cohort over the same time horizon, so deaths and disability both count, unlike HE-FM-DWT-005, where only disability weights change."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: Continuously discounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths and disability beginning at time zero
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability-Adjusted Life Year. The module describes Continuously discounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths and disability beginning at time zero as "Replaces the L standard years lost per death and the T years lived with the condition by their present values under continuous discounting at rate r, (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r and (1 minus e to the minus rT) over r, as in HE-FM-YLL-003 and HE-FM-YLD-002. Fox-Rushby and Hanson define DALYs for economic evaluation as the present value of future years of life lost plus the present value of future years lived with disability, and the original DALY used a 3% rate. Discounting shrinks the long stream of years lost to a death more than the shorter stream of illness, so it lowers the weight of deaths prevented. The function exp is the exponential function."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: DALY rate per 100,000 population for a cause
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Disability-Adjusted Life Year. The module describes DALY rate per 100,000 population for a cause as "Divides the DALYs from a cause by the population in which they arise and scales the result to 100,000 people, the form in which GBD 2021 reports all-age and age-specific rates. A rate removes the effect of population size but not of age structure; age-standardised rates weight age-specific rates by a standard population, as in HE-FM-INEQ-001."; HEO defines Disability-Adjusted Life Year as "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) measures health loss by adding years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability.".

column2: EQ-5D-3L utility as one minus a constant, level decrements and an N3 term
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept EQ-5D-3L Value Set. The module describes EQ-5D-3L utility as one minus a constant, level decrements and an N3 term as "Subtracts from full health a constant for any problem at all, the decrement attached to the level reported on each of the five dimensions and a single N3 decrement when any dimension is at level 3. The decrements are zero at level 1, so state 11111 scores 1, and the constant and N3 term are each charged once whatever the number of dimensions with problems. Any value set of this form can be scored by entering its own coefficients, and HE-FM-EQ3L-002 fixes them at the UK tariff."; HEO defines EQ-5D-3L Value Set as "EQ-5D-3L value sets are utility weights, elicited from a population's health state valuations, that score all 243 EQ-5D-3L states for QALY calculation.".

column2: UK MVH time trade-off EQ-5D-3L tariff from five reported levels
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept EQ-5D-3L Value Set. The module describes UK MVH time trade-off EQ-5D-3L tariff from five reported levels as "Scores a profile with the coefficients of Dolan's UK time trade-off tariff, the constant 0.081, the level 2 and level 3 decrements of each dimension and the N3 decrement 0.269. The level 2 indicator of a dimension is written min(l minus 1, 1) minus max(l minus 2, 0) and the level 3 indicator max(l minus 2, 0), which the site calculator can evaluate. The scale runs down to minus 0.594 for state 33333, below the value of dead."; HEO defines EQ-5D-3L Value Set as "EQ-5D-3L value sets are utility weights, elicited from a population's health state valuations, that score all 243 EQ-5D-3L states for QALY calculation.".

column2: QALY difference between two EQ-5D-3L states and the share due to N3
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept EQ-5D-3L Value Set. The module describes QALY difference between two EQ-5D-3L states and the share due to N3 as "Multiplies the utility gap between the state a treatment keeps patients in and the state it avoids by the years spent there, and finds what share of the gap the N3 decrement explains. Both utilities come from one value set of the main-effects form, and the QALY step is HE-FM-QALY-001 applied to one period, the decrement-times-duration loss of HE-FM-DISU-001 read as a gain. A large share shows that much of a modelled QALY gain rests on a single coefficient."; HEO defines EQ-5D-3L Value Set as "EQ-5D-3L value sets are utility weights, elicited from a population's health state valuations, that score all 243 EQ-5D-3L states for QALY calculation.".

column2: Per-person EVPI as the mean opportunity loss of the current decision
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Perfect Information. The module describes Per-person EVPI as the mean opportunity loss of the current decision as "In each draw s the opportunity loss L_s is the highest net benefit available in that draw less the net benefit, in the same draw, of the option d* chosen on current evidence. EVPI is the mean of L_s over the S equally weighted draws. Because d* is the option with the highest mean net benefit, the result equals the mean of the maxima less the maximum of the means in HE-FM-VOI-001, and it also shows which draws carry the loss. L_s is zero in every draw where d* is also the best option."; HEO defines Expected Value of Perfect Information as "Expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from removing all uncertainty in a funding decision, the upper limit on research value.".

column2: Two-option EVPI in QALYs from incremental net health benefit draws
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Perfect Information. The module describes Two-option EVPI in QALYs from incremental net health benefit draws as "With one new option and one comparator, the comparator's net benefit can be set to zero in every draw and the new option's to its incremental net health benefit INHB_s, its incremental QALYs less its incremental cost divided by the threshold. EVPI in QALYs is then the mean of the positive part of INHB_s less the positive part of its mean. Multiplying by the threshold gives the same EVPI in money, because net monetary benefit is the threshold times net health benefit in every draw."; HEO defines Expected Value of Perfect Information as "Expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from removing all uncertainty in a funding decision, the upper limit on research value.".

column2: EVPI as the probability of a wrong current decision times the mean loss when wrong
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Perfect Information. The module describes EVPI as the probability of a wrong current decision times the mean loss when wrong as "Splits the mean opportunity loss into how often the option chosen on current evidence is not the best option, P_err, and the mean loss in the draws where it is not, L_wrong. The product equals EVPI because the draws where the chosen option is best add no loss. P_err is one minus the acceptability of the chosen option (HE-FM-CEAC-003), so the formula links the acceptability curve to EVPI and shows why a small chance of a costly error can give a larger EVPI than a large chance of a small one."; HEO defines Expected Value of Perfect Information as "Expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from removing all uncertainty in a funding decision, the upper limit on research value.".

column2: Two-option EVPI for a normally distributed incremental net benefit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Perfect Information. The module describes Two-option EVPI for a normally distributed incremental net benefit as "When the incremental net benefit of the new option over its comparator is normal with mean mu_INB and standard deviation sigma_INB, EVPI has a closed form, sigma_INB times the unit normal loss integral at z, the absolute mean divided by the standard deviation. pdf_z is the standard normal density at z, computed in the formula, and cdf_z is the standard normal cumulative probability at z, which the site calculator cannot compute and so takes as an input from NORM.S.DIST or a table. The form needs no draws and has no Monte Carlo error. For a given sigma_INB the loss term is largest at z equal to zero, where EVPI is sigma_INB divided by the square root of 2 pi, about 0.3989 sigma_INB."; HEO defines Expected Value of Perfect Information as "Expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from removing all uncertainty in a funding decision, the upper limit on research value.".

column2: Two-level nested Monte Carlo EVPPI estimator from incremental net benefit
column10: Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information. The module describes Two-level nested Monte Carlo EVPPI estimator from incremental net benefit as "Draws K values of the parameters of interest theta_i in an outer loop and, for each, J values of the remaining parameters theta_c in an inner loop, averages the incremental net benefit of the new option over the inner draws and keeps the larger of that mean and zero, the value of standard care. The average of the K kept values, less the larger of zero and the mean of the inner means, estimates EVPPI for theta_i, the double-loop scheme of Brennan, Kharroubi, O'Hagan and Chilcott and of Algorithm 2 in the second ISPOR report. The calculator form is written for K = 2 outer and J = 2 inner draws, with INB_kj the run at outer draw k and inner draw j; larger loops add terms in the same pattern, as the Excel and the Computational Function do. With more than two options the maximum is taken over the inner means of every option, and Strong, Oakley and Brennan note that the value is unchanged when net benefits are expressed relative to a baseline option. When theta_i holds every parameter the inner runs at each outer draw are identical and the estimator becomes the per-person EVPI of HE-FM-VOI-001."; HEO defines Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information as "Expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) is the expected gain in net benefit from knowing selected model parameters exactly before deciding.".

column2: Single-loop EVPPI shortcut for a model linear in the remaining parameters
column10: Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information. The module describes Single-loop EVPPI shortcut for a model linear in the remaining parameters as "Replaces the inner loop by one model run for each draw of theta_i with the remaining parameters theta_c set at their mean. The second ISPOR report allows this when the model is linear or multilinear in theta_c, with no correlation between complementary parameters that are multiplied together, and prefers single-loop methods where they apply because they reduce Monte Carlo error. Here the incremental net benefit at draw k is alpha_k plus beta_k times theta_c, with alpha_k and beta_k depending on theta_i only, so its expectation over theta_c is that line evaluated at the mean mu_c. Brennan and colleagues show that the shortcut can be substantially inaccurate when even relatively small correlation or nonlinearity is present."; HEO defines Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information as "Expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) is the expected gain in net benefit from knowing selected model parameters exactly before deciding.".

column2: Regression-based EVPPI estimator from fitted incremental net benefits
column10: Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information. The module describes Regression-based EVPPI estimator from fitted incremental net benefits as "Regresses the incremental net benefit of each option against a baseline on the parameters of interest across the N runs of one probabilistic sample and treats the fitted values as the conditional expected net benefits, so no inner loop or extra model runs are needed. The estimate is the mean over runs of the largest fitted value, with zero for the baseline, less the largest mean fitted value. This is Equation 9 of Strong, Oakley and Brennan written for three options as incremental net benefits, which they note leaves the result unchanged and needs one regression fewer. Using the fitted values in both terms exploits the positive correlation between them and improves precision. Strong, Oakley and Brennan fit a generalised additive model or a Gaussian process, and Algorithm 4 of the second ISPOR report sets out the same scheme."; HEO defines Expected Value of Partial Perfect Information as "Expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) is the expected gain in net benefit from knowing selected model parameters exactly before deciding.".

column2: ENBS of one study design from its population EVSI and the study cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Net Benefit of Sampling. The module describes ENBS of one study design from its population EVSI and the study cost as "Gives the net value of one proposed design of sample size n as its population EVSI less the expected total cost of the study, the definition used by the ISPOR task force. Population EVSI comes from HE-FM-EVSI-004, which multiplies the design's per-person EVSI by the discounted number of people whose treatment the result will inform, scaled in the same way as population EVPI in HE-FM-VOI-002. A positive value means the design is expected to repay its cost, and the design with the greatest value among those feasible is the efficient one (HE-CF-ENBS-001)."; HEO defines Expected Net Benefit of Sampling as "Expected net benefit of sampling (ENBS) is a proposed study's population expected value of sample information minus its expected total cost.".

column2: Expected total cost of a two-arm study with the opportunity loss to participants
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Net Benefit of Sampling. The module describes Expected total cost of a two-arm study with the opportunity loss to participants as "Adds the three cost components that Fenwick and colleagues list, a fixed cost, a variable cost for each participant and the opportunity cost for participants who receive the option expected to be inferior while the study runs. Each such participant forgoes the absolute value of the expected incremental net benefit per person on current information, so with a share s_inf of the n participants on that arm the loss term is s_inf times n times abs(INB). The result is the C_n entered in HE-FM-ENBS-001."; HEO defines Expected Net Benefit of Sampling as "Expected net benefit of sampling (ENBS) is a proposed study's population expected value of sample information minus its expected total cost.".

column2: ENBS of a study run under only in research with the cost of waiting
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Net Benefit of Sampling. The module describes ENBS of a study run under only in research with the cost of waiting as "Subtracts from the population EVSI of a design its expected study cost and the net benefit forgone by people treated outside the study while it runs, when the new treatment is available only in research. When the new treatment is expected to be better, with INB above zero, each of the N_w people waiting forgoes INB. When it is not, standard care outside the study is already the expected best option and waiting costs nothing in this sense. Under approval with research N_w is zero and the result equals the ENBS of HE-FM-ENBS-001, so the same trial can have a different ENBS under the two arrangements."; HEO defines Expected Net Benefit of Sampling as "Expected net benefit of sampling (ENBS) is a proposed study's population expected value of sample information minus its expected total cost.".

column2: Ceiling on the ENBS of a study design from population EVPI
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Expected Net Benefit of Sampling. The module describes Ceiling on the ENBS of a study design from population EVPI as "No finite study delivers perfect information, so the population EVSI of any design is at most population EVPI (HE-FM-VOI-002) and the ENBS of a design costing C_n cannot exceed population EVPI less that cost. When the ceiling is zero or below for every feasible design, research is not worthwhile and the value of information process stops before any EVSI is computed, the first screen in the sequence set out by the ISPOR task force. A positive ceiling is necessary but not sufficient, so ENBS itself is still required."; HEO defines Expected Net Benefit of Sampling as "Expected net benefit of sampling (ENBS) is a proposed study's population expected value of sample information minus its expected total cost.".

column2: Stinnett and Mullahy confidence interval for incremental net health benefit from two trial arms
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Net Benefit Approach. The module describes Stinnett and Mullahy confidence interval for incremental net health benefit from two trial arms as "Estimates incremental net health benefit with the analogy estimator, the difference in arm mean effects less the difference in arm mean costs divided by lambda, and estimates its variance from each arm's sample variances of effect and cost, their within-arm correlation and the arm size (Stinnett and Mullahy, equations 6 and 7). The estimator is linear in the four sample means, so its variance is a direct sum of sample terms with no Taylor series approximation, and the interval is a normal (Wald) interval as in HE-FM-AN-001 (their equation 8). The statistic z_INHB, the estimate divided by its standard error, converts to the probability that net health benefit is positive through the standard normal cumulative distribution function, which the calculator lacks, so Excel NORM.S.DIST or R pnorm does that step. Multiplying every term by lambda gives the money-scale result of HE-FM-AN-004."; HEO defines Net Benefit Approach as "The net benefit approach is a cost-effectiveness decision framework that ranks options by net benefit at a stated threshold instead of by ratios.".

column2: Incremental net monetary benefit written through the ICER in each quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Net Benefit Approach. The module describes Incremental net monetary benefit written through the ICER in each quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane as "Rewrites incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002) as the effect difference times the gap between the threshold and the ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001), which holds whenever Delta_E is not zero. The sign of INMB is the sign of Delta_E times the sign of lambda minus R. With a health gain (north-east and south-east) a positive INMB means R below lambda, and with a health loss (south-west and north-west) it means R above lambda, so the same ratio can call for opposite decisions. This is the ambiguity between quadrants that Stinnett and Mullahy describe.
