Plotted against lambda, the expression is the line that Hoch and colleagues describe, with intercept minus Delta_C, slope Delta_E and a zero crossing at the ICER."; HEO defines Net Benefit Approach as "The net benefit approach is a cost-effectiveness decision framework that ranks options by net benefit at a stated threshold instead of by ratios.".

column2: Net-benefit regression coefficient on a treatment indicator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Net Benefit Approach. The module describes Net-benefit regression coefficient on a treatment indicator as "Each patient's net benefit at threshold lambda, lambda times the patient's effect minus the patient's cost, is regressed on a treatment indicator T_i, 1 for the new option and 0 for the comparator, in the model NB_i = alpha + beta T_i + epsilon_i. With no other regressors the fitted intercept is the comparator arm's mean net benefit and the coefficient is the difference in arm means, which equals incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002), so the confidence interval for beta is the interval for incremental net benefit. The calculator works from the arm means. Covariates added to the regression give an adjusted estimate of beta, which Hoch, Briggs and Willan proposed for imperfect randomisation and for subgroups."; HEO defines Net Benefit Approach as "The net benefit approach is a cost-effectiveness decision framework that ranks options by net benefit at a stated threshold instead of by ratios.".

column2: Threshold range in which a frontier strategy has the highest net monetary benefit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Frontier. The module describes Threshold range in which a frontier strategy has the highest net monetary benefit as "For a frontier strategy k whose neighbours on the frontier are i, the next less effective, and j, the next more effective, k has the highest net monetary benefit for every λ at or above lambda_in, the slope of the segment entering it, and at or below lambda_out, the slope of the segment leaving it. Both slopes are sequential ICERs (HE-FM-CEA-001), so the strategy chosen at λ is the frontier strategy with the largest ICER not above λ, the decision rule stated by Suen and Goldhaber-Fiebert, and it is the same strategy that HE-FM-NMB-003 selects. The slopes are the switching values at which two neighbours tie. For a middle strategy that is not on the frontier the range is empty, because lambda_in exceeds lambda_out exactly when D_M of HE-FM-EXD-001 is positive."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Frontier as "The cost-effectiveness frontier joins the strategies not ruled out by strict or extended dominance on a plot of expected cost against health effect.".

column2: Net monetary benefit a strategy gives up against the frontier strategy chosen at a threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Frontier. The module describes Net monetary benefit a strategy gives up against the frontier strategy chosen at a threshold as "Measures how far a strategy falls below the frontier at a value λ in net monetary benefit terms, as the net monetary benefit of the strategy s chosen at λ, the one with the highest value (HE-FM-NMB-003, the same strategy as HE-FM-CEF-001 picks), less that of strategy k, each from HE-FM-NMB-001. It is the incremental net monetary benefit of HE-FM-NMB-002 with s as the intervention and k as the comparator, so it is zero for the chosen strategy and not negative for any other. For a dominated or extendedly dominated strategy it is positive at every positive λ, since such strategies never have the highest net monetary benefit. When Q_k lies within the QALY range of the frontier, its smallest value arises at the slope of the frontier segment beneath Q_k, where it equals the saving of the blend of the two frontier neighbours in HE-FM-EXD-002, the vertical distance of k above the frontier."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Frontier as "The cost-effectiveness frontier joins the strategies not ruled out by strict or extended dominance on a plot of expected cost against health effect.".

column2: Gradient of an IQWiG efficiency frontier segment and the net cost at which a new intervention reaches the extended last segment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Cost-Effectiveness Frontier. The module describes Gradient of an IQWiG efficiency frontier segment and the net cost at which a new intervention reaches the extended last segment as "In the IQWiG efficiency frontier benefit B is on the vertical axis and total net cost per patient K on the horizontal axis, the reverse of the usual cost-effectiveness plane, so the gradient g of a segment is the incremental benefit per incremental cost and its reciprocal lambda_g is the sequential ICER of HE-FM-CEA-001. General Methods version 6.1 extended the last segment to judge a new intervention with more benefit and more cost than the comparators, and took the reciprocal of its gradient as the threshold for the net health benefit used to derive a price. K_max is the net cost per patient at which a new intervention with benefit B_new lies on that extension, where its net health benefit is zero. Version 8.0 (section 4.15) states that extending the last segment is no longer necessary, so K_max is a version 6.1 calculation."; HEO defines Cost-Effectiveness Frontier as "The cost-effectiveness frontier joins the strategies not ruled out by strict or extended dominance on a plot of expected cost against health effect.".

column2: Total health forgone for equity between a health-maximising and a fairer option
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Efficiency Trade-off. The module describes Total health forgone for equity between a health-maximising and a fairer option as "Gives the mean net health gain per person of each option as the population-share weighted sum of the two groups' net gains, and the health forgone for equity as the gain of the health-maximising option less the gain of the fairer option. Asaria and colleagues call this difference in total health the health opportunity cost of choosing the option that reduces inequality, and Cookson and colleagues describe counting it as equity constraint analysis. The share f_forgone expresses the same loss as a fraction of the health-maximising option's net gain. A positive H_forgone means a trade-off exists, and a value of zero or below means the fairer option costs no health."; HEO defines Equity-Efficiency Trade-off as "The equity-efficiency trade-off is the total health given up for a fairer distribution when the option that maximises health is not the fairest one.".

column2: Implied inequality aversion from the switching weight by inverting the Atkinson relative weight
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Equity-Efficiency Trade-off. The module describes Implied inequality aversion from the switching weight by inverting the Atkinson relative weight as "Inverts the live Atkinson relative weight HE-FM-ATK-004, in which a small gain to the worse-off group counts (h_better / h_worse) to the power epsilon times a gain to the better-off group. Setting that weight equal to the switching weight w_star, the w_s of HE-FM-WE-004 for the two options, and taking natural logarithms gives the approximate inequality aversion at which the two options tie. Cookson and colleagues note that an equity parameter implies a set of weights once combined with the existing distribution of health, and this formula reads the relation backwards. It is an approximation because the weights are taken at baseline health, while the exact switch solves the comparison of equally distributed equivalent health. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Equity-Efficiency Trade-off as "The equity-efficiency trade-off is the total health given up for a fairer distribution when the option that maximises health is not the fairest one.".

column2: Geometric distribution of cycles spent in a Markov state on one visit with a constant stay probability
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Assumption. The module describes Geometric distribution of cycles spent in a Markov state on one visit with a constant stay probability as "Gives the probability that one visit to state i lasts exactly d cycles, at least d cycles or at most d cycles, counting the cycle of entry, when the probability of staying for another cycle is the same p_ii in every cycle of the stay. Each cycle acts as a trial in which the person leaves with probability 1 minus p_ii, so the stay ends at the first exit and its length has the geometric distribution of Grinstead and Snell. Its mean, 1 divided by 1 minus p_ii, is the mean episode length L_j of HE-FM-MKCH-002 and is not restated. The median is the smallest whole number of cycles at or above d_star, the first d at which F_d reaches one half; when d_star is itself a whole number F_d equals exactly one half there and that number is the median."; HEO defines Markov Assumption as "The Markov assumption is that the next transition in a state-transition model depends only on the current state and model time, not on earlier history.".

column2: Memoryless residual stay and constant per-cycle exit probability of a geometric Markov sojourn
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Assumption. The module describes Memoryless residual stay and constant per-cycle exit probability of a geometric Markov sojourn as "Gives the probability that a stay already longer than a cycles lasts more than a + b cycles, and the probability of leaving in cycle d of the stay among those still in the state in that cycle. Neither depends on the time already spent, since R_ab equals p_ii to the power b whatever a is and h_d equals 1 minus p_ii at every d, which is the memoryless property that Grinstead and Snell derive for the geometric distribution. The first part is the conditional survival ratio of HE-FM-LTR-001 applied to the geometric stay, and the second divides f_d by G_d of HE-FM-MKA-001. Applied to a survival curve for time since entry, the same ratios test the assumption, since only a memoryless curve has the same per-cycle exit probability at every duration; HE-CF-MKA-001 carries out that check, and HE-FM-CUMH-002 gives the per-cycle probabilities of a fitted curve."; HEO defines Markov Assumption as "The Markov assumption is that the next transition in a state-transition model depends only on the current state and model time, not on earlier history.".

column2: Exponential residual time and median sojourn in a Markov state with a constant exit rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Assumption. The module describes Exponential residual time and median sojourn in a Markov state with a constant exit rate as "The continuous-time counterpart of HE-FM-MKA-002. With a constant total exit rate lambda the time spent in the state is exponential, with survival exp(minus lambda t) and mean 1 divided by lambda as in HE-FM-BTH-003 and HE-FM-CONT-002, which are not restated. S_res, the conditional survival ratio of HE-FM-LTR-001 applied to exponential survival, is the probability of staying a further time s after a time tau already spent, which equals exp(minus lambda s) whatever tau is, and t_med is the time by which half of all stays have ended. Grinstead and Snell state that the exponential is the only continuous density with the memoryless property, so in continuous time a constant exit rate and a stay that ignores time already spent go together. In a cycle model the stay probability is exp(minus lambda Delta), 1 minus the exit probability of HE-FM-TP-001, and t_med divided by Delta equals d_star of HE-FM-MKA-001."; HEO defines Markov Assumption as "The Markov assumption is that the next transition in a state-transition model depends only on the current state and model time, not on earlier history.".

column2: Mean stay of a discrete-cycle Markov state against the exponential mean at the same constant exit rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Markov Assumption. The module describes Mean stay of a discrete-cycle Markov state against the exponential mean at the same constant exit rate as "Compares the mean stay in a cycle model whose stay probability comes from a constant exit rate with the mean time in the state of the continuous process it represents. Here p_ii is 1 minus the exit probability of HE-FM-TP-001, D_mean turns the mean cycles of HE-FM-MKCH-002 into time by multiplying by the cycle length, and T_mean is the exponential mean of HE-FM-CONT-002. The geometric count credits a whole cycle for the cycle of entry and for every cycle begun in the state, so D_mean exceeds T_mean, and the excess gap_c, in cycles, is above one half and below one, and approaches one half as lambda times Delta shrinks. This is the overestimate from counting membership at the start of each cycle that Sonnenberg and Beck describe, a matter of counting that a half-cycle correction addresses, not of memory."; HEO defines Markov Assumption as "The Markov assumption is that the next transition in a state-transition model depends only on the current state and model time, not on earlier history.".

column2: Group health after a programme net of the group's share of the health opportunity cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distributional Cost-Effectiveness. The module describes Group health after a programme net of the group's share of the health opportunity cost as "Subtracts each group's share of the health opportunity cost from the QALYs the group gains, giving the group's net health benefit, and divides that by the number of people in the group to move the group's baseline health per person to its health under the programme. The health opportunity cost H_d is the incremental cost divided by the value of a QALY, the live record HE-FM-CET-002, and the shares o_1 and o_2 say who bears it. Because the shares add to 1, the total of the group net health benefits equals the total QALY gain less H_d, so the distribution of the opportunity cost changes who gains while total health stays the same. The line shows two groups, the more deprived group 1 and the less deprived group 2, and each further group adds a pair of terms of the same form."; HEO defines Distributional Cost-Effectiveness as "Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis (DCEA) is an economic evaluation showing who gains and loses health from a policy and its effect on inequality.".

column2: Change in mean health, EDE health and Atkinson index of a programme against its comparator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distributional Cost-Effectiveness. The module describes Change in mean health, EDE health and Atkinson index of a programme against its comparator as "Takes the mean health and the equally distributed equivalent health of the programme's distribution and of the comparator's, both at the same inequality aversion epsilon from the live records HE-FM-ATK-002 or HE-FM-ATK-003, or HE-CF-ATK-001 for groups of unequal size, and returns the change in mean health, the change in EDE health per person and across the population, the change in the inequality cost and the change in the Atkinson index. The inequality cost is mean health less EDE health, the health per person that a decision maker with that aversion would give up for full equality, so the change in EDE equals the change in mean health less the change in the inequality cost. A positive change in EDE health means the programme is preferred to the comparator at that epsilon. Each Atkinson index is HE-FM-ATK-001, and only the difference between the two is new here."; HEO defines Distributional Cost-Effectiveness as "Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis (DCEA) is an economic evaluation showing who gains and loses health from a policy and its effect on inequality.".

column2: Equity-efficiency impact plane quadrant of a programme against its comparator
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Distributional Cost-Effectiveness. The module describes Equity-efficiency impact plane quadrant of a programme against its comparator as "Places a programme on the equity-efficiency impact plane from the sign of its change in total health, net of the health opportunity cost, and the sign of its change in an inequality index, with the comparator at the origin. A win-win programme raises total health and lowers inequality and a lose-lose programme does the reverse, while win-lose and lose-win programmes need a trade-off analysis such as the change in EDE health of HE-FM-DCEA-002. The sources name the four quadrants without classifying a point on an axis, so the formula applies the tie rule of the live dominance record HE-FM-DOM-001, with less inequality taking the place of lower cost. No change on one axis with an improvement on the other counts as win-win, the mirror case counts as lose-lose, and no change on either axis gives no quadrant."; HEO defines Distributional Cost-Effectiveness as "Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis (DCEA) is an economic evaluation showing who gains and loses health from a policy and its effect on inequality.".

column2: Green Book social time preference rate from its Ramsey components with the health discount rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Time Preference. The module describes Green Book social time preference rate from its Ramsey components with the health discount rate as "Adds pure time preference delta and catastrophic risk L to give time preference rho, and adds the wealth effect, the elasticity of marginal utility mu times the growth rate g of real per capita consumption, to give the social time preference rate, as in paragraphs 2.2 to 2.8 of the Treasury's supplementary guidance on discounting (February 2026). With the Table 2.A values for years 1 to 30 the two parts are 1.5% and 2.0% and the rate is 3.5%. The health discount rate r_HD leaves out the wealth effect (paragraph 2.16), so it equals rho, 1.5%, which is broader than pure time preference because it keeps catastrophic risk. Freeman, Groom and Spackman, in their report for HM Treasury, and Attema and colleagues write the same sum as the Ramsey rule."; HEO defines Time Preference as "Time preference is the preference for benefits sooner and costs later; in health economics it is one reason future costs and QALYs are discounted.".

column2: Implied annual discount rate for health from a TEMPUS open-ended stated choice

With b = 1/(1 + r) the answer implies 20 b^2 = y b^s, which gives equation (1) of Cairns and van der Pol (2000). column2: Green Book discount factor for a year under the stepped long-term schedule

With 3.5%, 3.0% and 2.5% it reproduces the standard factors of Annex A Table A.1, 0.3459 for year 31 and 0.1468 for year 60, and with the health rates 1.5%, 1.286% and 1.071% it gives 0.4955 for year 50 as in Table A.2. For years up to 30 it is the single-amount factor of HE-FM-DR-001, and totals over a stream are in HE-CF-TPR-001."; HEO defines Time Preference as "Time preference is the preference for benefits sooner and costs later; in health economics it is one reason future costs and QALYs are discounted.".

column2: Isoelastic Atkinson health social welfare of three equal-sized groups for epsilon other than 1
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Social Welfare Function. The module describes Isoelastic Atkinson health social welfare of three equal-sized groups for epsilon other than 1 as "Adds h_i^(1-epsilon)/(1-epsilon) over the groups, the welfare function Atkinson derived from constant relative inequality aversion with its two constants set to 0 and 1, which leaves every ranking unchanged. The line is written for the three groups of the article's example, and with n people or groups the sum has n terms. At epsilon of 0 W is total health, the utilitarian rule of maximising total QALYs; as epsilon rises the weight on a small gain to group i, h_i^(-epsilon), shifts priority to the less healthy (HE-FM-ATK-004), and the ranking approaches the maximin rule of HE-FM-SWF-003. Solving W = n h_EDE^(1-epsilon)/(1-epsilon) for h_EDE gives the EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-002, so W and EDE health rank allocations identically, and W has meaning only in comparisons made at the same epsilon."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: Logarithmic health social welfare of three equal-sized groups at epsilon of 1
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Social Welfare Function. The module describes Logarithmic health social welfare of three equal-sized groups at epsilon of 1 as "At epsilon of 1 the isoelastic form of HE-FM-SWF-001 divides by zero, and Atkinson's welfare function becomes the natural logarithm, so W adds the logarithms of the groups' health. Once the constant n/(1-epsilon), which does not affect rankings, is taken away, HE-FM-SWF-001 tends to this form as epsilon tends to 1, so rankings change smoothly with epsilon through 1. The weight on a small gain to group i is 1/h_i, so a gain of 1% counts the same for every group. Dividing W by n and taking the exponential gives the geometric-mean EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-003. The function log is the natural logarithm."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: Maximin health social welfare of three groups as the Rawlsian limit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Social Welfare Function. The module describes Maximin health social welfare of three groups as the Rawlsian limit as "Sets social welfare equal to the health of the least healthy group, the Rawlsian or maximin form. Atkinson gives it as the limit of the isoelastic family as epsilon tends to infinity (HE-FM-SWF-001), and Dolan and Tsuchiya as the limit of the two-group CES form as r approaches infinity (HE-FM-SWF-004). Two allocations with the same minimum have the same W and are ranked as tied however the other groups fare, so a gain to a healthier group alone leaves W unchanged. The nested min written here returns the smallest of the three values."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: Wagstaff two-group CES health social welfare with a group weight and curvature
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Social Welfare Function. The module describes Wagstaff two-group CES health social welfare with a group weight and curvature as "Combines the health of two groups through a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) function, the iso-elastic form of Wagstaff 1991 that Asaria, Griffin and Cookson describe as the most commonly used in the health inequalities literature. The weight alpha pivots the welfare contours around the line of equal health and r sets their curvature. At r = -1 W is the weighted sum alpha h_a + (1-alpha) h_b, the inequality-neutral utilitarian case, and as r approaches infinity W approaches the smaller of the two health values, the maximin of HE-FM-SWF-003. With alpha = 0.5, W is the EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-002 for two groups with epsilon = 1 + r, so the isoelastic and CES families rank distributions identically. Unlike the weighted two-group social welfare of HE-FM-WE-004, whose weight on a group's QALYs is fixed, the weight here changes with the health gap (HE-FM-SWF-005)."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: Marginal rate of substitution and contour slope of the two-group CES health welfare
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Social Welfare Function. The module describes Marginal rate of substitution and contour slope of the two-group CES health welfare as "Divides the marginal welfare of health in group a by that in group b. The result is the health of group b that could be given up for one more unit to group a with W unchanged, and the social indifference curve through the point, drawn with h_a on the horizontal axis, has slope minus MRS. Dolan and Tsuchiya read the MRS as the equity weight on a marginal gain to group a relative to group b. At equal health it reduces to alpha/(1-alpha) for any r, which is how they identify alpha from survey choices, and with alpha = 0.5 it equals the Atkinson relative weight of HE-FM-ATK-004 with epsilon = 1 + r when group a is the less healthy, so the factor alpha/(1-alpha) is what this formula adds. Williams' fair innings equity weights come from these slopes at current health on the contour whose EDE is 70 QALYs."; HEO defines Social Welfare Function as "A social welfare function (SWF) combines individual health or wellbeing into overall social welfare, setting how equality is weighed against the total.".

column2: GBD age-weight function with its age and value of peak weight
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Age Weighting. The module describes GBD age-weight function with its age and value of peak weight as "Gives the weight on a year of life lived at age x as C times x times e to the minus beta x, the exponential form Murray used for the original DALY. The weight is zero at birth, rises through childhood and declines slowly after its peak, which falls where the slope C e to the minus beta x times (1 minus beta x) is zero, at the age 1/beta. The weight at the peak is C/(beta e). With the standard constants of 0.1658 and 0.04 the peak is at age 25 with a weight of about 1.525, as in the article."; HEO defines Age Weighting as "Age weighting values a year of healthy life by the age at which it is lived, as in the original GBD DALY, which gave years in young adulthood most weight.".

column2: Undiscounted age-weighted years of life lost per death with a modulation constant
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Age Weighting. The module describes Undiscounted age-weighted years of life lost per death with a modulation constant as "Integrates the weight of HE-FM-AGW-001 over the L years lost from the age at death a, which gives C/beta squared times the difference of (1 + beta a) e to the minus beta a and the same term at a + L. The modulation constant K mixes this with the unweighted L years, so K = 1 is the article's undiscounted age-weighted YLL and K = 0 returns the L standard years of HE-FM-YLL-001 for one death. The (1 minus K) L term is not printed in the sources cited, which give the K = 1 integral and the discounted form with K. It is derived here as the limit of the second term of HE-FM-AGW-003 as r falls to zero, and the numerical integral of HE-CF-AGW-002 confirms it. The whole expression is the r = 0 case of HE-FM-AGW-003, which cannot be evaluated directly at r = 0 because it divides by r."; HEO defines Age Weighting as "Age weighting values a year of healthy life by the age at which it is lived, as in the original GBD DALY, which gave years in young adulthood most weight.".

column2: Age-weighted continuously discounted years of life lost per death of the original DALY
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Age Weighting. The first term is the age-weighted integral, scaled by K, and the second term, with weight 1 minus K, is the continuously discounted years of HE-FM-YLL-003, so K = 0 returns that record and HE-FM-DISC-003 with an amount of 1 and its continuous rate rho set equal to r. With r = 0.03 and K = 1 it gives the YLL per death of the standard GBD 1990 DALY, which GBD 2010 and WHO later dropped. The undiscounted case is HE-FM-AGW-002."; HEO defines Age Weighting as "Age weighting values a year of healthy life by the age at which it is lived, as in the original GBD DALY, which gave years in young adulthood most weight.".

column2: Age-weighted continuously discounted years lived with disability per incident case
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Age Weighting. column2: One-stage expected gain of continuing over stopping at an interim look with a switching cost
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adaptive Value of Information. The module describes One-stage expected gain of continuing over stopping at an interim look with a switching cost as "Compares two expected rewards at an interim look in the model of Chick, Forster and Pertile, with outcomes observed at once and no discounting. Stopping now adopts the new technology only if P times the posterior mean exceeds the switching cost I, which is worth P times max(a, 0), with a the posterior mean less I divided by P. Continuing with m more pairs and then choosing is worth P times the expected positive part of a after updating, less the cost c of each pair, plus the participants' expected reward d_on times m times mu_t under online learning. The difference Delta is P times EVSI_I less the sampling cost plus that online term, where s_m is the preposterior standard deviation of HE-FM-EVSI-002 with n_t and m, and EVSI_I is the closed-form EVSI of HE-FM-EVSI-003 taken about the threshold I/P in place of zero. A positive Delta for some feasible m means that a one-stage plan beats stopping, the continuation condition of the KG* rule, which Chick and colleagues set out for unknown sampling variance (their section 4) and which here takes the normal distribution of their equation 6 as in their equation 14."; HEO defines Adaptive Value of Information as "Adaptive value of information applies VOI analysis to staged research, re-valuing further data at each interim look to decide whether to continue.".

column2: Per-step infection probability of a susceptible agent from k infectious contacts
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Agent-Based Model. The module describes Per-step infection probability of a susceptible agent from k infectious contacts as "A susceptible agent with k contacts with infectious agents in one step, each transmitting independently with probability p, escapes infection only if every contact fails, which happens with probability (1 minus p) to the power k, the binomial probability of no events in HE-FM-BINOM-002 with k in place of n. The probability of at least one transmission, P_inf, is the complement; the article writes it P. It rises with k but less than in proportion, because a second transmission to an agent already infected adds nothing, so the sum k times p overstates it and can exceed 1. With one contact the formula returns p and with no contacts it returns zero."; HEO defines Agent-Based Model as "An agent-based model (ABM) simulates individuals as agents that follow rules and interact, so outcomes such as infections, costs and QALYs emerge.".

column2: One-step infection update of a susceptible agent from its own uniform random number
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Agent-Based Model. The module describes One-step infection update of a susceptible agent from its own uniform random number as "Turns the per-step infection probability of HE-FM-ABM-001 into the agent's next state by comparing it with a uniform random number U drawn for that agent. The agent becomes infected, X_next equal to 1, when U is below P_inf, and otherwise stays susceptible with X_next equal to 0, so over many draws the share infected approaches P_inf. Drawing U from a stream reserved for the agent, the per-agent seed that Chhatwal and He describe for common random numbers, gives the same agent the same U under each strategy, so a strategy that lowers P_inf can avert that agent's infection and cannot cause it. A single draw against P_inf has the same distribution as one draw per contact against p, which the computational function under HE-FM-ABM-001 uses as an independent check."; HEO defines Agent-Based Model as "An agent-based model (ABM) simulates individuals as agents that follow rules and interact, so outcomes such as infections, costs and QALYs emerge.".

column2: Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a mean agent-based model outcome
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Agent-Based Model. The module describes Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a mean agent-based model outcome as "Inverts the Monte Carlo standard error of a mean over independent runs, s_run divided by the square root of the number of runs (the form of HE-FM-ANTV-002 with one observation per run, with the standard deviation taken with divisor R minus 1 as in HE-FM-BSE-001), to give the number of runs R_req whose standard error equals a chosen target e_target. s_run is the standard deviation of the outcome across a pilot set of runs, for example of mean cost per person or, for an increment, of the paired difference between strategies run with common random numbers. The result is rounded up to a whole number of runs. Halving the target multiplies the runs by four."; HEO defines Agent-Based Model as "An agent-based model (ABM) simulates individuals as agents that follow rules and interact, so outcomes such as infections, costs and QALYs emerge.".

column2: Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a share of agent-based model runs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Agent-Based Model. The module describes Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a share of agent-based model runs as "For an output that is a share of runs, such as the share in which an outbreak becomes a major one, each run gives a 0 or 1 result and the Monte Carlo standard error of the share is the binomial standard error, the square root of P_exp(1 minus P_exp) over the number of runs, the standard error of an estimated binomial probability in HE-FM-BINOM-004. Putting in the expected share and rearranging gives the number of runs R_prop for a target standard error e_share, equation 1 of Morris and colleagues. The product P_exp(1 minus P_exp) is largest at a share of 0.5, so 0.25 divided by the squared target is a worst-case count when the share is unknown."; HEO defines Agent-Based Model as "An agent-based model (ABM) simulates individuals as agents that follow rules and interact, so outcomes such as infections, costs and QALYs emerge.".

column2: Relative survival as all-cause survival over expected background survival
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Background Mortality. The module describes Relative survival as all-cause survival over expected background survival as "Divides the all-cause survival of the patient group at time t by the survival expected at the same time in a comparable group of the general population, matched on age, sex and calendar year. This is equation 14 of NICE DSU TSD 21, the survival-scale form of the additive hazard HE-FM-BTH-005. Because all-cause survival is the product of expected survival and survival from the excess hazard, relative survival equals exp of minus the cumulative excess hazard (HE-FN-CUMH-001), so it falls only while the excess hazard is above zero and levels off at the cure fraction in a mixture cure model (HE-FM-CRM-001). A value above 1 means that cumulative modelled mortality up to t is below that of the general population."; HEO defines Background Mortality as "Background mortality is the death rate a model's patients would face without the disease, usually taken from general population life tables by age and sex.".

column2: All-cause cycle death probability from independent background and disease-specific death probabilities
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Background Mortality. The module describes All-cause cycle death probability from independent background and disease-specific death probabilities as "Combines the probability of dying of other causes in a cycle, read from the life table at the cohort's attained age, with the probability of dying of the disease in the same cycle. A person survives the cycle only by escaping both, so the all-cause probability is 1 minus the product of the two survival probabilities. When both come from constant rates over the same cycle with HE-FM-TP-001, the result equals the probability from the summed hazard of HE-FM-BTH-005, the total compound rate that Sonnenberg and Beck form by adding the excess rate to the baseline rate. HE-FM-TP-004 splits the result between background and disease death states where a model keeps them apart."; HEO defines Background Mortality as "Background mortality is the death rate a model's patients would face without the disease, usually taken from general population life tables by age and sex.".

column2: Marginal expected survival and background hazard of a cohort mixing two sexes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Background Mortality. The module describes Marginal expected survival and background hazard of a cohort mixing two sexes as "Averages expected survival over the members of a cohort and weights each group's background hazard by its expected survival, the grouped form of equations 18 and 19 of NICE DSU TSD 21 for two groups such as women and men. Because the group with the higher hazard dies sooner, its weight in the marginal hazard shrinks over time, and the marginal background hazard falls below a fixed blend of the two hazards. The same form applies to age groups in a cohort with a spread of entry ages, where it avoids reading one hazard at the mean age. S_star is the expected survival of HE-FM-BGM-001 and h_star the background hazard of HE-FM-BTH-005 for the whole cohort."; HEO defines Background Mortality as "Background mortality is the death rate a model's patients would face without the disease, usually taken from general population life tables by age and sex.".

column2: Basic reproduction number of the SIR model as transmission rate times mean infectious period
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basic Reproduction Number. The module describes Basic reproduction number of the SIR model as transmission rate times mean infectious period as "In the simple susceptible, infectious and recovered (SIR) model, one infectious person in a fully susceptible population causes new infections at rate beta and stays infectious for a mean time D equal to 1/gamma, so R_0 is beta times D, or beta/gamma. Van den Driessche derives R_0 as the product of the transmission rate and the mean infectious time and shows that R_0 = 1 is a sharp threshold, with the number infectious falling steadily to zero below it and first rising above it. The WHO guide writes the same quantity for a homogeneously mixing population as p c D, the probability of transmission per contact times the contact rate times the duration of infectiousness, so beta here corresponds to p times c. Models with a latent stage, demography or several groups take R_0 from the next-generation matrix of HE-FM-BRN-005."; HEO defines Basic Reproduction Number as "The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of infections one typical case causes in a fully susceptible population, used in vaccine models.".

column2: Effective reproduction number as the basic reproduction number times the susceptible proportion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basic Reproduction Number. The module describes Effective reproduction number as the basic reproduction number times the susceptible proportion as "Once part of the population is immune, each case meets fewer people who can be infected. The WHO guide gives R_t = R_0 x_t for a homogeneously mixing population, where x_t is the proportion of the population still susceptible at time t, and Pitman and colleagues define the effective reproduction number in the same way. Vaccination and past infection lower x_t and so R_t, while R_0 stays the same because its definition assumes a fully susceptible population. R_t above 1 means new infections per generation are rising and below 1 falling. With an all-or-nothing vaccine of effectiveness E given to a proportion V before any spread, x_t equals 1 minus V times E, which is the starting susceptible proportion s_0 of HE-CF-ATR-001 when V times E is entered there as the fully protected proportion."; HEO defines Basic Reproduction Number as "The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of infections one typical case causes in a fully susceptible population, used in vaccine models.".

column2: Herd immunity threshold and critical vaccination coverage for a vaccine of effectiveness E
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basic Reproduction Number. The module describes Herd immunity threshold and critical vaccination coverage for a vaccine of effectiveness E as "Sustained spread stops once the susceptible proportion is below 1/R_0, so the proportion that must be immune is H = 1 minus 1/R_0, the herd immunity threshold of the WHO guide, which calls the matching level the critical effective immunisation level. Van den Driessche gives the same condition for a perfect vaccine, and Pitman and colleagues state that in a homogeneously mixing population coverage has to be greater than this value for herd immunity to occur. An all-or-nothing vaccine that fully protects a proportion E of those vaccinated immunises V times E of the population, so the critical coverage is V_c = H/E, the form Masterson and colleagues use, and when E is below H, V_c exceeds 1 and that vaccine alone cannot stop sustained spread. Pitman and colleagues and van den Driessche state the condition as coverage greater than the threshold, while the WHO guide writes p_c as at least 1 minus 1/R_0. At coverage exactly V_c the effective reproduction number of HE-FM-BRN-002 equals 1, the boundary that HE-CF-ATR-001 classifies as no major epidemic, since it returns a final attack rate of 0 whenever R_0 s_0 is 1 or less."; HEO defines Basic Reproduction Number as "The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of infections one typical case causes in a fully susceptible population, used in vaccine models.".

column2: Reproduction number from the early exponential growth rate under three generation interval shapes
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basic Reproduction Number. The module describes Reproduction number from the early exponential growth rate under three generation interval shapes as "In the early phase of an outbreak new infections grow as exp(r t), and Wallinga and Lipsitch show that the reproduction number implied by a growth rate r depends only on the generation interval distribution, through R = 1/M(minus r) with M its moment generating function. An exponential generation interval with mean T_c gives R = 1 plus r T_c; a latent stage and an infectious stage, each exponentially distributed with means T_E and T_I, give (1 plus r T_E)(1 plus r T_I); and a fixed interval gives exp(r T_c), the upper bound for a given growth rate and mean. In the SIR model T_c is the mean infectious period 1/gamma, so the exponential form is van den Driessche's R_0 = 1 plus r/gamma, the inverse of r = gamma(R_0 minus 1). A growth rate taken from an epidemic doubling time T_d, as used in HE-FM-CFR-003, is log(2)/T_d."; HEO defines Basic Reproduction Number as "The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of infections one typical case causes in a fully susceptible population, used in vaccine models.".

column2: Basic reproduction number of a two-group next-generation matrix as its dominant eigenvalue
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basic Reproduction Number. The module describes Basic reproduction number of a two-group next-generation matrix as its dominant eigenvalue as "When infected people differ by group or stage, element k_ij of the next-generation matrix K is the expected number of new cases in group i caused by one newly infected person in group j, as Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Roberts define it, and R_0 is the dominant eigenvalue of K, the definition proposed by Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Metz. For a compartmental model van den Driessche writes K as F times the inverse of V, with F the rates of new infections and V the other transitions, and R_0 as its spectral radius. For two groups the dominant eigenvalue is the larger root of lambda^2 minus T_K lambda plus D_K = 0, with T_K the trace and D_K the determinant, and the term under the square root equals (k_11 minus k_22)^2 plus 4 k_12 k_21, which is never negative for a matrix of non-negative entries. When D_K is zero, as for a matrix of rank one, R_0 is the trace. Larger matrices are handled by HE-CF-BRN-001."; HEO defines Basic Reproduction Number as "The basic reproduction number (R0) is the average number of infections one typical case causes in a fully susceptible population, used in vaccine models.".

column2: Foreign price or cost converted to the home currency at a market exchange rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket of Countries. The module describes Foreign price or cost converted to the home currency at a market exchange rate as "Multiplies a price or cost observed in another country's currency by the exchange rate expressed as home-currency units per unit of that currency, the p_i e_i term of the article's reference-price rule. The same step converts any cost record between currencies. A rate published the other way round, as local currency units per US dollar in the GLOBE Model final rule, is divided into the price instead. The converted prices feed the basket aggregates of HE-FM-BOC-003, and conversion at purchasing power parity is HE-FM-BOC-002."; HEO defines Basket of Countries as "The basket of countries is the set of foreign markets whose drug prices a regulator compares in external reference pricing to set a domestic price.".

column2: Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket of Countries. The module describes Cost converted between currencies at purchasing power parity as "Divides a cost in the source currency by the source country's PPP conversion factor, which gives international dollars, and multiplies by the target country's factor, which gives the target currency. Both factors are local currency units per international dollar, so the route through international dollars follows from their units (derived here), and a target factor of 1 returns international dollars. The World Bank describes PPPs as eliminating differences in price levels between countries in the process of conversion, and the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre Cost Converter page notes that pure exchange-rate conversion, the market rate of HE-FM-BOC-001, does not. Where the cost also comes from another price year, the year is moved first with HE-FM-COST-002 and HE-CF-BOC-001 sets out the two orders."; HEO defines Basket of Countries as "The basket of countries is the set of foreign markets whose drug prices a regulator compares in external reference pricing to set a domestic price.".

column2: Basket mean, lowest and highest price from five converted reference prices
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket of Countries. The module describes Basket mean, lowest and highest price from five converted reference prices as "Combines the converted prices c_1 to c_5 of a five-country basket, each from HE-FM-BOC-001, into the mean, the lowest and the highest price, three of the aggregation rules f in the article's P_ref. Kanavos and colleagues report that the lowest price in the basket is often used and that the average or the median is not uncommon, and Rémuzat and colleagues found the average price in use in 15 European countries and the lowest price in 7. The highest price is the PMPRB's highest international price. The median, baskets of other sizes and countries without a price are handled by HE-CF-BOC-002, and HE-FM-BOC-004 turns a reference price into a ceiling."; HEO defines Basket of Countries as "The basket of countries is the set of foreign markets whose drug prices a regulator compares in external reference pricing to set a domestic price.".

column2: Basket ceiling as a multiple of the reference price and the margin of a proposed price
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket of Countries. A positive margin means the price is above the ceiling and is cut or reviewed, and a margin of zero or below means it is accepted. The article's illustrative rule takes k = 1.25 on the basket mean, modelled on Japan's foreign average price adjustment, whose adjusted price is HE-FM-BOC-005, while the PMPRB test is k = 1 on the highest international price. column2: Euler step of one compartment from its inflows, outflows, births and deaths
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Compartmental Model. column2: Number of EQ-5D-5L health states and main-effects decrements, and the share valued directly
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept EQ-5D-5L Value Set. The module describes Number of EQ-5D-5L health states and main-effects decrements, and the share valued directly as "Counts the states that a descriptive system with K dimensions of L levels describes, the number of decrements a main-effects value set needs when level 1 carries none, and the share of states that respondents valued directly. For the EQ-5D-5L the count is 5 to the power 5, 3,125 states, and 5 dimensions times 4 levels above level 1 give 20 decrements, the size of the England model in HE-FM-EQ5L-002. The same counts give 243 states and 10 level decrements for the EQ-5D-3L, whose UK tariff in HE-FM-EQ3L-002 adds a constant and N3 to them. The share valued shows how much of a value set rests on model prediction."; HEO defines EQ-5D-5L Value Set as "EQ-5D-5L value set is a scoring algorithm, estimated from a general public valuation study, that gives each of the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L states a QALY utility.".

column2: Share of the life years gained over the model horizon observed within trial follow-up
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Life Years Gained. The module describes Share of the life years gained over the model horizon observed within trial follow-up as "Takes the restricted mean survival times of the two arms at a follow-up time tau and their mean survival over the model horizon, and returns the within-trial gain, the gain over the horizon, the share of that gain lying within follow-up and the gain lying after it. The restricted means come from HE-FM-ADMC-003 for a Kaplan-Meier curve or from the modelled curves, as in the article's step 6, and the horizon means from an extrapolation such as HE-FM-BTH-002 or HE-FN-CRM-001. The difference of two restricted means is the measure of Royston and Parmar and is not new here; the share phi and the gain after follow-up are derived here. HE-FM-ADMC-004 gives the share of one arm's mean survival that comes from its tail, whereas 1 minus phi is the difference between the arms in the area after tau divided by the gain over the horizon, which depends on both arms' means as well as their tail shares (derived here)."; HEO defines Life Years Gained as "Life years gained (LYG) are the extra years of mean survival an intervention gives over its comparator, without quality adjustment, in economic evaluation.".

column2: Cobb-Douglas gross investment in health from medical care, own time and schooling
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Production Function. The module describes Cobb-Douglas gross investment in health from medical care, own time and schooling as "Gross investment is the efficiency factor exp(rho_H E) times medical care raised to the power 1-K times own time raised to the power K, the exponential form of Grossman's estimating equation ln I = rho_H E + (1-K) ln M + K ln TH. The exponents sum to one, so doubling both inputs doubles I, and 1-K is the elasticity of gross investment with respect to medical care. Schooling enters as a factor-neutral efficiency shift, so one more year multiplies I by exp(rho_H) for the same inputs, a rise of about 3.05% when rho_H is 0.03. The result I is the gross investment of HE-FM-DFH-001."; HEO defines Health Production Function as "A health production function shows how medical care, other market goods and own time produce health, with education raising efficiency (Grossman model).".

column2: Least-cost split of an outlay between medical care and own time for Cobb-Douglas gross investment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Production Function. The module describes Least-cost split of an outlay between medical care and own time for Cobb-Douglas gross investment as "Spends the share 1-K of the outlay on medical care and the share K on own time, the cost shares that Grossman gives for the Cobb-Douglas form of HE-FM-HPF-001, and returns the gross investment the outlay buys. The quantities follow from Grossman's least-cost condition (derived here), under which the ratio of the marginal product of care, (1-K) I / M, to that of time, K I / TH, equals the ratio of the price of care to the wage. The chain therefore also returns both marginal products and their ratio, so the condition can be checked against P / W. With the outlay fixed, a higher wage buys fewer hours and leaves the units of care unchanged, so the mix shifts towards care."; HEO defines Health Production Function as "A health production function shows how medical care, other market goods and own time produce health, with education raising efficiency (Grossman model).".

column2: Unit cost of gross investment in health and the outlay for a target gross investment with schooling
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Production Function. The module describes Unit cost of gross investment in health and the outlay for a target gross investment with schooling as "Returns the cost of one unit of gross investment at the least-cost mix and the outlay needed for a target gross investment. For the Cobb-Douglas form of HE-FM-HPF-001 the unit cost is exp(-rho_H E) times (P / (1-K)) to the power 1-K times (W / K) to the power K, derived here by putting the least-cost split of HE-FM-HPF-002 into the production function. Because of constant returns and fixed prices it is both the average and the marginal cost of gross investment, the pi_(t-1) that HE-FM-DFH-002 takes as an input. One more year of schooling divides the unit cost by exp(rho_H), the exact form of Grossman's result that marginal cost falls by rho_H percent per unit of E, and a 1% rise in the wage raises it by about K percent."; HEO defines Health Production Function as "A health production function shows how medical care, other market goods and own time produce health, with education raising efficiency (Grossman model).".

column2: Mean and variance of specific stop-loss reimbursement over a three-level claims distribution
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attachment Point. The module describes Mean and variance of specific stop-loss reimbursement over a three-level claims distribution as "Gives the expected reimbursement per covered person, its second moment, variance and standard deviation when the person's annual eligible claims take one of three levels C_1 to C_3 with probabilities p_1 to p_3, and the remaining probability sits at claims that never reach the attachment point. Each level's payment is the specific layer rule of HE-FM-ASL-001 with a layer limit of U minus A, times the coinsurance rate c, and E_R is the probability-weighted mean of HE-FN-EV-001 over those payments, the net premium per person for the layer before any loading, carried here because the variance needs it. V_R is the second moment less the squared mean, following the expected value and second moment of the excess of loss cost function in Miccolis 1977. The record works from the discrete distribution of the article's worked example; the normal closed form for an aggregate total is the separate record HE-FM-ASL-005. For a group of n independent members the expected total is n times E_R and its standard deviation SD_R times the square root of n, the rule of HE-FM-ASL-003, which the computational function below applies. Raising A by an amount that passes no claim level and stays below the cap lowers E_R by c times that amount times the probability that claims exceed the old attachment point (derived), so expected reimbursement falls steeply while, as the worked examples show, the standard deviation falls more slowly."; HEO defines Attachment Point as "An attachment point is the claims level at which stop-loss insurance or health reinsurance starts to pay, per person (specific) or per group (aggregate).".

column2: Proportional rise in expected reimbursement of an uncapped specific excess layer under uniform claims inflation
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attachment Point. The module describes Proportional rise in expected reimbursement of an uncapped specific excess layer under uniform claims inflation as "Gives the expected reimbursement per member of an uncapped excess layer with full reimbursement before and after every claim level rises by the same inflation rate g while the attachment point stays fixed in money, the proportional rise rise_E in that expected reimbursement, and its ratio mult_E to g. Lee 1988 states that with the retention fixed the expected excess loss payment rises proportionally much more than the general rate of inflation. Miccolis 1977 shows that under a uniform inflation factor the expected loss limited at k equals the factor times the earlier expected loss limited at k divided by the factor (equation 17), from which E_g equals (1 + g) times the expected excess of current claims over A / (1 + g) (derived), so inflating claims has the same effect as lowering the attachment point in real terms, and without a cap mult_E is at least 1 (derived, checked over a grid of inputs). A coinsurance rate multiplies E_0 and E_g alike and cancels from rise_E; with a cap the top of the layer can already be used up and the rise can fall below g. The general price-year adjustment of a single cost is HE-FM-COST-002."; HEO defines Attachment Point as "An attachment point is the claims level at which stop-loss insurance or health reinsurance starts to pay, per person (specific) or per group (aggregate).".

column2: Immortal-time bias factor in a responder rate ratio from pre-response person-time counted as responder time
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Landmark Analysis. The module describes Immortal-time bias factor in a responder rate ratio from pre-response person-time counted as responder time as "Compares two constant-hazard rate ratios of responders against patients without a response, each of the form of HE-FM-HR-005. The naive ratio RR_naive adds the immortal time I, the person-time responders spent before responding, to the responders' person-time, while RR_split moves it to the side without a response up to the time status changes, as the extended Cox model with a time-varying covariate does in Giobbie-Hurder, Gelber and Regan. No death can fall in I, so the event counts are the same in both ratios and F, their ratio, equals PT_R PT_N divided by (PT_R + I)(PT_N + I) (derived here), which depends on person-time alone. F is 1 when I is zero and falls further below 1 as I grows (checked over a grid in Python), so the naive ratio always flatters responders, and dividing a naive rate ratio by F recovers the time-split ratio."; HEO defines Landmark Analysis as "A survival technique restricting analysis to patients event-free up to a predefined time point, then examining survival from that point forward.".

column2: Hedges' g from Cohen's d with the approximate correction factor J
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hedges' G. The module describes Hedges' g from Cohen's d with the approximate correction factor J as "Multiplies the uncorrected standardised mean difference d of HE-FM-CD-001 by a correction factor J that depends only on the degrees of freedom m of the standard deviation used to standardise, which for the pooled standard deviation is the total sample size less 2. The factor 1 minus 3 over (4m minus 1) is Hedges' algebraic approximation to an exact factor written with gamma functions, which HE-CF-HEDG-001 computes. Substituting for m gives 1 minus 3 over (4N minus 9) with N the total sample size, the form Review Manager prints. J is below 1, so g is always nearer zero than d, and J approaches 1 as the sample grows."; HEO defines Hedges' G as "A standardised effect size measure similar to Cohen's d but corrected for small sample size bias.".

column2: Large-sample variance and standard error of Hedges' g
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hedges' G. The module describes Large-sample variance and standard error of Hedges' g as "Gives the large-sample variance of d as a term for the precision of the mean difference, (n_1 + n_2) over n_1 n_2, plus a term that grows with the size of the effect, d squared over twice the total sample size. Multiplying d by the constant J multiplies its variance by J squared, so the variance of g is J squared times V_d and its square root is the standard error. J comes from HE-FM-HEDG-001 and d from HE-FM-CD-001. The inverse of V_g is the study's weight in HE-FM-ADMA-001 and HE-FM-ADMA-005, and HE-FM-AN-001 with SE_g gives the confidence interval."; HEO defines Hedges' G as "A standardised effect size measure similar to Cohen's d but corrected for small sample size bias.".

column2: Review Manager standard error of Hedges' adjusted g
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hedges' G. The module describes Review Manager standard error of Hedges' adjusted g as "Review Manager, the software Cochrane reviews use, gives the standard error of Hedges' adjusted g from the total sample size N, the two group sizes and the corrected estimate g, with N less 3.94 in the denominator of the effect term. It differs from SE_g of HE-FM-HEDG-002 because J is not applied as a multiplier and the effect term is g squared over twice (N less 3.94) in place of d squared over twice N, and it is slightly larger in small trials. Reproducing the weights of a Cochrane forest plot needs this form, while the article's interval uses HE-FM-HEDG-002. g comes from HE-FM-HEDG-001."; HEO defines Hedges' G as "A standardised effect size measure similar to Cohen's d but corrected for small sample size bias.".

column2: Expected overstatement of a population standardised effect by Cohen's d in small samples
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Hedges' G. The module describes Expected overstatement of a population standardised effect by Cohen's d in small samples as "Gives the mean of the uncorrected estimate d over repeated samples when the population standardised difference is delta, using Hedges' result that this mean is delta divided by the exact factor, here replaced by the approximate J of HE-FM-HEDG-001. Bias_d is the amount by which d overstates delta on average. The relative overstatement Bias_d over delta depends only on m, and with the approximate J it is about 25% at 4 degrees of freedom, about 4% at 20 and under 0.4% at 198 (computed here). It describes the estimator before any correction and does not shrink when more small studies are averaged."; HEO defines Hedges' G as "A standardised effect size measure similar to Cohen's d but corrected for small sample size bias.".

column2: Pigouvian subsidy bill, transfer to inframarginal users and bill per induced unit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Subsidy. The module describes Pigouvian subsidy bill, transfer to inframarginal users and bill per induced unit as "Multiplies the per-unit subsidy by the uptake it produces to give the bill to the public budget, and by the uptake there would have been without it to give the transfer to inframarginal users, people paid for doing what they would have done anyway. The rest of the bill is paid on the induced units, and dividing the whole bill by the induced units gives the public money paid out for each extra unit the subsidy brings about. The bill is a transfer and not a cost to society in itself; the social cost of raising it is the excess burden of HE-FM-DWL-004 with the bill as G, which HE-FM-PIGS-002 carries into the net welfare change. With linear demand the uptake under the subsidy is the private quantity of HE-FM-EXT-002 plus s / b."; HEO defines Pigouvian Subsidy as "A Pigouvian subsidy is a payment for an activity that benefits others, set equal to its marginal external benefit at the socially efficient level.".

column2: Net welfare change of a uniform or targeted Pigouvian subsidy with costly public funds
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Subsidy. The module describes Net welfare change of a uniform or targeted Pigouvian subsidy with costly public funds as "Measures the welfare gained as a per-unit subsidy s raises uptake from the private quantity Q_p of HE-FM-EXT-002 by s / b, the area between marginal social benefit and marginal cost over the induced units, and subtracts the excess burden of raising the bill, lambda times the bill of HE-FM-PIGS-001. W charges the excess burden on the whole bill of a uniform subsidy and W_T on a subsidy confined to the induced units. With the article's curves W reduces to the article's 15s minus 0.625s squared minus 0.2s(60 + s). At any rate S_g equals the deadweight loss of HE-FM-EXT-002 less the triangle of HE-FM-DWL-001 left between Q_p plus dQ and the efficient quantity, so at the Pigouvian rate it equals that deadweight loss and at a rate of d_0 it falls short by the overshoot loss (derived here and checked on a grid of curves). The general form in a, b, c, m and g is derived here from the article's example."; HEO defines Pigouvian Subsidy as "A Pigouvian subsidy is a payment for an activity that benefits others, set equal to its marginal external benefit at the socially efficient level.".

column2: Welfare-maximising uniform Pigouvian subsidy when public funds are costly
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Pigouvian Subsidy. The module describes Welfare-maximising uniform Pigouvian subsidy when public funds are costly as "Finds the uniform per-unit subsidy that maximises the net welfare W of HE-FM-PIGS-002 and the net welfare it gives. Setting the derivative of W to zero gives s_opt, which falls below the Pigouvian rate of HE-FM-EXT-002 whenever lambda is above zero and d_0 is positive, because each extra pound of rate is paid on every inframarginal unit as well as on the induced ones. With lambda of zero and a positive d_0, s_opt equals the Pigouvian rate and W_opt the deadweight loss of HE-FM-EXT-002. A subsidy adds net welfare only when the external benefit at the private quantity exceeds lambda times b times Q_p; otherwise the formula returns zero. The closed form is derived here from W and checked against the article's figures."; HEO defines Pigouvian Subsidy as "A Pigouvian subsidy is a payment for an activity that benefits others, set equal to its marginal external benefit at the socially efficient level.".

column2: Tipping-point shift for QALYs lost to follow-up at a cost-effectiveness threshold
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Loss to Follow-Up. The module describes Tipping-point shift for QALYs lost to follow-up at a cost-effectiveness threshold as "Sets the delta-adjusted QALY gain equal to the gain needed at threshold lambda, H_d = Delta_C / lambda (HE-FM-CET-002), and solves for the shift. With a shift delta for those lost from the new treatment arm and r times delta for those lost from usual care, the gain is Delta_E_obs plus (p_T minus r times p_C) times delta (HE-FM-LOCF-002 read as in HE-FN-LTFU-001), so the tipping-point shift is H_d minus Delta_E_obs, divided by p_T minus r times p_C (derived). Setting r = 0 confines the shift to the new treatment arm and gives the article's delta_star = (Delta_C / lambda minus Delta_E_obs) / p_T, and r = 1 applies the same shift to both arms, when only the difference in the proportions lost moves the gain. A negative delta_star is a QALY shortfall for those lost that the base case can absorb. When the denominator is positive the base-case conclusion holds for every shift that lies on the same side of delta_star as zero."; HEO defines Loss to Follow-Up as "Loss to follow-up occurs when trial participants stop providing data before follow-up ends, so later outcomes, costs and QALYs can be missing.".

column2: Crude-versus-adjusted ranking reversal condition for two providers' costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Case-Mix Adjustment. The module describes Crude-versus-adjusted ranking reversal condition for two providers' costs as "Compares two providers on crude cost per case and on the indirectly standardised cost index. The crude cost ratio rho is the product of the index ratio RI and the ratio mu of expected cost per case, the part of the crude gap that the case mix accounts for, so RI is rho divided by mu and equals I_1 / I_2 for the indices 100 A_h / E_h, which are 100 times R_h of HE-FM-CWT-003. The adjusted ranking reverses the crude one when rho minus 1 and RI minus 1 have opposite signs, which holds exactly when rho lies strictly between mu and 1 (derived here and checked numerically on 200,000 random inputs). A crude cost advantage therefore survives adjustment only when it is larger than the advantage in expected cost per case, and two providers with the same mix, mu equal to 1, cannot reverse. A tie in either ranking is not counted as a reversal."; HEO defines Case-Mix Adjustment as "Case-mix adjustment corrects comparisons of providers' costs or outcomes for differences in the patients they treat, so that like is compared with like.".

column2: Negative likelihood ratio of a negative result on both of two tests with conditional covariances
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Negative Likelihood Ratio. The module describes Negative likelihood ratio of a negative result on both of two tests with conditional covariances as "When two tests are combined so that a person is called negative only if both are negative, the combined sensitivity Se_par and specificity Sp_par follow from the single-test values and the conditional covariances, C_pos among people with the condition and C_neg among people without it, in the joint probabilities that Wang, Lin and Nelson give. The combined ratio LR_neg_12 is then the LR_neg of HE-FM-DXA-002 applied to Se_par and Sp_par. With both covariances zero, the conditional independence that the article warns about, LR_neg_12 equals the product of the two single-test ratios (derived). A positive C_pos raises the ratio above that product, so multiplying the ratios overstates the rule-out, while a positive C_neg on its own lowers it below the product (derived)."; HEO defines Negative Likelihood Ratio as "Negative Likelihood Ratio (LR-): (1 minus sensitivity) over specificity, the factor by which a negative test multiplies disease odds in decision models.".

column2: Copas probit probability that a study with standard error s is published
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Copas Model. The module describes Copas probit probability that a study with standard error s is published as "Under the selection equation of the Copas model a study is published when a latent propensity Z = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s + delta is above zero, with delta standard normal, so its marginal probability of publication is the standard normal distribution function at the index u = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s. Phi(gamma_0) is the probability of publishing a study with an infinitely large standard error, and gamma_1 sets how fast the probability rises as the standard error shrinks. The site calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_u is entered as a named input from NORM.S.DIST(u, TRUE) or pnorm(u), the convention of HE-FM-MCID-004. That record's normal share above a threshold returns the same number with a threshold of zero, a standard deviation of 1 and a mean of u; the Copas form adds the index in the study's precision with its two selection parameters."; HEO defines Copas Model as "The Copas model is a selection model for publication bias in meta-analysis that re-estimates the pooled effect under assumed rates of non-publication.".

column2: Expected number of unpublished studies implied by Copas selection parameters for two standard error groups
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Copas Model. The module describes Expected number of unpublished studies implied by Copas selection parameters for two standard error groups as "Copas and Shi translate a pair of selection parameters into the expected number of unpublished studies, M, the sum over the published studies of (1 minus P_i) / P_i, with P_i the publication probability of HE-FM-COPAS-001 at study i's standard error. The formula is written for two groups of published studies that share a standard error within each group, n_1 at s_1 and n_2 at s_2, as in the article's example of two large and ten small trials; each further standard error adds a term of the same form, which the R and Python code of HE-CF-COPAS-001 handles. Each published study with probability P stands in expectation for (1 minus P) / P unpublished studies of the same precision, so groups with a low publication probability dominate M; in the article's moderate scenario 18.57 of the 18.68 come from the ten small trials. The step that turns P into M is the same algebra as the bed turnover interval of HE-FM-BTO-004 in another setting; the Copas content is the chain from gamma_0, gamma_1 and the standard errors."; HEO defines Copas Model as "The Copas model is a selection model for publication bias in meta-analysis that re-estimates the pooled effect under assumed rates of non-publication.".

column2: Grossman demand for the health stock as a ratio between two states with the implied gross investment
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Derived Demand for Healthcare. The module describes Grossman demand for the health stock as a ratio between two states with the implied gross investment as "Grossman's demand function for the health stock, ln H = eps ln W minus eps ln pi minus eps ln delta with the intercept suppressed, is written as the ratio of the stock demanded after a change to the stock demanded before it, so that the intercept cancels. With pi held fixed a 1% rise in the wage raises the stock demanded by eps percent, while a 1% rise in the marginal cost of gross investment or in the depreciation rate lowers it by eps percent. The wage also raises pi through the own time input, so with pi taken from HE-FM-HPF-003 the net wage elasticity of the stock is (1-K) eps and schooling raises it by rho_H eps per year, Grossman's reduced form for health. The second step applies HE-FM-DFH-001 with net investment small, so gross investment is about delta H and its ratio is the depreciation ratio times H_ratio (derived here), which for a change in delta alone is (delta_1 / delta_0) to the power 1-eps and rises with depreciation when eps is below 1. The function follows from the pure investment condition HE-FM-DFH-002 once the marginal efficiency schedule has the constant elasticity eps."; HEO defines Derived Demand for Healthcare as "Derived demand for healthcare is the idea that people want medical care mainly as an input for producing health, the thing they actually value.".

column2: Grossman reduced-form demand for medical care with its wage, price, schooling and depreciation elasticities
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Derived Demand for Healthcare. The module describes Grossman reduced-form demand for medical care with its wage, price, schooling and depreciation elasticities as "Grossman's reduced-form demand function for medical care, ln M = [(1-K) eps + K] ln W minus [(1-K) eps + K] ln P plus rho_H (eps minus 1) E plus (1-eps) ln delta, with intercepts suppressed and the small net disinvestment term left out, is written as the ratio of care demanded after and before a change. It follows from the health stock demand of HE-FM-DDHC-001, gross investment of about delta H from HE-FM-DFH-001, the unit cost pi of HE-FM-HPF-003 and the least-cost care M = (1-K) C / P of HE-FM-HPF-002, and every coefficient contains eps, the parameter of the demand for health. The price elasticity splits into a scale part, minus (1-K) eps, through the smaller health stock demanded when care is dearer, and a substitution part, minus K, towards own time. Schooling changes care by rho_H (eps minus 1) per year and depreciation by the elasticity 1-eps, so with eps below 1 the more educated use less care and people whose health depreciates faster use more. For a change in the price of care alone the ratio is HE-FM-XPE-003 with the own-price elasticity e_MP."; HEO defines Derived Demand for Healthcare as "Derived demand for healthcare is the idea that people want medical care mainly as an input for producing health, the thing they actually value.".

column2: Net days in accounts receivable from net receivables and average daily net patient revenue
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Days in Accounts Receivable. The module describes Net days in accounts receivable from net receivables and average daily net patient revenue as "Divides the net patient receivables on the balance sheet at the end of a period by the average daily net patient service revenue of the same period, the HFMA MAP Key FM-1 net days in accounts receivable, so that receivables of providers of any size read on one scale of days.
