The measure applies to providers paid claim by claim, where each episode of care has to be coded, billed, adjudicated and collected before it turns into cash. Applied to one payer group the same formula gives that group's own days figure, and the overall figure is the revenue-weighted mean of the group figures by the weighted-mean identity of HE-FM-CRAT-001. Multiplying DAR by r_bar returns the receivables balance, the input to the carrying cost and the cash released that HE-FN-DAR-001 describes."; HEO defines Days in Accounts Receivable as "Days in accounts receivable (AR days) is a provider's net receivables divided by average daily net patient revenue, giving days of revenue still unpaid.".

column2: Heterotrait-monotrait ratio for two constructs with two indicators each
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Discriminant Validity. The module describes Heterotrait-monotrait ratio for two constructs with two indicators each as "With two indicators per construct each within-construct mean is a single correlation, r_i1i2 or r_j1j2, and the between-construct mean rbar_ij has four terms, so the heterotrait-monotrait ratio is rbar_ij divided by the square root of r_i1i2 times r_j1j2. This is Eq. 6 of Henseler, Ringle and Sarstedt with K_i and K_j both equal to 2, and HE-CF-DISV-001 takes any numbers of indicators. The authors describe the ratio as an estimate of the correlation between the two constructs, so a value clearly below 1 indicates constructs that differ. Used as a criterion, a value above a cut-off of 0.85 or 0.90 points to a lack of discriminant validity, a level the authors call debatable. In the article's example the questionnaire and the clinician rating serve as the two indicators of physical functioning and of mood."; HEO defines Discriminant Validity as "Discriminant validity is evidence that a health measure correlates less with measures of other constructs than with its own, as predicted in advance.".

column2: Returns to scale of a Cobb-Douglas hospital production function with free output elasticities
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Healthcare Production Function. The module describes Returns to scale of a Cobb-Douglas hospital production function with free output elasticities as "Gives a provider's activity from labour and capital in the Cobb-Douglas form that hospital studies estimate, with the output elasticities alpha and beta left free, and returns the degree of returns to scale RTS, their sum, with the output Q_s and the ratio g_s when every input is multiplied by s. Sielska and Nojszewska define economies of scale as the sum of the output elasticities, the percentage change in output when all inputs rise by 1%, and g_s equals s to the power RTS for any s (derived), so returns to scale are decreasing when RTS is below 1 and increasing when it is above 1. With alpha + beta = 1 the function is the constant-returns HE-FM-HPF-001, under which g_s always equals s. The marginal products alpha Q / L and beta Q / K have the form of those in HE-FM-HPF-002, each exponent times output over the input, a form that holds at any RTS (derived), although HE-FM-HPF-002 computes them only for exponents summing to one. RTS is a property of the estimated function and is the same at every size, unlike scale efficiency HE-FM-EFF-003, a ratio of frontier scores for one unit."; HEO defines Healthcare Production Function as "A healthcare production function gives the maximum care output, such as visits or hospital episodes, obtainable from given staff, capital and technology.".

column2: Time trade-off utility of a chronic state under the linear QALY model
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Utility. The module describes Time trade-off utility of a chronic state under the linear QALY model as "The time trade-off utility is the ratio of the years in full health T_y to the years in the state T_x that the respondent judges equal. The rule follows from the indifference once full health is valued at 1, immediate death at 0 and utility of life duration is linear in years, as Lipman, Brouwer and Attema set out, and it gives one respondent's value for one state judged at least as good as immediate death. The standard gamble asked about the same state gives the indifference probability itself as the utility (HE-FN-UTIL-001), and the two methods tend to give different values (HE-ER-UTIL-001)."; HEO defines Utility as "Utility is a numerical measure of preference; in health economics, a health utility values a health state on a scale where 1 is full health and 0 is dead.".

column2: Phelps second-order expected welfare loss at a coinsurance rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard in Health Insurance. The module describes Phelps second-order expected welfare loss at a coinsurance rate as "Adds two losses that move in opposite directions as cover changes. The first is the risk premium of the spending the patient still bears, one half of r times the variance of that spending, which is sigma squared times C squared when insurance pays the share 1 minus C of every bill. The second is the welfare-loss triangle of insurance-induced care, one half of (1 minus C) squared times eps times mu, which is HE-FM-MH-002 with the demand slope written as eps mu over the square of the full price (derived, for a straight-line demand curve with elasticity eps at the full price). Lowering C cuts the first term and raises the second, both quadratically, so the expected loss has a single minimum at the rate given by HE-FM-MHHI-002. Phelps prints the sum as his equation (4), with the elasticity entered as a negative number and subtracted."; HEO defines Moral Hazard in Health Insurance as "Moral hazard in health insurance is extra healthcare use when cover lowers the price patients pay, and any reduced effort to stay healthy once insured.".

column2: Phelps optimal coinsurance rate from risk aversion, spending variance and price elasticity
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Moral Hazard in Health Insurance. The module describes Phelps optimal coinsurance rate from risk aversion, spending variance and price elasticity as "Gives the coinsurance rate that minimises the expected welfare loss of HE-FM-MHHI-001, found by setting its derivative with respect to C to zero. The rate is eps mu over eps mu plus r sigma squared, which Phelps puts in words as the moral hazard loss over the sum of the moral hazard loss and the risk premium. It rises with the price elasticity and falls with risk aversion and with the variance of spending, so a large, barely price-sensitive risk such as hospital care calls for near-complete cover and small, predictable, price-sensitive spending for a high rate. Phelps also gives it in relative terms with the coefficient of variation and the share of income at risk (his equation (7)), the same rule divided through by mu (derived)."; HEO defines Moral Hazard in Health Insurance as "Moral hazard in health insurance is extra healthcare use when cover lowers the price patients pay, and any reduced effort to stay healthy once insured.".

column2: Integer optimum of the 0-1 funding problem for four indivisible programmes with its gaps to a funding rule and to the divisible fill
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Integer Programming. The module describes Integer optimum of the 0-1 funding problem for four indivisible programmes with its gaps to a funding rule and to the divisible fill as "Each of the 15 packages that fund at least one of four programmes contributes its total QALYs when its total cost is at most the budget and zero when it is not, and H_star is the largest contribution, the optimum of the article's binary problem of maximising the sum of q_i x_i subject to the sum of c_i x_i at most B with each x_i equal to 0 or 1. Funding nothing gives zero, so H_star is zero when no programme fits. G_rule is the health that a funding rule's package, with health H_rule, leaves unbought at the same budget, the loss of benefit that Crown and colleagues say optimisation shows for the choice finally made, and with H_rule taken from HE-FM-CELT-003 it is the gain of the optimum over the league table. L_ind is the health the divisible fill of HE-FM-CELT-001, H_div, buys above the optimum, the health lost purely because programmes cannot be split (derived). The formula is written out for four programmes so that it runs as calculator text, and HE-CF-IPH-001 does the same search for any number."; HEO defines Integer Programming as "Integer programming chooses which indivisible health programmes or medicines to fund to maximise health gain, such as QALYs, within a fixed budget.".

column2: Plant capacity utilisation from output efficiency with fixed inputs and with all inputs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Capacity Utilisation. The module describes Plant capacity utilisation from output efficiency with fixed inputs and with all inputs as "Divides the output efficiency score of a hospital or other unit measured with only its fixed inputs, such as beds and rostered staff, constraining output and its variable inputs unrestricted, by its output efficiency score with all inputs constraining output, both from one data envelopment analysis under constant returns to scale. The all-input score E_V carries the technical inefficiency of the unit, so dividing by it leaves the part of the shortfall from capacity output that is due to unused plant, the Johansen definition of plant capacity that Valdmanis and colleagues adopt. A value of 1 means that the unit, once on the frontier, could not raise its outputs in proportion without more fixed inputs, and a value below 1 shows unused plant capacity that could treat proportionately more patients. In 68 Thai public hospitals in 1999 the mean was 0.954. Unlike a bed occupancy ratio, the measure sets outputs against what the fixed inputs could produce."; HEO defines Capacity Utilisation as "Capacity utilisation is the share of available health care capacity, such as staffed beds, theatre sessions or scanner time, that is used over a period.".

column2: Current health expenditure as a percentage of gross domestic product
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Spending as GDP Share. The module describes Current health expenditure as a percentage of gross domestic product as "Divides current health expenditure by gross domestic product for the same country and year and multiplies by 100. The WHO Global Health Expenditure Database defines its indicator che_gdp in this way, with both parts held in million current national currency units, so no exchange rate or purchasing power parity enters the share. The OECD uses the same ratio in Health at a Glance and keeps GDP as the denominator for every country. The share moves whenever either part moves, so a value read on its own says nothing about the level of spending."; HEO defines Health Spending as GDP Share as "Health spending as GDP share is current health expenditure divided by gross domestic product, used to compare health spending across countries and years.".

column2: Lifetime infection risk of an unvaccinated child and infections per birth in an endemic infection with vaccination at birth
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vaccination Externalities. The module describes Lifetime infection risk of an unvaccinated child and infections per birth in an endemic infection with vaccination at birth as "In an endemic infection with lifelong immunity, births and deaths at rate mu and a share v of each birth cohort given a fully protective vaccine at birth, the susceptible share settles at 1/R_0 while the infection persists, so the force of infection lambda settles where the unvaccinated births mu(1 minus v) balance the outflow (lambda + mu)/R_0 from the susceptible pool. An unvaccinated child then leaves the susceptible state by infection or by death, and its lifetime chance of infection lambda/(lambda + mu), the long-horizon limit of HE-FM-TP-004 (derived), becomes pi = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus v)), Eq. 15 of Bauch and Earn and equation (15) of Goodkin-Gold and colleagues, which falls as coverage rises and is zero at or above the threshold H of HE-FM-BRN-003. The same expression is 1 minus 1/R_t with R_t = R_0(1 minus v) from HE-FM-BRN-002 (derived), but HE-FM-BRN-003 is defined for the basic reproduction number and returns an immune share, not a probability of infection. Infections per birth n are the unvaccinated share times that risk, the pathway probability of HE-FM-CHN-002 with factors 1 minus v and pi, which equals (1 minus v) minus 1/R_0 below H (derived from the endemic infected share in Eq. 14 of Bauch and Earn), so each extra vaccination below H removes exactly one infection in total; the share infected in a closed epidemic without births is the final size of HE-CF-ATR-001, a different quantity."; HEO defines Vaccination Externalities as "Vaccination externalities are the benefits one person's vaccination gives others by cutting disease spread, benefits that person ignores when choosing.".

column2: Private and external benefit of one vaccination at a given coverage in an endemic infection
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vaccination Externalities. The module describes Private and external benefit of one vaccination at a given coverage in an endemic infection as "Splits the value of one more vaccination at coverage v, with a loss L per infection valued the same by the family and by society, into the marginal private benefit to the vaccinated child, L times the lifetime risk pi it avoids (the expected value of HE-FM-CHN-001 with branch values L and 0), and the marginal external benefit to unvaccinated children, L/(R_0(1 minus v)), which is L times 1 minus pi below the threshold H and zero at or above it. Below H the two add to L, because each extra vaccination there removes exactly one infection in total (HE-FM-VEXT-001), so the marginal social benefit of HE-FM-EXT-001 stays at L while its split moves towards the external side as coverage rises (derived). Goodkin-Gold and colleagues derive the same split, the marginal private benefit theta H Phi_I, the marginal social benefit theta H and the marginal externality theta H/((1 minus theta Q/mu) R_0) below the eradication quantity and zero above it, with theta of 1 and Q/mu equal to v for a fully protective vaccine. The external share is 0.5 at the article's 60% coverage and 0.8 at 75%, so a subsidy set at the marginal external benefit, as in HE-FM-EXT-002 with linear curves, depends on the coverage at which that benefit is read."; HEO defines Vaccination Externalities as "Vaccination externalities are the benefits one person's vaccination gives others by cutting disease spread, benefits that person ignores when choosing.".

column2: Coverage reached by voluntary vaccination when families weigh private cost against expected loss from infection
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vaccination Externalities. The module describes Coverage reached by voluntary vaccination when families weigh private cost against expected loss from infection as "A family that bears a private cost c per vaccination, counting any price and its own time and travel, and expects a loss L if the child is infected vaccinates while L times pi exceeds c, so in a homogeneous population uptake settles where the unvaccinated child's lifetime risk equals r = c/L. Solving pi(v) = r with HE-FM-VEXT-001 gives v_vol = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus r)), the convergently stable Nash equilibrium P* of Bauch and Earn's vaccination game with r read as their relative risk r_v/r_i, and, with P/(theta H) equal to r, theta times d(P)/mu, the share immunised under the demand d(P) of Goodkin-Gold and colleagues, which for a fully protective vaccine is the share vaccinated. When r is at least the risk with no vaccination, 1 minus 1/R_0, nobody vaccinates, and writing max(1 minus r, 1/R_0) in the denominator returns that 0 and avoids a division by zero for r of 1 or more (derived; it equals the piecewise result on a grid of R_0 and r). For any r above zero v_vol is below the threshold H of HE-FM-BRN-003, Bauch and Earn's result that voluntary vaccination cannot eradicate the disease, and free provision lowers c and raises v_vol without reaching H while any private cost remains."; HEO defines Vaccination Externalities as "Vaccination externalities are the benefits one person's vaccination gives others by cutting disease spread, benefits that person ignores when choosing.".

column2: Erlang loss refusal probability, annual refusals and achieved occupancy of a six-bed unit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Capacity Planning. The module describes Erlang loss refusal probability, annual refusals and achieved occupancy of a six-bed unit as "Gives, for a unit of six staffed beds with Poisson arrivals, the share of arriving patients who find all six beds occupied and are refused, the Erlang loss formula of de Bruin and colleagues written out term by term, with the offered load a equal to arrivals per day times the mean stay. Refusals a year are the annual arrivals times that share, and the achieved occupancy is the load actually carried, a times one minus the refusal probability, over the six beds, de Bruin and colleagues' occupancy rate for the loss model, which takes the form of HE-FM-ALOS-002 solved for o with the patients admitted, not the patients arriving, as the discharges. Achieved occupancy is always below a / 6 because refused patients use no bed-days. The model needs only the mean stay, not the shape of the length of stay distribution. Other numbers of beds follow the same pattern with terms up to a^N / N!, which HE-CF-CAPP-001 computes by recursion."; HEO defines Capacity Planning as "Capacity planning estimates the beds, staff, theatre time and equipment a health service needs to meet expected demand to a stated standard of access.".

column2: Linear partial value score of a technology on one MCDA criterion
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept MCDA in HTA. The module describes Linear partial value score of a technology on one MCDA criterion as "Places a technology's performance on one criterion on a 0 to 100 scale whose ends are the worst and best performance of the criterion's fixed range, so equal changes in performance earn equal changes in score. The same line serves a criterion on which lower performance is better, such as a rate of adverse events, by entering the worse, higher level as x_worst, as the first ISPOR MCDA task force appendix does for its criterion B. Zero marks the bottom of the chosen range, not an absence of value, so differences in score can be compared but ratios cannot. Where equal changes in performance are not equally valued, the score is read from an elicited nonlinear partial value function instead."; HEO defines MCDA in HTA as "MCDA in HTA uses multi-criteria decision analysis to appraise health technologies on explicit, often weighted, criteria such as health gain and severity.".

column2: Swing-weighted additive value of a technology on three MCDA criteria
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept MCDA in HTA. The module describes Swing-weighted additive value of a technology on three MCDA criteria as "Divides each criterion's swing points by the total points to give weights that sum to one, then multiplies each partial value score by its criterion's weight and adds the three products, the additive (weighted-sum) model that both ISPOR MCDA task force reports describe as the usual aggregation in health care. With partial values on a 0 to 100 scale the overall value is on the same scale. The weights act as scaling constants for the ranges over which the swings were judged, so a change of range calls for new points. The formula is written for three criteria, the article's health gain, severity and strength of evidence; more criteria add terms in the same way, and HE-CF-MCDH-001 applies it to several technologies."; HEO defines MCDA in HTA as "MCDA in HTA uses multi-criteria decision analysis to appraise health technologies on explicit, often weighted, criteria such as health gain and severity.".

column2: Incentive and participation slacks of a two-type procurement menu
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Mechanism Design. The module describes Incentive and participation slacks of a two-type procurement menu as "A purchaser offers two contracts, (t_L, q_L) intended for a low-cost supplier and (t_H, q_H) for a high-cost one, and cannot observe which type it faces. Each type's information rent is its transfer less its cost on its own contract, and each incentive slack is that rent less what the type would earn by taking the other contract at its own cost. The menu is incentive feasible when both incentive slacks and both rents are at least zero, inequalities (2.9) to (2.12) of Laffont and Martimort. These are the article's incentive compatibility and participation constraints for one participant with two types and an outside option of zero. A low-cost type that takes the high-cost contract earns the high-cost type's rent plus (theta_H minus theta_L) q_H, which is why a menu that leaves both types no rent fails. Each rent takes the form of the margin in HE-FM-CTH-001 with no reimbursed share (derived), there computed per case of hospital care; the incentive slacks, which value one type's cost on the other type's contract, have no live counterpart."; HEO defines Mechanism Design as "Mechanism design uses game theory to set rules, such as auctions, tenders or matching schemes, under which self-interested choices serve a chosen goal.".

column2: Second-best two-type procurement menu with a linear marginal value of output
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Mechanism Design. The module describes Second-best two-type procurement menu with a linear marginal value of output as "The purchaser values output at S(q) and, knowing only that the supplier is low-cost with probability nu, chooses the menu that maximises expected S(q) less the transfer subject to the constraints of HE-FM-MECH-001. In Laffont and Martimort's solution the low-cost type produces its first-best output, the high-cost type's output is set where the marginal value equals the virtual cost theta_H + nu / (1 minus nu) (theta_H minus theta_L), and the low-cost type receives the information rent (theta_H minus theta_L) q_H while the high-cost type receives none. With a linear marginal value S'(q) = a minus b q, an illustrative form chosen here, both outputs solve in closed form (derived). The output step takes the form of HE-FM-CTH-002 and the first-best output that of HE-FM-CTH-003, which compute stays of hospital care; here the cost fed in is the virtual cost of (2.28). The max function sets q_H to zero when (2.28) has no positive solution, the authors' shut-down case."; HEO defines Mechanism Design as "Mechanism design uses game theory to set rules, such as auctions, tenders or matching schemes, under which self-interested choices serve a chosen goal.".

column2: Smallest effort bonus, expected payment and limited liability rent for a binary effort choice
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Principal-Agent Problem. The module describes Smallest effort bonus, expected payment and limited liability rent for a binary effort choice as "A risk-neutral agent, such as a general practice, chooses a high effort that costs it c per patient or a low effort that costs nothing, and is paid a bonus for each patient whose recorded indicator is met, which happens with probability p_H after high effort and p_L otherwise. The smallest bonus that satisfies the incentive constraint, p_H b minus c at least p_L b, is b_star = c / (p_H minus p_L), the gap between the transfers (4.20) and (4.19) of Laffont and Martimort, and the principal also charges a fixed fee F per patient, the smaller of the liability limit ell and p_L b_star, which combines the two cases of their Proposition 4.2 (derived). The expected payment, the two-branch expected value of HE-FM-CHN-001 with branches b_star minus F and minus F, is the second-best cost of inducing effort, and the rent R is that payment less c, the form of the HE-FM-CTH-001 margin with no reimbursed share. With ell = 0 the rent is c p_L / (p_H minus p_L), which equals what the agent would earn without the effort and, for p_L above 0, c / (p_H / p_L minus 1) (derived), the limited liability rent (4.21) that the authors describe as the extra payment caused by moral hazard combined with limited liability. At ell equal to p_L b_star the rent (4.21) of the second case of their Proposition 4.2 falls to zero, and for a larger ell the first case applies, with no rent."; HEO defines Principal-Agent Problem as "The principal-agent problem arises when patients or payers rely on providers who know more than they do, act unobserved and may pursue other interests.".

column2: Pure-strategy best-reply check of each cell of a 2 x 2 game with strict and weak equilibria
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Nash Equilibrium. The module describes Pure-strategy best-reply check of each cell of a 2 x 2 game with strict and weak equilibria as "Tests each of the four strategy pairs of a two-player game in which each player has two strategies. A cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium when the row player's payoff in it is at least its payoff from switching rows against the same column, and the column player's payoff in it is at least its payoff from switching columns against the same row, which is Definition 5.1 of Tadelis applied cell by cell as in his section 5.1.1. The cell is a strict equilibrium when both comparisons hold with a strict inequality, Definition 7 of Slantchev, and a cell that passes the weak test but fails the strict one is a weak equilibrium, because some player has an alternative that does exactly as well. Each output is 1 for a pass and 0 for a fail. A game in which no cell passes, such as matching pennies, still has an equilibrium in mixed strategies (HE-FM-NASH-002)."; HEO defines Nash Equilibrium as "A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies, one per player, from which no player, such as a payer, provider or patient, gains by changing strategy alone.".

column2: Mixed-strategy equilibrium probabilities of a 2 x 2 game from the indifference conditions
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Nash Equilibrium. The module describes Mixed-strategy equilibrium probabilities of a 2 x 2 game from the indifference conditions as "In a mixed equilibrium of a game in which each player has two strategies, each player randomises over both, which it is willing to do only if both give it the same expected payoff, so each player's mixing probability is set by the other player's payoffs. Equating the row player's expected payoffs from its two strategies, q u_11 + (1 minus q) u_12 = q u_21 + (1 minus q) u_22, gives the probability q_star that the column player chooses its first strategy, and the column player's indifference gives the probability p_star that the row player chooses its first strategy. Slantchev states this condition for 2 x 2 games and solves it for the equilibrium probabilities; the closed forms are that equation solved (derived). The pair is a mixed equilibrium when both values are above 0 and below 1, which is what Proposition 1 of Slantchev requires when each player mixes over two strategies (derived); when q_star is not, the row player has a strictly dominant strategy (derived, for games without the ties of HE-AS-NASH-005), and likewise p_star for the column player. The algebra is that of the decision curve threshold HE-FM-DCA-004, p_t = L / (G + L), and of the blend weight in HE-FM-EXD-002, with a_1 and a_2 in place of G and L, but HE-VR-DCA-013 to HE-VR-DCA-015 define p_t as a patient's risk and G and L as a patient's benefit and harm, while here the probability is the other player's equilibrium choice, set by the payoffs of the player it leaves indifferent and an equilibrium only as a pair with p_star. When a_1 and a_2 are both negative, as in the angioplasty game, listing the row player's strategies in the other order makes both positive and leaves q_star unchanged (derived). Each player's expected payoff at the equilibrium is HE-FM-CHN-001 applied to its payoffs against the other's mix."; HEO defines Nash Equilibrium as "A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies, one per player, from which no player, such as a payer, provider or patient, gains by changing strategy alone.".

column2: Symmetric Nash equilibrium use of a shared resource by N users and the share of its rent dissipated
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Tragedy of the Commons. The module describes Symmetric Nash equilibrium use of a shared resource by N users and the share of its rent dissipated as "Each of N identical users chooses q_i to maximise q_i (a less c less k Q), where Q is the use of all users together. Setting the derivative to zero gives a less c less k Q less k q_i equal to zero, and with identical users the unique equilibrium gives each user (a less c) / (k (N + 1)), the result Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher state as Proposition 1. The chain then gives total use, the net value of each unit at that use and the rent V_E, the net value to the group. Q_s is the joint optimum, the efficient quantity of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b and g equal to k and m equal to zero (also the equilibrium at N = 1), V_s the rent it yields, (a less c) squared / (4k), which equals the open-access deadweight loss of HE-FM-PIGT-002 with the same b, g and m (derived), and d_E the share of V_s lost at the equilibrium, which equals ((N less 1) / (N + 1)) squared (derived, checked on a grid). Use rises and the rent falls as users are added, and the rent tends to zero as N grows, the open-access outcome."; HEO defines Tragedy of the Commons as "The tragedy of the commons is the overuse of a shared resource, such as antibiotic effectiveness, when each user keeps the gain but the cost falls on all.".

column2: Per-unit fee that brings N users of a shared resource to the joint optimum, with use and revenue under the fee
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Tragedy of the Commons. The module describes Per-unit fee that brings N users of a shared resource to the joint optimum, with use and revenue under the fee as "A fee t_s on each unit raises every user's cost to c plus t_s, so use under the fee is the equilibrium of HE-FM-TOTC-001 with that cost. Setting the resulting total equal to the joint optimum (a less c) / (2k) gives t_s, the optimal Pigouvian amount Delaney and Jacobson state for their common pool resource game. It equals the loss one more unit imposes on the other N less 1 users at the optimum, k (N less 1) Q_s / N, the marginal external cost of HE-FM-EXT-001 valued at the efficient quantity as in HE-FN-PIGT-001 (derived). The user already bears their own share, so the fee is below the whole marginal external cost k Q_s, the t_star of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b and g equal to k and m equal to zero, and tends to it, (a less c) / 2, as N grows (derived). Revenue R_t is paid by the users to the authority as a transfer and does not reduce the group's net value. A quota of Q_s / N units per user reaches the same use."; HEO defines Tragedy of the Commons as "The tragedy of the commons is the overuse of a shared resource, such as antibiotic effectiveness, when each user keeps the gain but the cost falls on all.".

column2: Expected lowest cost, expected price and winner's margin in a second-price reverse auction with uniform costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Auction Theory. The module describes Expected lowest cost, expected price and winner's margin in a second-price reverse auction with uniform costs as "A purchaser buys from the lowest of N bidding suppliers whose unit costs are independent draws from a uniform distribution on the interval [c_low, c_high]. Under the second-price rule each supplier bids its cost and the winner is paid the second-lowest bid, so the expected price is the expected second-lowest cost. Klemperer prints the expected k-th highest of n uniform draws as v_low + ((n + 1 minus k) / (n + 1)) (v_high minus v_low); the lowest cost is the N-th highest and the second-lowest the (N minus 1)-th highest, which give E_c1 and E_p. By revenue equivalence the first-price rule has the same expected price (HE-FM-AUCT-002). The winner's expected margin is the gap between the two, (c_high minus c_low) / (N + 1) (derived), and both the price and the margin fall towards c_low and zero as N rises."; HEO defines Auction Theory as "Auction theory in health economics studies how bidding rules in tenders set the price and supply of medicines, vaccines and medical equipment.".

column2: Symmetric first-price equilibrium bid and expected winning bid in a reverse auction with uniform costs
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Auction Theory. The module describes Symmetric first-price equilibrium bid and expected winning bid in a reverse auction with uniform costs as "Under the first-price rule the lowest bidder wins and is paid its own bid, so a supplier bids above its cost, trading a higher price on winning against a lower chance of winning. With N suppliers whose costs are independent and uniform on the interval [c_low, c_high], the symmetric equilibrium bid adds to the supplier's cost c the expected gap to the lowest of the other N minus 1 costs, given that they all exceed c, which is (c_high minus c) / N. Klemperer prints the selling form, a bid of v_low + ((n minus 1) / n) (v minus v_low); the procurement form is derived by mirroring each cost to the value c_low + c_high minus c on the same range and checked here by a best-response search and by simulation. Because the bid is linear in cost, the expected winning bid is the bid at the expected lowest cost E_c1 of HE-FM-AUCT-001 (derived), and it equals that formula's expected price E_p, revenue equivalence for this case."; HEO defines Auction Theory as "Auction theory in health economics studies how bidding rules in tenders set the price and supply of medicines, vaccines and medical equipment.".

column2: Shared savings payment of an accountable care organisation with the minimum savings rate gate and payment limit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accountable Care Organization. The module describes Shared savings payment of an accountable care organisation with the minimum savings rate gate and payment limit as "Computes the payment CMS makes to an accountable care organisation for a performance year in which its assigned beneficiaries' average per capita spending E falls below the updated benchmark B. The savings ratio g_S must reach the minimum savings rate MSR, and once it does the final sharing rate, s times the quality factor q, applies to all the savings on a first dollar basis, as 42 CFR 425.605(d) and 425.610(e) state. The payment may not exceed the performance payment limit PPL, a share c_P of total benchmark expenditure, 10% in the BASIC track and 20% in ENHANCED; that last step is the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point. Because the gate is a test and not a deductible, the payment jumps from zero to s q MSR N B at the MSR when the cap does not bind (derived), USD 2.4 million for the article's Level E ACO. A low revenue BASIC ACO that beats its benchmark but not its MSR is paid under 425.605(h) at half the sharing rate, entered as s halved with MSR set to 0."; HEO defines Accountable Care Organization as "An accountable care organization (ACO) is a provider group that shares in savings if its patients' spending beats a benchmark and quality targets are met.".

column2: Shared losses of a two-sided BASIC accountable care organisation with the minimum loss rate and loss recoupment limit
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accountable Care Organization. The module describes Shared losses of a two-sided BASIC accountable care organisation with the minimum loss rate and loss recoupment limit as "Computes what an ACO in BASIC Level C, D or E repays CMS when its per capita spending E exceeds the updated benchmark B. The loss ratio g_L must reach the minimum loss rate MLR, which mirrors the MSR, and the fixed 30% shared loss rate r_L then applies to the whole excess, the loss counterpart of HE-FM-ACO-001. The amount may not exceed the loss recoupment limit LRL, a share rho_R of the ACO participants' Medicare fee-for-service revenue, never more than a share rho_B of total benchmark expenditure, as 42 CFR 425.605(d)(1)(iii) to (v) and (i)(2) set out. The final min step is the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point. With the article's case 3 figures a 3% overspend gives USD 2.16 million, the article's result, whenever the limit is at least that amount."; HEO defines Accountable Care Organization as "An accountable care organization (ACO) is a provider group that shares in savings if its patients' spending beats a benchmark and quality targets are met.".

column2: Shared losses of an ENHANCED track accountable care organisation with the quality-based loss rate
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Accountable Care Organization. The module describes Shared losses of an ENHANCED track accountable care organisation with the quality-based loss rate as "Computes what an ACO in the ENHANCED track repays CMS when per capita spending E exceeds the benchmark B by at least the MLR. The shared loss rate r_E is 1 minus 75% of the quality score Q, held to at least 40% and at most 75%, and is 75% when the ACO meets neither quality standard, as 42 CFR 425.610(f)(4) sets for performance years from 2024. Entering Q = 0 for an ACO that meets neither standard returns the same 75%, since the ceiling binds for every score up to one third, and the floor of 40% binds for every score of 0.8 or more (derived, checked on a grid of 1,001 scores). Losses apply to the whole excess and may not exceed 15% of total benchmark expenditure under 425.610(g), the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point; there is no revenue-based limit in this track."; HEO defines Accountable Care Organization as "An accountable care organization (ACO) is a provider group that shares in savings if its patients' spending beats a benchmark and quality targets are met.".

column2: Two-step floating catchment area accessibility for two practices and three neighbourhoods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Geographic Accessibility of Healthcare. The module describes Two-step floating catchment area accessibility for two practices and three neighbourhoods as "Step one divides each practice's full-time-equivalent GPs by the population of the neighbourhoods within the threshold travel time d_0 of it, giving the practice's supply ratio. Step two gives each neighbourhood the sum of the supply ratios of the practices within d_0 of it. Each comparison such as (d_1X <= d_0) is 1 when the travel time is within the threshold and 0 otherwise, so a neighbourhood outside a practice's catchment adds nothing to its denominator and takes nothing from its ratio. The result is in GPs per head of population, and the article reports it per 10,000 people. Neighbourhoods A, B and C of the article are 1, 2 and 3 here; more practices or neighbourhoods add terms of the same pattern, which HE-CF-ACCS-001 computes for any number of sites."; HEO defines Geographic Accessibility of Healthcare as "Accessibility is the dimension of health care access concerned with how easily people can reach services, given location, travel time, distance and cost.".

column2: Gravity accessibility with a population demand adjustment for two practices and three neighbourhoods
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Geographic Accessibility of Healthcare. The module describes Gravity accessibility with a population demand adjustment for two practices and three neighbourhoods as "Each practice's demand potential adds the neighbourhood populations weighted by travel time raised to the power minus beta, so nearer residents compete for its GPs more than distant ones. Each neighbourhood's score adds, over both practices, the practice's GPs weighted the same way and divided by its demand potential. Every practice counts, with no threshold, and a larger beta makes distance matter more. It is Wang's equation 1 and Luo and Wang's equation 6, the improved gravity model that Guagliardo attributes to Joseph and Bantock, written for the article's example, and HE-CF-ACCS-002 computes it for any number of sites. The scores are in GPs per head, and their population-weighted mean equals total GPs over total population, as for HE-FM-ACCS-001."; HEO defines Geographic Accessibility of Healthcare as "Accessibility is the dimension of health care access concerned with how easily people can reach services, given location, travel time, distance and cost.".

column2: Non-inferiority and superiority readings of a risk difference against a margin
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Active Control Trial. The module describes Non-inferiority and superiority readings of a risk difference against a margin as "Forms the difference in the proportion of patients with a favourable outcome, test minus active control, and its two-sided Wald interval, then reads the lower limit against minus the non-inferiority margin M and against zero. The chained steps are live records, d as HE-FM-ARR-001 with the subtraction reversed for a favourable outcome, as HE-AS-ARR-002 states, SE_d as the sum of the two arm variances of HE-FM-BINOM-004 (the rule of HE-VR-AN-002 and HE-FM-NMA-001), and L_d and U_d as HE-FM-AN-001. The new step is the decision, which ICH E9 section 3.3.2 and CPMP/EWP/482/99 section II.3 state as the interval lying wholly above minus the margin, and which the FDA guidance writes as the upper bound for control minus test lying below M. NI and SUP equal 1 when the reading is shown and 0 otherwise, so a trial can show non-inferiority without superiority, and when both are shown the superiority claim is allowed by CPMP/EWP/482/99 section IV.1."; HEO defines Active Control Trial as "An active control trial is a randomised trial testing a new treatment against a known effective treatment, not placebo, for superiority or non-inferiority.".

column2: Sullivan active life expectancy over three age bands with life expectancy and dependent years
column24: The module lists this formula on the formulae page of the HEO concept Active Life Expectancy. The module describes Sullivan active life expectancy over three age bands with life expectancy and dependent years as "Weights the person-years that a period life table assigns to each age band after the starting age x by the share of the band free of dependency, adds them and divides by the survivors at x, as Sullivan's method does. The article's three bands (65 to 74, 75 to 84, and 85 and over) are written term by term; more bands add terms in the same way, and the last band is open-ended so that all remaining life is counted. Setting every pi_i to 0 returns life expectancy e_x, person-years over survivors (Imai and Soneji equation 7). That first part is HE-FM-ASF-002 with U_t of 1 and r of 0, its single-year L_t summed within each band to give L_i over l_x (derived), and is cited, not restated. DLE_x, the expected years lived dependent, is the difference and s_A is the share of remaining life lived active. The sum has the form of HE-FM-ASF-002 with r of 0 and U_t replaced by 1 minus pi_i, a use that record does not cover because its U_t is a utility norm (HE-VR-ASF-007); here the weight is a prevalence share with dependent time counting zero."; HEO defines Active Life Expectancy as "Active life expectancy (ALE) is the average number of years a person of a given age can expect to live free of dependency in activities of daily living.".

column2: Trial adverse event counts to a per-cycle probability
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Adverse Event Rate. The module describes Trial adverse event counts to a per-cycle probability as "Takes the counts in a trial safety table, the number of patients with an adverse event and the number at risk, with the follow-up period and the model cycle length, and returns the probability of a first episode in one model cycle. It computes the trial proportion with HE-FM-AER-001 and then rescales it with HE-FM-AER-004 through the implied constant rate, so the inputs are counts rather than the proportion the formula takes. The general conversion from an annual probability is HE-CF-TP-002 on the Transition Probability page."; HEO defines Adverse Event Rate as "Adverse event rate (AE rate) is the count of adverse events, or of patients with one, divided by the patients or person-time at risk in a stated period.".

column2: AIC, AIC differences and Akaike weights for candidate survival curves
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Akaike Information Criterion. The module describes AIC, AIC differences and Akaike weights for candidate survival curves as "Takes the maximised log-likelihoods and parameter counts of a set of candidate survival models fitted to the same data, and returns three vectors: AIC, the AIC difference from the best-scoring model and the Akaike weight of each model. It chains HE-FM-AIC-001, HE-FM-AIC-002 and HE-FM-AIC-003, and the second and third steps use the whole vector produced by the step before, so the inputs are lists of models rather than the single values the formulae take."; HEO defines Akaike Information Criterion as "Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic ranking models fitted to the same data, such as survival curves in HTA, by fit penalised per parameter.".

column2: Alpha spent and stopping hazard ratio at a group sequential look
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Alpha Spending. The module describes Alpha spent and stopping hazard ratio at a group sequential look as "Takes the counts a trial report gives, deaths at the current and previous looks and the planned final deaths, with the overall one-sided level and the critical value at the look, and returns the cumulative alpha spent under both Lan-DeMets functions, the increment at the look and the hazard ratio needed to stop. It chains HE-FM-ASP-001, HE-FM-ASP-002, HE-FM-ASP-003, HE-FM-ASP-004 and HE-FM-ASP-005. The critical value is an input because, from the second look onwards, it comes from recursive numerical integration over the joint normal distribution of the test statistics, which a spreadsheet formula cannot do; the function computes only the closed-form parts."; HEO defines Alpha Spending as "Alpha spending is a group sequential trial method that spreads the type I error rate (alpha) across interim and final analyses as information accrues.".

column2: Therapy price to annuity instalment, nominal total and present value
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Annuity Payment. The module describes Therapy price to annuity instalment, nominal total and present value as "Takes the terms that a payer and a manufacturer negotiate, the upfront price, the number of yearly instalments and the financing rate, together with the discount rate of the evaluation, and returns the instalment, the nominal total and the present value that enters the economic evaluation. It chains HE-FM-AP-001, which sets the instalment at the financing rate, and HE-FM-AP-002, which values the instalments at the discount rate, so the second step uses the result of the first and the two rates play different parts. A financing rate of zero, as in an interest-free split, is handled as a separate case because the general instalment formula then divides zero by zero."; HEO defines Annuity Payment as "Annuity payment is an agreement to pay for a one-off therapy in yearly instalments, not upfront, with later ones sometimes stopping if the therapy fails.".

column2: Delta-method, Fieller and net benefit intervals from trial summary statistics
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Asymptotic Normality. The module describes Delta-method, Fieller and net benefit intervals from trial summary statistics as "Takes the summary statistics a trial-based analysis produces, the incremental mean cost and effect, their standard errors and covariance, and a threshold, and returns three large-sample intervals in one pass: the delta-method interval for the ICER (HE-FM-AN-002), Fieller's interval (HE-FM-AN-003) and the incremental net benefit interval with the probability that net benefit is positive (HE-FM-AN-004). The delta-method and net benefit intervals are Wald intervals (HE-FM-AN-001) applied to the ratio and to a linear combination of the differences; Fieller's method applies the normal approximation to the two differences themselves. The procedure branches on the sign of the Fieller coefficient a, so it reports whether Fieller's set is a bounded interval, two unbounded pieces or the whole real line, rather than returning two roots that may bound nothing."; HEO defines Asymptotic Normality as "Asymptotic normality means an estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal in large samples, the basis of Wald confidence intervals.".

column2: Annual event rate to a model-cycle transition probability
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Transition Probability. The module describes Annual event rate to a model-cycle transition probability as "Takes the inputs a model usually holds, an event rate per year and a cycle length in months, and returns the transition probability for one cycle. It converts the cycle length into years and then applies the constant-rate formula HE-FM-TP-001. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the formula needs an interval in the same time unit as the rate, and the function builds that interval from the cycle length."; HEO defines Transition Probability as "A transition probability is the chance of moving from one health state to another, or staying, during one cycle of a Markov or state-transition model.".

column2: Annual probability to a model-cycle transition probability
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Transition Probability. The module describes Annual probability to a model-cycle transition probability as "Takes an annual probability, the form in which many sources report risk, and a cycle length in months, and returns the cycle probability in two steps. It first recovers the implied constant rate with HE-FM-TP-002 and then converts that rate to the cycle probability with HE-FM-TP-001, so two formulae are chained inside one function and the second step uses the result of the first. The answer equals the single-step rescaling formula HE-FM-TP-003, which gives a cross-check."; HEO defines Transition Probability as "A transition probability is the chance of moving from one health state to another, or staying, during one cycle of a Markov or state-transition model.".

column2: Atkinson index from subgroup health levels and population shares
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Atkinson Index. The module describes Atkinson index from subgroup health levels and population shares as "Takes the inputs a distributional cost-effectiveness analysis usually holds, the mean health of each population subgroup and the share of the population in each subgroup, together with a chosen epsilon, and returns mean health, the equally distributed equivalent health and the Atkinson index. It weights each group by its population share, as in Atkinson's measure for discrete distributions, and switches to the share-weighted geometric mean when epsilon equals 1, where the general formula HE-FM-ATK-002 is undefined. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: HE-FM-ATK-002 and HE-FM-ATK-003 need one value per person or per equal-sized group, and the function accepts groups of any size."; HEO defines Atkinson Index as "The Atkinson index measures inequality in health or income using a social welfare function with an explicit inequality aversion parameter, epsilon.".

column2: AUC from predicted risks and observed outcomes
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Area Under Curve. The module describes AUC from predicted risks and observed outcomes as "Takes the data a validation study holds, one predicted risk or test score and one observed outcome per person, and returns the AUC. It splits the people into those with and without the outcome, compares every case with every non-case, counts the concordant and tied pairs and then applies HE-FM-AUC-001. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the formula needs pair counts, and the function builds them from patient-level data."; HEO defines Area Under Curve as "Area under the curve (AUC), or C-statistic, is the probability a test or risk model scores a random case above a random non-case (0.5 chance, 1 perfect).".

column2: DerSimonian and Laird meta-analysis from study estimates and standard errors
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis. The module describes DerSimonian and Laird meta-analysis from study estimates and standard errors as "Takes the two columns an aggregate data synthesis starts from, each study's effect estimate and its standard error, and returns the full DerSimonian and Laird analysis in one pass: the common-effect estimate and standard error (HE-FM-ADMA-001), Cochran's Q (HE-FM-ADMA-002), I-squared (HE-FM-ADMA-003), tau2 (HE-FM-ADMA-004) and the random-effects mean, standard error and 95% confidence interval (HE-FM-ADMA-005). The inputs differ from the formulae's variables: the formulae take variances and previously computed statistics, while the function squares the standard errors itself and each step uses the vector or statistic produced by the step before."; HEO defines Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis as "Aggregate data meta-analysis pools study-level summary results, such as effect estimates and standard errors, from several studies into one estimate.".

column2: AR(1) QALY variance and between-arm standard error for any visit schedule
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Autoregressive Correlation. The module describes AR(1) QALY variance and between-arm standard error for any visit schedule as "Takes a visit schedule in years, the utility variance at each visit, a correlation per year and the number of patients per arm, and returns the variance of each patient's QALY total and the standard error of the difference in mean QALYs between two arms. It derives the trapezium weights from the visit times, builds the continuous-time AR(1) correlation matrix of HE-FM-AR1-002 from the elapsed times, and evaluates the double sum behind HE-FM-AR1-003 for any number of visits. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the weights and the correlations are computed from the schedule rather than entered."; HEO defines Autoregressive Correlation as "Autoregressive correlation is a structure for repeated measures in which correlation falls by a constant factor with each time step between measurements.".

column2: Average length of stay from admission and discharge dates
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Length of Stay. The module describes Average length of stay from admission and discharge dates as "Takes patient-level admission and discharge dates and a reporting period, and returns the average length of stay for the discharges in that period. It selects stays by discharge date, computes each stay as the number of changes of calendar day from admission to discharge, sums them to bed-days and divides by the number of discharges, so its inputs are dates rather than the bed-day and discharge totals of HE-FM-ALOS-001. A stay that began before the period is counted in full, and a same-day stay counts as zero days."; HEO defines Average Length of Stay as "Average length of stay (ALOS) is the mean number of days inpatients spend in hospital: total bed-days divided by discharges over the same period.".

column2: Hourly arrival overflow probability and expected cover cost
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Arrival Process. The module describes Hourly arrival overflow probability and expected cover cost as "Takes the inputs of a capacity check, an hourly arrival rate, the number of arrivals the service can absorb in an hour, the number of hours at that rate and the cost of each overflow hour, and returns the probability that an hour overflows, the expected overflow hours and their expected cost. It sums the Poisson probabilities of HE-FM-ARRP-001 from 0 up to the capacity, takes the complement and scales it by hours and cost, so its inputs differ from the formula's variables. Running it once per rate period and adding the results gives the cost for a day with a peak, as in the article's assessment unit example."; HEO defines Arrival Process as "Arrival process is the pattern in time, random or scheduled, by which patients or other entities enter a queueing model or simulation of a health service.".

column2: Antithetic pairs of exponential survival times with a pair-mean standard error
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Antithetic Variates. The module describes Antithetic pairs of exponential survival times with a pair-mean standard error as "Takes a hazard and a vector of uniform random numbers, one per pair, and returns the antithetic estimate of mean survival and its standard error. For each uniform number U it samples a survival time by the inverse distribution function and a partner from 1-U, averages the two, and treats the pair means as an independent sample, so it combines HE-FM-ANTV-001 with the pair-mean standard error of HE-FM-ANTV-002. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: sigma2 and rho are not entered but follow from the exponential distribution, with rho equal to 1-pi^2/6."; HEO defines Antithetic Variates as "Antithetic variates are a variance reduction method that pairs each random draw with its mirror image so errors tend to cancel in Monte Carlo simulation.".

column2: Final attack rate by iteration and infections averted by pre-epidemic vaccination
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Attack Rate. The module describes Final attack rate by iteration and infections averted by pre-epidemic vaccination as "Takes the inputs of a vaccination scenario, a basic reproduction number, the coverage reached before the epidemic, the population size and the cost per person vaccinated, and returns the final attack rate with and without the programme, the infections averted and the cost per infection averted. The final size relation has z on both sides and cannot be rearranged to give z directly, so the function solves it by fixed-point iteration: starting from z = s_0, it repeats the update z = s_0(1 minus exp(minus R_0 z)), which falls steadily to the positive solution whenever R_0 s_0 exceeds 1. The inputs therefore differ from those of HE-FM-ATR-005, which runs the other way, from an observed final attack rate to R_0."; HEO defines Attack Rate as "Attack rate is the proportion of an at-risk population that develops the disease during an outbreak or other defined period: a risk, not a true rate.".

column2: Plan design and spending distribution to actuarial value
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Value. The module describes Plan design and spending distribution to actuarial value as "Takes a plan design, the deductible, the member's coinsurance rate and the out-of-pocket maximum, together with a spending distribution for the standard population, and returns the actuarial value. It applies the member cost-sharing formula HE-FM-AV-002 to the allowed cost of each spending group, takes the plan payment as the remainder and then forms the ratio HE-FM-AV-001, so its inputs are the plan terms rather than the plan payments that the ratio needs. This is the core of what the federal AV Calculator does with its continuance tables, without the copayment, service-type and interpolation steps."; HEO defines Actuarial Value as "Actuarial value (AV) is the share of the total allowed cost of covered care that a health plan is expected to pay for a standard population.".

column2: Group size and attachment factor to expected aggregate stop-loss payment
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Aggregate Stop-Loss. The module describes Group size and attachment factor to expected aggregate stop-loss payment as "Takes the inputs an analyst usually holds about a self-funded group, the number of members, the mean and standard deviation of net claims per member and the attachment factor, and returns the carrier's expected aggregate stop-loss payment and its share of expected claims. It chains HE-FM-ASL-003 (pooled mean and standard deviation), HE-FM-ASL-002 (attachment point), HE-FM-ASL-004 (standardised distance) and HE-FM-ASL-005 (normal expected excess), so its inputs differ from the symbols of the expected payment formula, which needs the attachment point and the distribution of total claims. The calculator version takes Q_z as an input because it has no normal distribution function; the Excel, R and Python versions compute it."; HEO defines Aggregate Stop-Loss as "Aggregate stop-loss is insurance that reimburses a self-funded employer for total health claims above an agreed attachment point in a plan year.".

column2: Insurer annual figures to medical loss ratio rebate
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Administrative Cost Ratio. The module describes Insurer annual figures to medical loss ratio rebate as "Takes the items an insurer reports for a year, earned premium, taxes and licensing and regulatory fees, incurred claims and quality improvement expenditure, together with the market standard, and returns the rebate in the order the regulation sets. It computes the medical loss ratio with HE-FM-ACR-002, rounds it to three decimal places as 45 CFR 158.221(c) requires, and only then applies the rebate formula HE-FM-ACR-004. The inputs therefore differ from those of the rebate formula, which takes the rounded ratio as given, and the rounding step changes the result."; HEO defines Administrative Cost Ratio as "Administrative cost ratio is the share of an insurer's premium income, or a health system's spending, used for administration rather than claims or care.".

column2: New benefit costing from base use to gross premium in actuarial analysis
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Actuarial Analysis. The module describes New benefit costing from base use to gross premium in actuarial analysis as "Takes the figures an analyst usually holds when costing a new benefit, a base utilisation rate per 1,000 members, an allowance for induced use, the allowed cost per unit, the member coinsurance rate, the loadings and the membership, and returns the expected claims cost, the gross premium, the scheme totals and the pooled standard deviation of the average cost. It chains the expected claims cost formula HE-FM-ACTA-001, the gross premium formula HE-FM-ACTA-002 and the pooled standard deviation formula HE-FM-ACTA-003, with a two-point (use or no use) model for one member's cost. Its inputs differ from the formulae's variables: the utilisation rate per person and the unit cost to the scheme are built inside the function."; HEO defines Actuarial Analysis as "Actuarial analysis uses probability and statistics to estimate expected health insurance claims for pricing premiums or contributions and holding reserves.".

column2: IPW incremental net monetary benefit from patient-level data
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Average Treatment Effect. The module describes IPW incremental net monetary benefit from patient-level data as "Takes patient-level data as an analysis file holds it, one treatment flag, propensity score, cost and QALY total per patient, together with a value per QALY, and returns the incremental cost, the incremental QALYs and the incremental net monetary benefit. It applies the estimator HE-FM-ATE-003 twice with the same weights, once to costs and once to QALYs, and then the incremental net monetary benefit formula HE-FM-NMB-002, so three steps run inside one function. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the formula takes one outcome vector, and the function takes two outcomes and a value per QALY."; HEO defines Average Treatment Effect as "The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean change in costs or health outcomes if a whole population received a treatment rather than its comparator.".

column2: Survival and mean survival from a piecewise-constant bathtub hazard schedule
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bathtub Hazard. The module describes Survival and mean survival from a piecewise-constant bathtub hazard schedule as "Takes a bathtub hazard schedule as a model usually holds it, a list of cut points in years and one hazard per interval, and returns survival at each cut point, the life-years lived in each interval and mean survival. It applies HE-FM-BTH-001 interval by interval, carrying survival forward, and closes the schedule with the open final interval of HE-FM-BTH-002. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the formula handles one interval at a time, while the function builds the interval lengths from the cut points and chains the results."; HEO defines Bathtub Hazard as "A bathtub hazard is a U-shaped hazard that is high soon after an event such as surgery, falls to a lower stable level, then rises again as patients age.".

column2: Threshold, patience and outside option to a negotiated price per patient
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bargaining Theory. The module describes Threshold, patience and outside option to a negotiated price per patient as "Takes the inputs a price negotiation usually starts from, a threshold, the incremental QALYs and other costs per patient, the manufacturer's reservation price, the two parties' discount factors, which party opens and the value of any competing option to the payer, and returns the negotiated price, the cost per QALY at that price and the payer's net monetary benefit. It chains four formulae: the payer's maximum price (HE-FM-BARG-002), the manufacturer's share from alternating offers (HE-FM-BARG-003, taking the responder's share when the payer opens), the Nash bargaining price (HE-FM-BARG-001) and the outside option rule (HE-FM-BARG-004). The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the formula needs a weight and a maximum price, and the function builds both from the threshold and the parties' patience."; HEO defines Bargaining Theory as "Bargaining theory explains how negotiating parties divide the gains from reaching agreement, as when a payer and a manufacturer agree a drug price.".

column2: Partial pooling of a basket trial table and its tumour-type mix response
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Basket Trial. The module describes Partial pooling of a basket trial table and its tumour-type mix response as "Takes a basket trial's results as reported, responders and evaluable patients per basket, together with a common mean response, a between-basket standard deviation and the tumour-type shares expected in practice, and returns the partially pooled response for every basket and the expected response for that mix. It applies HE-FM-BSKT-001 to each basket and then HE-FM-BSKT-002 to the results, so two formulae are chained over a whole table. The inputs therefore differ from the formulae's variables: the function takes count vectors and a standard deviation, squares the standard deviation itself, and returns the mix response without a separate step."; HEO defines Basket Trial as "A basket trial tests one targeted treatment in several diseases, usually tumour types, that share the same biomarker, with each disease forming a basket.".

column2: Two-sector Baumol scenario from a starting share of hours
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Baumol Effect. The module describes Two-sector Baumol scenario from a starting share of hours as "Takes the inputs of a simple two-sector scenario, the starting share of hours in health care, annual productivity growth in each sector, annual wage growth and a horizon, and returns the unit cost indices, the relative cost, the hours ratio and share needed to hold the output mix, and real output growth in each sector. It chains HE-FM-BAUM-002 and HE-FM-BAUM-003, so the later steps use the results of the earlier ones, and its inputs differ from the formulas' symbols: it starts from a share of hours rather than a ratio and includes the wage, which drops out of the relative cost. Holding total hours fixed, it checks that both sectors still produce more."; HEO defines Baumol Effect as "The Baumol effect is the rising relative cost of labour-intensive services such as health care as their pay tracks faster productivity growth elsewhere.".

column2: Health inequality indices from group mean health and population shares
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Health Inequality. The module describes Health inequality indices from group mean health and population shares as "Takes the inputs a health inequality analysis usually holds, the mean health of each group in order from the most to the least disadvantaged and the share of the population in each group, and returns the slope index of inequality, both forms of the relative index of inequality and the concentration index. It first builds each group's midpoint rank from the shares, then the population-weighted mean, covariance and variance, and then applies HE-FM-HINQ-002 to HE-FM-HINQ-005. The inputs therefore differ from the formulas' variables, which take the ranks, covariance and variance as given."; HEO defines Health Inequality as "Health inequality is a measurable difference in health between individuals or groups, described without judging whether the difference is unfair.".

column2: Kakwani index from group shares of income and health payments
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Vertical Equity. The module describes Kakwani index from group shares of income and health payments as "Takes the inputs a financing incidence table usually holds, the share of the population, of ability to pay and of one health payment in each group, and returns the Gini coefficient of ability to pay, the concentration index of the payment and the Kakwani index. It cumulates the shares, adds the trapezoids of HE-FM-VEQ-002 for each curve, and subtracts as in HE-FM-VEQ-001. Each trapezoid uses the identity L_t plus L_(t-1) equals twice L_t minus s_t, where s_t is the group's own share. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: HE-FM-VEQ-001 needs the two indices already computed, and the function builds them from group shares, for groups of any size."; HEO defines Vertical Equity as "Vertical equity is the principle that those in greater need should get appropriately more care, and those more able to pay should pay more.".

column2: Horizontal inequity index from group shares, actual use and need-expected use
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Horizontal Equity. The module describes Horizontal inequity index from group shares, actual use and need-expected use as "Takes the inputs a horizontal equity table usually holds, the population share, mean actual use and mean need-expected use of each income group from poorest to richest, and returns the concentration indices of actual and need-expected use and the horizontal inequity index. It builds each group's fractional rank at the midpoint of its interval, applies the grouped covariance form of the concentration index (HE-FM-HINQ-005) to each column, written as in the article for a mean rank of one half, and then applies HE-FM-HEQ-003. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: HE-FM-HEQ-003 needs the two indices already computed, and the function builds them from group means, for groups of any size."; HEO defines Horizontal Equity as "Horizontal equity is equal treatment of equals in health care: equal care for people in equal need and equal payments from those with equal ability to pay.".

column2: Grid posterior over the between-study standard deviation in a Bayesian meta-analysis
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis. The module describes Grid posterior over the between-study standard deviation in a Bayesian meta-analysis as "Takes the trial estimates and standard errors of a pairwise meta-analysis and a prior for the between-study standard deviation tau, and returns the posterior median of tau and the posterior probability that the mean effect mu is below zero by numerical integration over a fine grid of tau values. At each grid value it applies HE-FM-BMA-001 to get the conditional posterior mean and precision of mu, weights the grid value by its prior density times the marginal likelihood of the data with mu integrated out, and normalises the weights. The inputs differ from the formula's variables: the formula takes one fixed tau2, while the function takes a prior over tau and a grid and averages over them. This is the numerical integration route that Turner and colleagues describe as an alternative to MCMC for a summary-data meta-analysis."; HEO defines Bayesian Meta-Analysis as "Bayesian meta-analysis combines prior distributions with results from several studies to give posterior and predictive distributions for an effect.".

column2: Bed turnover rate from daily available bed counts
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bed Turnover. The module describes Bed turnover rate from daily available bed counts as "Takes a series of daily available bed counts and the discharges of the same period, and returns the average daily number of available beds and the turnover rate. It averages the daily counts first and then applies HE-FM-BTO-001, so its inputs are the daily counts rather than the single bed figure B_bar. Averaging daily counts matters when wards open or close during the year: a mean of the opening and closing counts misstates capacity if beds were closed for part of the period."; HEO defines Bed Turnover as "Bed turnover is the number of discharges, including deaths, per available hospital bed over a period, using the average number of beds available.".

column2: Reported mean and standard error to a fitted beta with its interval and a PSA draw
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Beta Distribution. The module describes Reported mean and standard error to a fitted beta with its interval and a PSA draw as "Takes the inputs a model usually holds for a bounded parameter, a reported mean, its standard error and a uniform random number, and returns the fitted beta parameters, the central 95% interval and a sampled value. It checks the existence condition, applies the method-of-moments formula HE-FM-BETA-003 and then inverts the cumulative beta distribution numerically, which has no closed form: Excel BETA.INV searches for the value whose cumulative probability equals the target, and R qbeta and Python scipy.stats.beta.ppf return the same inverse. The inputs therefore differ from the formula's variables: the uniform draw u and the interval levels are extra, and the outputs include quantiles that the formula cannot give."; HEO defines Beta Distribution as "The beta distribution is a probability distribution on values between zero and one, used in decision models to represent uncertainty in probabilities.".

column2: Sequential incremental benefit-cost comparison of mutually exclusive options
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Benefit-Cost Ratio. The module describes Sequential incremental benefit-cost comparison of mutually exclusive options as "Takes the present-value benefits and costs of any number of mutually exclusive options, including doing nothing, and returns the option with the largest net present value by applying the incremental ratio HE-FM-BCRX-002 step by step. The options are sorted by cost; the cheapest becomes the current choice, and each more costly option replaces it only if its incremental ratio over the current choice exceeds one. The inputs are lists of options rather than the two named options X and Y of the formula, and each comparison is made against the current choice, not against the next cheaper option."; HEO defines Benefit-Cost Ratio as "Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is a health programme's monetised benefits divided by its costs, in present values, used to summarise a cost-benefit analysis.".

column2: BIC, BIC differences and posterior model probabilities for candidate survival curves
column24: The module lists this computational function on the formulae page of the HEO concept Bayesian Information Criterion. The module describes BIC, BIC differences and posterior model probabilities for candidate survival curves as "Takes the maximised log-likelihoods and parameter counts of a set of candidate survival models fitted to the same data, together with one penalty count, and returns three vectors: BIC, the difference from the smallest BIC and the approximate posterior probability of each model.
